lsj_entry_text: ἐξήγ-ησις, εως, ἡ, statement, narrative, ἐ. ποιήσασθαι Th. 1.72 ; ὑπέρ τινος Plb. 6.3.1 . explanation, interpretation, περὶ τοὺς νόμους Pl. Lg. 631a ; ἐνυπνίων D.S. 2.29 ; Ἐ. τῶν Ἐμπεδοκλέους, title of a work by Zeno Eleaticus; so in Gramm., Sch. Il. 8.296 .
greek_sentence: Ὅπερ εἴρηταί μοι πολλάκις ἄμεινον ἀναμνῆσαι καὶ νῦν, ὡς ἡ μὲν ἐξήγησις ἐπὶ τῶν ἀσαφῶν γίγνεται λέξεων, οὐ μὴν [515] οἵ γε ἐξηγηταὶ τοῦτο μόνον ἐν τοῖς ὑπομνήμασι πράττουσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ κατασκευάζουσι τὰ λεγόμενα διὰ τῶν συγγραμμάτων, εἰς ἃ τὰς ἐξηγήσεις ποιοῦνται.
english_sentence_A: What I have said many times it is better to recall now as well: that exegesis takes place with respect to unclear expressions, yet [515] the exegetes do not do this alone in their commentaries, but also establish the things said in the treatises on which they make their exegeses.
english_sentence_B: What I have often said, it is better to recall now too: that exegesis is applied to unclear expressions, yet [515] the exegetes do not do only this in their commentaries; they also argue in support of what is said in the writings on which they compose their exegeses.

lsj_entry_text: ἐμός, ή, όν, possess. Pron. of 1st pers.: (ἐγώ, ἐμοῦ):— mine; contr. with the Art., οὑμός, τοὐμόν, τοὐμοῦ, τὠμῷ, τἀμά, Trag. (not Com., τἀμὰ γὰρ διοίχεται is paratrag. in Ar. Ec. 393 ), rarely in Prose, οὑμός Pl. Ep. 354c ; τἀμά Id. Plt. 258b ; οὑμός even in Il. 8.360 ; and (acc. to some Gramm.) τὠμῷ 11.608 , Od. 4.71 ; τἠμῇ Il. 9.654 :—poet. ἀμός (q.v.): with a Subst.: subjectively, mine, of me, ἐμὰ δάκρυα Il. 1.42 ; χεῖρες ἐμαί ib. 166 ; ἐμός τε πατὴρ καὶ σός Hes. Op. 633 : with the Art., τὸν ἐμὸν χόλον Il. 4.42 , etc.: in Poets sts. joined with gen., to strengthen the possessive notion, ἐμὸν αὐτοῦ mine own, 6.446 , Od. 2.45 ; δαὴρ . . ἐμὸς ἔσκε κυνώπιδος Il. 3.180 ; θρῆνον ἐμὸν τὸν αὐτῆς A. Ag. 1323 ; τἀμὰ δυστήνου κακά S. OC 344 , cf. El. 252 ; τὸν ἐμὸν αὐτοῦ . . βίον Ar. Pl. 33 . mine, i.e. favourable to me, τεκμήρια ἐμά, οὐ τούτων Antipho 2.4.10 . objectively, relating to me, against me, ἐμὴ ἀγγελίη Il. 19.336 ; τὸν ἐμὸν γάμον Od. 2.97 ; τὴν ἐμὴν αἰδῶ respect for me, A. Pers. 699 (troch.); τἀμὰ νουθετήματα warnings to me, S. El. 343 ; τὠμῷ πόθῳ by love for me, Id. OT 969 ; αἱ ἐμαὶ διαβολαί slanders against me, Th. 6.90 ; δωρεὰ ἐμή a gift to me, X. Cyr. 8.3.32 ; sts. with another gen. added, τὰς ἐμὰς Λαΐου διαφθοράς murder of L. by me, S. OT 572 ; τοὐμὸν αἷμα πατρός his blood shed by me, ib. 1400 ; τὰ ἐμὰ δῶρα Κύπριδος (Dind. for Κύπρις) her gifts to me, E. Hel. 364 (anap.). without a Subst., mine, οὐ γὰρ ἐμὸν παλινάγρετον my word, Il. 1.526 ; τὸ μὲν ἐμόν [ἐστι] 'tis my counsel, Pi. I. 8(7).42 : in Trag. and Prose, it is my duty, my business, E. Ion 1020 , Pl. Lg. 664b . ἐμοί my friends, Il. 20.205 ; οἱ ἐμοί X. Cyr. 3.2.28 , etc.; ὁ ἐμὸς Ἡράκλειτος my dear Heraclitus, Arr. Epict. 2.2.17 . τὰ ἐμά my property, Pl. Prt. 310e , etc.; of children, S. El. 538 , OC 922 ; τὸ τύπτειν καὶ ἐμὲ καὶ τὰ ἐμὰ ἀδίκως Pl. Grg. 508e ; of servants. PEdgar 4.6 (iii B.C.), etc.; but also τὰ ἐμά or τὸ ἐμόν, my part, my affairs, my interest, οὕτω τὸ ἐμὸν ἔχει things stand thus with me, Hdt. 4.127 ; τὰ τούτου μᾶλλον ἢ τοὐμόν S. Aj. 124 ; ἔρρει τἀμὰ παντελῶς X. Cyr. 6.1.3 ; τὸ ἐμὸν εὖ πράττει Pl. R. 463e , etc.; in full, τοὐμὸν μέρος S. Tr. 1215 : hence in Trag. and Att. , my conduct (almost periphr. for ἐγώ), Id. El. 1302 , Tr. 1068 , Ar. Th. 105 ; τὸ μὲν οὖν ἐμὸν οὐκ ἐμποδὼν ὑμῖν ἔσται Lys. 8.19 , cf. Pl. Grg. 452c , etc.: abs., τό γε ἐμόν for my part, as far as concerns me, Hdt. 1.108 , Pl. Prt. 338c , Sph. 237b . ἡ ἐ. (sc. γῆ) my country, Th. 6.78 ; also (sc. γνώμη) my opinion, ἐὰν ἡ ἐ. νικᾷ Pl. R. 397d ; κατά γε τὴν ἐ. Ar. Ec. 153 , Pl. Plt. 277a .
greek_sentence: δι᾿ οὖν τοῦτο τὸ ἔθος ἀναγκάζομαι κᾀγὼ συναγορεύειν οἷς οὐκ ἀρέσκομαι, προσαποφαίνεσθαί τε τοῖς ἐξηγήσεως δεομένοις ὡς τὰ πολλὰ καὶ τὴν ἐμὴν γνώμην· οὐ μὴν τὰς ἀποδείξεις γράφω τῶν ἀληθῶν μοι δοξάντων εἶναι, κατὰ τὰ τοιαῦτα ὑπομνήματα, γέγραπται γὰρ ὑπὲρ τούτων ἰδίᾳ καθ᾿ ἕκαστον· ἀλλὰ τὰ κεφάλαια μόνα τῶν ἀποδεδειγμένων ἐν ἑτέραις πραγματείαις ἀναμιμνήσκω, καθάπερ καὶ νῦν ἐπὶ τῆς ὀδύνης ποιήσω.
english_sentence_A: On account of this custom, then, I too am compelled to speak in support of things with which I am not satisfied, and in addition, for the most part, to declare my own opinion too on the matters requiring exegesis; yet I do not write the demonstrations of what has seemed to me to be true in commentaries of this sort, for these matters have been written about separately, each on its own; rather, I recall only the main points of what has been demonstrated in other treatises, just as I shall do now too in the case of pain.
english_sentence_B: Because of this custom, then, I too am compelled to argue in support of things with which I am not satisfied, and, for the most part, to declare my own opinion as well on the passages that need exegesis. I do not, however, write out in commentaries of this kind the demonstrations of the things that have seemed to me to be true, for these have been written about separately, each on its own.

lsj_entry_text: ἀληθ-ής [α], Dor. ἀλαθής, ές, (λήθω, = λανθάνω : ἀληθὲς τὸ μὴ λήθῃ ὑποπῖπτον EM 62.51 ):—unconcealed, so true, real, opp. false, apparent: Hom. , opp. ψευδής,in phrases ἀληθέα μυθήσασθαι, εἰπεῖν, ἀγορεύειν, ἀληθὲς ἐνισπεῖν, Il. 6.382 , Od. 13.254 , 3.254 , 247 , al.; in Hdt. and Att. τὸ ἀληθές, by Trag. crasis τἀληθές, Ion. τὠληθές ( Hdt. 6.68 , 69 ), or τὰ ἀληθῆ, by crasis τἀληθῆ, etc.; ἀληθέϊ λόγῳ χρᾶσθαι Hdt. 1.14 , etc.; οἱ ἀληθέϊ λόγῳ βασιλέες 1.120 ; ἀληθεστάτη πρόφασις Th. 1.23 . of persons, etc., truthful, honest (not in Hom. , v. infr.), ἀ. νόος Pi. O. 2.92 ; κατήγορος A. Th. 439 ; κριτής Th. 3.56 ; οἶνος ἀ. `in vino veritas', Pl. Smp. 217e ; ὁ μέσος ἀ. τις Arist. EN 1108a20 . of oracles, true, unerring, ἀλαθέα μαντίων θῶκον Pi. P. 11.6 , cf. S. Ph. 993 , E. Ion 1537 ; of dreams, A. Th. 710 . of qualities or events, true, real, φίλος E. Or. 424 ; ἀ. τὸ πραχθέν Antipho 1.6 ; genuine, ἀ. εἶναι δεῖ τὸ σεμνόν, οὐ κενόν Men. 596 . realizing itself, coming to fulfilment, ἀρά A. Th. 944 . Adv. ἀληθῶς, Ion. -θέως, truly, Simon. 5.1 , Hdt. 1.11 , al., A. Supp. 315 , etc. actually, in reality, γένος τόδε Ζηνός ἐστιν ἀ. ib. 585 ; ἀ. οὐδὲν ἐξῃκασμένα Id. Ag. 1244 , cf. Th. 1.22 , etc.; τὴν ἀ. μουσικήν (sc. οὖσαν) Antiph. 209.6 :—ὡς ἀ. in the true way, really, E. Or. 739 , Pl. Phd. 63a , etc.; ἡ μὲν γὰρ ὡς ἀ. μήτηρ D. 21.149 : Comp. -εστέρως Pl. R. 347e , -έστερον Antipho 3.3.4 : Sup. -έστατα X. Mem. 4.8.1 . neut. as Adv., proparox. ἄληθες; indeed? really? ironically, S. OT 350 , Ant. 758 , E. Cyc. 241 , Ar. greek_sentence: περὶ οὖν ὀδύνης γενέσεως εἴρηται μέν μοι κᾀν τῷ καθ᾿ Ἱπποκράτην στοιχείων περὶ τῶν, εἴρηται δὲ κᾀν ταῖς τῶν συμπτωμάτων αἰτίαις ὡς ἐν τοῖς αἰσθητικοῖς σώμασιν ἡ ὀδύνη γίγνεται μεταβολὴν ἀθρόαν εἰς τὸ παρὰ φύσιν λαμβάνουσι, καὶ ὡς ἔστιν ἡ μεταβολὴ διττὴ, ποτὲ μὲν ἀλλοιουμένων αὐτῶν ἀθρόως τε καὶ βιαίως κατὰ ποιότητα, ποτὲ δὲ τῆς συνεχείας λυομένης.
english_sentence_A: Concerning the genesis of pain, then, it has been stated by me both in the work On the Elements according to Hippocrates (the Greek here reads τῷ καθ᾿ Ἱπποκράτην στοιχείων περὶ τῶν, with the word order disturbed), and it has been stated also in the Causes of Symptoms, that pain arises in sentient bodies when they undergo a sudden change toward the condition contrary to nature, and that the change is twofold: sometimes when they are altered suddenly and violently in quality, sometimes when their continuity is dissolved.
english_sentence_B: Rather, I recall only the main heads of what has been demonstrated in other treatises, just as I shall do now in the case of pain. Concerning the genesis of pain, then, I have spoken both in my work On the Elements according to Hippocrates and in the Causes of Symptoms: that pain arises in sentient bodies when they undergo a sudden change into what is contrary to nature, and that the change is twofold, occurring sometimes when they are altered suddenly and violently in quality, and sometimes when continuity is dissolved.

greek_sentence: εἰ μὲν οὖν ταῦτα πραχθείη, κενωθήσεταί τι τοῦ αἵματος ἧττόν τε διατεινόμενα τὰ πεπονθότα μόρια πρὸς τοῦ λοιποῦ πρᾳότερον ὀδυνήσεται· μὴ γιγνομένου δὲ ἐλάττονος τοῦ κατὰ τὴν φλεγμονὴν αἵματος ἢ καὶ πνεύματος ἀτμώδους ἐκ τῆς θερμασίας γεννηθέντος αὐξάνεσθαι συμβαίνει τὴν ὀδύνην.
english_sentence_A: If, then, these things are accomplished, some of the blood will be evacuated, and the affected parts, being less distended by what remains, will suffer pain more mildly; but if the blood in the inflammation does not become less, or if also vaporous pneuma is generated from the heat, it comes about that the pain increases.
english_sentence_B: If, then, this should be accomplished, some of the blood will be evacuated, and the affected parts, being less distended, will thereafter suffer pain more mildly; but if the blood in the inflammation does not become less, or if vaporous pneuma has also been generated from the heat, it comes about that the pain increases.

greek_sentence: οὐ γίγνεται δὲ ἔλαττον τὸ αἷμα διὰ τὴν ἐν τῷ παντὶ σώματι περιουσίαν τῶν χυμῶν· [517] ἐπὶ γὰρ τὸ θερμαινόμενον μέρος ἕλκεται πλέον ἢ διαφορεῖται, φύσιν ἐχόντων τῶν θερμαινόντων ὥσπερ διαφορεῖν τὸ περιεχόμενον οἶς ἂν πλησιάζῃ μορίοις, οὕτως ἕλκειν τὸ περιττεῦον ἐκ τῶν γειτνιώντων.
english_sentence_A: But the blood does not become less, because of the superabundance of the humours in the whole body; [517] for more is drawn towards the part being heated than is dispersed, since heating agents have the nature, just as they disperse what is contained in whatever parts they are applied to, so also to draw the excess from the neighbouring parts.
english_sentence_B: But the blood does not become less, on account of the superabundance of the humours in the whole body; [517] for more is drawn to the part being warmed than is dispersed, since warming agents have the nature that, just as they disperse what is contained in whatever parts they come near, so they draw the superfluity from the neighbouring parts.

lsj_entry_text: φλεβοτομ-ία, Ion. -ιη, ἡ, blood-letting, Hp. Coac. 288 , Nat.Hom. 11 , Aristid. Or. 49(25).34 (pl.), Gal. 6.256 ; φλεβοτομίας ποιεῖσθαι Polybus ap. Arist. HA 512b17 .
greek_sentence: ὅταν οὖν τὰ θερμάσματα μὴ λύῃ τὴν ὀδύνην, προκενωτέον ἐστί σοι τὸ πᾶν σῶμα διὰ κενώσεως· ἀξιόλογος δὲ κένωσις ἐπὶ τῶν ὀξέως νοσούντων ἥ τε διὰ τῆς γαστρὸς καὶ ἡ διὰ τῆς φλεβοτομίας, ὧν τὴν ἑτέραν ἀξιοῖ παραλαμβάνειν ὁ Ἱπποκράτης, διδάσκων σκοποὺς τῆς μᾶλλον ὠφελῆσαι δυναμένης.
english_sentence_A: When, therefore, the heating applications do not dissolve the pain, you must first evacuate the whole body by means of an evacuation; and a noteworthy evacuation in those suffering from acute diseases is both that through the belly and that through phlebotomy, one or the other of which Hippocrates thinks fit to employ, teaching the indications of the one that is able to benefit more.
english_sentence_B: Whenever, then, the warm applications do not resolve the pain, you must first evacuate the whole body by means of evacuation. The evacuation worth mentioning in those who are acutely ill is that through the belly and that through phlebotomy, of which Hippocrates thinks fit to employ one or the other, teaching the indications for the one able to benefit more.

greek_sentence: τὸ μὲν οὖν κεφάλαιον τοῦ προκειμένου λόγου τοῦτό ἐστι, τῶν δὲ κατὰ μέρος αὐτῷ λεγομένων ὅσα μὴ σαφῆ τοῖς πολλοῖς ἐστι διὰ τῶν ἐφεξῆς δηγήσομαι· τοῖς πολλοῖς δὲ εἶπον, ἐπειδὴ τοῖς προγεγυμνασμένοις ἀκούειν λέξεως παλαιᾶς ὀλίγα παντάπασιν ἀσαφῆ γίνεται.
english_sentence_A: This, then, is the chief point of the discourse before us; and of the things said by him in detail, as many as are not clear to the many I shall explain in what follows. I said 'to the many', since for those who have been previously trained in understanding ancient diction, altogether few things are obscure.
english_sentence_B: This, then, is the main point of the argument before us; of the particular things he says, I shall explain in what follows whatever is not clear to the many. I said 'to the many', since to those previously trained in hearing ancient diction very few things indeed are unclear.

lsj_entry_text: θάλψις, εως, ἡ, ( θάλπω) warming, fomenting, Hp. Acut. 21 , S.E. M. 7.354 , Ruf. Sat.Gon. 47 . opp. ψῦξις, of seasons, Hp. Aph. 3.1 ; heat, heating property, Gal. 18(1).228 . cherishing, PLond. 5.1727.10 (vi A.D.).
greek_sentence: περιστέγειν δὲ ἱματίῳ τὴν θάλψιν χρή· πλείω τε γὰρ χρόνον ἂν διαρκέσει καὶ παραμενεῖ, καὶ ἅμα ὡς μὴ ἡ ἀτμὶς πρὸς τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ κάμνοντος φέρηται, ἢν μὴ ἄρα δοκέῃ καὶ τοῦτο χρήσιμον πρός τι εἷναι· ἔστι γὰρ ὅτε δεῖ πρός τι.
english_sentence_A: And one must cover the warming application closely with a cloth; for thus it will both last and remain for a longer time, and at the same time so that the vapour may not be carried to the breath of the patient, unless indeed this too should seem to be useful for some purpose; for there are times when it is needed for some purpose.
english_sentence_B: One must cover the warming all round with a cloak; for in this way it will last and persist for a longer time, and at the same time the vapour will not be carried to the breath of the patient, unless indeed this too should seem useful for some purpose; for there are times when it is needed for some purpose.

greek_sentence: ἐνταῦθα μὲν οὖν ἐπιγέγραπται τὸ πρῶτον εἶδος τῆς πυριάσεως, ἐφεξῆς δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ δεύτερον μεταβαίνων ἐρεῖ· Ἔτι δὲ καὶ κριθαὶ ἢ καὶ ὄροβοι ἐν ὄξει κεκραμένῳ σμικρῷ [523] ὀξύτερον ἢ ὡς ἂν πίῃ τις διέντα καὶ ἀναζέσαντα εἰς μαρσύππιά τε ἀποῤῥάψαντα προστιθέναι καὶ πίτυρα τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον.
english_sentence_A: Here, then, the first kind of fomentation has been set down, and next, passing on to the second, he will say: "Further, also barley or bitter vetch, in vinegar mixed so as to be a little [523] sharper than one would drink it — having soaked and boiled them up and sewn them into little bags, apply them; and bran in the same way." Both barley and bitter vetch he bids one boil in vinegar and water not as whole seeds, but having first pounded them; this is clear also from his saying "having soaked", and in any case one might be taught from the matter itself that this is what Hippocrates intends.
english_sentence_B: Here, then, the first kind of fomentation has been set down; next, passing on to the second, he will say: "Further, barley or bitter vetch, too, breaking them up in vinegar diluted to be a little [523] sharper than one would drink it, and boiling them up and sewing them into small bags, one should apply them; and bran in the same way." He bids that both barley and bitter vetch be boiled in vinegar and water not as whole seeds, but after first pounding them.

Both barley and bitter vetch he bids one boil in vinegar and water not as whole seeds, but having first pounded them; this is clear also from his saying "having soaked", and in any case one might be taught from the matter itself that this is what Hippocrates intends.
english_sentence_B: This is clear from his saying 'breaking them up', and besides, one could learn from the matter itself that Hippocrates means this.

english_sentence_A: He effects the evacuations in accordance with the inclination of the humours that are producing the inflammation; for the dictum "they are to be led in the direction in which they incline, through the suitable [528] regions" is most true.
english_sentence_B: He makes the evacuations according to the inclination of the humours that produce the inflammation; for the precept that one must draw off where it inclines, through the suitable [528] regions, is most true.

english_sentence_A: So when the sympathetic affection shows itself above, one must cut a vein at the elbow, the one that is able more and more quickly to draw back and evacuate the blood from the affected part; but when it shows itself below, it is fitting to effect the evacuation by purgation.
english_sentence_B: When, then, the sympathetic affection gives its sign upwards, one must cut a vein at the elbow, the one that is able more, and more quickly, to draw the blood away from the affected part by revulsion and to evacuate it; but when it gives its sign downwards, it is proper to make the evacuation by means of purging. He rightly said that heaviness arises about the arm, and not pain.

greek_sentence: εὖ δὲ εἶπε βάρος γίγνεσθαι περὶ τὸν βραχίονα καὶ οὐ πόνον· τοῦ μὲν γὰρ ἐνταῦθα μᾶλλον ἠθροῖσθαι τὸ αἷμα καὶ ῥέπειν σημεῖόν ἐστι τὸ βάρος ἐπὶ πλήθει γιγνόμενον· αἱ δὲ τάσεις καὶ κατὰ συμπάθειαν μόνην εἰώθασι γίγνεσθαι, τῶν συνεχῶν τοῖς φλεγμαίνουσι τεινομένων ἄνευ τοῦ πλεονάζειν ἐν αὐτοῖς τὸ αἷμα· διὰ τοῦτο οὖν αὐτὸ κενοῦν κελεύει τὸ πλεονάζον αἷμα τέμνοντα φλέβα τὴν ἔνδον.
english_sentence_A: And he did well to say that heaviness arises about the upper arm, and not pain; for heaviness, which comes about from fullness, is a sign that the blood has collected there to a greater degree and is inclining there; whereas tensions are wont to arise also through sympathetic affection alone, the parts continuous with the inflamed ones being stretched without the blood being in excess in them. For this reason, therefore, he bids one evacuate the excess blood itself by cutting the inner vein.
english_sentence_B: For heaviness, arising as it does from plethora, is a sign that the blood has collected there in greater quantity and is inclining there; but tensions are wont to arise even through sympathetic affection alone, when the parts continuous with the inflamed ones are stretched without the blood being in excess in them. For this very reason, then, he bids one evacuate the excess blood by cutting the inner vein.

greek_sentence: ἐντεῦθεν γὰρ ἀποφυομένη ταπεινοτέρα φέρεται διὰ τῆς καρδίας ἐπὶ τὴν ῥάχιν κατακαμπτομένη.
english_sentence_A: For growing off from there it is carried lower, bending down through the heart toward the spine.
english_sentence_B: Its offshoots, before it reaches the heart, are large veins into the diaphragm and small ones into the lower part of the thorax itself, the part of the eight ribs, which is nourished by a single azygos vein. In some animals this vein branches off above the heart; in others, as also in human beings, it branches off at the part where the vena cava already [530] touches the auricle of the heart.

greek_sentence: τούτων οὖν τῶν δύο φλεβῶν ἀκολούθως ἐφεξῆς εἰσιν αἱ εἰς τὰς χεῖρας ἀφικνούμεναι διὰ τῶν μασχαλῶν· αἱ δ᾿ ὠμιαῖαι καλούμεναι μετὰ τὸ σχισθῆναι εἰς τὰς σφαγίτιδας τὴν κοίλην ἀφ᾿ ἑκατέρας μία πεφύκασιν ἐκτὸς ἤδη τοῦ θώρακος, ἔχουσι δὲ τὰς ῥίζας κοινὰς ταῖς ἐπιπολαίοις σφαγίτισιν.
english_sentence_A: Next in order after these two veins, accordingly, are those that arrive at the arms through the armpits; while the so-called humeral veins, after the hollow vein has been split into the jugulars, grow one from each of them, now outside the thorax, and have their roots in common with the superficial jugulars.
english_sentence_B: The remaining four high ribs of the thorax are nourished by another pair of veins, which branch off from the vena cava before it divides into the jugular veins. Next in order after these two veins come those that reach the arms through the armpits.

english_sentence_A: From the superficial jugulars, then, almost all the superficial parts about the neck and the head are nourished, just as also all the deep parts are nourished from the deep jugulars.
english_sentence_B: The so-called shoulder veins arise, one from each of the jugulars, after the vena cava has divided into the jugular veins, and they arise already outside the thorax; they have their roots in common with the superficial jugular veins. From the superficial jugular veins, then, nearly all the superficial parts of the neck and the head are nourished, just as all the deep parts are nourished from the deep jugular veins.

greek_sentence: εἰκότως οὖν ἡ μὲν ὠμιαία τὰ τῶν κλειδῶν ἄνωθεν μέρη κενοῖ θᾶττόν τε καὶ μᾶλλον, ὅσα κατὰ τράχηλόν τέ ἐστι καὶ κεφαλήν· ἡ δὲ διὰ τῆς μασχάλης τὰ κατὰ τὸν θώρακα καὶ τούτων αὐτῶν μᾶλλον τὰ ὑψηλὰ καὶ μάλιστα ἐπὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων· ἐπειδὴ τὰ ταπεινὰ πάντα μία φλὲψ ἑτέρα τρέφει κατωτέρω τῆς καρδίας ἀποφυομένη τῆς κοίλης φλεβός.
english_sentence_A: Reasonably, then, the humeral vein evacuates more quickly and to a greater degree the parts above the collar-bones, namely all those that lie in the neck and head; whereas the vein that passes through the armpit evacuates the parts in the thorax, and of these themselves more the upper ones, and especially in human beings; since all the lower parts are nourished by one other vein, which branches off from the vena cava lower down than the heart.

Il. 16.186 , Od. 3.112 ; κύνες, ἔλαφος, πτώξ, ἵππος, Il. 3.26 , 8.248 , 17.676 , 23.347 , etc.; οἰωνόν, ταχὺν ἄγγελον 24.292 , cf. Od. 15.526 ; τ. βαδιστής a quick walker, E. Med. 1182 ; σφοδροὶ καὶ τ. X. Cyr. 2.1.31 . of things, τ. πόδες Il. 6.514 , cf. Od. 13.261 , etc.; τ. ἰός, ὀϊστοί, Il. 4.94 , Od. 22.3 , etc.; πτερά Ar. Av. 1453 ; -ύτατα ἅρματα Pi. R. 553d ; short, τ. ἐλπίδες fleeting hopes, Pi. P. 1.83 ; ἐπαυρέσεις Th. 2.53 ; ἀτραπός Ar. Ra. 127 ; ταχεῖ σὺν χρόνῳ S. OC 1602 ; τ. διήγησις short, rapid, Arist. Rh. 1416b30 . Adv., regul. ταχέως, quickly, opp. βραδέως, Il. 23.365 , Hes. Th. 103 , etc.:—rarely in sense perhaps (cf. τάχα 11 ), Plb. 16.25.8 . the Adv. is also expressed by periphr., διὰ ταχέων in haste, Th. 1.80 , 3.13 , Pl. Ap. 32d , X. An. 1.5.9 ; ἐκ ταχείας S. english_sentence_A: Now whatever upper part of it, after its division, is carried toward the outer side of the forearm, this is cut beside the division itself, since it lies most directly in line with the first root of the vein, and for this reason it also most quickly empties the regions above the collar-bones; the oblique part carried into the bend empties these less [533] than this one, but more than the others; while the part carried from the inner side of the great vein, itself also oblique, empties the aforesaid parts least of all, but the upper parts of the thorax most, because of its roots, which are very close both to the vein carried through the armpit to the arm and to the vein nourishing the upper parts of the thorax.

english_sentence_A: The measure of evacuation proper to the affection, then, has been stated; but when the faculty at times prevents evacuating to that extent, one must know that the benefit to the inflamed part will be less, yet it is more fitting to refrain from breaking down the faculty than from evacuating the excess blood.
english_sentence_B: The measure of evacuation proper to the affection has thus been stated. But when the strength sometimes prevents evacuating to that extent, one must know that the benefit to the inflamed part will be less; yet it is more fitting to refrain from breaking down the strength than to evacuate the superabundant blood.

english_sentence_A: Both of these stop pain; and many other of the purgatives also stop it, but these are the strongest of those that I know.

greek_sentence: Ὅτι τὰ καθαρτικὰ φάρμακα διὰ τῆς πείρας εὑρίσκεται τίνα τε καθαίρει χυμὸν καὶ εἰ ὅλως καθαίρει, μεμάθηκας ἐν τοῖς περὶ τῆς τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων δυνάμεως· ὅτι μέντοι χρεία καθάρσεως ἐστιν, εἰ ῥέπουσιν οἱ πλεονάζοντες χυμοὶ κάτω καὶ τῷ λόγῳ μὲν ἐπενοήθη, τὴν μαρτυρίαν δὲ καὶ βεβαίωσιν ἐκ τῆς πείρας ἔσχεν.
english_sentence_A: That the cathartic drugs are discovered through experience—both which humour each purges and whether it purges at all—you have learned in the books on the power of simple drugs; that, however, there is need of purgation if the humours in excess incline downward, was both conceived by reason and received its testimony and confirmation from experience.
english_sentence_B: That purgative drugs are discovered through experience, both which humour they purge and whether they purge at all, you have learned in the books On the Capacity of Simple Drugs. That there is, however, a need for purging if the superabundant humours tend downwards was both conceived by reason and received its testimony and confirmation from experience.

english_sentence_A: Hippocrates himself, then, has taught you the powers of the drugs he gives in such affections, saying that black hellebore evacuates what is more critical, [537] while peplion is more effective at breaking down flatulence.
english_sentence_B: Hippocrates himself, then, has taught you the powers of the drugs that he gives in affections of this kind, when he said that black hellebore evacuates things more critical, [537] and that peplion is more apt to break up flatulences.

english_sentence_A: And since all purgative drugs harm the stomach, and especially its mouth, because it is most sinewy and most sensitive, the admixture of the aromatic substances was devised, so that the power of the purgative drugs might not touch the mouth of the stomach by itself and unmixed.
english_sentence_B: And since all purgative drugs do harm to the stomach, and above all to its mouth, because this is the most sinewy and most sensitive part, the admixture of fragrant substances was devised, so that the power of the purgative drugs should not come into contact with the mouth of the stomach alone and unmixed.

greek_sentence: ἡ γάρ τοι στάσις ἐν ταῖς μίξεσι τῶν καθαιρόντων γίνεται φαρμάκων, οὐχ ὅταν αὐτῶν τὸ μὲν χολῆς, εἰ τύχῃ, τὸ δὲ φλέγματος ᾖ κενωτικὸν (ἀμφότερα γὰρ ἐκκενοῦσθαι δύναται κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον) ἀλλ᾿ ὅταν τὸ μὲν εὐθέως, τὸ δὲ μετὰ πολὺ τῆς προσφορᾶς πεφύκῃ κινεῖν τὴν κάθαρσιν· ἀνώμαλος γὰρ οὕτως ἡ κένωσις γίγνεται προσενεχθέντων ἅμα.
english_sentence_A: For variance in the mixtures of purgative drugs arises not when one of them is, say, evacuative of bile and the other of phlegm (for both can be evacuated at the same time), but when one is naturally such as to set the purgation in motion immediately and the other long after its administration; for in this way the evacuation becomes uneven when they are administered together.
english_sentence_B: For conflict in mixtures of purgative drugs arises not when one of them is, say, evacuative of bile and the other of phlegm (for both can be evacuated at the same time), but when the one is naturally disposed to set the purging in motion at once, and the other long after its administration; for in this way, when they have been administered together, the evacuation becomes irregular.

greek_sentence: ὅταν οὖν, φησὶ, μὴ μόνον ὀξὺ τὸ πάθος ᾖ, καθάπερ ἐστὶν ἡ πλευρῖτις, ἀλλὰ καὶ μετὰ πυρετοῦ σφοδροτάτου, πολλῷ μᾶλλον εὐλαβητέον ἐστὶ τὴν δόσιν τοῦ καθαίροντος φαρμάκου καὶ διὰ φλεβοτομίας κενωτέον μᾶλλον, εἰ καὶ πρὸς ὑποχόνδριόν ἐστιν ἡ ὀδύνη περαινομένη, μικροτέρας μὲν ὠφελείας ἢ τῆς διὰ καθάρσεως ἑπομένης, ἀσφαλεστέρας δὲ μακρῷ, μᾶλλον δὲ κίνδυνον μὲν [539] οὐδ᾿ ὁντιναοῦν τῆς διὰ φλεβοτομίας ἐχούσης, μεγίσταις δὲ ἀποτυχίαις τῆς διὰ καθάρσεως περιπιπτούσης, καὶ μάλισθ᾿ ὅταν ἀπείρως τις ἔχῃ τῆς τοῦ κάμνοντος φύσεως.
english_sentence_A: When, therefore, he says, the affection is not only acute, as pleurisy is, but is also accompanied by a most violent fever, one must be far more cautious about the administration of the purging drug and should rather evacuate by means of phlebotomy, even if the pain is extending toward the hypochondrium; for the benefit that follows is smaller than that which follows from purgation, but far safer—or rather, the evacuation through phlebotomy carries no danger [539] whatsoever, whereas that through purgation falls into the greatest failures, and especially when one is inexperienced in the nature of the patient.
english_sentence_B: When, then, he says, the affection is not only acute, as pleurisy is, but is also accompanied by a most violent fever, one must be much more cautious about the giving of the purging drug, and must rather evacuate by phlebotomy, even if the pain extends to the hypochondrium. For the benefit that follows from phlebotomy is smaller than that which follows from purging, but far safer; or rather, the one through phlebotomy carries no danger [539] whatsoever, whereas the one through purging runs into the greatest failures, and especially when one is unacquainted with the nature of the patient.

lsj_entry_text: μικρός and σμικρός, ά, όν, Dor. , Ion. μικκός (q.v.): σμικρός is corroborated by metre in Il. 17.757 , Hes. Op. 361 , and might be restored in Il. 5.801 , Od. 3.296 (μικρός codd.); it is prob. the only form in Hdt. ( μικρός Hdt. 2.74 codd.): freq. in Lyr. and prob. always in Trag. (exc. where metre requires μικρός, as S. Aj. 161 (anap., Comp. )); most freq. in Pl. ; but in Th. , also Ar. and other Com., μικρός prevails, σμικρός being found Th. 4.13 , 7.75 , 8.81 , Ar. Ach. 523 , V. 5 ; Att. Inscrr. have σμικρός IG 12.313.111 , al., μικρός ib. 369.10 , al.:—small, little, in Size, μ. ἔην δέμας Il. 5.801 ; μ. λίθος Od. 3.296 ; κίρκον, ὅ τε σμικρῇσι φόνον φέρει ὀρνίθεσσιν Il. 17.757 ; σμ. ἄστεα Hdt. 1.5 ; μεγάθεϊ σμικροί Id. 2.74 : with Dims., μ. πολίχνιον, γῄδιον, παιδάρια, Isoc. 5.145 , X. Cyr. 8.3.38 , Ages. 1.21 : as a Com. exaggeration, δικαστηρίδιον μ. πάνυ Ar. V. 803 ; σκαλαθυρμάτι' ἄττα μ. Id. Nu. 630 , etc.: c. inf., μικροὶ δ' ὁρᾶν Id. Pax 821 : as a term of reproach, Κλειγενὴς ὁ μικρός Id. Ra. 709 , cf. Pl. Prt. 323d , Arist. EN 1123b7 , Alex. 98.7 ; Ἀμύντας ὁ μ. Arist. Pol. 1311b3 ; οἱ ἐν μικρῷ μεγάλοι short but stoutly built, Philostr. Gym. 36 ; ὁ μ. δάκτυλος SIG 1172.4 (Lebena). in Quantity, σμικρὸν ἐπὶ σμικρῷ καταθεῖναι Hes. Op. 361 ; μέλιτος μικρόν Ar. V. 878 ; μ. ὄψον, ἀργυρίδιον, X. Mem. 3.14.1 , Ar. Pl. 240 , cf. Antiph. 44 . in Amount or Importance, petty, trivial, slight, σμ. πρόφασις Thgn. 323 ; ἔπος, ἔγκλημα, ῥοπή, etc., S. OC 443 , Tr. 361 , OT 961 , etc.; ἐκ σμικροῦ λόγου on some slight pretext, Id. OC 620 ; ἐν σμικρῷ λόγῳ παρῆκεν as of small account, ib. 569 ; αἰτίας μικρᾶς πέρι E. Andr. 387 , etc.; οὐδὲ μικρόν, = οὐδὲ γρῦ , D. 19.37 ; of persons, of small account, opp. μέγας, σμ. ἐν σμικροῖς, μέγας ἐν μεγάλοις Pi. P. 3.107 ; ἄριστ' ἂν καὶ μέγας ὀρθοῖθ' ὑπὸ μικροτέρων S. Aj. 161 (anap.), etc.; σμ. τίθησί με Id. OC 958 ; βίος ὁ μ., = μέτριος , E. Fr. 504 ; τίνος σμικροτάτου μεταβαλόντος, σμικρότατος τὴν δύναμιν, Pl. R. 473b ; of the mind, οὐ σμικρὸν φρονεῖ S. Aj. 1120 ; of style, mean, [ Φίλιστοσ] μικρὸς ταῖς ἐκφράσεσιν D.H. Vett.Cens. 3.2 ; of festivals, of lesser importance, Ἁλίεια τὰ μεγάλα καὶ τὰ μ. SIG 1067.14 (Cedreae). of Time, short, Pi. O. 12.12 , Ar. Pl. 126 , etc.; εἰς μ. χρόνον Pl. R. 498d ; ἐν μικρῷ (sc. χρόνῳ) shortly, X. Cyn. 5.32 , Eq. 8.7 ; πρὸ μικροῦ Poll. 1.72 ; ἔτι μικρὸν καὶ καταλιθοβολήσουσί με LXX Ex. 17.4 . of Age, young, Ostr.Bodl. i237 (ii B.C.), etc. Adverbial usages, regul. Adv. σμικρῶς, but little, Pl. Criti. 107d ; μικρῶς by a little, prob. in Archim. Stom. 1 : Sup. σμικρότατα X. Mem. 3.11.12 . σμικροῦ or μικροῦ within a little, almost, Id. Cyr. 1.4.8 , D. 18.151 , etc.; in full, μικροῦ δεῖν, v. δεῖ 11 , δέω (B) 1 ; μικροῦ τινος ἀπελείφθη τοῦ μή . . Ach.Tat. 7.13 ; but μικροῦ πρίασθαι for a little, cheap, X. Mem. 2.10.4 . σμικρῷ by a little, with Comp. , Pl. Plt. 262c , etc.; also σμικρῷ πρόσθεν a little before, Id. Lg. 719b , etc.; μικρῷ ἄνωθεν D. 44.6 . μικρόν a little, σμικρὸν ὑπολείπεσθαι, σμ. τι παρακλίνειν, X. An. 5.4.22 , Pl. Cra. 410a ; of Time, X. An. 3.1.11 , etc.; repeated, μικρὸν μικρόν Antiph. 10 : pl., of Degree, σμικρὰ γεωμετρίας ἔμπειροι Pl. R. 527a , etc.; σμίκρ' ἄττα διατρίψαντες Id. Prt. 316a ; μικρὰ διακινήσω σε περὶ τοῦ πράγματος Sosip. 1.22 ; περιπάτησον μικρὰ μετ' ἐμοῦ Men. Sam. 243 , cf. Plu. Luc. 31 . with Preps., ἐπὶ σμικρόν but a little, S. El. 414 , Antipho 6.18 , Hdt. 4.129 . κατὰ μικρόν into small pieces, X. An. 7.3.22 ; so κατὰ μικρὰ γενομένης τῆς δυνάμεως ib. 5.6.32 ; also, little by little, κατὰ μικρὸν ἀεί Ar. V. 702 , cf. Nu. 741 ; opp. συλλήβδην, Pl. R. 344a ; καὶ κατὰ σμ. or μ. ever so little, Id. Sph. 241c , Isoc. 3.10 , D. 2.22 . παρὰ μικρόν within a little, παρὰ μ. ἐλθεῖν c. inf., to be within an ace of doing, E. Heracl. 295 (anap.), cf. Isoc. 7.6 , etc.; παρὰ μ. ἦλθον ἀποθανεῖν Id. 17.42 ; τὸ παρὰ μ. ὥσπερ οὐδὲν ἀπέχειν δοκεῖ Arist. Ph. 197a30 ; but τὸ παρὰ μ. σῴζεσθαι to be only just saved, Id. Rh. 1371b11 , cf. Simp. in Ph. 344.10 ; gradual, imperceptible change, Arist. Pol. 1303a20 ; οὐδὲ παρὰ μ. ἦν κρεῖττον c. inf., Plb. 12.20.7 ; [ ἡ τύχη] παρὰ μ. εἰς ἑκάτερα ποιεῖ μεγάλας ῥοπάς Id. 15.6.8 , cf. Isoc. 4.59 ; but also παρὰ μ. ποιεῖσθαι, ἡγεῖσθαι, to think little of . . , D. 61.51 , Isoc. 5.79 . μετὰ μικρόν a little after, Ev.Matt. 26.73 . besides regul. Comp. and Sup. μικρότερος, -ότατος ( Ar. Eq. 789 , D. Prooem. 48 , etc.), there are the irreg. ἐλάσσων, ἐλάχιστος, from ἐλαχύς, and μείων, μεῖστος, also μειότερος; v. μείων. [ι by nature; ι only in late Poetry, Epigr. ap. Phleg. Fr. 36.17 J. ] (Perh. cf. Lat. mīca, mīcidus, OHG. smāhi, ONorse smár 'little'.)

Prose, Jahresh. 12.136 (Erythrae), IG 12(5).22 (Ios), 5(2).343.34 (Orchom. Arc. )) and the neut. ὅττι Od. 9.402 , al., cf. ὄττι Alc. 45 .—In some forms only the second part is inflected, viz. gen. ὅτου Th. 1.23 , al., Ep. ὅττεο Od. 1.124 , later Ion. ὅτεο Jahresh.l.c., contr. ὅττευ Od. 17.121 , ὅτευ ib. 421 , Hdt. 1.7 ; Lesb. ὄττω Sapph. Supp. 5.3 ; dat. ὅτῳ Th. 1.36 , al.; perh. also in Ion. , Emp. 2.5 , Democr. 99 , Hp. VC 14 ; Ep. ὅτεῳ Od. 2.114 , and as disyll., Il. 12.428 , 15.664 ; so Hdt. 1.86 , al., Democr. 100 , Heraclit. 15 , SIG 194.21 (Amphipolis, iv B. C.); Arc. ὀσ<*>έοι IG 5(2).262.14 (Mantinea, v B. C.); Ep. acc. ὅτινα Od. 8.204 , 15.395 ; Delph. gen. ὅτινος IG 22.1126.37 (iv B. C.), also Berl.Sitzb. 1927.167 (Cyrene); Delph. dat. ὅτινι IG 22.1126.25 ; Cret. dat. sg. ὄτιμι Leg.Gort. 7.51 , 8.7 , al.: pl., nom. masc. Arg. ὄττινες Mnemos. 44.65 (iii B. C.); neut. ὅτινα Il. 22.450 ; gen. ὅτεων Od. 10.39 , Hdt. 8.65 , Att. ὅτων S. OT 414 , X. An. 7.6.24 (cj.), Oec. 3.2 (cj.) (also in Hes. Fr. 238 , Anaxag. 12 , Hp. Aër. 21 ); dat. ὁτέοισι(ν) Il. 15.491 , Hdt. 2.82 , Att. ὅτοισι S. Ant. 1335 , Ar. Eq. 758 , ὅτοις S. Tr. 1119 ; acc. ὅτινας Il. 15.492 , Aeol. ὄττινας Sapph. 12 : in a few forms only the first part is inflected, Cret. gen. sg. ὦτι prob. in Leg.Gort. 1.5 , 2.50 , 11.50 , al., GDI 4993 ii 10 : neut. pl. ἄτι Leg.Gort. 2.47 , al.: of the forms with double inflexion Hom. has only ὅν τινα Il. 2.188 , al., ἥν τινα 3.286 , al., οἵ τινες Od. 4.94 , al., οὕς τινας Il. 4.240 , al., ἅς τινας Od. 8.573 ; ᾧτινι first in Hes. Op. 31 , ἧστινος A. Ag. 1358 , ᾗ τινι δή Th. 8.87 , οἷστισι Ar. Pax 1279 : Att. Inscrr. have ἧστινος ᾗτινι along with masc. and neut. ὅτου ὅτῳ, and this rule holds with few exceptions in Trag. and Att. Prose before iv B. C.; ᾡτινιοῦν occurs in Lys. 1.37 , etc.: ὅτῳ rarely as fem., E. IT 1071 .—For the Ion. and Ep. form ἅσσα, Att. ἅττα, v. ἅσσα .—On the concord and construction cf. ὅς B. 1.1 , 3 , 11.3 , 111.2a ,b:—Radic. sense, any one who, anything which, whosoever, whichsoever; ὣς ἀπόλοιτο καὶ ἄλλος, ὅτις τοιαῦτά γε ῥέζοι Od. 1.47 ; ἀθανάτων ὅς τίς σε φυλάσσει 15.35 , etc.: freq. without express antec., χαίρει δέ μιν ὅς τις ἐθείρῃ Il. 21.347 ; ἆσσον ἴτω ὅς τις δέπας οἴσεται 23.667 : hence freq. in maxims or sentiments, οὐκ ἔστιν ὅ. πάντ' ἀνὴρ εὐδαιμονεῖ Ar. Ra. 1217 ; μακάριος ὅ. οὐσίαν καὶ νοῦν ἔχει Men. 114 ; οὗτος βέλτιστος ἂν εἴη, ὅ. . . Lys. 3.4 , etc.: freq. in such phrases as ὅστις εἶ, ὅστις ἐστί, v. ὅς B. 111.2 ; ἔστιν ὅ., freq. with a neg., οὐ γὰρ ἔην ὅς τίς σφιν . . ἡγήσαιτο Il. 2.687 ; οὐκ ἔστιν ὅτῳ μείζονα μοῖραν νείμαιμ' ἢ σοί A. Pr. 293 (anap.), cf. 989 , 1070 (anap.), etc.; εἰσὶν οἵτινες S. Fr. 354.5 ; οὐδὲν ὅ τι οὐ . . everything, Hdt. 5.97 , Th. 7.87 :—in these phrases the case of ὅστις commonly depends on that of οὐδείς; but sts. the reverse, v. οὐδείς 1.2 : also joined with Sup. , τρόπῳ ὅτῳ ἂν δύνωνται ἰσχυροτάτῳ Foed. ap. Th. 5.23 ; ὅντινα ἀφανέστατον δύναιντο τρόπον Paus. 10.1.5 : in Trag. and Att. sts. strengthd. by an antec. πᾶς, but only in sg., ἅπας δὲ τραχὺς ὅ. ἂν νέον κρατῇ A. Pr. 35 , cf. Th. 8.90 (πάντες ὅσοι being commonly used in pl., not πάντες οἵτινες; but πᾶσιν . . ὅστις ἐρωτᾷ IG 12.410 ). referring to a definite object, prop. only when a general notion is implied, Πολυκράτεα . . , δι' ὅντινα κακῶς ἤκουσε, not the man through whom, but one through whom . . , Hdt. 3.120 ; τελευταῖόν σε προσβλέψαιμι νῦν, ὅστις πέφασμαι φύς τ' ἀφ' ὧν οὐ χρῆν may I see thee now for the last time, I who am one born from sinful parentage, S. OT 1184 , cf. A. Pr. 38 , Ag. 1065 ; but in quite definite sense, βωμόν, ὅστις νῦν ἔξω τῆς πόλεώς ἐστι Th. 6.3 : sts. even with οὗτος or ὅδε as antec., Hdt. 1.167 , 2.99 , 6.47 , E. Hipp. 943 , Theoc. 8.87 . ἐφ' ὅτῳ, = ἐφ' ᾧτε , D.S. 16.4 ; so ἐφ' ὅτῳ τε Delph. 3(2).236 (ii B. C.). in indirect questions, Hom. , etc., εἴπ' ἄγε μοι καὶ τόνδε . . , ὅς τις ὅδ' ἐστί Il. 3.192 , cf. 167 , etc.; ἔσπετε νῦν μοι, Μοῦσαι, ὅς τις δὴ κτλ. who it was that . . , 14.509 ; ξεῖνος ὅδ', οὐκ οἶδ' ὅς τις Od. 8.28 : in dialogue, when the person questioned repeats the question asked by τίς, as οὗτος τί ποιεῖς;—ὅ τι ποιῶ ; Ar. Ra. 198 ; ἀλλὰ τίς γὰρ εἶ;—ὅστις ; πολίτης χρηστός Id. Ach. 595 , cf. Pl. 462 , Pl. Euthphr. 2c , etc. rare and late in direct questions, ὅ τι ἐστὶ τὸ ἐμποδίζον ; A.D. Adv. 140.12 ; ἀνθ' ὅτου . . ; = why? Jul. Ep. 82p.109B. -C.; cf. ὅπως. limited or made more indefinite by the addition of Particles: ὅστις γε being one who (cf. ὅσγε), S. OT 1335 , OC 810 , Ar. Ra. 1184 . ὅστις δή (v. δή IV. 1 ), freq. used without any distinct relative force, θεῶν ὅτεῳ δή to some one or other of the gods, Hdt. 1.86 ; ὅτευ δὴ χρήματος δεησόμενον Id. 3.121 ; ᾗ τινι δὴ γνώμῃ Th. 8.87 , etc.; also ὅ τι δήκοτε πρήξοντα Hdt. 6.134 ; ὅστις δήποτ' ὤν Pl. Phdr. 273c ; ὡς ἀπετύγχαν' ὁτουδήποτε D. 19.167 ; ὁτῳδήτινι τρόπῳ PFay. 21.11 (ii A. D.); so ὁστισοῦν, ὁτιοῦν anybody (anything) whatsoever, Th. 4.16 , Pl. Smp. 198b , etc.; μετὰ ὁτουοῦν τρόπου Th. 8.27 ; ὁτῳοῦν Pl. Tht. 175a ; εἷς ὁστισοῦν any one person, Arist. Pol. 1286a31 : freq. with neg., μηδ' ἂν ὁστισοῦν τυγχάνῃ ὤν Pl. Euthphr. 5e , cf. Phd. 78d , etc.; οὐδ' ὁτιοῦν not the least mite, nothing whatsoever, Ar. Nu. 344 , Pl. 385 ; μηδοτιοῦν Thgn. 64 : rarely, = whoever (whatever), as subject of a verb, ὁτιοῦν ἔτυχε τῶν ἐπὶ μέρους ( v.l. ὅτι ἄν ) Arist. Mu. 391a22 . ὁστισδηποτοῦν D. 40.8 , Aeschin. 1.164 . so also ὅστις alone, Pl. Hp.Ma. 282d , etc.: with neg., μηδὲ οἵτινες none at all, X. HG 1.5.9 ; οὐδ' ἧστινος ἂν ἀσχολίας τὸ πρᾶγμα προσεδεῖτο Plb. 9.14.6 . ὅστις ποτε whoever, A. Ag. 160 (lyr.), cf. Hdt. 8.65 . ὅστις περ (cf. ὅσπερ), mostly in neut., ὅ τι πέρ ἐστ' ὄφελος Ar. Ec. 53 , cf. Pl. R. 492e : in masc., D. 21.225 . ὅστις τε, where τε is otiose as in ὅστε, Il. 23.43 , al. neut. ὅ τι used abs. as a Conj., v. ὅ τι . ἐξ ὅτου from which time, S. OC 345 , Tr. 326 , Ar. greek_sentence: ὅταν οὖν, φησὶ, μὴ μόνον ὀξὺ τὸ πάθος ᾖ, καθάπερ ἐστὶν ἡ πλευρῖτις, ἀλλὰ καὶ μετὰ πυρετοῦ σφοδροτάτου, πολλῷ μᾶλλον εὐλαβητέον ἐστὶ τὴν δόσιν τοῦ καθαίροντος φαρμάκου καὶ διὰ φλεβοτομίας κενωτέον μᾶλλον, εἰ καὶ πρὸς ὑποχόνδριόν ἐστιν ἡ ὀδύνη περαινομένη, μικροτέρας μὲν ὠφελείας ἢ τῆς διὰ καθάρσεως ἑπομένης, ἀσφαλεστέρας δὲ μακρῷ, μᾶλλον δὲ κίνδυνον μὲν [539] οὐδ᾿ ὁντιναοῦν τῆς διὰ φλεβοτομίας ἐχούσης, μεγίσταις δὲ ἀποτυχίαις τῆς διὰ καθάρσεως περιπιπτούσης, καὶ μάλισθ᾿ ὅταν ἀπείρως τις ἔχῃ τῆς τοῦ κάμνοντος φύσεως.
english_sentence_A: When, therefore, he says, the affection is not only acute, as pleurisy is, but is also accompanied by a most violent fever, one must be far more cautious about the administration of the purging drug and should rather evacuate by means of phlebotomy, even if the pain is extending toward the hypochondrium; for the benefit that follows is smaller than that which follows from purgation, but far safer—or rather, the evacuation through phlebotomy carries no danger [539] whatsoever, whereas that through purgation falls into the greatest failures, and especially when one is inexperienced in the nature of the patient.
english_sentence_B: When, then, he says, the affection is not only acute, as pleurisy is, but is also accompanied by a most violent fever, one must be much more cautious about the giving of the purging drug, and must rather evacuate by phlebotomy, even if the pain extends to the hypochondrium. For the benefit that follows from phlebotomy is smaller than that which follows from purging, but far safer; or rather, the one through phlebotomy carries no danger [539] whatsoever, whereas the one through purging runs into the greatest failures, and especially when one is unacquainted with the nature of the patient.

greek_sentence: αὐτὸ μὲν γὰρ τὸ καθαρτικὸν φάρμακον, ὡς ἂν ὀλίγον ὂν, εἰς τὸν πυθμένα τῆς κοιλίας ἀφικνεῖται· κατὰ δὲ τὴν δίοδον ὁ στόμαχος, ὅσον τε ὑψηλότερον τῆς γαστρὸς, οὐ μόνον τῆς ποιότητος τοῦ καθαίροντος [542] φαρμάκου, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς οὐσίας προσιζούσης ἐν τῇ διόδῳ, μεταλαμβάνων μεγάλως βλάπτεται· χρήσιμος οὖν ὁ χυλὸς τῆς πτισάνης ἐπιῤῥοφούμενος, ὡς ἂν ἀποῤῥύψαι μὲν καὶ κατασῦραι κάτω τὸ προσπεπλασμένον ἐν τῇ διόδῳ δυνάμενος, ἐπικεράσαι δὲ καὶ ὑπαλλάξαι τὴν ἐνιζηκυῖαν τοῖς μορίοις ποιότητα τοῦ φαρμάκου.
english_sentence_A: For the purgative drug itself, being small in quantity, arrives at the bottom of the belly; but along its passage the gullet, and whatever part of the stomach lies higher up, since it partakes not only of the quality of the purging [542] drug but also of its substance, which settles upon it in the passage, is greatly harmed. The juice of ptisan supped after it is therefore useful, inasmuch as it is able to wash off and drag downward what has been plastered on in the passage, and to temper and alter the quality of the drug that has lodged in the parts.

greek_sentence: Φημὶ γὰρ ἄμεινον εἶναι αὐτίκα ἄρξασθαι τὸ ἐπίπαν ῥοφεῖν, μᾶλλον ἢ προκενεαγγήσαντα ἄρξασθαι τοῦ ῥοφήματος ἢ τριταῖον ἢ τεταρταῖον ἢ πεμπταῖον ἢ ἑκταῖον ἢ ἑβδομαῖον, ἤν γε μὴ προκριθῇ ἡ νοῦσος ἐν τουτέῳ τῷ χρόνῳ.
english_sentence_A: For I say that it is better, on the whole, to begin taking gruel at once, rather than, having first emptied the vessels, to begin the gruel on the third or fourth or fifth or sixth or seventh day, if indeed the disease has not reached its crisis beforehand within this period of time.

greek_sentence: ἐὰν οὖν αὕτη τῇ πέμπτῃ τῶν ἡμερῶν μέλλῃ γίνεσθαι καὶ μὴ δύνηται τοῖς πόμασι μόνοις χρώμενος ὁ κάμνων ἐξαρκέσαι, βέλτιον εἶναί φησιν εὐθέως ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς αὐτῷ δίδοσθαι τῆς πτισάνης, οὐ κατὰ τὴν τρίτην ἢ τὴν τετάρτην ἡμέραν ἄρξασθαι τῆς δόσεως.

english_sentence_B: Even if, without ptisane, you should regulate the patient's regimen on drinks alone, he requires that you carry out the preliminary preparations mentioned, that is, either to perform phlebotomy, or to administer a clyster, or to use a suppository.

greek_sentence: Οἶδα δὲ καὶ τοὺς ἰητροὺς τὰ ἐναντιώτατα ἢ ὡς δεῖ ποιέοντας· βούλονται γὰρ ἅπαντες ὑπὸ τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν νούσων προταριχεύσαντες τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἢ δύο ἢ τρεῖς ἡμέρας ἢ καὶ πλείονας οὕτω προσφέρειν τὰ ῥοφήματα καὶ τὰ ποτά.
english_sentence_A: And I know that physicians too do the very opposite of what is required; for they all wish, at the beginnings of diseases, first to dry people out, as if curing them like salt-fish, for two or three days or even more, and only then to administer the gruels and the drinks.
english_sentence_B: I know, however, that physicians too do the very opposite of what ought to be done: for all of them wish, at the beginnings of diseases, first to dry people out like salt-fish for two or three days or even more, and only then to administer the gruels and the drinks.

greek_sentence: καὶ ἴσως τι καὶ εἰκὸς δοκέει αὐτέοισιν εἶναι, μεγάλης τῆς μεταβολῆς γενομένης τῷ σώματι, μέγα τι κάρτα [547] καὶ ἀντιμεταβάλλειν· τὸ δὲ μεταβάλλειν μὲν εὖ ἔχει μὴ ὀλίγον, ὀρθῶς μέντοι μεταβιβαστέη καὶ ἡ μεταβολὴ καὶ ἔκ γε τῆς μεταβολῆς ἡ πρόσαρσις τῶν γευμάτων ἔτι μᾶλλον.
english_sentence_A: And perhaps it also seems to them somewhat reasonable that, when a great change has taken place in the body, one should also make a very great [547] counter-change in return; now, to change by no small degree is indeed good, yet the change must be carried through correctly, and, following upon the change, the offering of foods still more so.
english_sentence_B: "And perhaps it seems to them also somewhat reasonable that, a great change having taken place in the body, one should make in return some very great [547] counter-change. Now to change is indeed good, and not a little; yet the change must be conducted correctly, and, following on the change, the bringing-in of foods still more so." He censures those physicians who, having kept the patients in complete abstinence from food during the first days, transfer them all at once, some to the administration of gruels, others to that of drinks.

greek_sentence: ὅσοι δ᾿ οὕτω μεταβάλλουσιν, ἴσως οἴονται, φησὶ, κατὰ λόγον μεταβάλλειν ἐπὶ μεγάλῃ τῇ τοῦ σώματος μεταβολῇ, ἀξιόλογον καὶ τὴν τῆς διαίτης ὑπαλλαγὴν ποιούμενοι.
english_sentence_A: Those who make the change in this way perhaps think, he says, that they are changing in due proportion, in response to the great change of the body, by making the alteration of the regimen also a considerable one.
english_sentence_B: Those who change in this way perhaps think, he says, that they are changing in accordance with reason in response to the great change of the body, making a considerable alteration of the regimen as well.

greek_sentence: τοῦτο μὲν οὖν αὐτὸ καλῶς ὑπειληφέναι φησὶν αὐτοὺς, οὐ μὴν ἅπασάν γε μεταβολὴν, ἀλλά τινα οἰητέον [548] εἶναι, περὶ ἧς τὸ μέν τι προείρηκε, τὸ δέ τι καὶ λέξει κατασκευάζων τῷ λόγῳ, φυλάττεσθαι τὰς ἀθρόας μεταβολάς.
english_sentence_A: This point itself, then, he says they have grasped correctly; one must not, however, suppose it to be just any change, but a particular change, [548] concerning which he has partly spoken already and will partly go on to speak, establishing by his argument that sudden (wholesale) changes are to be guarded against.
english_sentence_B: He says, then, that they have rightly supposed this very point; yet one must think that it is not every change, but a certain kind of change [548] that is right. About this he has said something already, and will say more, establishing by argument that sudden changes must be guarded against.

greek_sentence: Τὴν εἰρημένην ὀλίγον ἔμπροσθεν ἀθρόαν μεταβολὴν τῆς διαίτης, καθ᾿ ἣν ταῖς πρώταις ἡμέραις ἐν ἀσιτίᾳ παντελεῖ φυλάξαντες τοὺς κάμνοντας ἄρχονται τρέφειν περὶ τετάρτην ἡμέραν, μάλιστα μὲν βλάπτειν φησὶν, ἐὰν ἐπὶ τὴν ὅλην πτισάνην μεταβάλλωσιν, ἔλαττον δ᾿ ὅταν ἐπὶ τὸν χυλόν· ἥκιστα δὲ, τουτέστιν ἐλάχιστα βλάπτειν τοὺς ἐπὶ μόνα τὰ ποτὰ παραγινομένους.
english_sentence_A: The sudden change of regimen mentioned a little earlier, according to which, after keeping the patients in complete abstinence from food during the first days, they begin to nourish them around the fourth day, he says harms most if they change over to whole ptisane, less when they change to the juice, and least—that is, it harms least—those who go over to drinks alone.
english_sentence_B: The sudden change of regimen spoken of a little before, in which, having kept the patients in complete abstinence from food during the first days, they begin to feed them about the fourth day, he says does most harm if they change over to whole ptisan, less when they change to the juice; and 'least', that is, it does the least harm to those who are brought over to drinks alone.

greek_sentence: [549] Χρὴ δὲ καὶ τὰ μαθήματα ποιέεσθαι ἐν τῇ διαίτῃ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἔτι ὑγιαινόντων, οἷα ξυμφέρει· εἰ γὰρ δὴ τοῖσί γε ὑγιαίνουσι φαίνονται διαφέροντα μεγάλα τὰ τοῖα ἢ τοῖα διαιτήματα, ἐν ἄλλῳ τινί που καὶ ἐν τῇσι μεταβολῇσι, πῶς οὐχὶ καὶ ἐν τῇσι νούσοισι διαφέρει μεγάλα καὶ τουτέων ἐν τῇσιν ὀξυτάτῃσι μάλιστα;
english_sentence_A: [549] One must also acquire the lessons, in the regimen of people while they are still healthy, as to what sorts of things are beneficial; for if indeed in the healthy such-and-such regimens as against such-and-such others appear to differ greatly, in some other respect, I suppose, and especially in the changes, how do they not differ greatly in diseases as well, and most of all among these in the most acute?
english_sentence_B: [549] One must also draw one's lessons, in the regimen of people while they are still healthy, as to what sort of things are beneficial. For if in the healthy, at any rate, regimens of this kind or of that kind evidently make great differences, both in some other respect and in changes, how will they not also make great differences in diseases, and of these most of all in the most acute?

greek_sentence: [549] Χρὴ δὲ καὶ τὰ μαθήματα ποιέεσθαι ἐν τῇ διαίτῃ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἔτι ὑγιαινόντων, οἷα ξυμφέρει· εἰ γὰρ δὴ τοῖσί γε ὑγιαίνουσι φαίνονται διαφέροντα μεγάλα τὰ τοῖα ἢ τοῖα διαιτήματα, ἐν ἄλλῳ τινί που καὶ ἐν τῇσι μεταβολῇσι, πῶς οὐχὶ καὶ ἐν τῇσι νούσοισι διαφέρει μεγάλα καὶ τουτέων ἐν τῇσιν ὀξυτάτῃσι μάλιστα;
english_sentence_A: [549] One must also acquire the lessons, in the regimen of people while they are still healthy, as to what sorts of things are beneficial; for if indeed in the healthy such-and-such regimens as against such-and-such others appear to differ greatly, in some other respect, I suppose, and especially in the changes, how do they not differ greatly in diseases as well, and most of all among these in the most acute?
english_sentence_B: [549] One must also draw one's lessons, in the regimen of people while they are still healthy, as to what sort of things are beneficial. For if in the healthy, at any rate, regimens of this kind or of that kind evidently make great differences, both in some other respect and in changes, how will they not also make great differences in diseases, and of these most of all in the most acute?

greek_sentence: Ἀποδεικνύειν ἤρξατο τὴν προειρημένην ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ περὶ τῆς διαίτης δόξαν, ἐλέγχων ἅμα καὶ τοὺς ἐναντίως διαιτῶντας· ἵνα δὲ σαφὴς ὁ λόγος γένηται, τὸ κεφάλαιον αὐτοῦ σύμπαν ἄμεινόν μοι δοκεῖ προειπεῖν.
english_sentence_A: He has begun to demonstrate the opinion about regimen which he has previously stated, at the same time also refuting those who prescribe regimen in the opposite way; and so that the argument may become clear, it seems to me better to state beforehand the whole main point of it.
english_sentence_B: He has begun to demonstrate the opinion about regimen that he stated earlier, refuting at the same time those who prescribe regimen in the contrary way. So that the argument may become clear, it seems better to me to state its whole chief point beforehand.

greek_sentence: ἔστι δὲ τῶν εἰς αὐτὸ λαμβανομένων λημμάτων τὸ μὲν ἕτερον ἀξίωμα καθόλου τοιοῦτον· ἐὰν τοῖς ὑγιαίνουσι βλάβην φέρουσιν αἱ ἀθρόαι τῆς διαίτης ἐπὶ τἀναντία μεταβολαὶ, πολὺ μᾶλλον τοῖς νοσοῦσιν· ὃ καὶ πολυειδῶς ἐστιν ἑρμηνεύειν, ἄλλοτε εἰς ἄλλην λέξιν μεταλαμβάνοντας, οἷον οὕτως· ἐπὶ τῶν κατὰ δίαιταν [550] ἀθρόων μεταβολῶν οἱ ὑγιαίνοντες ἧττον βλάπτονται τῶν νοσούντων· ἢ οὕτως, οἱ νοσοῦντες βλάπτονται μᾶλλον τῶν ὑγιαινόντων· ἢ οὕτως, τὰ βλαβερὰ τοὺς ὑγιαίνοντας ἧττον βλάπτει τῶν νοσούντων· καὶ ἔτι γενικώτερον τοῦδε· τοὺς ἰσχυροτέρους ἧττον βλάπτει, τοὺς δ᾿ ἀσθενεστέρους μᾶλλον τὰ βλαβερά· ἔξεστι δὲ καὶ ἄλλως ἑρμηνεύειν τὴν αὐτὴν τοῦ λόγου δύναμιν, ἤτοι τὸ καθ᾿ αὑτὸ καὶ πρώτως χρήσιμον εἰς τὸ ἀποδεικνύμενον ἢ διά τινος τῶν περιεχόντων ἀξιωμάτων ἢ λημμάτων αὐτό.
english_sentence_A: Of the premises taken for it, the one is a universal axiom of the following sort: if sudden changes of regimen to the opposite bring harm to the healthy, much more so to the sick; and this can be expressed in many forms, transposing it now into one wording, now into another, for example thus: in the case of sudden changes in [550] regimen the healthy are harmed less than the sick; or thus: the sick are harmed more than the healthy; or thus: harmful things harm the healthy less than the sick; and still more generally than this: harmful things harm the stronger less and the weaker more. It is also possible to express the same force of the argument in other ways, either as what is in itself and primarily useful for the thing being demonstrated, or by means of one of the axioms or premises that contain it.

greek_sentence: ἔστι δὲ τῶν εἰς αὐτὸ λαμβανομένων λημμάτων τὸ μὲν ἕτερον ἀξίωμα καθόλου τοιοῦτον· ἐὰν τοῖς ὑγιαίνουσι βλάβην φέρουσιν αἱ ἀθρόαι τῆς διαίτης ἐπὶ τἀναντία μεταβολαὶ, πολὺ μᾶλλον τοῖς νοσοῦσιν· ὃ καὶ πολυειδῶς ἐστιν ἑρμηνεύειν, ἄλλοτε εἰς ἄλλην λέξιν μεταλαμβάνοντας, οἷον οὕτως· ἐπὶ τῶν κατὰ δίαιταν [550] ἀθρόων μεταβολῶν οἱ ὑγιαίνοντες ἧττον βλάπτονται τῶν νοσούντων· ἢ οὕτως, οἱ νοσοῦντες βλάπτονται μᾶλλον τῶν ὑγιαινόντων· ἢ οὕτως, τὰ βλαβερὰ τοὺς ὑγιαίνοντας ἧττον βλάπτει τῶν νοσούντων· καὶ ἔτι γενικώτερον τοῦδε· τοὺς ἰσχυροτέρους ἧττον βλάπτει, τοὺς δ᾿ ἀσθενεστέρους μᾶλλον τὰ βλαβερά· ἔξεστι δὲ καὶ ἄλλως ἑρμηνεύειν τὴν αὐτὴν τοῦ λόγου δύναμιν, ἤτοι τὸ καθ᾿ αὑτὸ καὶ πρώτως χρήσιμον εἰς τὸ ἀποδεικνύμενον ἢ διά τινος τῶν περιεχόντων ἀξιωμάτων ἢ λημμάτων αὐτό.
english_sentence_A: Of the premises taken for it, the one is a universal axiom of the following sort: if sudden changes of regimen to the opposite bring harm to the healthy, much more so to the sick; and this can be expressed in many forms, transposing it now into one wording, now into another, for example thus: in the case of sudden changes in [550] regimen the healthy are harmed less than the sick; or thus: the sick are harmed more than the healthy; or thus: harmful things harm the healthy less than the sick; and still more generally than this: harmful things harm the stronger less and the weaker more. It is also possible to express the same force of the argument in other ways, either as what is in itself and primarily useful for the thing being demonstrated, or by means of one of the axioms or premises that contain it.
english_sentence_B: Of the premisses taken up for it, the one is a universal axiom of this kind: if sudden changes of regimen to the opposite bring harm to the healthy, much more do they to the sick. This can also be expressed in many forms, transposing it now into one wording, now into another, for instance thus: in sudden changes in [550] regimen the healthy are harmed less than the sick; or thus: the sick are harmed more than the healthy; or thus: harmful things harm the healthy less than the sick; and, still more generally than this: harmful things harm the stronger less, and the weaker more.

greek_sentence: καὶ τοὺς μέν γε μὴ μεμαθηκότας ἀριστᾷν, ἢν ἀριστήσωσιν, εὐθέως ἀῤῥώστους ποιέει καὶ βαρέας ὅλον τὸ σῶμα καὶ ἀσθενεῖς καὶ ὀκνηρούς· ἢν δὲ καὶ ἐπιδειπνήσωσιν, ὀξυρεγμιώδεας, ἐνίοισι δὲ ἂν καὶ σπατίλη γένοιτο, ὁκόταν παρὰ τὸ ἔθος ἀχθοφορήσῃ ἡ κοιλίη εἰθισμένη ἐπιξηραίνεσθαι καὶ μὴ δὶς διογκοῦσθαι μηδὲ δὶς ἕψειν τὰ σιτία.
english_sentence_A: And those who are not accustomed to take the midday meal, if they do take it, it straightaway makes weak and heavy in the whole body and feeble and sluggish; and if they also take dinner afterwards, prone to acid eructation, and in some there might even come about loose stool (σπατίλη), whenever the belly, contrary to its habit, carries a burden, being accustomed to be dried out and not to be distended twice nor to concoct the food twice.
english_sentence_B: Those, at any rate, who have not learned to take a midday meal, if they do take one, it at once renders feeble and heavy in the whole body, and weak and sluggish; and if they also take supper on top of it, subject to acid eructations; and in some there may even be watery stools, when, contrary to custom, the belly bears a load, being accustomed to dry out in the interval and not to be distended twice nor twice to concoct the foods.

greek_sentence: πρώτη μὲν οὖν ἐστι μεταβολὴ ἡ νῦν προκεχειρισμένη, τοῦ ἔθους ἐπὶ τῶν ἀηθῶν μὲν ἀριστᾷν, ἀριστησάντων δέ ποτε· φησὶ γὰρ ἀῤῥώστους τε καὶ βαρεῖς ὅλον τὸ σῶμα γίγνεσθαι καὶ ἀσθενεῖς καὶ ὀκνηρούς.
english_sentence_A: The first change, then, is the one now taken in hand, that of habit in the case of those who are unaccustomed to take the morning meal (ariston) but have on some occasion taken it; for he says that they become infirm and heavy in the whole body and weak and sluggish.
english_sentence_B: The first change, then, is the one now taken in hand: the change of habit in those who are unaccustomed to take the midday meal but who have on some occasion taken it. For he says that they become debilitated and heavy in the whole body, and weak and sluggish.

greek_sentence: συμβαίνει δὲ αὐτοῖς ταῦτα βαρυνομένης τῆς δυνάμεως ὑπὸ τῆς τροφῆς ὡς ὑπὸ φορτίου· οὐ γὰρ δὴ κατά γε τὸν ἴδιον λόγον ἀῤῥωστούσης, ὡς ἐπὶ τῆς ἐνδείας εἴωθε γίγνεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: These things happen to them because the faculty is weighed down by the nourishment as by a burden; for it is certainly not infirm on its own account, as is wont to happen in the case of deficiency.
english_sentence_B: These things happen to them because the faculty is weighed down by the nourishment as by a burden; for it is not, at any rate, debilitated on its own account, as usually happens in deficiency.

greek_sentence: διὰ τοῦτο οὖν ἐνταῦθα μὲν προσέθηκε τῷ λόγῳ, τὸ βαρέας ὅλον τὸ σῶμα γίγνεσθαι καὶ ὀκνηροτέρους τοὺς δὶς διαιτηθέντας· ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν εἰθισμένων ἀριστᾷν, οὐκ ἀριστησάντων δὲ, τὴν μὲν ἀσθένειαν τῆς δυνάμεως ἔγραψε, τὸ δὲ βάρος οὐ προσέγραψε· κατὰ γὰρ τὸν ἑαυτῆς λόγον ἡ δύναμις ἐν ταῖς τοιαύταις μεταβολαῖς ἀῤῥωστεῖ.
english_sentence_A: For this reason, then, here he added to his statement that those who have been fed twice become heavy in the whole body and more sluggish; whereas in the case of those accustomed to take the morning meal who have not taken it, he wrote of the weakness of the faculty, but did not add the heaviness; for in changes of that kind the faculty is infirm on its own account.
english_sentence_B: For this reason, then, he added here to his account that those who have been dieted twice become heavy in the whole body and more sluggish; whereas in the case of those accustomed to take the midday meal who have not taken it, he wrote of the weakness of the faculty but did not add the heaviness; for in such changes the faculty is debilitated on its own account.

english_sentence_B: The pale-yellow (ōchron) colour is in truth such as is that of the so-called ochre (ōchra), when it is given the acute accent on the first syllable in pronouncing its name; and it comes about in this way, when the bile that is called pale-yellow, bitter and yellow (xanthē) is mixed with the watery residue.

lsj_first_sense_gloss: the sour fumes caused by indigestion
greek_sentence: ἐμάθομεν δὲ ὅτι διά τε τὴν ψύξιν τῆς γαστρὸς αἱ ὀξυρεγμίαι γίνονται καὶ διὰ φλέγμα πολλάκις ἠθροισμένον ἐν αὐτῇ καὶ διὰ πλῆθος σιτίων ἢ καὶ συμμέτρων μὲν ὄντων, ἀλλὰ ψυχρῶν τῇ δυνάμει.
english_sentence_A: To the things he said happen in the case of those who have taken a midday meal contrary to habit, he added this as well: 'and if they also dine afterwards, they become subject to acid eructations.' We have learned that acid eructations arise both on account of chilling of the stomach and on account of phlegm often collected in it and on account of an abundance of foods, or even foods that are moderate in quantity but cold in capacity.
english_sentence_B: To the things he said happen in those who have taken a midday meal contrary to habit, he added this as well: 'and if they also take supper afterwards, they are subject to acid eructations.' We have learnt that acid eructations arise both through the chilling of the stomach, and through phlegm often accumulated in it, and through a quantity of foods, or even when these are moderate but cold in their power.

greek_sentence: πάντων δὲ τῶν προειρημένων κοινόν ἐστι τὸ νικᾶσθαι τὴν ἔμφυτον θερμασίαν τῆς γαστρὸς ὑπὸ τῶν σιτίων, οὐ νικᾷν οὐδὲ κρατεῖν οὐδὲ κατεργάζεσθαι δυναμένην καλῶς αὐτά· καθάπερ εἰ καὶ φλογὶ μικρᾷ πλῆθος ἐπισωρεύσαις ξύλων, ἢ καὶ χωρὶς πλήθους ἐπιτιθείης χλωρὰ καὶ ὑγρά.
english_sentence_A: Common to all the aforesaid is that the innate heat of the stomach is overcome by the foods, being unable to overcome or master or work them up properly; just as if you were to heap a great quantity of wood upon a small flame, or even without any great quantity were to put on green and moist wood.

greek_sentence: ἐγκοιμηθῆναι γὰρ χρὴ ὥσπερ νύκτα ἀγαγόντα μετὰ τὸ δεῖπνον, τοῦ μὲν χειμῶνος ἀριγέως, τοῦ δὲ θέρεος ἀθαλπέως· ἢν δὲ καθεύδειν μὴ δύνανται, βραδεῖαν συχνὴν περίοδον πλανηθέντα μὴ στασίμως, δειπνῆσαι μηδὲν ἢ ὀλίγα καὶ μὴ βλαβερὰ, ἔτι δὲ ἔλασσον πιεῖν καὶ μὴ ὑδαρές.
english_sentence_A: For one must sleep after dinner as though passing the night, in winter without being chilled, in summer without being overheated; but if they cannot sleep, having wandered about on a slow, lengthy circuit without standing still, they should dine on nothing, or on a little and nothing harmful, and further drink less, and not watery (wine).
english_sentence_B: For one should sleep after dinner, as though passing a night, in winter without being chilled, in summer without being overheated; but if they cannot sleep, after wandering about on a slow, long circuit, not in a standing manner, they should take no dinner, or a little and nothing harmful, and further drink less, and not watery."

greek_sentence: ἔτι δὲ μᾶλλον ἂν πονήσειεν ὁ τοιοῦτος, εἰ τρὶς σιτέοιτο τῆς ἡμέρας ἐς κόρον, ἔτι δὲ μᾶλλον, εἰ πλεονάκις· καίτοιγε [557] πολλοί εἰσιν, οἳ εὐφόρως φέρουσι τρὶς σιτεόμενοι τῆς ἡμέρης εἰς πλῆθος, οἳ ἂν οὕτως ἐθισθῶσιν.
english_sentence_A: Still more would such a person suffer if he were to take food three times a day to satiety, and still more if more often; and yet [557] there are many who bear it easily, taking food three times a day in quantity—those who have been accustomed to it in this way.
english_sentence_B: "And such a person would suffer still more if he were to eat three times a day to satiety, and still more if more often; and yet [557] there are many who bear it easily to eat three times a day in abundance, if they have become so accustomed." It was not necessary for these things to be said now, for his purpose was to teach that sudden changes of habits harm us, not how such harms ought to be treated. But since he saw fit to do this too, let us also follow what he wrote.

greek_sentence: Οὐκ ἦν ἀναγκαῖον εἰρῆσθαι νῦν ταῦτα, προὔκειτο γὰρ αὐτῷ διδάξαι τὰς ἐξαπιναίας μεταβολὰς τῶν ἐθῶν βλάπτειν ἡμᾶς, οὐχ ὅπως χρὴ τὰς τοιαύτας βλάβας ἐκθεραπεύειν· ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ τοῦτο ἔδοξεν αὐτῷ πρᾶξαι, καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀκολουθήσωμεν οἷς ἔγραψε, μάλιστα μὲν ἐπὶ πλέον κοιμηθῆναι κελεύων, εἰ δὲ καθεύδειν μὴ δύναιντο περιπατῆσαι σχολαίως συχνὴν περίοδον, ὡς μὲν οἱ πλεῖστοι τῶν ἐξηγουμένων λέγουσι, μετὰ τὸ δεῖπνον, ὡς δὲ ἡ διάνοια τῶν εἰρημένων βούλεται, μετὰ τὸ ἄριστον· τὸ γὰρ ὥσπερ νύκτα ἀγαγόντα περὶ τῶν ἡμερινῶν ὕπνων, οὐ τῶν ἐν τῇ νυκτὶ προσήκει λέγεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: It was not necessary for these things to be said now, for his purpose was to teach that sudden changes of habits harm us, not how one ought to treat such harms thoroughly; but since he decided to do this too, let us also follow what he wrote, where he bids them above all to sleep longer, and, if they are not able to sleep, to walk at leisure over a long circuit—after dinner, as most of the commentators say, but, as the sense of what has been said requires, after the midday meal; for the phrase "as if passing the night" is properly said of daytime sleeps, not of those during the night.
english_sentence_B: He bids them above all to sleep for a longer time, and, if they cannot sleep, to walk slowly a long circuit: after the dinner, as most of the commentators say, but after the midday meal, as the sense of what is said requires. For the phrase 'as though having passed a night' is properly said of sleep by day, not of sleep at night.

lsj_entry_text: ἕτερος, α, ον, only Att. - Ion. with ἕ-, Dor. ἅτερος [α] IG 4.914.9 (Epid.), etc. (and Att. in crasis, v.infr.), Aeol. ἄτερος Alc. 41.5 , etc.:— but ἅτερος [α], Att. crasis for ὁ ἅτερος, Com.Adesp. 14.23 D. , al., Ion. οὕτερος (fr. ὁ ἕτ-) Hdt. 1.34 , etc., Dor. ὥτερος Theoc. 7.36 ; neut. θάτερον A. Ph. 597 , etc., Ion. τοὐτέρου Semon. 7.113 , Dor. θατέρω Ti.Locr. 94a , θωτέρω Epich. 71 (dub. l.); dat. θατέρῳ A. Pr. 778 ; fem. nom. ἡτέρα IG 22.1498.76 , 1615.14 , 87 (iv B.C.), S. OC 497 , Ar. Art. exc. in Poets ; freq. of natural pairs, σκαιῇ (sc. χειρὶ) ἔγχος ἔχων, ἑτέρηφι δὲ λάζετο πέτρον Il. 16.734 ; τῇ ἑτέρῃ μὲν . . τῇ δ' ἑτέρῃ . . 14.272 , cf. X. greek_sentence: δυοῖν οὖν θάτερον ἢ ἐπανορθωτέον ἐστὶν ὡς ἡμαρτημένην μὲν τοιαύτην [558] γραφὴν καὶ οὕτω γραπτέον· ἐγκοιμηθῆναι γὰρ χρὴ ὥσπερ νύκτα ἀγαγόντα, μετὰ τὸ ἄριστον, τοῦ μὲν χειμῶνος ἀριγέως, τοῦ δὲ θέρεος ἀθαλπέως· ἢ εἴπερ φυλάττοιμεν τὴν μετὰ τὸ δεῖπνον, οὕτως ἀκουστέον τῆς λέξεως· ἐγκοιμηθῆναι γὰρ χρὴ ὥσπερ μετὰ τὸ δεῖπνον ἐκοιμᾶτο πρόσθεν, οὕτω νῦν μετὰ τὸ ἄριστον ὥσπερ νύκτα ἀγαγόντα.
english_sentence_A: So one of two things: either such a reading must be corrected as faulty and written thus: "for one must sleep, as though passing the night, after the luncheon, in winter without being chilled, in summer without being overheated"; or, if we keep the reading "after the dinner", the wording must be understood thus: "for one must sleep—just as previously he used to sleep after the dinner, so now after the luncheon—as though passing the night." As for his bidding him dine either on nothing at all or on few and light things, the reasoning is evident: he wants the stomach to rest and to recover from the fatigue which it suffered when it was weighed down because the man had taken luncheon contrary to his custom.
english_sentence_B: One of two things, then: either such a reading must be corrected as erroneous, and it must be written thus: 'for he should sleep, as though passing a night, after the midday meal, in winter without being chilled, in summer without being overheated'; or, if we retain the reading 'after the evening meal', [558] the phrase must be understood thus: 'for he should sleep just as he used to sleep previously after the evening meal, so now after the midday meal, as though passing a night.' As for his bidding him take either no evening meal at all or a small and light one, the reasoning is evident: for he wishes the stomach to rest and to recover from the fatigue it was suffering, weighed down as it was because the man took a midday meal contrary to his habit.

english_sentence_A: Consistent with this too is drinking less, yet not watery drink: for one must guard against sloshing and moisture and cooling when the stomach has been weighed down by the quantity of food; and the drink that is given should itself not be watery, but such as thoroughly warms and strengthens the stomach.

english_sentence_A: And most of those who have gone without the morning meal are unable to eat up their dinner; and when they have dined they weigh down the belly and sleep badly, much more than if they had also taken the morning meal beforehand.
english_sentence_B: "And most of those who have gone without the midday meal are unable to eat up their dinner; and when they have dined they are heavy in the belly and rest badly in bed much more than if they had taken the midday meal beforehand as well." Those who are bitter-bilious by nature, when they remain without the midday meal contrary to their custom, turn away from food, because their stomach has been harmed.

english_sentence_B: Those of them who force themselves and take it are weighed down, and for this reason they rest badly in bed, as he himself said; this means the same as their continuing in a bad state in bed.

greek_sentence: [561] Ὁκότ᾿ οὖν ταῦτα τοιαῦτα γίγνεται τοῖσιν ὑγιαίνουσιν ἕνεκεν ἡμίσεος ἡμέρης διαίτης μεταβολῆς παρὰ τὸ ἔθος οὔτι προσθεῖναι λυσιτελέειν φαίνεται οὔτε ἀφελέειν.
english_sentence_A: [561] When, therefore, these things turn out in this way for the healthy on account of a change of regimen for half a day contrary to custom, it appears advantageous neither to add nor to take away.
english_sentence_B: [561] When, therefore, such effects as these come about in the healthy on account of a change of regimen for half a day contrary to custom, it appears profitable neither to add anything nor to take anything away.

greek_sentence: ἐφεξῆς δὲ πάλιν ἐπὶ τὴν διήγησιν τῶν συμβαινόντων τοῖς ὑγιαίνουσιν ἐπανέρχεται κατὰ τὴν ἐχομένην ῥῆσιν ἔχουσαν οὕτως· Εἰ τοίνυν οὗτος ὁ παρὰ τὸ ἔθος μονοσιτήσας, ὅλην τὴν ἡμέρην κενεαγγήσας, δειπνήσειεν ὁκόσον εἴθιστο εἰκὸς αὐτὸν, [562] εἰ τότε ἀνάριστος ἐὼν ἐπόνεε καὶ ἠῤῥώστει, δειπνήσας δὲ τότε βαρὺς ἦν, πολὺ μᾶλλον βαρύνεσθαι· εἰ δέ γε ἔτι πλείονα χρόνον κενεαγγήσας ἐξαπίνης μεταδειπνήσειεν, ἔτι μᾶλλον ἂν βαρύνοιτο.
english_sentence_A: Next he returns again to the narration of what happens to healthy people, in the following passage, which runs thus: "If, then, this man who contrary to his habit took one meal, having kept his vessels empty for the whole day, should dine as much as he was accustomed, it is likely that he, [562] if at that time, being without his midday meal, he suffered and was weak, and having dined at that time was heavy, would be weighed down much more; and if, having kept his vessels empty for a still longer time, he should suddenly dine afterwards, he would be weighed down still more." What he says is of this sort.
english_sentence_B: Next, in the following passage, he again returns to the account of what happens to the healthy. It runs thus: "If, then, this man who contrary to custom has taken only a single meal, having had his vessels empty the whole day, should dine on as much as he was accustomed to, it is likely that, [562] if at that time, being without his midday meal, he suffered and was weak, and having dined he was then heavy, he would be weighed down much more; and if, having had his vessels empty for a still longer time, he should suddenly take a late dinner, he would be weighed down still more." What he says is this.

lsj_entry_text: μικρός and σμικρός, ά, όν, Dor. , Ion. μικκός (q.v.): σμικρός is corroborated by metre in Il. 17.757 , Hes. Op. 361 , and might be restored in Il. 5.801 , Od. 3.296 (μικρός codd.); it is prob. the only form in Hdt. ( μικρός Hdt. 2.74 codd.): freq. in Lyr. and prob. always in Trag. (exc. where metre requires μικρός, as S. Aj. 161 (anap., Comp. )); most freq. in Pl. ; but in Th. , also Ar. and other Com., μικρός prevails, σμικρός being found Th. 4.13 , 7.75 , 8.81 , Ar. Ach. 523 , V. 5 ; Att. Inscrr. have σμικρός IG 12.313.111 , al., μικρός ib. 369.10 , al.:—small, little, in Size, μ. ἔην δέμας Il. 5.801 ; μ. λίθος Od. 3.296 ; κίρκον, ὅ τε σμικρῇσι φόνον φέρει ὀρνίθεσσιν Il. 17.757 ; σμ. ἄστεα Hdt. 1.5 ; μεγάθεϊ σμικροί Id. 2.74 : with Dims., μ. πολίχνιον, γῄδιον, παιδάρια, Isoc. 5.145 , X. Cyr. 8.3.38 , Ages. 1.21 : as a Com. exaggeration, δικαστηρίδιον μ. πάνυ Ar. V. 803 ; σκαλαθυρμάτι' ἄττα μ. Id. Nu. 630 , etc.: c. inf., μικροὶ δ' ὁρᾶν Id. Pax 821 : as a term of reproach, Κλειγενὴς ὁ μικρός Id. Ra. 709 , cf. Pl. Prt. 323d , Arist. EN 1123b7 , Alex. 98.7 ; Ἀμύντας ὁ μ. Arist. Pol. 1311b3 ; οἱ ἐν μικρῷ μεγάλοι short but stoutly built, Philostr. Gym. 36 ; ὁ μ. δάκτυλος SIG 1172.4 (Lebena). in Quantity, σμικρὸν ἐπὶ σμικρῷ καταθεῖναι Hes. Op. 361 ; μέλιτος μικρόν Ar. V. 878 ; μ. ὄψον, ἀργυρίδιον, X. Mem. 3.14.1 , Ar. Pl. 240 , cf. Antiph. 44 . in Amount or Importance, petty, trivial, slight, σμ. πρόφασις Thgn. 323 ; ἔπος, ἔγκλημα, ῥοπή, etc., S. OC 443 , Tr. 361 , OT 961 , etc.; ἐκ σμικροῦ λόγου on some slight pretext, Id. OC 620 ; ἐν σμικρῷ λόγῳ παρῆκεν as of small account, ib. 569 ; αἰτίας μικρᾶς πέρι E. Andr. 387 , etc.; οὐδὲ μικρόν, = οὐδὲ γρῦ , D. 19.37 ; of persons, of small account, opp. μέγας, σμ. ἐν σμικροῖς, μέγας ἐν μεγάλοις Pi. P. 3.107 ; ἄριστ' ἂν καὶ μέγας ὀρθοῖθ' ὑπὸ μικροτέρων S. Aj. 161 (anap.), etc.; σμ. τίθησί με Id. OC 958 ; βίος ὁ μ., = μέτριος , E. Fr. 504 ; τίνος σμικροτάτου μεταβαλόντος, σμικρότατος τὴν δύναμιν, Pl. R. 473b ; of the mind, οὐ σμικρὸν φρονεῖ S. Aj. 1120 ; of style, mean, [ Φίλιστοσ] μικρὸς ταῖς ἐκφράσεσιν D.H. Vett.Cens. 3.2 ; of festivals, of lesser importance, Ἁλίεια τὰ μεγάλα καὶ τὰ μ. SIG 1067.14 (Cedreae). of Time, short, Pi. O. 12.12 , Ar. Pl. 126 , etc.; εἰς μ. χρόνον Pl. R. 498d ; ἐν μικρῷ (sc. χρόνῳ) shortly, X. Cyn. 5.32 , Eq. 8.7 ; πρὸ μικροῦ Poll. 1.72 ; ἔτι μικρὸν καὶ καταλιθοβολήσουσί με LXX Ex. 17.4 . of Age, young, Ostr.Bodl. i237 (ii B.C.), etc. Adverbial usages, regul. Adv. σμικρῶς, but little, Pl. Criti. 107d ; μικρῶς by a little, prob. in Archim. Stom. 1 : Sup. σμικρότατα X. Mem. 3.11.12 . σμικροῦ or μικροῦ within a little, almost, Id. Cyr. 1.4.8 , D. 18.151 , etc.; in full, μικροῦ δεῖν, v. δεῖ 11 , δέω (B) 1 ; μικροῦ τινος ἀπελείφθη τοῦ μή . . Ach.Tat. 7.13 ; but μικροῦ πρίασθαι for a little, cheap, X. Mem. 2.10.4 . σμικρῷ by a little, with Comp. , Pl. Plt. 262c , etc.; also σμικρῷ πρόσθεν a little before, Id. Lg. 719b , etc.; μικρῷ ἄνωθεν D. 44.6 . μικρόν a little, σμικρὸν ὑπολείπεσθαι, σμ. τι παρακλίνειν, X. An. 5.4.22 , Pl. Cra. 410a ; of Time, X. An. 3.1.11 , etc.; repeated, μικρὸν μικρόν Antiph. 10 : pl., of Degree, σμικρὰ γεωμετρίας ἔμπειροι Pl. R. 527a , etc.; σμίκρ' ἄττα διατρίψαντες Id. Prt. 316a ; μικρὰ διακινήσω σε περὶ τοῦ πράγματος Sosip. 1.22 ; περιπάτησον μικρὰ μετ' ἐμοῦ Men. Sam. 243 , cf. Plu. Luc. 31 . with Preps., ἐπὶ σμικρόν but a little, S. El. 414 , Antipho 6.18 , Hdt. 4.129 . κατὰ μικρόν into small pieces, X. An. 7.3.22 ; so κατὰ μικρὰ γενομένης τῆς δυνάμεως ib. 5.6.32 ; also, little by little, κατὰ μικρὸν ἀεί Ar. V. 702 , cf. Nu. 741 ; opp. συλλήβδην, Pl. R. 344a ; καὶ κατὰ σμ. or μ. ever so little, Id. Sph. 241c , Isoc. 3.10 , D. 2.22 . παρὰ μικρόν within a little, παρὰ μ. ἐλθεῖν c. inf., to be within an ace of doing, E. Heracl. 295 (anap.), cf. Isoc. 7.6 , etc.; παρὰ μ. ἦλθον ἀποθανεῖν Id. 17.42 ; τὸ παρὰ μ. ὥσπερ οὐδὲν ἀπέχειν δοκεῖ Arist. Ph. 197a30 ; but τὸ παρὰ μ. σῴζεσθαι to be only just saved, Id. Rh. 1371b11 , cf. Simp. in Ph. 344.10 ; gradual, imperceptible change, Arist. Pol. 1303a20 ; οὐδὲ παρὰ μ. ἦν κρεῖττον c. inf., Plb. 12.20.7 ; [ ἡ τύχη] παρὰ μ. εἰς ἑκάτερα ποιεῖ μεγάλας ῥοπάς Id. 15.6.8 , cf. Isoc. 4.59 ; but also παρὰ μ. ποιεῖσθαι, ἡγεῖσθαι, to think little of . . , D. 61.51 , Isoc. 5.79 . μετὰ μικρόν a little after, Ev.Matt. 26.73 . besides regul. Comp. and Sup. μικρότερος, -ότατος ( Ar. Eq. 789 , D. Prooem. 48 , etc.), there are the irreg. ἐλάσσων, ἐλάχιστος, from ἐλαχύς, and μείων, μεῖστος, also μειότερος; v. μείων. [ι by nature; ι only in late Poetry, Epigr. ap. Phleg. Fr. 36.17 J. ] (Perh. cf. Lat. mīca, mīcidus, OHG. smāhi, ONorse smár 'little'.)
greek_sentence: εἰ ὁ παρὰ τὸ ἔθος ἀναρίστητος μείνας, εἶτα δειπνήσας τῶν εἰθισμένων ἐλάττω τῆς νυκτὸς ἐβαρύνθη, πολὺ μειζόνως βαρυνθήσεται ὁ πλείω ἢ ὅσα εἴθιστο δειπνήσας· ὁ δ᾿ ἐπὶ πλείονα χρόνον κενεαγγήσας, εἰ ἐξαπίνης μεταδειπνήσειεν, ἔτι μᾶλλον ἂν βαρυνθείη.
english_sentence_A: If the man who remained without his midday meal contrary to his habit, and then dined on less than his accustomed amount, was weighed down during the night, he who dines on more than he was accustomed to will be weighed down much more greatly; and he who has kept his vessels empty for a longer time, if he should suddenly dine afterwards, would be weighed down still more.
english_sentence_B: If the man who remained without his midday meal contrary to custom, and then dined on less than his accustomed amounts, was weighed down during the night, the man who dined on more than he was accustomed to will be weighed down much more greatly; and the man who has had his vessels empty for a longer time, if he should suddenly take a late dinner, would be weighed down still more.

english_sentence_A: For of those who remain without their midday meal contrary to their habit, some extend the abstinence from food for a shorter time, others for a longer; these latter, then, he says, will be weighed down still more.

greek_sentence: καὶ τὸ δεῖπνον συχνῷ ἔλασσον ποιήσασθαι ἢ ὅσον εἴθιστο καὶ μὴ ξηρὸν, ἀλλὰ τοῦ πλαδαρωτέρου τρόπου· καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα πιεῖν μὴ ὑδαρὲς μήτε ἔλασσον ἢ κατὰ λόγον τοῦ βρώματος· καὶ τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ ὀλίγα ἀριστῆσαι, ὡς ἐκ προσαγωγῆς ἀφίκηται εἰς τὸ ἔθος.
english_sentence_A: And to make the evening meal considerably smaller than what he was accustomed to, and not dry, but of the moister kind; and after this to drink what is not watery nor less than in proportion to the food; and on the following day to take a small morning meal, so that he may arrive at his custom by gradual approach.
english_sentence_B: And to make his dinner considerably smaller than he was accustomed to, and not dry, but of the moister kind; and after this to drink, not watery wine, nor less than is in proportion to the food; and on the following day to take a small midday meal, so that he may come back to his habit by gradual approach.

greek_sentence: καίτοι τούτου ἐναντιώτατον οἱ πολλοὶ ποιοῦσι· κωλυθέντες γὰρ ὑπό τινος ἀσχολίας ἀριστῆσαι κατὰ τὸ δεῖπνον ἀξιοῦσιν ἀπολαμβάνειν καὶ τὴν παραλελειμμένην ἐπὶ τοῦ ἀρίστου τροφὴν, οὐκ εἰδότες ὅτι δεῖται μὲν ὄντως τὸ σῶμα τῆς παραλελειμμένης τροφῆς, οὐ δύναται δὲ αὐτὴν ἡ γαστὴρ κατεργάσασθαι, βεβλαμμένη διὰ τὴν [564] μακροτέραν ἀσιτίαν.
english_sentence_A: And yet most people do the very opposite of this: for when they have been prevented by some business from taking the morning meal, they think it right at dinner to recover also the nourishment omitted at the morning meal, not knowing that the body does indeed need the omitted nourishment, but that the stomach cannot work it up, having been harmed by the [564] longer abstinence from food.
english_sentence_B: And yet most people do the very opposite of this: for when they have been prevented by some occupation from taking their midday meal, they think fit at dinner to make up also the food that was omitted at the midday meal, not knowing that, although the body does truly need the omitted food, the stomach cannot work it up, having been harmed by the [564] longer abstinence from food.

lsj_entry_text: ὑγρός, ά, όν: Comp. ὑγρότερος Pl. Tht. 162b , etc.: Sup. -ότατος X. greek_sentence: ἀλλ᾿ ὅ γε Ἱπποκράτης ὥσπερ ἐλάττονα κελεύει δοθῆναι τὴν τροφὴν, οὕτως καὶ ὑγροτέραν· αὕτη γὰρ οἰκεῖον ἴαμα τῇ τε γαστρὶ καὶ παντὶ τῷ σώματι γενήσεται κατεξηρασμένοις.
english_sentence_A: But Hippocrates, just as he orders the nourishment to be given in smaller quantity, so also orders it to be moister; for this will be a proper remedy both for the stomach and for the whole body, which have been dried out.
english_sentence_B: But Hippocrates, just as he orders the food to be given in smaller quantity, so also orders it moister; for this will be a proper remedy both for the stomach and for the whole body, since they have been dried out.

english_sentence_A: For the watery will relax the tone of the stomach, while the lesser quantity is unsuitable for a stomach that has been dried out.
english_sentence_B: For the watery will slacken the tone of the stomach, and the lesser amount is unsuitable for a stomach that has been dried out.
