greek_sentence: εὔδηλον δ᾿ ὅτι τῶν ἔξωθέν εἰσι συμβεβηκότων αἱ τοιαῦται διαφοραί· καθόσον γὰρ ἐν τῷ χρόνῳ δριμύτεροί τε καὶ θερμότεροι γίγνονται, μεταβάλλοντες ἅμα τούτοις καὶ χρόαν καὶ σύστασιν καὶ ὀσμὴν, [629] κατὰ τοσοῦτον ὁ χρόνος διαφοράν τινα ἐν τοῖς οἴνοις ἐργάζεσθαι δοκεῖ· εἰ δέ γε καὶ μηδὲν τούτων ὑπήλλαττεν, οὐδ᾿ ἂν ἐλέγετο πρός τινων παλαιὸς ὁ οἶνος ἢ νέος· ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ νῦν οὕτω λέγουσιν, ὡς τῶν ἐτῶν αὐτοῦ δεόμενοι κατὰ πρῶτον λόγον, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς ἄμα τοῖς ἔτεσιν ἐνδεικνύμενοι τὴν δύναμιν· οὐ γὰρ διὰ τὸν χρόνον οἱ οἶνοι τὰς ὠφελείας καὶ βλάβας ἔχουσιν, ἀλλ᾿ ἐκ τῆς τῶν οἰκείων διαφορῶν τούτων᾿ ὑπαλλαγῆς.
english_sentence_A: It is quite clear that differences of this kind belong to the things that are accidents from outside; for insofar as in the course of time wines become more pungent and hotter, changing along with these also their colour, consistency and smell, [629] to that extent time seems to produce a certain difference in wines; but if it altered none of these things, wine would not be called by anyone old or new; yet even now people do not speak in this way as though they required its years in the primary sense, but as indicating its power together with the years; for it is not on account of time that wines have their benefits and harms, but from the alteration of these proper differences of theirs.
english_sentence_B: For inasmuch as in the course of time wines become sharper and hotter, changing together with these qualities their colour, consistency and smell as well, [629] to that extent time seems to produce some difference in wines. But if it altered none of these things, the wine would not be called old or new by anyone.

greek_sentence: κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς οὖν τοῦ χρόνου μνημονεύομεν ἐν ταῖς τῶν οἴνων διαφοραῖς, οὐ κυρίως οὐδὲ πρώτως.
english_sentence_A: Accidentally, therefore, do we mention time among the differences of wines, not in the strict sense nor primarily.
english_sentence_B: For it is not on account of time that wines have their benefits and harms, but from the alteration of these proper differences of theirs. It is therefore accidentally that we mention time among the differences of wines, not properly, nor primarily.

greek_sentence: καὶ αὐτῶν μέντοι τῶν οἰκείων ἐν αὐτοῖς διαφορῶν, αἱ μὲν εἰς ὠφέλειάν τε καὶ βλάβην ἀναφέρονται κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον λόγον, αἱ δὲ οὐ κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον, ἀλλὰ κατὰ συμβεβηκός· γλυκύτης μὲν καὶ αὐστηρότης κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον λόγον, οὕτω δὲ καὶ ἡ ἰσχὺς καὶ ἀσθένεια καὶ λεπτότης καὶ πάχος· αἱ δὲ κατὰ τὴν χρόαν τε καὶ ὀσμὴν οὐ πρώτως, ἀλλὰ κατὰ συμβεβηκός· ἐπεὶ τῶν οἴνων οἱ μὲν ὑδατώδεις τέ εἰσι καὶ λευκοὶ καὶ κιῤῥοὶ καὶ μέλανες, οἱ δὲ ὑδατώδεις καὶ ἄοδμοι [630] ὥσπερ ὕδωρ, ἢ εὐώδεις ὅσπερ ὥρωμα καὶ μύρον.
english_sentence_A: And indeed, of the proper differences in them themselves, some are referred to benefit and harm in their own right, others not in their own right but accidentally: sweetness and austerity in their own right, and likewise also strength and weakness and thinness and thickness; whereas the differences in colour and odour are not primary but accidental, since among wines some are watery-coloured and white and tawny and dark, while others are watery and odourless [630] like water, or fragrant like an aromatic (ὥρωμα) and perfume.
english_sentence_B: And indeed, of the differences proper to wines themselves, some are referred to benefit and harm according to their own proper account, others not according to their own account but incidentally. english_sentence_A: The sweet wine is less heavy on the head than the vinous one and less apt to affect the phrenes, and somewhat more purgative than the other by way of the intestine; but it is productive of enlarged viscera, of the spleen and of the liver.

english_sentence_A: It is therefore not suitable either for the bitter-bilious; for indeed it is thirst-producing for such people; moreover it is also flatulent for the upper bowel, though not hostile to the lower bowel itself in proportion to the flatulence, and yet [631] the flatulence arising from sweet wine is not very easily passed, but lingers about the hypochondria.
english_sentence_B: It is therefore not suitable for the bitter-bilious either; for indeed it causes thirst in such people at least. Moreover, it is also productive of flatus in the upper intestine, yet it is not hostile to the lower intestine itself, as might be expected in proportion to the flatus; although [631] the flatus from sweet wine is not very easily passed, but lingers about the hypochondria.

greek_sentence: οὐκ ἐπιτήδειος οὖν οὐδὲ τοῖσι πικροχόλοισι· καὶ γὰρ οὖν διψώδης τοῖσί γε τοιουτέοισίν ἐστιν· ἀτὰρ καὶ φυσώδης ἐντέρου τοῦ ἄνω, οὐ μὴν πολέμιός γε αὐτῷ τῷ κάτω ἐντέρῳ ὡς κατὰ λόγον τῆς φύσης, καίτοι γε [631] οὐ πάνυ πορίμη ἐστὶν ἡ ἀπὸ τοῦ γλυκέος οἴνου φύση, ἀλλ᾿ ἐγχρονίζει περὶ ὑποχόνδρια.
english_sentence_A: It is therefore not suitable either for the bitter-bilious; for indeed it is thirst-producing for such people; moreover it is also flatulent for the upper bowel, though not hostile to the lower bowel itself in proportion to the flatulence, and yet [631] the flatulence arising from sweet wine is not very easily passed, but lingers about the hypochondria.
english_sentence_B: It is therefore not suitable for the bitter-bilious either; for indeed it causes thirst in such people at least. Moreover, it is also productive of flatus in the upper intestine, yet it is not hostile to the lower intestine itself, as might be expected in proportion to the flatus; although [631] the flatus from sweet wine is not very easily passed, but lingers about the hypochondria.

english_sentence_A: Wine is called sweet in respect of its gustatory quality, in respect of which it is also austere and pungent—to leave aside the watery wine, which has not entirely fallen away from being astringent, even if it has the quality of astringency altogether slackened.
english_sentence_B: Wine is called sweet according to the gustatory quality, the same quality according to which a wine is also austere and acrid, to pass over the watery wine, which has not entirely lost the property of astringing, even if it has the quality of astringency altogether relaxed.

english_sentence_A: People call watery the wine that resembles water in both colour and consistency; for it appears transparent like water, and bright and clear and thin in consistency; and such a wine is at once also similar to water in its power, affecting neither a weak head nor weak nerves, because it does not heat perceptibly either.
english_sentence_B: Watery wine is the name people give to the wine that resembles water both in colour and in consistency; for it appears transparent like water, and bright and pure, and thin in consistency. And it follows directly that such a wine is also close to water in its power, affecting neither a weak head nor weak nerves, because it does not even heat perceptibly.

english_sentence_A: At any rate the Theraean and the Scybelite are sweet wines to an outstanding degree, both being thick and black; sweet too are those produced in Maeonia, the Therinos and the Karyinos, which differ from those mentioned in thickness and blackness to the same degree as they fall short of them in sweetness; and moreover what is called hepsēma and siraion, which is produced from must being boiled down, in proportion as it is rendered sweeter than wine, appears to that same extent both blacker in colour and thicker in consistency.

english_sentence_A: It has been shown, then, also in the fourth book On the Powers of Simple Drugs that every sweet humour comes into being through heat, not however heat that is immoderate and vehement, as the acrid humour does in things that heat vehemently, for acridity is inseparable from these; but in actual use sweet wine is seen to heat moderately, and its thirst-provoking character belongs to it both on account of its heat and on account of its thickness.
english_sentence_B: Now it has been shown in the fourth book On the Power of Simple Drugs that every sweet flavour comes about through heat, though not heat that is immoderate and violent, as the pungent flavour does in things that heat violently, for pungency is inseparable from these. Rather, in use sweet wine appears to heat moderately, and its thirst-producing character belongs to it on account of both its heat and its thickness.

greek_sentence: οὕτως γοῦν καὶ τὸ γλεῦκος εἰς ὅσον ὁμιλήσει τῷ πυρὶ πλέονι χρόνῳ, [633] παχύτερόν τε καὶ μελάντερον καὶ γλυκύτερον γίνεται· τό γε μὴν ὑπεροπτηθὲν εἰς πικρότητα μεταβάλλει, καθάπερ καὶ τὸ μέλι, καίτοι πάντων γλυκύτατον ὂν, ἀλλ᾿ ὅμως καὶ τοῦτο πικρότητα προσλαμβάνει κατὰ τὴν ἐπὶ πλεῖστον ἕψησιν.
english_sentence_A: Thus, at any rate, must too, to the extent that it has contact with the fire for a longer time, [633] becomes thicker, blacker and sweeter; what has been over-cooked, however, changes into bitterness, just as honey too, although it is the sweetest of all things, nevertheless also takes on bitterness upon very prolonged boiling.
english_sentence_B: Thus, at any rate, must too, the longer it is in contact with the fire, [633] becomes thicker, darker and sweeter; but when it has been over-cooked it changes into bitterness, just as honey does too: although it is the sweetest of all things, nevertheless it also takes on bitterness when boiled for a very long time.

english_sentence_A: Since, then, sweet wine heats the viscus, and is also, as has been said, thick in consistency, its particular powers, which it displays when drunk, follow upon the secondary qualities; for colour, in its own right, has no power for benefit or harm.

lsj_entry_text: βραδυ-πόρος, ον, slow-passing, of food, Hp. Acut. 62 , Ruf. ap. Orib. 5.3.4 , Philagr.ib. 5.19.4 ; of humours, Gal. 7.341 : generally, slow, ὅρασις Plu. 2.626a ; β. πέλαγος slow to pass, ib. 941b .
greek_sentence: εἰς ὅσον οὖν παχύς τ᾿ ἐστὶ κατὰ σύστασιν ὁ τοιοῦτος οἶνος, τοσοῦτον καὶ βραδύπορος, ὥστ᾿ οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἐκφράξει τι τῶν ἐμπεφραγμένων μορίων, ἀλλὰ καὶ προσεμφράξει· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο βλαβερώτατος ἥπατι πάσχοντι, καὶ μάλισθ᾿, ὅταν ἤτοι φλεγμονή τις ἢ σκίῤῥος ᾖ [634] κατὰ τοῦτο· μετριωτέραν δ᾿ ἐργάζεται τὴν βλάβην, ὅταν ὑπὸ παχέων χυμῶν ἐμφράττηται τὸ σπλάγχνον ἢ δι᾿ ἀτονίαν πάσχῃ, καθάπερ ἐν τοῖς ἰδίως ἡπατικοῖς ὀνομαζομένοις πάθεσιν.
english_sentence_A: To the extent, then, that such a wine is thick in consistency, to that extent it is also slow in passing, so that not only will it not clear any of the parts that have become obstructed, but it will even add further obstruction; and for this reason it is most harmful to a liver that is affected, and especially whenever there is either some inflammation or a scirrhus [634] in it; but it produces a more moderate harm whenever the viscus is obstructed by thick humours or is affected through atony, as in the affections properly called hepatic.
english_sentence_B: To the extent, then, that such a wine is thick in consistency, to that same extent it is also slow in passage, so that not only will it not clear any of the obstructed parts, but it will even add to the obstruction. For this reason it is most harmful to a liver that is affected, and especially when there is either some inflammation or a scirrhus [634] in it.

english_sentence_A: To the extent, then, that such a wine is thick in consistency, to that extent it is also slow in passing, so that not only will it not clear any of the parts that have become obstructed, but it will even add further obstruction; and for this reason it is most harmful to a liver that is affected, and especially whenever there is either some inflammation or a scirrhus [634] in it; but it produces a more moderate harm whenever the viscus is obstructed by thick humours or is affected through atony, as in the affections properly called hepatic.
english_sentence_B: To the extent, then, that such a wine is thick in consistency, to that same extent it is also slow in passage, so that not only will it not clear any of the obstructed parts, but it will even add to the obstruction. For this reason it is most harmful to a liver that is affected, and especially when there is either some inflammation or a scirrhus [634] in it.

english_sentence_A: For, having been distributed through many veins and worked up beforehand in them, it falls into the wide spaces of the bronchi, first into those of the smaller ones, and from those it is taken up into the larger, carrying up along with itself also the thick humours, than which it is not only warmer but also thinner. And you have learned that the lung is cleared of the thick and viscous humours by coughs; for those humours which are watery and perfectly thin flow around the breath that is sent out in the coughs; for this breath is, as it were, [635] a kind of hand that carries up the thick humours together with itself.
english_sentence_B: For, having been distributed through many veins and worked up beforehand in them, it falls into the cavities of the bronchia, first into those of the smaller ones, and from those it is taken on into the larger, carrying up along with itself the thick humours as well, than which it is not only hotter but also thinner. You have learned that the lung is cleansed of thick and viscous humours by coughs; for those humours that are watery and exactly thin flow around the breath that is sent out in coughing, since this breath is, as it were, [635] a hand that carries the thick humours up along with itself.

english_sentence_B: But such wine has no other good when given to those who are febrile: it will indeed be able to do less harm than the vinous wine that heats strongly, but it has nothing else beneficial beyond what has been said, except that it contributes a little to the passage of the contents of the belly.

greek_sentence: οὐκ ἐπιτήδειόν γε μὴν τὸν γλυκὺν οἶνον οὐδὲ τοῖς πικροχόλοις εἶναί φησι, τουτέστι τοῖς τὴν πικρὰν χολὴν ἀθροίζουσιν, εἴθισται γὰρ τοῖς ἰατροῖς χολὴν μὲν ἁπλῶς ὀνομάζειν τὴν ὠχράν τε καὶ ξανθὴν, τὴν μέλαιναν δὲ χολὴν, ὅλον τοῦτο λέγειν, οὐχ ἁπλῶς χολήν· ἀλλ᾿ αὕτη μὲν ὀξεῖα, πικρὰ δ᾿ ἡ ξανθὴ, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τοὺς πικροχόλους Ἱπποκράτης ὀνομάζει τοὺς πλεονάζουσαν ἔχοντας τὴν τοιαύτην χολήν.
english_sentence_A: He says moreover that sweet wine is not suitable even for the bitter-bilious, that is, for those who accumulate bitter bile; for physicians are accustomed to call the pale and yellow bile simply "bile", but black bile they call by this whole expression, not simply "bile"; and the latter is acid, whereas the yellow is bitter, and for this reason Hippocrates names "bitter-bilious" those who have such bile in excess.
english_sentence_B: Yet he says that sweet wine is not suitable for the bitter-bilious either, that is, for those who accumulate bitter bile. For physicians are accustomed to call 'bile' without qualification the pale and the yellow, but in the case of black bile to say this whole expression, not simply 'bile'.

greek_sentence: οὐ μόνον δ᾿ ὅτι ἡ πολλὴ θερμασία τοὺς τοιούτους χυμοὺς ἐργάζεται πικροὺς, ἀνεπιτήδειός ἐστιν ὁ γλυκὺς οἶνος τοῖς πυρέττουσι, καὶ μάλισθ᾿ ὅταν ὦσι θερμοὶ καὶ ξηροὶ τὴν κρᾶσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ διότι παχεῖς ὄντες οὔτ᾿ ἐπ᾿ οὖρα διεξέρχονται ταχέως οὔτε διαπνέονται ταχέως, ὥστ᾿ οὐ συνάγουσιν ἑαυτοῖς οὐδὲ συνεκκενοῦσι τοὺς χολώδεις χυμούς.
english_sentence_A: And sweet wine is unsuitable for those with fever, and especially when they are hot and dry in temperament, not only because abundant heat makes such humours bitter, but also because, being thick, they neither pass out quickly by way of the urines nor are transpired quickly, so that they do not gather up the bilious humours along with themselves nor evacuate them together with themselves.
english_sentence_B: Sweet wine is unsuitable for those who are feverish, and especially when they are hot and dry in their mixture, not only because great heat makes such juices bitter, but also because, being thick, they neither pass through quickly to the urine nor are quickly dispersed by transpiration, so that they do not draw together with themselves, nor evacuate along with themselves, the bilious humours. These alone, then, have one good: loosening the belly; so that if they do not do this, they do harm in every way.

greek_sentence: ἀναγωγὸς τοῦ πτυέλου μάλιστα πάντων οἴνων ἐστὶν ὁ γλυκὺς, ὅταν σφόδρα μὴ παχὺς ᾖ, καθάπερ γε κᾀπειδὰν μὴ πολὺ ᾖ πρὸς τὸν κιῤῥὸν ἀποκεχωρηκὼς, ὡς ἐκλελύσθαι τὸ πάχος αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν γλυκύτητα.
english_sentence_A: Of all wines the sweet is most apt to bring up sputum, whenever it is not very thick, just as also when it has not departed far toward the tawny, so that its thickness and its sweetness have been dissolved.

greek_sentence: ὁ δὲ μετὰ τὸν οὐκ ἐσχάτως παχὺν οἶνον γλυκὺν, ἐπιτήδειος εἰς τὴν τῶν ἐκ πνεύμονος ἀναγωγὴν ὁ ὑδατώδης οἶνός ἐστι, τήν τε δύναμιν ῥωννὺς καὶ τοὺς χυμοὺς ὑγραίνων τε καὶ τέγγων μετρίως· ὁ δ᾿ αὐτὸς καὶ τοῖς πυρέττουσιν ἀκινδυνότερον δίδοται τῶν ἄλλων οἴνων ἁπάντων.

english_sentence_A: And next after the sweet wine that is not extremely thick, the watery wine is suitable for the bringing-up of the matters from the lung, since it strengthens the faculty and moistens and wets the humours moderately; and the same wine is also given to those with fever with less danger than all the other wines.
english_sentence_B: Next after the sweet wine that is not extremely thick, the watery wine is suitable for the bringing up of what comes from the lung, since it both strengthens the faculty and moderately moistens and softens the humours; the same wine is also given to those in fever with less danger than all the other wines.

greek_sentence: αὐστηρῷ ἐν ταύτῃσι τῇσι νούσοισιν [645] ἐς τάδε ἂν χρήσαιο· εἰ καρηβαρίη μὲν μὴ ἐνείη, μηδὲ φρενῶν ἅψις μηδὲ τὸ πτύελον κωλύοιτο τῆς ἀνόδου, μηδὲ τὸ οὖρον ἴσχοιτο, τὰ διαχωρήματα δὲ πλαδαρώτερα καὶ ξυσματωδέστερα εἴη· ἐν δὴ τοῖσι τοιουτέοισι πρέποι ἂν μάλιστα μεταβάλλειν ἐκ τοῦ λευκοῦ καὶ ὁκόσα τουτέοισιν ἐμφερέα.

greek_sentence: ὁ δὲ κατὰ τὴν Κιλικίαν Ἀναβάτης αὐστηρός τε ἅμα καὶ γλυκύς ἐστιν, ἐξ ἐναντίων ποιοτήτων συγκείμενος· διὸ καὶ μοχθηρὸς ὑπάρχει, μήτ᾿ ἀναδιδόμενος μήθ᾿ ὑπερχόμενος, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ πλέον τε παραμένων τῇ ἄνω γαστρὶ καὶ πνευματῶν αὐτήν.
english_sentence_A: The Anabates in Cilicia is at once both austere and sweet, being compounded of opposite qualities; for which reason it is also a bad wine, being neither distributed nor passing downward, but remaining for too long in the upper belly and filling it with wind.
english_sentence_B: The Anabates of Cilicia, however, is at once both astringent and sweet, being composed of opposite qualities; for this reason it is also bad, being neither distributed nor passing down, but remaining for a longer time in the upper belly and filling it with wind.

english_sentence_A: For these conditions, then, he says that the tawny wine is also fitting, not meaning simply every tawny wine, but the austere tawny wine; for in the case of both one must understand what was said at the beginning of the passage in this way: 'tawny wine and dark, the austere ones, you would use in these diseases for the following purposes.' For the tawny is twofold, just as the dark is too, the one sweet, the other austere; there being also a third in each case, from the intermixture of both qualities.
english_sentence_B: For these conditions, then, he says that tawny wine is also fitting, not meaning simply every tawny wine, but the austere tawny; for in both cases one must understand what was said at the beginning of the passage, thus: 'Tawny wine and dark, the austere ones, you might use in these diseases for the following purposes.' For tawny wine is twofold, as is the dark also: the one sweet, the other austere; and there is also a third kind alongside each, arising from an admixture of both qualities.

greek_sentence: εἰκότως οὖν ἐκώλυσε χρῆσθαι τοῖς αὐστηροῖς οἴνοις, εἴτε κιῤῥοὶ τὴν χρόαν εἴτε μέλανές εἰσιν, ἐν δὲ ταῖς καρηβαρίαις καὶ ταῖς βλάβαις τῶν φρενῶν, τουτέστιν ὅπου ὁ πυρετὸς αὐτῶν ἥψατο· καὶ προσέτι γε κᾀκεῖνα τῶν κατὰ θώρακά τε καὶ πνεύμονα νοσημάτων, ἐν οἷς ἴσχεται τὸ πτύελον, ἀνεπιτηδείους τοὺς τοιούτους οἴνους εἶναί [647] φησι καὶ τῶν οὔρων ἐπεχομένων, διὰ τὸ πάχος δηλονότι καὶ τὴν στύψιν.
english_sentence_A: Reasonably, then, he forbade the use of the astringent wines, whether they are tawny in colour or dark, in cases of heaviness of the head and injuries of the mind, that is, wherever the fever has laid hold of these parts; and in addition he says that such wines are also unsuitable in those diseases of the thorax and lung in which the sputum is held back, [647] and when the urine is retained, evidently on account of their thickness and their astringency.

english_sentence_B: With good reason, then, he forbade the use of austere wines, whether they are tawny in colour or dark, in cases of heaviness of the head and of damage to the mind (φρενῶν), that is, wherever the fever has affected these parts. And further he says [647] that such wines are unsuitable also in those diseases of the thorax and lung in which the sputum is held back, and when the urine is retained, evidently on account of their thickness and their astringency.

greek_sentence: Προξυνιέναι δὲ δεῖ ὅτι τὰ μὲν ἄνω πάντα καὶ τὰ κατὰ τὴν κύστιν ἧσσον βλάψει, ἢν ὑδαρέστερος ᾖ· τὰ δὲ κατ᾿ ἔντερον καὶ μᾶλλον ὀνήσει, ἢν ἀκρητέστερος ᾖ.
english_sentence_A: One must understand beforehand that it will harm all the upper parts and the parts about the bladder less, if it is more watery; but the parts about the intestine it will benefit even more, if it is more unmixed.
english_sentence_B: 'One must understand beforehand that it will harm all the upper parts, and those in the region of the bladder, less if it is more watery; but it will benefit the parts in the intestine more if it is more unmixed.' The more unmixed wine, as he has said, is more suitable for the conditions in the intestine.

lsj_entry_text: στῦψις, εως, ἡ, contraction, astringency, Thphr. Od. 32 , Diph.Siph. ap. Ath. 3.80f , Dsc. 1.39 , Sor. 1.81 , Phylotim. ap. Orib. 4.10.2 , Aret. SA 2.2 ; of food which has a costive effect, Hp. Acut. 10 , cf. Aen.Gaz. Ep. 20 ; contraction of the skin, Sch. Il. 14.216 . in dyeing, steeping of the fabric in an astringent solution, to prepare it for taking the dye, Arist. Col. 794a29 (pl.). in perfumery, thickening of oil with certain drugs to make it retain the scent longer, Dsc. 1.6 (pl.).
greek_sentence: Ὁ ἀκρατέστερος οἶνος, ὡς εἴρηκε, τοῖς κατ᾿ ἔντερον μᾶλλον ἐπιτήδειός ἐστιν· εἰκότως οὖν ὀνίνησιν αὐτὰ τῷ λόγῳ τῆς στύψεως, δι᾿ ἣν καὶ τὸ βοηθεῖν ὅλως εἶχεν· ἀλλὰ ταύτην γε τὴν στύψιν ἐκλύει κεραννύμενος ὑδαρὴς καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἧττον ὀνίνησιν αὐτά.
english_sentence_A: The more unmixed wine, as he has said, is more suitable for the parts about the intestine; reasonably, then, it benefits them by reason of its astringency, through which it also had its capacity to help at all; but when it is mixed watery, it loses this astringency, and for this reason it benefits them less.
english_sentence_B: With good reason, then, it benefits them by reason of its astringency, through which it had its capacity to help at all. But when it is mixed so as to be watery, it dissolves this astringency, and for this reason benefits them less.

greek_sentence: καθάπερ δὲ ταῦτα μᾶλλον ὀνίνησιν τῷ λόγῳ τῆς στύψεως, ὅταν ἀκρατέστερος ᾖ, οὕτω τὰ κατὰ θώρακα καὶ κεφαλὴν μᾶλλον βλάπτει· ταῦτα δ᾿ ἐστὶν ἃ ἐδήλωσεν εἰπὼν, τὰ μὲν ἄνω βλάπτει πάντα.
english_sentence_A: And just as it benefits these parts more by reason of its astringency when it is more unmixed, so it harms the parts about the thorax and the head more; and these are what he indicated when he said, "it harms all the upper parts."
english_sentence_B: And just as it benefits these parts more by reason of its astringency when it is more unmixed, so it harms the parts in the thorax and the head more. These are what he indicated when he said: 'it harms all the upper parts.'

lsj_entry_text: ἔκ-κρισις, εως, ἡ, separation, Arist. Mete. 342a15 , Onos. 9.1 (pl.). secretion, of the animal functions, Arist. PA 689a16 , GA 727a2 ; τῶν ὑγρῶν Eun. Hist. p.263 D. = ἔκκριμα , of excrement, Hp. Aph. 2.15 ; of the menses, Arist. HA 583a2 , etc.
greek_sentence: βλάπτει δὲ καὶ τὰ δεόμενα δι᾿ οὔρων ἐκκαθαίρεσθαι τὰ σώματα· πασῶν γὰρ τῶν ἐκκρίσεων ἐφεκτικός ἐστιν ὁ αὐστηρὸς [648] οἶνος.
english_sentence_A: And it also harms those bodies that need to be purged through the urine; for the austere [648] wine is retentive of all the excretions.
english_sentence_B: It also harms those bodies that need to be cleansed out through the urine; for austere [648] wine is retentive of all excretions.

english_sentence_A: Having said these things about wines, Hippocrates passes straight on to melikraton, having set out nearly all the other points concerning wines, but leaving one unworked-out, which I went through as a side matter: that for those with fever the most suitable wine is the watery one.
english_sentence_B: Having said these things about wines, Hippocrates passes straight on to honey-water (melikraton). He has set out almost everything else concerning wines, but has left one point unworked out, which I went through by way of a side-issue: that for those who are feverish the most suitable wine is the watery one.

greek_sentence: ἔστι δ᾿ οὗτος ὁ λευκὸς μὲν τὴν χρόαν, λεπτὸς δὲ τὴν σύστασιν, ἐπιφανῆ μηδεμίαν ἔχων ποιότητα τῶν τοῖς ἄλλοις οἴνοις ὑπαρχουσῶν, μήτ᾿ αὐστηρότητα, μήτε στρυφνότητα, μήτε γλυκύτητα, μήτε δριμύτητα, μήτ᾿ ὀσμήν· τῷ γὰρ τοιούτῳ καὶ τὰς τοῦ ὕδατος κακίας καὶ τὰς τοῦ οἴνου ἐκπεφευγέναι μόνῳ τῶν πάντων οἴνων ὑπάρχει.
english_sentence_A: This is the wine white in colour, thin in consistency, having no manifest quality of those that belong to the other wines—neither austerity, nor harshness, nor sweetness, nor pungency, nor odour; for it belongs to such a wine alone of all wines to have escaped both the faults of water and those of wine.
english_sentence_B: This is the wine that is white in colour and thin in consistency, and that has no evident quality of those belonging to the other wines: neither austerity, nor acerbity, nor sweetness, nor pungency, nor smell. For to such a wine alone of all wines it belongs to have escaped both the defects of water and those of wine.

greek_sentence: γεννῶνται δὲ καθ᾿ ἕκαστον ἔθνος ἔνιοι τοιοῦτοι, κατὰ μὲν τὴν Ἰταλίαν ὁ ἄτονος Σαβῖνος, ὃν καὶ διδόασι τοῖς πυρέττουσιν· ἐν Ἀσίᾳ δὲ ὅ τε Τιτακαζηνὸς καὶ Τιβῖνος.
english_sentence_A: Some such wines are produced in each nation: in Italy the slack Sabine, which they also give to those with fever; in Asia the Titacazene and the Tibine.
english_sentence_B: Some such wines are produced in each nation: in Italy the weak Sabine, which they also give to the feverish; and in Asia the Titakazene and the Tibine.

greek_sentence: ἀκηκοὼς δὲ αὐτοῦ τὰ γνωρίσματα ῥᾳδίως εὑρήσεις καθ᾿ ἕκαστον ἔθνος οἴνους τοιούτους, ἐν οἷς χωρίοις πάνυ τι λεπτοὶ καὶ ὑδατώδεις οἶνοι γίγνονται· ἐγὼ γοῦν καὶ κατὰ τὴν Κιλικίαν καὶ Φοινικίην καὶ Παλαιστίνην καὶ Σκῦρον καὶ Κρήτην εὗρον οἴνους τοιούτους· ἀλλ᾿ ὅμως οἷον εἴρηκα καὶ κατὰ πάντα τὰ χωρία τεθέαμαι καὶ τό γε [649] θαυμασιώτερον, ὅτι καὶ κατ᾿ Αἴγυπτον· παχεῖς γὰρ οἶνοι καὶ ὀσμὴν ἔχοντες καὶ ἰσχυροὶ σφόδρα ἐν τοῖς θερμοῖς χωρίοις γεννῶνται· κατὰ δὲ τὴν Ἰταλίαν καὶ Βιθυνίαν καὶ τὴν Ἀσίαν θαυμαστὸν οὐδέν ἐστι πολλοὺς ὑδατώδεις γίνεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: And having heard its distinguishing marks, you will easily find wines of this kind among each people, in those regions where very thin and watery wines are produced; I at any rate have found wines of this kind in Cilicia and Phoenicia and Palestine and Scyros and Crete; but nevertheless, as I have said, I have observed them in all regions, and — what is [649] more remarkable — even in Egypt; for it is thick wines, possessing odour and exceedingly strong, that are produced in the hot regions; whereas in Italy and Bithynia and Asia it is nothing remarkable that many watery wines are produced.
english_sentence_B: Having heard its distinguishing marks, you will easily find such wines in each nation, in those regions where very thin and watery wines are produced. I at any rate found such wines in Cilicia, Phoenicia, Palestine, Scyros and Crete; but nevertheless I have seen wine of the kind I have described in all regions, and, what is [649] more remarkable, even in Egypt; for thick wines, wines that have an odour and are very strong, are produced in hot regions.

lsj_entry_text: ὀλιγο-φόρος, ον, that can bear but little, of weak wine, that will bear but little water, Hp. Acut. 56 , Gal. 6.807 , cf. Sch. Ar. Pl. 854 .
greek_sentence: οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ τοῦτ᾿ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν, ὡς ἠγνόει τὸν τοιοῦτον οἶνον· αὐτὸς γοῦν ὀλίγον ὕστερον ἐν τῷ τοῦ μελικράτου λόγῳ τάδε γράφει· ἀτὰρ καὶ οἴνου λεπτοῦ καὶ ὀλιγοφόρου καὶ ἀνόσμου, ἐνίῃ μὲν ἰσχυρότερον, ἐνίῃ δὲ καὶ ἀσθενέστερον· ταῦτ᾿ εἶπε παραβάλλων τὸ μελίκρατον οἴνῳ λεπτῷ καὶ ὀλιγοφόρῳ, τουτέστιν ὀλίγον ὕδωρ φέροντι καὶ ἀνόσμῳ.
english_sentence_A: For it is not even possible to say this, that he was ignorant of such a wine; he himself at any rate writes the following a little later, in the discussion of melikraton: 'but also than thin wine, which bears little water and is odourless, in one respect stronger, in another also weaker'; he said these things comparing melikraton with thin and oligophoros wine, that is, wine that bears little water, and odourless.
english_sentence_B: For one cannot even say that he did not know such a wine: he himself, at any rate, a little later, in his account of melicrat, writes as follows: 'but also, compared with a wine that is thin, of little bearing (oligophoros) and without odour, it is in some respects stronger and in some respects weaker.' He said this comparing melicrat with a wine that is thin and oligophoros, that is, one that bears little water, and odourless.

greek_sentence: τοῖς μὲν οὖν ἄλλοις ἅπασιν ἐπιτηδειότατόν ἐστιν ἐπὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις νοσήμασι τὸ μελίκρατον, ἦττον δὲ τοῖς πικροχόλοις ὠφέλιμον· ἐκχολοῦται γὰρ ἐν αὐτοῖς, ἐὰν μὴ φθάσῃ διεξελθεῖν ἢ κατ᾿ ἔντερον ἢ κύστιν, ὡς εἴ γε διεξέλθοι, πρὸς τῷ [651] μὴ βλάψαι μηδὲν ὀνίνησι μέγιστα, συνυπάγεται γὰρ αὐτῷ χολώδη περιττώματα.
english_sentence_A: For all the others, then, melikraton is most suitable in such diseases, but it is less beneficial to the bitter-bilious; for in them it is turned into bile, unless it first passes out, either by way of the intestine or by way of the bladder, since if it does pass out, in addition to [651] doing no harm it is of the greatest benefit, for bilious residues are carried off together with it.
english_sentence_B: For all others, then, honey-water is most suitable in such diseases, but it is less beneficial to the bitter-bilious; for in them it turns into bile unless it first manages to pass through, either by way of the intestine or the bladder; since if it does pass through, besides [651] doing no harm at all, it benefits very greatly, for bilious residues are carried down together with it.

greek_sentence: συνεδείξατο γοῦν τῷ λόγῳ τῷδε καὶ περὶ τῆς κράσεως αὐτοῦ· συμφέρει γὰρ αὑτοῦ ὑδαρέστερον ἐπὶ τῶν τοιούτων φύσεων δίδοσθαι τὸ μελίκρατον, ὅπως μήτε διψῶδες εἴη μήτε χολοποιόν.
english_sentence_A: At any rate, by this statement he also indicated something about its mixture: for in the case of such natures it is advantageous that the melikraton be given more watery than it otherwise is, so that it may be neither thirst-provoking nor bile-producing.
english_sentence_B: At any rate, by this statement he also indicated at the same time something about its mixing; for in such natures it is beneficial for the honey-water to be given more watery than it usually is, so that it may be neither thirst-provoking nor bile-producing.

R. 410e , (φύω): origin, φ. οὐδενός ἐστιν ἁπάντων θνητῶν οὐδὲ . . τελευτή Emp. 8.1 (cf. Plu. 2.1112a ); φ. βούλονται λέγειν γένεσιν τὴν περὶ τὰ πρῶτα Pl. english_sentence_A: For it is softening of the lung, moderately brings up sputum, and is soothing of cough; [652] for it has something detergent in it, which renders the sputum viscous more than is moderate.
english_sentence_B: Why it is less productive of thirst than sweet wine has been stated by me earlier, when I showed that in so far as both are sweet, to that extent they are readily turned into bile; but in so far as honey-water is thinner and more penetrating, so as to pass everywhere, to that extent it becomes less productive of thirst than the wine. english_sentence_A: Why it is less thirst-provoking than sweet wine has been stated by me earlier, when I showed that insofar as both are sweet, to that extent they are easily turned into bile; but insofar as melikraton is thinner and more penetrative, so as to pass everywhere, in this respect it becomes less thirst-provoking than the other; since, if ever it remains in the stomach for a longer time, it too will be no less thirst-provoking than sweet wine.

greek_sentence: Διὰ τί μὲν ἧττον οἴνου ἐστὶ γλυκέος διψῶδες ἔμπροσθεν εἴρηταί μοι, δεικνύντι καθ᾿ ὅσον μέν εἰσιν ἄμφω γλυκέα, κατὰ τοσοῦτον ἐκχολοῦσθαι ῥᾳδίως αὐτά· καθ᾿ ὅσον δὲ λεπτότερόν τ᾿ ἐστὶ καὶ ποριμώτερον, ὡς ἰέναι πάντῃ, τὸ μελίκρατον, κατὰ τοῦτο ἧττον αὐτοῦ γίνεσθαι διψῶδες· ὡς εἴ γέ ποτε κατὰ τὴν γαστέρα μείνῃ χρόνῳ πλείονι καὶ αὐτὸ διψῶδες οὐχ ἧτον ἔσται τοῦ γλυκέος οἴνου.
english_sentence_A: Why it is less thirst-provoking than sweet wine has been stated by me earlier, when I showed that insofar as both are sweet, to that extent they are easily turned into bile; but insofar as melikraton is thinner and more penetrative, so as to pass everywhere, in this respect it becomes less thirst-provoking than the other; since, if ever it remains in the stomach for a longer time, it too will be no less thirst-provoking than sweet wine.
english_sentence_B: This in itself happens rarely. But passing more quickly than sweet wine through the stomach and the whole intestine, and further also through the liver as far as the kidneys and bladder, belongs to honey-water not rarely but always.

english_sentence_A: This latter, however, happens rarely; whereas passing more quickly than sweet wine through the stomach and the whole intestine, and further through the liver as far as the kidneys and bladder, belongs to melikraton not rarely but always.
english_sentence_B: For these reasons, then, it is less productive of thirst than sweet wine. Hippocrates, however, did not put it thus.

greek_sentence: διὰ ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ἧττόν ἐστι διψῶδες τοῦ γλυκέος οἴνου· ὁ δὲ Ἱπποκράτης οὐχ οὕτως εἶπεν, ἀλλ᾿ ἑτέρως ταὐτὸν ἐνδειξάμενος αὐτοῦ τὴν δύναμιν ἐξ ὧν ἐργάζεται κατὰ τὸν πνεύμονα· δῆλον γὰρ ὡς οὐκ ἂν εἰργάζετο ταῦτα, μὴ διεξερχόμενόν γε καὶ διαῤῥύπτον αὐτοῦ τὰς ὁδούς.
english_sentence_A: For these reasons, then, it is less thirst-provoking than sweet wine; but Hippocrates did not put it in this way, but indicated the same thing differently, pointing to its power from the things it effects in the lung; for it is clear that it would not effect these things if it did not pass through and thoroughly cleanse its passages.
english_sentence_B: He indicated the same thing in another way, showing its power from what it effects in the lung. For it is clear that it would not effect these things unless it passed through and cleansed the lung's passages.

lsj_entry_text: ὀξυ-μελίκρατον, Ion. ὀξύ-κρητον, τό, mixture of vinegar and honey, oxymel, Hp. Loc.Hom. 17 :—also ὀξύμελι, ιτος, τό, Id. Acut. 19 , 59 , Lys. Fr. 42 , Arist. Pr. 922a6 , cf. Dsc. 5.14 , Gal. 15.677 .
greek_sentence: τὸ γὰρ ἰσχυρῶς ἀνάγειν οὐκ ἔχει, καθάπερ τὸ ὀξύμελι· τό γε μὴν παρηγορικὸν ἔχει, μηδ᾿ ὅλως ἔχοντος αὐτὸ τοῦ ὀξυμέλιτος· ἐπεγείρει γὰρ ἐκεῖνο τὰς βῆχας, ἐρεθίζον τε καὶ τραχῦνον, ἐκ τοῦ ῥύπτειν σφοδρῶς.
english_sentence_A: For it does not have the capacity to bring it up strongly, as oxymel does; it does, however, possess the soothing quality, which oxymel does not possess at all, for that stirs up coughs, irritating and roughening, as a result of its cleansing vigorously.
english_sentence_B: For it does not have the property of bringing up strongly, as oxymel does; it does, however, have the soothing property, which oxymel does not have at all, for that provokes coughs, irritating and roughening by its vehement cleansing. Melicrat, and above all the watery kind, has only a very small share of the cleansing faculty.

greek_sentence: μελικράτῳ δὲ καὶ μάλιστα τῷ ὑδαρεῖ τῆς ῥυπτικῆς δυνάμεως ὀλιγίστης μέτεστιν· καλεῖται δ᾿ ἡ τοιαύτη καὶ σμηκτικὴ, καὶ νῦν ὁ Ἱπποκράτης ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνης ἐποιήσατο τὸ σμηγματῶδες ὄνομα, περὶ τοῦ μελικράτου γράψας, ἔχει γὰρ σμηγματῶδές τι· μετρίας αὐτῷ μετεῖναι τῆς τοιαύτης δυνάμεως αἰνιξάμενος ἐκ τοῦ προσθεῖναι τῷ σμηγματῶδες τὸ τὶ, βραχύτητα δηλοῦν οἷς ἂν οὕτω προσκέηται.
english_sentence_A: Melikraton, and especially the watery kind, has only the very smallest share of the cleansing faculty; such a faculty is also called smectic (scouring), and here Hippocrates formed from it the term "smegmatic" (soap-like), writing about melikraton, "for it has something smegmatic," hinting that it has a share in a moderate degree of such a faculty by adding to "smegmatic" the word "something," which indicates smallness in whatever it is thus attached to.
english_sentence_B: Such a faculty is also called abstersive, and here Hippocrates formed from it the word "soap-like" (σμηγματῶδες), writing of melicrat "for it has something soap-like". He hinted that it has a moderate share of such a faculty by adding "something" to "soap-like", since this word indicates smallness in whatever it is so attached to.

greek_sentence: μελικράτῳ δὲ καὶ μάλιστα τῷ ὑδαρεῖ τῆς ῥυπτικῆς δυνάμεως ὀλιγίστης μέτεστιν· καλεῖται δ᾿ ἡ τοιαύτη καὶ σμηκτικὴ, καὶ νῦν ὁ Ἱπποκράτης ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνης ἐποιήσατο τὸ σμηγματῶδες ὄνομα, περὶ τοῦ μελικράτου γράψας, ἔχει γὰρ σμηγματῶδές τι· μετρίας αὐτῷ μετεῖναι τῆς τοιαύτης δυνάμεως αἰνιξάμενος ἐκ τοῦ προσθεῖναι τῷ σμηγματῶδες τὸ τὶ, βραχύτητα δηλοῦν οἷς ἂν οὕτω προσκέηται.
english_sentence_A: Melikraton, and especially the watery kind, has only the very smallest share of the cleansing faculty; such a faculty is also called smectic (scouring), and here Hippocrates formed from it the term "smegmatic" (soap-like), writing about melikraton, "for it has something smegmatic," hinting that it has a share in a moderate degree of such a faculty by adding to "smegmatic" the word "something," which indicates smallness in whatever it is thus attached to.
english_sentence_B: Such a faculty is also called abstersive, and here Hippocrates formed from it the word "soap-like" (σμηγματῶδες), writing of melicrat "for it has something soap-like". He hinted that it has a moderate share of such a faculty by adding "something" to "soap-like", since this word indicates smallness in whatever it is so attached to.

greek_sentence: Λέλεκταί μοι καὶ πρόσθεν ὅτι τῷ διεξέρχεσθαι ῥᾳδίως ἁπάσας τὰς μεταξὺ κοιλίας τε καὶ νεφρῶν ὁδοὺς, οὐρητικόν ἐστι τὸ μελίκρατον· ἐδείχθη δὲ καὶ ὅτι κακοπραγοῦντος τοῦ ἥπατος οὐ προσήκει πίνειν αὐτὸ, βλάπτει δὲ καὶ σπλῆνα φλεγμαίνοντα, καὶ πολὺ δὴ μᾶλλον ἔντερά τε καὶ γαστέρα, ταχέως γὰρ ἐκπυρούμενον ὑπὸ τῆς κατὰ τὴν φλεγμονὴν θερμασίας εἰς χολὴν μεταβάλλει.

english_sentence_A: For perhaps on account of its sweetness the viscera take pleasure in honey, just as the stomach does too, so that they draw it in both more quickly and more all at once; and indeed one might also reckon that the other sweet things have the same property as this, namely that they are disposed toward the viscera in the same way as toward the belly.
english_sentence_B: For perhaps the viscera delight in honey because of its sweetness, just as the stomach also does, so that they draw it in more quickly and more all at once. greek_sentence: φανεῖται δ᾿ ἡ γαστὴρ ἥδεσθαι τούτοις· καὶ γὰρ μετὰ τὸ καταπιεῖν αὐτὰ, φανερῶς πώς ἐστιν ἡδομένη πρὸς τῶν εἰλημμένων, ὥσπερ αὖ πάλιν ἀνιωμένη [656] τοῖς τραχύνουσί τε καὶ πικροῖς, οὐκ ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ λαμβάνεσθαι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ μετὰ τὸ ληφθῆναι ἄχρι χρόνου τινός.
english_sentence_A: And the stomach will appear to take pleasure in these things; for indeed after swallowing them it is in some way manifestly pleased by what has been taken, just as, conversely, it is distressed [656] by things that are roughening and bitter, not only in the very act of taking them but also for some time after they have been taken.
english_sentence_B: And the stomach will be seen to take pleasure in these; for after it has swallowed them it is, in a way, manifestly pleased by what has been taken, just as, conversely, it is distressed [656] by things that roughen and by bitter things, not only in the very act of their being taken but also after they have been taken, for some time.

english_sentence_A: Hence no one administers these, except sometimes as a drug, on account of humours gathered contrary to nature in the stomach; but when it is in its natural state, all such things are distressing to it, and sweet things alone are pleasant.
english_sentence_B: Hence no one even administers them, except sometimes as a drug, on account of humours that have accumulated contrary to nature in the stomach; but when the stomach is in its natural state, all such things are distressing to it, and only sweet things are pleasant.

greek_sentence: οὕτως οὖν εἰκός ἐστι καὶ τὰ σπλάγχνα χαίρειν τῷ μὲν γλυκεῖ χυμῷ, ταχέως δ᾿ αὐτοῦ καὶ πλεῖστον ἐπισπώμενα, καθ᾿ ὃν μὲν ὑγιαίνει χρόνον, ἀπολαύειν τε καὶ τρέφεσθαι, καθ᾿ ὃν δὲ πυρετώδη [657] τέ ἐστι καὶ φλεγμαίνει, μεταβάλλειν ἐστὶ τὸ χολῶδες αὐτό.
english_sentence_A: So then it is likely that the viscera too rejoice in the sweet humour, and, drawing it in quickly and in very great quantity, during the time when they are healthy enjoy it and are nourished, but during the time when they are feverish [657] and inflamed change it into the bilious.

greek_sentence: ὁρᾶται γοῦν καὶ τὰ καλούμενα συκωτὰ διὰ τῆς τῶν ἰσχάδων ἐδωδῆς, μέγιστά τε καὶ ἥδιστα γιγνόμενα, προφανῶς τοῦ ἥπατος εὐτροφοῦντος ἐπὶ τῇ τῶν γλυκέων ἐδωδῇ· ἀλλ᾿ ἐν ταῖς φλεγμοναῖς τε καὶ τοῖς πυρετοῖς οὐκ εἰς εὐτροφίαν, ἀλλ᾿ εἰς χολῆς γένεσιν, ἡ τῶν τοιούτων προσφορὰ μεταβάλλεται, τοῦ μὲν πυρετώδους θερμοῦ πλεονάζοντος, ἐλλείποντος δὲ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν, ὅπερ εὔκρατον ἦν.
english_sentence_A: At any rate the so-called sykota (fig-fed livers) are seen, through the eating of dried figs, to become very large and most delicious, the liver evidently being well nourished upon the eating of sweet things; but in inflammations and fevers the administration of such things is converted not into good nourishment but into the generation of bile, since the feverish heat is in excess and the natural heat, which was well-tempered, is deficient.

english_sentence_B: For sweet wine too carries off bilious matters, but honey-water is sometimes evacuant of good bilious matters, and sometimes of bad ones. These are the bilious matters that are quite unmixed, those containing tawny or yellow and thick bile.

greek_sentence: Λέλεκται καὶ πρόσθεν ὡς ἐκχολουμένου τοῦ μέλιτος ἐν ταῖς ὀξείαις νόσοις καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο βλάπτοντος ἡμᾶς, βραδυπόρου δ᾿ ὄντος τοῦ ὕδατος καὶ μένοντος ἐπὶ πλεῖστον [660] ἐν τοῖς ὑποχονδρίοις καὶ διὰ τοῦτ᾿ ὄντος φευκτοῦ· τὸ μικτὸν ἔξ ἀμφοῖν ἐπιτήδειον γίνεται, κατὰ τὴν τοιαύτην κρᾶσιν συντιθέμενον, ὅταν ὕδατι πλείονι μέλιτος μιχθῇ τοσοῦτον, ὡς ὁδοποιεῖν τε καὶ πρὸς τὴν ἀνάδοσιν ἄγειν αὐτό.
english_sentence_A: It has also been said earlier that, since honey turns into bile in acute diseases and in this respect harms us, while water is slow to pass and remains for a very long time [660] in the hypochondria and on this account is to be avoided, the mixture of both becomes suitable, when it is compounded in the following blending: whenever to a greater quantity of water only so much honey is mixed as to open a way for it and lead it toward distribution.
english_sentence_B: It has also been said before that, since honey turns to bile in acute diseases and in this respect harms us, while water is slow of passage and remains for a very long time [660] in the hypochondria and for this reason is to be avoided, the mixture made from both becomes suitable, when it is compounded according to such a blend, namely when so much honey is mixed with a larger quantity of water as both to open a way for it and to carry it on to distribution.

english_sentence_A: For both the urines become more readily passed and the bringing up of the sputa quicker when they are mixed in this way; but if much honey is mixed in, it produces thirst and makes the sputum viscous.

greek_sentence: καὶ διὰ τῶν κλυστήρων δὲ ἐνιέμενον, ὅσῳπερ ἂν ἀκρατέστερον ᾖ, τοσοῦτον μᾶλλον ἐκκριτικὸν γίνεται τὸ τοιοῦτον· καὶ τῶν κατακορέως χολωδῶν, τουτέστι τῶν ἱκανῶς τοιούτων καὶ τῶν ἀφρωδῶν διαχωρημάτων αἴτιον ὑπάρχει· τὸ γὰρ ἐπισπᾶσθαι τὰ τοιαῦτα μᾶλλον ἔχει τῷ δάκνειν τε καὶ ῥύπτειν τὸ ἔντερον· ἔτι δὲ καὶ αὐτὸ μεταβάλλον εἰς χολὴν ξανθὴν συναύξει καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο τῶν χολωδῶν διαχωρημάτων τὸ πλῆθος, ὅθεν οὐδ᾿ ἐπαινεῖ [661] τὴν χρῆσιν αὐτοῦ.
english_sentence_A: And when injected through clysters, too, the more undiluted it is, the more evacuant such a mixture becomes; and it is the cause of stools that are intensely bilious, that is, of those that are considerably such, and of frothy stools. For it is more capable of drawing such matters by its biting and scouring of the intestine; and moreover, itself changing into yellow bile, it also in this way increases the quantity of the bilious stools, whence he does not even approve [661] its use.
english_sentence_B: And when it is injected by means of clysters, the less diluted such a thing is, the more excretory it becomes; and it is the cause of intensely bilious evacuations, that is, those that are sufficiently such, and of frothy ones. english_sentence_A: So you too, mindful of these things, whenever, either after melikraton has been drunk or even without it, someone passes stools that are at once frothy and intensely bilious, know that the fever is colliquative, and on this account desist from the use of melikraton and proceed to the juice of ptisane, watching to see some sign, even a slight one, through the urines, of the concoction of the disease; for if at that moment you give cold water as well, you will benefit the patient most greatly.
english_sentence_B: You too, then, remembering these things, whenever someone, either after melicrat has been drunk or even without it, passes evacuations that are at once frothy and intensely bilious, know that the fever is colliquative, and for this reason refrain from the use of melicrat, and turn to the juice of ptisan, watching to see some sign, even a small one, through the urine, of the concoction of the disease; for at that time, by giving cold water as well, you will be of the greatest benefit.

greek_sentence: τίνα γε μήν ἐστιν ἃ συμβαίνει πρὸς τῶν εἰρημένων διαχωρημάτων σίνεα, παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἄκουε λέγοντος· οὔτε γὰρ ἐξ ὑποχονδρίων καῦμα σβέννυσιν, ἀλλ᾿ [663] ὁρμᾷ· τοῦτο δὲ εἶπεν, ἐπειδὴ πολλάκις ἡ τῶν χολωδῶν ὑποχώρησις αὐτίκα σβέννυσι τὸ ἐξ ὑποχονδρίων καῦμα· διὰ τοῦτ᾿ οὖν ἐπὶ τῶν κακοηθῶν χολωδῶν προσέθηκεν, ὅτι μὴ σβέννυται, ἀλλὰ τοὐναντίον ἅπαν αὐξάνεται τοῖς τὰ τοιαῦτα διαχωροῦσι καὶ οὐ παύεται τὸ καῦμα ἐκ τῶν ὑποχονδρίων, ἀλλὰ καὶ σφοδρότερον γίγνεται καὶ ῥιπτάζονται, τουτέστιν ἄσην τε καὶ δυσφορίαν ἔχουσιν, ἐπειδὴ τῆς ἐν τοῖς ὑποχονδρίοις διαθέσεως φλογώδους τὰ τοιαῦτα διαχωρήματα συμπτώματα· καὶ μέντοι καὶ ὅτι κατὰ τὴν τῶν ἐντέρων διέξοδον ἡ δριμύτης αὐτῶν ξυσματώδη διάθεσιν ἐργάζεται.
english_sentence_A: What, then, the harms are that result from the stools just mentioned, hear from him himself as he says: "for it neither quenches the burning heat from the hypochondria, but [663] rather stirs it up." greek_sentence: ταύτης μὲν οὖν τῆς διαθέσεως αἴτια γίγνεται τὰ κατακορῆ χολώδη, τῆς δὲ ἐν τοῖς ὑποχονδρίοις σημεῖα· ὅ γε μὴν Ἱπποκράτης, ὡς ἔφην, εἴωθεν ἐνίοτε καὶ τοῖς τῶν αἰτίων ἐνδεικτικοῖς ῥήμασιν ἐπὶ τῶν σημείων χρῆσθαι.
english_sentence_A: Of this latter condition, then, the intensely saturated bilious stools are causes, whereas of the condition in the hypochondria they are signs; Hippocrates, however, as I said, is accustomed sometimes to use the words that indicate causes even in the case of signs.

english_sentence_A: "So then, using melikraton without gruels in place of another drink in these diseases, you would have good fortune in many cases and would not have ill fortune in many; to whom it should be given and to whom it should not be given, the most important points have been stated, and the reasons why it should not be given." He has now too made it most plainly clear, advising the use of melikraton alone until the disease has reached its crisis.
english_sentence_B: Without gruels, then, if you use melicrat instead of any other drink in these diseases, you would have much success and not many failures. To whom it should be given and to whom it should not be given, the most important points have been stated, and also the reasons for which it should not be given.

greek_sentence: τὰ μὲν γὰρ καθαιροῦντα τὴν δύναμιν, ὡς αἱμοῤῥαγία καὶ διαχώρησις πολλὴ καὶ ἱδρὼς ἄμετρός τε καὶ κατά τι συμβεβηκὸς ἀσιτία, καταγυιοῦν εἰκότως ἂν λέγοιτο· τὰ δὲ μηδ᾿ ὅλως τρέφοντα, καθάπερ τὸ ὕδωρ οὔτε καταγυιοῦν, οὔτε ῥωννύναι τὴν δύναμιν ἀληθῶς ἄν τις εἴποι, πλὴν κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς ἐνίοτε· τὸ γὰρ ὕδωρ οὐχ ὡς τροφὴ τὴν δύναμιν ἀνακτᾶται τῶν καμνόντων, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς φάρμακον εἰς συμμετρίαν κράσεως ἄγον τὰ διὰ τὴν ἀμετρίαν αὐτῆς ἀῤῥωστοῦντα.
english_sentence_A: For the things that pull down the faculty, such as haemorrhage and copious evacuation and immoderate sweat and, in some accidental way, abstinence from food, might reasonably be said to enfeeble; whereas of things that do not nourish at all, such as water, one could not truly say either that they enfeeble or that they strengthen the faculty, except sometimes accidentally; for water restores the faculty of the sick not as nourishment but as a drug, bringing to a due proportion of mixture those things that are weak on account of its disproportion.

greek_sentence: ἔνιοι δὲ ἀντὶ τοῦ ᾗ τὸ ἐνίῃ γράφουσιν οὕτως· ἀτὰρ καὶ οἴνου ὀλιγοφόρου καὶ λεπτοῦ καὶ ἀνόσμου ἐνίῃ μὲν ἰσχυρότερον, ἐνίῃ δὲ ἀσθενέστερον.
english_sentence_A: "But also in relation to wine that is white and thin and bears little water and is odourless, in one respect it is stronger, in another weaker." Some write the passage without the "is", thus: "but also in relation to wine that is thin and bears little water and is odourless, in one respect stronger, in another weaker." Others write ἐνίῃ instead of ᾗ, thus: "but also in relation to wine that bears little water and is thin and odourless, in one respect (ἐνίῃ) stronger, in one respect weaker." From all of them, nonetheless, the same force and meaning is indicated, since he says that melikraton is in some respect stronger than such a wine, and in some respect weaker.
english_sentence_B: 'Moreover, compared with white, thin, oligophoros (of little bearing) and odourless wine, it is in one respect stronger, in another weaker.' Some people write the phrase without the 'is', thus: 'Moreover, compared with thin, oligophoros and odourless wine, in one respect stronger, in another weaker.' Others write 'in some respects' (eniēi) instead of 'in one respect' (hēi), thus: 'Moreover, compared with oligophoros, thin and odourless wine, in some respects stronger, in some respects weaker.' From all of them, however, the same meaning and sense is made clear: he is saying that melicrat is in some respect stronger than such a wine, and in some respect weaker.

english_sentence_A: "But also in relation to wine that is white and thin and bears little water and is odourless, in one respect it is stronger, in another weaker." Some write the passage without the "is", thus: "but also in relation to wine that is thin and bears little water and is odourless, in one respect stronger, in another weaker." Others write ἐνίῃ instead of ᾗ, thus: "but also in relation to wine that bears little water and is thin and odourless, in one respect (ἐνίῃ) stronger, in one respect weaker." From all of them, nonetheless, the same force and meaning is indicated, since he says that melikraton is in some respect stronger than such a wine, and in some respect weaker.
english_sentence_B: 'Moreover, compared with white, thin, oligophoros (of little bearing) and odourless wine, it is in one respect stronger, in another weaker.' Some people write the phrase without the 'is', thus: 'Moreover, compared with thin, oligophoros and odourless wine, in one respect stronger, in another weaker.' Others write 'in some respects' (eniēi) instead of 'in one respect' (hēi), thus: 'Moreover, compared with oligophoros, thin and odourless wine, in some respects stronger, in some respects weaker.' From all of them, however, the same meaning and sense is made clear: he is saying that melicrat is in some respect stronger than such a wine, and in some respect weaker.

greek_sentence: κατὰ τοὐναντίον γὰρ ὁ πολλοῦ δεόμενος ὕδατος εἰς εὐκρασίαν ὀνομάζεται πολυφόρος, ἐν ἴσῳ τῷ πολὺ φέρειν ὕδατος δεόμενος εἰς τὴν εὔκρατον μίξιν· ὁ δ᾿ ὀλιγοφόρος οἶνος ἔκλυτός τε καὶ ἀσθενὴς καὶ ἄχρηστος εἰς ποτὸν γίνεται, εἰ πλέονι κεράσεις ὕδατι.
english_sentence_A: For, conversely, the wine that needs much water for a good blend is named "bearing much water," which is the same as saying that it needs to bear much water for the well-blended mixture; whereas the wine bearing little water becomes slack and weak and useless for drink if you mix it with more water.
english_sentence_B: For that wine is so called which requires the smallest admixture of water in order to be drunk. Conversely, the wine that needs much water to reach a good temperament (eukrasia) is named 'of much bearing' (polyphoros), which is as much as to say 'needing to bear much water to make the well-tempered mixture'.

greek_sentence: καὶ μὴν καὶ τὸ ἄοδμον αὐτοῦ μέγιστον γνώρισμα τῆς ἀσθενείας τε καὶ ψυχρότητός ἐστιν, ὕδατι καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο ἐοικὼς, ὥσπερ γε καὶ τῶν ἰσχυρὰν ἐχόντων ὀσμὴν μέγιστον τοῦτ᾿ ἔστι τῆς ῥώμης σημεῖον.
english_sentence_A: And indeed its being without odour too is the greatest token of its weakness and coldness, since in this respect also it resembles water, just as, in the case of wines that have a strong smell, this is the greatest sign of their strength.
english_sentence_B: The wine of little bearing, by contrast, becomes slack, weak and useless for drinking if you mix it with more water. Moreover, its being odourless is the greatest mark of its weakness and coldness, since in this respect too it resembles water; just as, among wines that have a strong smell, this is the greatest sign of their strength.

lsj_entry_text: ὀλίγ-ιστος, v. ὀλίγος.
greek_sentence: ὁ μὲν γὰρ ὑδατώδης οἶνος ὀλιγίστην μὲν ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ τῆς ἀμπέλου μεταβολὴν ἔσχηκεν, ὀλιγίστην δὲ καὶ τοῦ γεώδους στοιχείου τὴν μίξιν, ὥστε ὕδωρ εἶναι, βραχὺ γεώδους τε [670] καὶ θερμῆς οὐσίας προσειληφὸς, ἢ μετειληφὸς, εἴς τε τὴν τούτων ἕνωσιν ὀλιγίστης κατεργασίας δεηθείς.
english_sentence_A: For the watery wine has undergone the least change in the wood of the vine, and has also the least admixture of the earthy element, so that it is water which has taken on in addition, or taken a share of, a small amount of earthy and [670] hot substance, and has required very little elaboration for the union of these.
english_sentence_B: For the watery wine has undergone very little change in the wood of the vine, and has also had very little admixture of the earthy element, so that it is water that has taken in, or received a share of, a little earthy [670] and hot substance, and has needed very little elaboration for the union of these.

greek_sentence: ὁ μὲν γὰρ ὑδατώδης οἶνος ὀλιγίστην μὲν ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ τῆς ἀμπέλου μεταβολὴν ἔσχηκεν, ὀλιγίστην δὲ καὶ τοῦ γεώδους στοιχείου τὴν μίξιν, ὥστε ὕδωρ εἶναι, βραχὺ γεώδους τε [670] καὶ θερμῆς οὐσίας προσειληφὸς, ἢ μετειληφὸς, εἴς τε τὴν τούτων ἕνωσιν ὀλιγίστης κατεργασίας δεηθείς.
english_sentence_A: For the watery wine has undergone the least change in the wood of the vine, and has also the least admixture of the earthy element, so that it is water which has taken on in addition, or taken a share of, a small amount of earthy and [670] hot substance, and has required very little elaboration for the union of these.
english_sentence_B: For the watery wine has undergone very little change in the wood of the vine, and has also had very little admixture of the earthy element, so that it is water that has taken in, or received a share of, a little earthy [670] and hot substance, and has needed very little elaboration for the union of these.

greek_sentence: ὁ δ᾿ ἐναντίος οἰνώδης τε καὶ πολυφόρος οὔθ᾿ ὑπὸ βραχείας κατεργασίας γίγνεται τοιοῦτος, ὡς ἂν ἐπὶ πλεῖστον ἀφιστάμενος ὕδατος, ἀξιόλογον δὲ διὰ τοῦτ᾿ αὐτὸ τὴν θερμασίαν καὶ τὴν ὀδμὴν ἐπικτᾶται.
english_sentence_A: But the opposite wine, vinous and able to bear much water, does not become such through a small elaboration, inasmuch as it departs very far from water, and for this very reason it acquires in addition a considerable heat and odour.
english_sentence_B: The opposite wine, vinous and 'polyphoros' (one that bears much water), does not become such through brief elaboration, inasmuch as it stands at the greatest remove from water, and for this very reason it acquires considerable heat and smell.

english_sentence_B: Indeed, the unmixedness both of wine and of honey makes a great difference as regards the strength of both.

english_sentence_A: Some people, in comparisons of this kind, reason fallaciously, not only against others willingly, but also against themselves unwillingly; and some, having at any rate made trial of certain less diluted mixtures, attach the power observed in those not only to unmixed wines alone, but also to wines mixed in whatever manner; just as, conversely, others, having made trial of more watery mixtures, have pronounced on the basis of those about all wines mixed in whatever manner.
english_sentence_B: In comparisons of this kind some people reason fallaciously, misleading not only others willingly but also themselves unwillingly. Some, having at least had experience of certain less diluted wines, attach the power they observed in those not only to the unmixed alone but also to wines mixed in any way whatever; just as, again, others, having had experience of more watery ones, have pronounced on the basis of those about all wines mixed in any way whatever.

english_sentence_A: Some people, in comparisons of this kind, reason fallaciously, not only against others willingly, but also against themselves unwillingly; and some, having at any rate made trial of certain less diluted mixtures, attach the power observed in those not only to unmixed wines alone, but also to wines mixed in whatever manner; just as, conversely, others, having made trial of more watery mixtures, have pronounced on the basis of those about all wines mixed in whatever manner.
english_sentence_B: In comparisons of this kind some people reason fallaciously, misleading not only others willingly but also themselves unwillingly. greek_sentence: οὐ μὴν οὕτως ἐχρῆν ποιεῖσθαι τὰς κρίσεις τῶν πραγμάτων, ἀλλὰ λογίσασθαι δεῖν ἀνάλογον τὸ μελίκρατον ἐν τῇ κράσει τῶν πινομένων οἴνων κατὰ τὴν τοῦ ὕδατος μίξιν, ὡς μὴ τὸν οἶνον ἀκρατέστερον εἶναι, τὸ δὲ μελίκρατον ὑδαρέστερον, εἰ μέλλεις δικαίαν ποιεῖσθαι τὴν παραβολὴν αὐτῶν· ἐπεὶ δὲ χαλεπόν ἐστι τὴν ἀναλογίαν ἀκριβῶς ἐν τῇ μίξει φυλάξαι, διὰ τοῦτο ἐπ᾿ αὐτὰ τὰ ὄντως ἄμικτα καὶ κυρίως ἄκρατα καλούμενα μετήνεγκε τὸν λόγον ὁ Ἱπποκράτης, οἴνῳ μηδ᾿ ὅλως κεκραμένῳ παραβάλλων τὸ μέλι· καί φησι διπλάσιον οἶνον [672] πινόμενον ἧττον τρέφειν ἁπλοῦ πλήθους μέλιτος.
english_sentence_A: Yet one ought not to have made one's judgements of the matters in this way, but one ought to reckon the melikraton as proportionate, in its blending, to the wines that are drunk, in respect of the admixture of water, so that the wine is not the less diluted and the melikraton the more watery, if you are going to make a fair comparison of them. But since it is difficult to preserve the proportion exactly in the mixing, for this reason Hippocrates transferred the discussion to the things themselves that are really unmixed and properly called unmixed (ἄκρατα), comparing honey with wine not diluted at all; and he says that a double quantity of wine [672] when drunk nourishes less than a single quantity of honey.

greek_sentence: ἐπεὶ δὲ πλείω γένη τῶν οἴνων εἰσὶν, οὐ τοὺς ἰσχυροὺς καὶ κεφαλὴν πλῆξαι δυναμένους καὶ παραφροσύνας ἐργάσασθαι προεχειρίσατο κατὰ τὸν λόγον, ἀλλὰ τὸν ἀσθενῆ καὶ ὑδατώδη καὶ τούτῳ παραβάλλων τὸ μέλι τροφιμώτερον ἀπέδειξεν.
english_sentence_A: And since there are several kinds of wines, he did not take up in his discussion the strong ones, which are able to strike the head and produce derangements (παραφροσύναι), but the weak and watery one, and comparing honey with this he showed it to be more nourishing.
english_sentence_B: But since it is difficult to preserve the proportion exactly in the mixing, for this reason Hippocrates transferred the argument to the things themselves that are truly unmixed and properly called neat, comparing honey with wine not mixed at all. And he says that wine drunk in double quantity [672] nourishes less than a single amount of honey.

greek_sentence: δύναται γὰρ εἰ τύχοι κύαθον ἕνα μέλιτος ἢ καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν λαμβάνειν ἢ ὅσον βούλεται μιγνὺς ὕδατι προσφέρεσθαι καὶ τοῦτο καθ᾿ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν πιεῖν· ἢ πάλιν οἴνου κυάθους δύο ἑκάστης ἡμέρας ὡς αὐτὸς βούλεται κεραννὺς ὕδατι προσφέρεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: For he can, say, take one kyathos of honey either by itself or, mixing in as much water as he wishes, take it so and drink this each day; or again take two kyathoi of wine each day, diluting it with water as he himself wishes.
english_sentence_B: Rather, if after the quantity of each has been measured it is administered in whatever way he wishes, the difference holds none the less. For he can, for example, take one cyathus of honey either by itself, or mixed with as much water as he wishes, and drink this each day; or again take two cyathi of wine each day, mixed with water as he himself wishes.

greek_sentence: γνωσθήσεται γὰρ ἐκ τῆς τοιαύτης πείρας ἐπὶ πλέον τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὁμοίως ἐχόντων κατ᾿ ἄλλα καὶ μέντοι καὶ μᾶλλον ἐφ᾿ ἑνὸς, οὐ κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον, ἡ ἑκατέρου δύναμις ἀκριβής· εἰ γὰρ μὴ κατὰ τινα φύσεως ἰδιότητα ταράττοι τὴν γαστέρα τὸ μέλι, [673] πλείοσιν ἡμέραις ἐξαρκέσουσιν οἱ τῷ μέλιτι χρώμενοι.
english_sentence_A: For from such a trial the precise power of each will come to be known, on a larger number of people who are in a similar condition in other respects, and indeed still more on a single person, though not at the same time; for if the honey does not disturb the belly on account of some peculiarity of nature, [673] those who use the honey will hold out for more days.
english_sentence_B: For from an experiment of this kind, made on a larger number of people who are alike in other respects, and indeed still more on a single person, though not at the same time, the exact power of each will be known. For unless honey disturbs the belly through some peculiarity of nature, [673] those who use honey will hold out for more days.

english_sentence_A: Either is possible: for perhaps [677] it was then first coming into common use; and perhaps too he finds fault with the term, as indicating either that the drug is composed of vinegar and honey alone, or as signifying a variety of honey, as if one were to speak thus: 'sour honey has such-and-such a power.' Concerning the addition of 'so-called', then, the matter is clear; let us proceed to what is actually useful.
english_sentence_B: Both are possible: for perhaps [677] it was then first coming into common use; or perhaps he also finds fault with the word, as suggesting either that the drug is composed of vinegar and honey alone, or as indicating a variety of honey, as if someone were to say: 'sharp honey has such-and-such a power.' Concerning the addition of 'so-called', then, the matter is clear; let us go on to what is itself useful.

lsj_entry_text: σύν-θεσις, εως, ἡ, putting together, composition, combination, Pl. Phd. 93a , R. 611b ; τῶν λίθων Arist. EN 1174a23 , cf. IG 42(1).103.56 (Epid., iv B.C.), 7.3073.92 (Lebad., ii B.C.); τῶν σπονδύλων Sor. 1.102 ; storage, τῶν μήλων (quinces in a ῥίσκος) Phylarch. 10 J. ; but ἐλαιῶν ς. a preserve of olives, Gp. 9.28.2 . in concrete sense, junction, ὀστῶν Arist. PA 658b19 ; συνθέσεις (λέγω τὰς γωνίας) Id. Pr. 910b14 . in various technical senses: in Grammar, composition, γραμμάτων τε συνθέσεις, i.e. syllables and words, A. Pr. 460 , cf. Arist. Metaph. 1092a26 ; ς. ἔκ τε ῥημάτων γιγνομένη καὶ ὀνομάτων, i.e. sentences, Pl. Sph. 263d , cf. Cra. 431c , Arist. Po. 1458a28 , Gal. 15.487 ; περὶ συνθέσεως ὀνομάτων, title of work by D.H. ; also, the juxtaposition of letters in a word, Arist. Rh.Al. 1434b34 ; of an author's composition, Isoc. 10.11 ; so ἡ τῶν μέτρων ς. metrical composition, Arist. Po. 1449b35 ; ἡ τῶν ἐπῶν ς. D.S. 5.74 ; ἡ τοῦ παίωνος ξ. the way the paeon is made up, Plu. 2.1143d ; the constitution of things, Hp. Virg. 1 . Math., synthesis of a problem (opp. ἀνάλυσις), Archim. Sph.Cyl. 2.7 , explained in Papp. 634 ; ἡ κατὰ ς. ἀγωγή synthetic procedure, Id. 412.2 . Math., ς. λόγου transformation of a ratio known as componendo, Euc. 5 Def. 14 ; κατὰ -σιν, = componendo, Archim. Aequil. 2.9 . Math., addition, Ph. 1.11 , Plu. 2.1018c , Dioph. 1 Intr.; καθ' ἁντινοῦν -σιν however many times added, i.e. whatever number of times taken (multiplied), Archim. Spir. 1 :—also as Pythag. name for 2 , Anatol. ap. Theol.Ar. 8 . in Logic, union of noun and verb or of two objects of thought in a statement, Arist. Int. 16a12 , de An. 430a27 ; also ὁ παρὰ τὴν ς. [λόγος] the fallacy of composition, opp. διαίρεσις, Id. SE 177a33 . in Physics, composition of substances, parts of organisms, from their elementary constituents, Id. PA 646a12 , Top. 151a23 ; opp μίξις (combination), Id. GC 328a6 . in Medicine, compounding of essences and drugs, τῶν μύρων Thphr. Od. 14 , al., cf. D.S. 4.45 , Aglaïas 8 . combination of parts so as to form a whole, γενέσεις καὶ ς. Pl. R. 533b ; ἡ τῶν στρωμάτων ς. Id. Plt. 280b , cf. Arist. PA 645a35 , Metaph. 1014b37 ; in plants, Thphr. HP 5.5.2 . in concrete sense, a social or political combination, Arist. Pol. 1276b7 ; a military formation, Ael. Tact. 18.5 . agreement, treaty, Pi. P. 4.168 , Fr. 205 ; πὸς τὰς συνθέσις in accordance with the agreements, IG 5(2).343.41 , 60 (Orchom. Arc. , iv B.C.); ἐκ συνθέσεως by arrangement, D.S. 13.112 , etc.; συνθέσεις περὶ γάμων Plu. lsj_entry_text: βρόγχος, ὁ, trachea, windpipe, Hp. Epid. 5.68 , Arist. Pr. 900a13 , Gal. UP 7.11 , etc. generally, throat, Hp. Aph. 6.37 , Aret. SA 1.6 . gulp, draught, ψυχροῦ Apollon. ap. Arr. Epict. 3.12.17 . = βάτραχος , Hsch.
greek_sentence: εἰ γὰρ ἀνάγοι μὲν τὰ ἐγκέρχνοντα καὶ ὄλισθον ἐμποιήσειε καὶ ὥσπερ εἰ διαπτερώσειε τὸν βρόγχον, παρηγορήσειε τὸν πνεύμονα, μαλθακτικὸν γὰρ αὐτέου· καὶ εἰ μὲν ταῦτα συγκυρήσειε, μεγάλην ἂν ὠφελείην ποιήσειεν· ἔστι δ᾿ ὅτε τὸ κάρτα ὀξὺ οὐκ ἐκράτησε τῆς ἀναγωγῆς τοῦ πτυέλου, ἀλλὰ προσεγλίσχρηνέ τε καὶ ἔβλαψεν.
english_sentence_A: For if it should bring up what causes rasping, and produce slipperiness, and, as it were, sweep the windpipe clean as with a feather, it would soothe the lung, for it is emollient of it; and if these things should concur, it would produce great benefit; but there are times when the very acid kind did not master the bringing up of the sputum, but rendered it more viscous and did harm." In the cases where there is need of acid oxymel, in these he teaches the harm that sometimes arises from it; for in cases where one would not at all use such a drug in acid form, it is superfluous to enumerate such harms.
english_sentence_B: For if it should bring up the matter that causes rattling, and produce slipperiness, and, as it were, clear out the windpipe as with a feather, it would soothe the lung, for it is emollient to it; and if these things should come about together, it would produce great benefit. But there are times when the very acid [oxymel] has not prevailed in the bringing up of the sputum, but has instead made it more viscid and done harm.

lsj_entry_text: ὀξύς, εῖα, ύ, Ion. fem. ὀξέα Hdt. 9.23 , al., v.l. in Hp. Mul. 1.64 , al. (in codd. freq. ὀξέη, and so Babr. 73.1 metri gr.) : ὀξεῖα, poet. for neut. pl. ὀξέα, Hes. Sc. 348 :—sharp, keen, whether of a point or an edge, in Hom. and Hes. mostly of weapons or anything made of metal, ἄκων Il. 10.335 , al.; ἄορ 21.173 , Hes. Sc. 457 ; βέλος Il. 4.185 , etc.; also of non-metallic substances, λᾶας 16.739 ; μοχλός Od. 9.382 ; σκόλοπες Il. 12.56 , 64 ; ὀξεῖα κορυφή, of a mountain-peak, Od. 12.74 ; so πάγοι ὀξέες 5.411 ; λίθος ὀξὺς πεποιημένος sharpened so as to serve as a knife, Hdt. 7.69 , cf. 3.8 ; κυρβασίας ἐς ὀξὺ ἀπηγμένας brought to a point, Id. 7.64 ; ὄρεα ἐς ὀ. τὰς κορυφὰς ἀ. Id. 2.28 ; τὸ ὀ. the apex of a triangle, ib. 16 ; of the heart, Arist. Resp. 478b5 ; τὸ ὀ. τοῦ ᾠοῦ Id. GA 752b8 ; ὀ. γωνία an acute angle, Id. Top. 107a16 , al., Euc. 1 Def. 12 , Archim. Spir. 16 ; Χρόνος ὀξὺς ὀδόντας Simon. 176 ; ἡ ὀξεῖα, name of a surgical instrument, Hermes 38.282 , Heliod. ap. Orib. 44.23.59 ; but also, a pointed splinter of bone, ib. 46.20.5 . in reference to the senses, of feeling, sharp, keen, ὀδύναι Il. 11.268 ; ὀ. ἠέλιος the piercing sun, h.Ap. 374 ; ὀξειᾶν ἀκτίνων πατήρ, i.e. the Sun, Pi. O. 7.70 ; Σείριος ὀξὺς ἐλλάμπων Archil. 61 ; πῦρ ὀ. Anaxipp. 1.12 ; so χιὼν ὀξεῖα Pi. P. 1.20 ; so also of grief and the like , ἄχος Il. 19.125 ; μελεδῶναι Od. 19.517 : and generally, sharp, severe, μάχη ὀξέα . . γίνεται keenly contested, Hdt. 9.23 ; ὀ. πυρετός Hp. VM 16 ( Sup. ); [ἡ νόσοσ] ὀξεῖα φοιτᾷ καὶ ταχεῖ' ἀπέρχεται S. Ph. 808 ; νόσοι, μανίαι, Pi. O. 8.85 , N. 11.48 ( Comp. ), cf. Hp. Acut. tit., Archig. ap. Gal. 9.887 ; πάθαι Pi. P. 3.97 ; ἐπιμομφά Id. O. 10(11).9 , etc. of the sight, ὀξύτατον ὄμμα Id. N. 10.62 ; ὄψις . . ὀξυτάτη τῶν διὰ τοῦ σώματος . . αἰσθήσεων Pl. Phdr. 250d : freq. in neut. as Adv., ὀξύτατον δέρκεσθαι to be keenest of sight, Il. 17.675 ; ὀξύτατα καθορᾶν Pl. R. 516c ; so ὀξὺ νοεῖν notice a thing sharply, Il. 3.374 ; ὀξὺ προϊδεῖν Od. 5.393 ; ὀξύτερον βλέπει Ar. Pl. 1048 , Lys. 1202 (lyr.) : prov., ὀξύτερον τοῦ Λυγκέως βλέπειν Id. Pl. 210 , cf. Macar. Prov. 6.41 ; also ὀξὺ ἄκουσεν heard with sharp ear, Il. 17.256 , cf. Pl. Lg. 927b ; ὀξεῖαν ἀκοὴν . . λόγοις διδούς keen attention, S. El. 30 . of things that affect the sight, dazzling, bright, αὐγὴ Ἠελίου Il. 17.372 ; [Ἠελίου] ὀξύτατον πέλεται φάος εἰσοράασθαι 14.345 : hence of colours, Ar. Pax 1173 (v. φοινικίς 2 ) ; αἱ ὀξεῖαι χροιαί Arist. Phgn. 806b4 ; πορφύρα Plu. Cat.Mi. 6 , PHolm. 20.36 ; [ἐσθὴσ] ὀξυτέρα καὶ τηλαυγεστέρα Ael. NA 4.46 . of sound, shrill, piercing, ἀϋτή Il. 15.313 ; ὀξὺ βοήσας 17.89 ; ὀξὺ δὲ κωκύσασα 18.71 ; ὀξὺ λεληκώς 22.141 ; ὀξέα κεκληγώς 17.88 , etc.; of whinnying horses, ὀξεῖα χρέμισαν Hes. Sc. 348 ; of young pigs, ὀξὺ κεκράγατε Ar. Ach. 804 ; of the scream of birds of prey, ὀξέα κλάζων S. Ant. 112 (anap.) ; of metals, ἰάχεσκε σάκος ὀξέα καὶ λιγέως Hes. Sc. 233 ; also of the wail of the nightingale (cf. ὀξύφωνος), ὄρνιθος ὀ. φθόγγον S. Ant. 424 ; so ἐπηλάλαξαν τὸν ὀ. νόμον shrieked their shrill song, A. Th. 952 (lyr.) ; ὀξὺ μέλος, of the grasshopper, Ar. Av. 1095 (lyr.). of musical tones, in a technical sense, high-pitched, opp. βαρύς, φθόγγοι Pl. Ti. 80a , X. Cyn. 6.20 ; ὀξυτάτη χορδή Pl. Phdr. 268d ; φωνὴ ὀξεῖα, βαρεῖα, μέση Arist. Rh. 1403b29 ; τῷ ὀξεῖ ἐν φωνῇ μὲν ἐναντίον τὸ βαρύ, ἐν ὄγκῳ δὲ τὸ ἀμβλύ Id. Top. 106a13 . in Music, δι' ὀξειῶν ( Dor. -ᾶν) interval of a fifth, Philol. 6 , Arist. Pr. 920a24 . ἡ ὀξεῖα (sc. προσῳδία) the acute accent, D.T. 630.1 , A.D. Pron. 35.10 , al.; τὸν τόνον φυλάσσειν ὀ. ib. 60.1 ; ὀ. συλλαβή Pl. Cra. 399b ; ὀ. στοιχεῖον S.E. M. 1.113 . of taste, sharp, pungent, acid, φακῆ X. Cyr. 6.2.31 ; ὄξος Diph. 18.1 ; οἶνος Alex. 141.12 ; ἐξ ὀξέος καὶ ἁλμυροῦ ξυνθεὶς ζύμωμα Pl. Ti. 74c . of smell, Arist. de An. 421a30 ; ὀξύτατον ὄζειν τινός Ar. Ach. 193 . metaph., of the inner sense, sharp, keen, hasty, esp. quick to anger, passionate, epith. of Ares, Il. 2.440 ,al. ; μένος ὀξύ h.Hom. 8.14 ; καρδίη ὀξυτέρη Thgn. 366 ; θυμὸς ὀ. S. OC 1193 ; νέος καὶ ὀ. Pl. Grg. 463e ; οἱ ἀκρόχολοι ὀξεῖς Arist. EN 1126a18 : so in ὀξύ-θυμος, -κάρδιος, -χολος. sharp, quick, δεινοὶ καὶ ὀξεῖς Pl. Ap. 39b : c. inf., ἐπινοῆσαι ὀ. Th. 1.70 ; γνῶναι . . ὀξύτατοι τὰ ῥηθέντα D. 3.15 ; also εἰς πάντα τὰ μαθήματα ὀξεῖς Pl. R. 526b ; τὰς ἐνθυμήσεις ὀξύς Luc. Salt. 81 . of motion, quick, swift, post- Hom. , ὀξυτάτους ἵππους Hdt. 5.9 ( v.l. ὠκυτάτους ) ; ἱερακίσκος Ar. Av. 1112 ; ὀξυτέρῳ χαλινῷ S. Ant. 108 (lyr.) ; of a report, ὀξεῖα βάξις διῆλθ' Ἀχαιούς Id. Aj. 998 ; ὀξεῖαν ἐκβάλλει ῥοήν, of a dying man, Id. Ant. 1238 , cf. A. Ag. 1389 ; of a flame, fierce, Thphr. HP 5.9.3 ; ᾄξας ὀξὺς νότος ὥς S. Aj. 258 (anap.) ; τὸ εὔψυχον . . ὀξεῖς ἐνδείκνυνται are quick in displaying, Th. 4.126 ; opp. βραδύς, Id. 8.96 ; opp. ῥάθυμος, Arist. EE 1240a2 ; opp. ἡσύχιος, Id. english_sentence_A: He says that the thick sputa's becoming thoroughly viscous, deriving no benefit from the administration of the sharp oxymel, happens to those who are in any case in a deadly condition, that is, those in whom the disease is quite unconcocted; for these bring up nothing by expectoration.
english_sentence_B: "This happens most of all to those who are in any case in a deadly condition and are unable to cough and to bring up by hawking what is lodged within." That the thick sputa become glutinous, deriving no benefit from the administration of the sharp oxymel, he says happens to those who are in any case in a deadly condition, that is, those in whom the disease is very unconcocted; for these bring up nothing.

greek_sentence: [681] Ἐπειδὴ προείρηκεν ὑπὸ τοῦ ὀξέος ὀξυμέλιτος οὐδὲν ὀνίνασθαι τοὺς καὶ ἄλλως ὀλεθρίως ἔχοντας, ἔνιοι δὲ σπανίως ἐξ αὐτῶν σώζονται βοηθούμενοι, διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τὴν τούτου σπανίαν βοήθειαν οὐ παρέλιπεν· ἔστι δ᾿ αὕτη διὰ τοῦ ὀξέος ἱκανῶς ὀξυμέλιτος, ὅταν ὁ κάμνων ἰσχυρὸς ᾖ τὴν δύναμιν.
english_sentence_A: [681] Since he has said beforehand that those who are in any case in a deadly condition derive no benefit from the sharp oxymel, while some of them, rarely, are saved when they are aided, for this reason he did not omit even this rare aid that it affords; and this consists in oxymel that is sufficiently sharp, whenever the patient is strong in his faculty.
english_sentence_B: [681] Since he has said before that those who are otherwise in a deadly condition derive no benefit from the sharp oxymel, though some of them are on rare occasions saved when they are given aid, for this reason he did not omit this rare remedy for it either. This remedy is by means of very sharp oxymel, when the patient is strong in his capacity.

greek_sentence: ἄλλως γὰρ οὐδὲν ὀνίνησι τὸ τοιοῦτον ὀξύμελι, δυοῖν θάτερον ἐργασάμενον, ἢ μηδ᾿ ὅλως τεμὸν, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπιγλισχραῖνον τὰ γλίσχρα, ἢ τεμὸν καὶ ἀποῤῥύψαν, ἀθρόαν δὲ ἀναγωγὴν καὶ κένωσιν κινῆσαν, τῆς δυνάμεως μὴ φερούσης, ἀκολουθήσει πνιγῆναι τὸν ἄνθρωπον.
english_sentence_A: For otherwise such oxymel is of no benefit at all, having done one of two things: either not cutting at all but rendering the viscous matters still more viscous, or cutting and scouring away, and stirring up an all-at-once bringing up and evacuation, and, the faculty not bearing it, it will follow that the man is suffocated.
english_sentence_B: For otherwise such an oxymel is of no benefit, since it produces one of two things: either it does not cut at all but makes the viscous matters more viscous still; or, having cut and scoured them away, it sets in motion an all-at-once bringing up and evacuation, and, the capacity not bearing it, it will follow that the person is choked.

greek_sentence: ἄλλως γὰρ οὐδὲν ὀνίνησι τὸ τοιοῦτον ὀξύμελι, δυοῖν θάτερον ἐργασάμενον, ἢ μηδ᾿ ὅλως τεμὸν, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπιγλισχραῖνον τὰ γλίσχρα, ἢ τεμὸν καὶ ἀποῤῥύψαν, ἀθρόαν δὲ ἀναγωγὴν καὶ κένωσιν κινῆσαν, τῆς δυνάμεως μὴ φερούσης, ἀκολουθήσει πνιγῆναι τὸν ἄνθρωπον.

lsj_entry_text: ὀξυ-μελίκρατον, Ion. ὀξύ-κρητον, τό, mixture of vinegar and honey, oxymel, Hp. Loc.Hom. 17 :—also ὀξύμελι, ιτος, τό, Id. Acut. 19 , 59 , Lys. Fr. 42 , Arist. Pr. 922a6 , cf. Dsc. 5.14 , Gal. 15.677 .
greek_sentence: Ἢν μηδὲν ἀναπτύῃ τι διὰ πάχος καὶ γλισχρότητα τῶν πτυσμάτων, οὐ μὴν ἀσθενῆ γε τὴν δύναμιν, ὀξύμελι κελεύει δίδοσθαι τὸ λίαν ὀξὺ, κατ᾿ ὀλίγον τε καὶ ἀκροχλίαρον, ὅπερ [682] ἐστὶν ἄκρως χλιαρόν (ἄκρως δὲ ἐστι χλιαρὸν ὅπερ ἂν ᾖ μέσον ἀκριβῶς τοῦ τε ψυχροῦ καὶ τοῦ θερμοῦ)· ἰσχυρὰν γὰρ ἔχον αὐτὸ τὴν δύναμιν εὐλαβεῖται πολὺ προσφέρειν εἰς ἅπαξ.
english_sentence_A: If someone brings up nothing at all because of the thickness and viscosity of the sputa, yet does not have his power weak, he orders that the very sharp oxymel be given, a little at a time and ἀκροχλίαρον, which [682] is lukewarm to the exact degree (and that is lukewarm to the exact degree which is precisely midway between the cold and the hot); for since it has a strong power, he is cautious about administering much of it at once.
english_sentence_B: If [the patient] brings nothing up by expectoration because of the thickness and viscosity of the sputa, but has a capacity that is by no means weak, he directs that oxymel be given, the very acid kind, little at a time and akrochliaron, which [682] is 'extremely lukewarm' (and that is extremely lukewarm which is exactly midway between the cold and the hot); for since it has a strong power, he is wary of administering much at once.

english_sentence_A: [683] The oxymel that is only slightly sour, however, moistens the mouth and the pharynx, and it is conducive to bringing up sputum and allays thirst; to the hypochondrium and to the viscera in that region it is kindly, and it prevents in that region the harms that come from honey; for the bilious element in honey is checked.

greek_sentence: τῆς οὖν τοῦ μελικράτου δυνάμεως [684] τὰ ἄλλα μὲν πάντα ἐχούσης, ὧν δεῖται τὰ τοιαῦτα νοσήματα, καθ᾿ ἓν δὲ μόνον ἐναντιουμένης αὐταῖς, ὅταν ὑπερθερμανθὲν ἐκχολωθῇ, τὴν τοιαύτην αὐτοῦ μεταβολὴν ἡ τοῦ ὄξους μίξις κωλύουσα κάλλιστον ἐργάζεται φάρμακον.
english_sentence_A: Since, then, the power of melikraton [684] possesses all the other things that such diseases require, and is opposed to them in one respect only, namely when, having been overheated, it is turned into bile, the admixture of vinegar, by preventing such a change in it, produces a most excellent remedy.
english_sentence_B: Since, then, the power of melicrat [684] possesses all the other things that such diseases require, and is contrary to them in one respect only, namely when, having been overheated, it turns bilious, the admixture of vinegar, by preventing this change in it, makes a most excellent remedy.

greek_sentence: ἄδιψόν τε γὰρ ἔσται καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τὰ πτύελα, τά γε μὴ παντάπασι παχέα καὶ γλίσχρα, ῥᾳδίως ἀνάξει· τούτοις δ᾿ ἀμφοτέροις αὐτοῖς ἔργοις ἕπεται καὶ ἡ τῶν κατὰ τὸ στόμα καὶ τὴν φάρυγγα μορίων ὑγρότης.

greek_sentence: Περὶ τοῦ μετρίως ὀξέος ὀξυμέλιτος ἔτι διαλεγόμενος εἴρηκε ταῦτα, πολλὴν δὲ τὴν χρῆσιν ἔχοντος ἐπὶ τῶν κατὰ πνεύμονα καὶ θώρακα παθῶν, ἀξιολογωτάτην τε τὴν ὠφέλειον, [685] διὰ τὴν ἔμμετρον μίξιν ὕδατός τε καὶ ὄξους καὶ μέλιτος.
english_sentence_A: He has said these things while still discussing the moderately sour oxymel, which has extensive use in the affections of the lung and thorax, and a most notable benefit, [685] on account of the well-proportioned mixture of water, vinegar and honey.

english_sentence_A: For oxymel of this kind, cutting the thick and flatulent pneuma in the hypochondrium and breaking up the flatus and thoroughly cleansing all the passages, guides the serous and bilious residues toward the urine.
