greek_sentence: τὸ γὰρ τοιοῦτον ὀξύμελι, τέμνον τε τὸ παχὺ καὶ φυσῶδες ἐν ὑποχονδρίῳ πνεῦμα καὶ καταῤῥηγνύον τὰς φύσας διακαθαῖρόν τε τὰς διεξόδους πάσας, ἐπ᾿ οὖρα ποδηγεῖ τοῖς ὀῤῥώδεσί τε καὶ χολώδεσι περιττώμασιν.
english_sentence_A: For oxymel of this kind, cutting the thick and flatulent pneuma in the hypochondrium and breaking up the flatus and thoroughly cleansing all the passages, guides the serous and bilious residues toward the urine.
english_sentence_B: For such an oxymel, cutting the thick and flatulent pneuma in the hypochondrium, breaking up the flatulences and cleansing all the passages, leads the way to the urine for the serous and bilious residues.

english_sentence_A: We know that he always calls the moisture arising in the parts beyond what is in accordance with nature plados; this, then, he says, oxymel produces, scraping away whatever of the thick or viscous humours is plastered on from the parts above, cutting this and bringing it down toward excretion.
english_sentence_B: We know that he always calls the moisture that arises in the parts beyond what is natural 'sodden moisture' (plados). This, then, he says, the oxymel produces, scraping off from the parts above whatever thick or viscous humours are plastered on there, and cutting this and drawing it down to excretion.

greek_sentence: εὐπετεῖς δὲ κατὰ τοιαύτην τὴν δύναμιν ἐργάζεται καὶ τὰς ἐξ ἥπατος ἐπαγωγὰς τῶν περιττωμάτων, ὥστε πασῶν τῶν ἄνωθεν ὑγροτήτων ἀθροιζομένων ἐν τοῖς ἐντέροις καὶ μάλιστα τοῖς κάτω, διὰ μὲν τὸ πλῆθος [686] αὐτῶν τὸν πλάδον ἐγγίνεσθαι, διὰ δὲ τὴν ποιότητα ξύεσθαι τὸ ἔντερον.
english_sentence_A: And by virtue of such a power it also renders easy the conveyances of the residues from the liver, so that, when all the moistures from above are collected in the intestines, and especially in the lower ones, through their quantity [686] the sodden moistness (pladōs) arises, while through their quality the intestine is scraped.
english_sentence_B: By a power of this kind it also makes easy the drawing-down of the residues from the liver, so that, since all the moistures from above are collected in the intestines, and especially in the lower ones, sogginess arises through their quantity [686] and the intestine is scraped through their quality.

english_sentence_B: For oxymel, having a detergent power, would in time scrape the intestine; and so would the bilious residue that descends together with it, since it has the same power. Hence, even without oxymel, if it ever happens to be in excess, it scrapes the intestine.

greek_sentence: οὖσα δὲ τοιαύτη λυπεῖται πρὸς ἁπάντων [687] τῶν διεξερχομένων καὶ μάλιστα τῶν ἐχόντων τινὰ δῆξιν· λυπηθὲν δὲ τὸ ἔντερον, εἰ μὴ παραχρῆμα τὴν ἔκκρισιν τῶν δακνόντων ποιήσαιτο, πρὸς τὴν ἄνω χώραν ἀναπέμπει τὰ διεξερχόμενα.
english_sentence_A: And being such, it is pained by all [687] the things that pass through it, and especially by those that have some biting quality; and the intestine, once pained, if it does not immediately effect the excretion of the biting matters, sends back what is passing through toward the upper region.

And the intestine, once distressed, if it does not at once effect the excretion of the biting things, sends the things passing through back up to the upper region.

greek_sentence: φυσικὴν γὰρ ἐνέργειαν ἔχει τὰ ἔντερα τὴν περισταλτικὴν, ὡς ἐν τοῖς περὶ τῶν φυσικῶν δυνάμεων ὑπομνήμασι δέδεικται· ταχύτητος δ᾿ ἔργον ἐστὶν ἀπωθεῖσθαι τὰ περιεχόμενα πρὸς τῶν μερῶν ἐκείνων ἐν οἶς περιέχεται.
english_sentence_A: For the intestines have a natural activity, the peristaltic one, as has been shown in the commentaries On the Natural Faculties; and it is the work of swiftness (ταχύτητος) to thrust away the contents from those parts in which they are contained.
english_sentence_B: For the intestines have the peristaltic as their natural activity, as has been shown in the commentaries On the Natural Faculties; and it is the work of swiftness (?) that the contents are thrust away by those parts in which they are contained.

greek_sentence: καὶ τοῦτό γε σαφῶς φαίνεται κᾀν τῷ κατὰ φύσιν ἔχειν συμβαῖνον, ὅταν ὑπιούσης ἀθρόως ποτὲ χολῆς εἰς τὰ κάτω τῶν ἐντέρων ἐπίσχωμεν τὴν ἔκκρισιν ἢ τῷ παρεῖναι τοιαύτην πρᾶξιν, ἣν μὴ διακόπτειν δυνατόν ἐστιν, ἢ τῷ μὴ παρεῖναι πλησίον ἀπόπατον· ἐν γὰρ τοῖς τοιούτοις καιροῖς ἀνατρεχούσης αἰσθανόμεθα τῆς χολῆς οὕτως ὡς μηκέτι ἐκκριθῆναι.
english_sentence_A: And this is clearly seen to happen even in the natural state, when, as bile is at some time descending all at once into the lower intestines, we hold back the excretion either because some such activity is in hand which cannot be interrupted, or because there is no privy near at hand; for on such occasions we perceive the bile running back up in such a way that it is no longer excreted.
english_sentence_B: And this is clearly seen to happen even when one is in the natural state, when, bile having at some time descended all at once into the lower parts of the intestines, we hold back the excretion, either because some activity is at hand which it is not possible to interrupt, or because there is no privy nearby. For on such occasions we perceive the bile running back up, so that it is no longer excreted.

greek_sentence: οὕτως οὖν ἡ καὶ ξυσματώδης ἐν τοῖς ἐντέροις διάθεσις ἐνίοτε μὲν τὴν ἔκκρισιν εἰς τὸ κάτωθεν ἐργάζεται ταχέως, οὐχ ὑπομένουσα τὴν τῶν πασχόντων ἀνίαν, ἐνίοτε δὲ κάτωθεν πρὸς τὴν ἄνωθεν χώραν, ὅταν μὴ παραχρῆμα τὸ διεξερχόμενον ἐκπέσῃ διὰ τῆς ἔδρας, ἀλλ᾿ ὁ κατ᾿ αὐτὴν μῦς ὁ κυκλοτερῶς συσταλεὶς καὶ σφίγξας τὸ πέρας τοῦ ἀπευθυσμένου, τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς περισταλτικῆς κινήσεως ἐκ τῶν κάτω μερῶν ἄνω ποιήσηται.
english_sentence_A: Thus, then, the scraping (ξυσματώδης) condition in the intestines sometimes produces the excretion downward quickly, not enduring the distress of the parts affected, and sometimes from below toward the region above, whenever what is passing through does not fall out at once through the seat, but the muscle at it, having contracted in a circle and constricted the end of the rectum, makes the beginning of the peristaltic movement from the lower parts upward.
english_sentence_B: In the same way, then, the scraping condition in the intestines sometimes quickly brings about excretion downwards, not enduring the distress of the affected parts, and sometimes from below towards the upper region, when what is passing through is not immediately expelled through the seat, but the muscle at that place, contracting circularly and constricting the end of the rectum, makes the beginning of the peristaltic motion from the lower parts upwards.

english_sentence_A: It also happens that the faculty is harmed because of the biting that follows in the passage; for the parts that are being scraped, even if what passes through has the slightest biting, are distressed violently; and we know that every pain is dissolvent of the faculty and for this reason also chilling to the extremities.

And we know that every pain is dissolutive of the strength, and for this reason also cooling to the extremities.

Smp. 186c , al.; ἐν κεφαλαίοις ὑπομνῆσαι, ἀποδείξειν, περιλαβεῖν τι, Th. 6.87 , Lys. 13.33 , Isoc. 2.9 ; βραχυτάτῳ κ. μαθεῖν Th. 1.36 ; τύπῳ καὶ ἐπὶ κεφαλαίου (v.l. -αίῳ), opp. ἀκριβέστερον, Arist. EN 1107b14 ; ἐπὶ κ. Plb. 1.65.5 , 3.5.9 ; ἐπὶ κεφαλαίων D. 19.315 , etc.; esp. in an argument, summing up, ἐν κεφαλαίοις Pl. Ti. 26c ; κεφαλαίῳ δέ . . , Lat. denique, Decr. ap. D. 18.164 ; τὸ δ' οὖν κ. ib. 213 ; τὸ δὲ κ. τῶν λόγων, ἄνθρωπος εἶ Men. 531.10 ; συναγαγεῖν τὸ κ. to sum up, Arist. Metaph. 1042a4 . metaph., of persons, the head or chief, ὅ τι περ κ. τῶν κάτωθεν, of Pericles, Eup. 93 ; τὸ κ. οὐδέπω λογίζομαι, τὸν δεσπότην Men. Pk. 173 ; ὅ τι περ τὸ κ. Luc. Harm. 3 , Gall. 24 , Philops. 6 ; τὰ κ. τῶν μαθημάτων, of philosophers, Id. Pisc. 14 ; τὸ κ. τοῦ πολέμου App. BC 5.50 ; οἳ τὸ τῆς στάσεως κ. ἦσαν ib. 43 ; τὸν Θαλῆν τῶν σοφῶν τὸ κ. Jul. Or. 3.125d : hence, of qualities, etc., σχεδόν τι τὸ κ. τῶν κακῶν (sc. avarice) Apollod. Gel. 4 ; τὸ κ. τῆς εὐδαιμονίας ἡ διάθεσις Diog.Oen. 57 . Rhet., head, topic of argument, D.H. Comp. 1 , Rh. 10.5 , Str. 1.2.31 . of money, capital, opp. interest or income, Pl. Lg. 742c , D. 27.64 , etc. sum total, IG 12.91.23 , al., Lys. 19.40 , D. 27.10 ; πολλοῦ κ. for a large sum, Act. Ap. 22.28 , cf. Aristeas 24 , Plu. Fab. 4 , etc.; κ. ἀργυρικά PRyl. 133.15 (i A.D.); also σιτικὰ καὶ ἀργυρικὰ κ. PSI 4.281.31 (ii A.D.). crown, completion of a thing, τὸ μὲν κ. τῶν ἀδικημάτων the crowning act of wrong, D. 27.7 ; δύο ταῦτα ὡσπερεὶ κ. ἐφ' ἅπασι . . ἐπέθηκε Id. 21.18 . chapter, section, PGnom.Prooem., Ammon. in Int. 1.17 , al., Chor.in Hermes 17.223 ; distd. from τίτλος, Suid. s.h.v.

lsj_entry_text: ὀξύς, εῖα, ύ, Ion. fem. ὀξέα Hdt. 9.23 , al., v.l. in Hp. Mul. 1.64 , al. (in codd. freq. ὀξέη, and so Babr. 73.1 metri gr.) : ὀξεῖα, poet. for neut. pl. ὀξέα, Hes. Sc. 348 :—sharp, keen, whether of a point or an edge, in Hom. and Hes. mostly of weapons or anything made of metal, ἄκων Il. 10.335 , al.; ἄορ 21.173 , Hes. Sc. 457 ; βέλος Il. 4.185 , etc.; also of non-metallic substances, λᾶας 16.739 ; μοχλός Od. 9.382 ; σκόλοπες Il. 12.56 , 64 ; ὀξεῖα κορυφή, of a mountain-peak, Od. 12.74 ; so πάγοι ὀξέες 5.411 ; λίθος ὀξὺς πεποιημένος sharpened so as to serve as a knife, Hdt. 7.69 , cf. 3.8 ; κυρβασίας ἐς ὀξὺ ἀπηγμένας brought to a point, Id. 7.64 ; ὄρεα ἐς ὀ. τὰς κορυφὰς ἀ. Id. 2.28 ; τὸ ὀ. the apex of a triangle, ib. 16 ; of the heart, Arist. Resp. 478b5 ; τὸ ὀ. τοῦ ᾠοῦ Id. GA 752b8 ; ὀ. γωνία an acute angle, Id. Top. 107a16 , al., Euc. 1 Def. 12 , Archim. Spir. 16 ; Χρόνος ὀξὺς ὀδόντας Simon. 176 ; ἡ ὀξεῖα, name of a surgical instrument, Hermes 38.282 , Heliod. ap. Orib. 44.23.59 ; but also, a pointed splinter of bone, ib. 46.20.5 . in reference to the senses, of feeling, sharp, keen, ὀδύναι Il. 11.268 ; ὀ. ἠέλιος the piercing sun, h.Ap. 374 ; ὀξειᾶν ἀκτίνων πατήρ, i.e. the Sun, Pi. O. 7.70 ; Σείριος ὀξὺς ἐλλάμπων Archil. 61 ; πῦρ ὀ. Anaxipp. 1.12 ; so χιὼν ὀξεῖα Pi. P. 1.20 ; so also of grief and the like , ἄχος Il. 19.125 ; μελεδῶναι Od. 19.517 : and generally, sharp, severe, μάχη ὀξέα . . γίνεται keenly contested, Hdt. 9.23 ; ὀ. πυρετός Hp. VM 16 ( Sup. ); [ἡ νόσοσ] ὀξεῖα φοιτᾷ καὶ ταχεῖ' ἀπέρχεται S. Ph. 808 ; νόσοι, μανίαι, Pi. O. 8.85 , N. 11.48 ( Comp. ), cf. Hp. Acut. tit., Archig. ap. Gal. 9.887 ; πάθαι Pi. P. 3.97 ; ἐπιμομφά Id. O. 10(11).9 , etc. of the sight, ὀξύτατον ὄμμα Id. N. 10.62 ; ὄψις . . ὀξυτάτη τῶν διὰ τοῦ σώματος . . αἰσθήσεων Pl. Phdr. 250d : freq. in neut. as Adv., ὀξύτατον δέρκεσθαι to be keenest of sight, Il. 17.675 ; ὀξύτατα καθορᾶν Pl. R. 516c ; so ὀξὺ νοεῖν notice a thing sharply, Il. 3.374 ; ὀξὺ προϊδεῖν Od. 5.393 ; ὀξύτερον βλέπει Ar. Pl. 1048 , Lys. 1202 (lyr.) : prov., ὀξύτερον τοῦ Λυγκέως βλέπειν Id. Pl. 210 , cf. Macar. Prov. 6.41 ; also ὀξὺ ἄκουσεν heard with sharp ear, Il. 17.256 , cf. Pl. Lg. 927b ; ὀξεῖαν ἀκοὴν . . λόγοις διδούς keen attention, S. El. 30 . of things that affect the sight, dazzling, bright, αὐγὴ Ἠελίου Il. 17.372 ; [Ἠελίου] ὀξύτατον πέλεται φάος εἰσοράασθαι 14.345 : hence of colours, Ar. Pax 1173 (v. φοινικίς 2 ) ; αἱ ὀξεῖαι χροιαί Arist. Phgn. 806b4 ; πορφύρα Plu. Cat.Mi. 6 , PHolm. 20.36 ; [ἐσθὴσ] ὀξυτέρα καὶ τηλαυγεστέρα Ael. NA 4.46 . of sound, shrill, piercing, ἀϋτή Il. 15.313 ; ὀξὺ βοήσας 17.89 ; ὀξὺ δὲ κωκύσασα 18.71 ; ὀξὺ λεληκώς 22.141 ; ὀξέα κεκληγώς 17.88 , etc.; of whinnying horses, ὀξεῖα χρέμισαν Hes. Sc. 348 ; of young pigs, ὀξὺ κεκράγατε Ar. Ach. 804 ; of the scream of birds of prey, ὀξέα κλάζων S. Ant. 112 (anap.) ; of metals, ἰάχεσκε σάκος ὀξέα καὶ λιγέως Hes. Sc. 233 ; also of the wail of the nightingale (cf. ὀξύφωνος), ὄρνιθος ὀ. φθόγγον S. Ant. 424 ; so ἐπηλάλαξαν τὸν ὀ. νόμον shrieked their shrill song, A. Th. 952 (lyr.) ; ὀξὺ μέλος, of the grasshopper, Ar. Av. 1095 (lyr.). of musical tones, in a technical sense, high-pitched, opp. βαρύς, φθόγγοι Pl. Ti. 80a , X. Cyn. 6.20 ; ὀξυτάτη χορδή Pl. Phdr. 268d ; φωνὴ ὀξεῖα, βαρεῖα, μέση Arist. Rh. 1403b29 ; τῷ ὀξεῖ ἐν φωνῇ μὲν ἐναντίον τὸ βαρύ, ἐν ὄγκῳ δὲ τὸ ἀμβλύ Id. Top. 106a13 . in Music, δι' ὀξειῶν ( Dor. -ᾶν) interval of a fifth, Philol. 6 , Arist. Pr. 920a24 . ἡ ὀξεῖα (sc. προσῳδία) the acute accent, D.T. 630.1 , A.D. Pron. 35.10 , al.; τὸν τόνον φυλάσσειν ὀ. ib. 60.1 ; ὀ. συλλαβή Pl. Cra. 399b ; ὀ. στοιχεῖον S.E. M. 1.113 . of taste, sharp, pungent, acid, φακῆ X. Cyr. 6.2.31 ; ὄξος Diph. 18.1 ; οἶνος Alex. 141.12 ; ἐξ ὀξέος καὶ ἁλμυροῦ ξυνθεὶς ζύμωμα Pl. Ti. 74c . of smell, Arist. de An. 421a30 ; ὀξύτατον ὄζειν τινός Ar. Ach. 193 . metaph., of the inner sense, sharp, keen, hasty, esp. quick to anger, passionate, epith. of Ares, Il. 2.440 ,al. ; μένος ὀξύ h.Hom. 8.14 ; καρδίη ὀξυτέρη Thgn. 366 ; θυμὸς ὀ. S. OC 1193 ; νέος καὶ ὀ. Pl. Grg. 463e ; οἱ ἀκρόχολοι ὀξεῖς Arist. EN 1126a18 : so in ὀξύ-θυμος, -κάρδιος, -χολος. sharp, quick, δεινοὶ καὶ ὀξεῖς Pl. Ap. 39b : c. inf., ἐπινοῆσαι ὀ. Th. 1.70 ; γνῶναι . . ὀξύτατοι τὰ ῥηθέντα D. 3.15 ; also εἰς πάντα τὰ μαθήματα ὀξεῖς Pl. R. 526b ; τὰς ἐνθυμήσεις ὀξύς Luc. Salt. 81 . of motion, quick, swift, post- Hom. , ὀξυτάτους ἵππους Hdt. 5.9 ( v.l. ὠκυτάτους ) ; ἱερακίσκος Ar. Av. 1112 ; ὀξυτέρῳ χαλινῷ S. Ant. 108 (lyr.) ; of a report, ὀξεῖα βάξις διῆλθ' Ἀχαιούς Id. Aj. 998 ; ὀξεῖαν ἐκβάλλει ῥοήν, of a dying man, Id. Ant. 1238 , cf. A. Ag. 1389 ; of a flame, fierce, Thphr. HP 5.9.3 ; ᾄξας ὀξὺς νότος ὥς S. Aj. 258 (anap.) ; τὸ εὔψυχον . . ὀξεῖς ἐνδείκνυνται are quick in displaying, Th. 4.126 ; opp. βραδύς, Id. 8.96 ; opp. ῥάθυμος, Arist. EE 1240a2 ; opp. ἡσύχιος, Id. EN 1116a9 ; ὀ. παράγγελμα Onos. 10.2 ; ὀ. καιρός an urgent crisis, Id. 6.1 , al.; ὁ ὀ. δρόμος the express post, POxy. 900.7 (iv A. D.), 2115.6 (iv A. D.) ; ὀξεῖς οἱ πόδες αὐτῶν ἐκχέαι αἷμα Ep.Rom. 3.15 : esp. in Adv. (v. infr.). regul. Adv. ὀξέως quickly, soon, βοηθεῖν, μεταχειρίσαι, Th. 6.10 , 12 , etc.; sharply, ὁρᾶν, αἰσθάνεσθαι, Pl. R. 567b , Phdr. 263c ; poet. ὀξείως Epigr.Gr. 986.3 (Philae) : Comp. ὀξυτέρως Hp. Epid. 3.17 .β' ; ὀξυτέρως ἀποθῄνσκειν ib. 1.2 ; but, neut. ὀξύ and pl. ὀξέα as Adv., v. supr. 11.2 , 3 : Comp. ὀξύτερον Th. 2.8 , Pl. Tht. 190a : Sup. ὀξύτατον Il. 17.675 , Pl. Lg. 741d ; or ὀξύτατα Id. R. 401e , al. (Cf. ὀξίνα, ὄκρις.)

lsj_entry_text: μέλας ( μέλας Rhian. 58 , where μέγας is corrupt for μέλας), μέλαινα, μέλαν; gen. μέλανος, μελαίνης, μέλανος, etc.; Ep. dat. μείλανι (metri gr.) Il. 24.79 : Aeol. nom. μέλαις, from Μέλανς, Choerob. in Theod. 1.123 , Greg.Cor. p.599 S. , hence restored in Sapph. 57 :—black, dark: in Hom. generally, dark in colour, οἶνος Od. 5.265 ; μέλαν αἷμα, κῦμα, Il. 4.149 , 23.693 ; γαῖα μέλαινα 2.699 , cf. Sapph. Supp. 5.2 ; ὕδωρ μέλαν Αἰσήποιο Il. 2.825 , cf. Od. 4.359 , νηῦς μ., from its being pitched over, Il. 1.300 , al.; of men, dark, swarthy, μέλανας δὲ ἀνδρικοὺς ἰδεῖν Pl. R. 474e ; ἰσχυρός τις ἦν, μ. D. 21.71 ; τὰ μ. black marks about the ears of dogs, X. Cyn. 5.23 . dark, murky, ἕσπερος Od. 1.423 ; εὐφρόνα Pi. N. 7.3 . metaph., black, dark, θάνατος Il. 2.834 , etc.; κήρ ib. 859 , etc.; ὀδύναι 4.117 , etc. (the origin of the metaphor is seen in the phrases θανάτου μ. νέφος, ἄχεος νεφέλη μ., 16 . 350 , 18.22 ); μ. τύχα, ἀρά, A. Supp. 89 (lyr.), Th. 832 (lyr.); Ἐρινύς ib. 993 (lyr.), cf. Eu. 52 ; ἄτα Id. Ag. 769 (lyr.); Ἄρης ib. 1511 (lyr.); Ἅιδης S. OT 29 ; Ἅιδου μ. ἀνάγκα E. Hipp. 1388 (lyr.), etc.; ἡμέραι μέλαιναι, = Lat. dies atri, Plu. Luc. 27 . of the voice, indistinct, Arist. Top. 106a25 , Philostr. VA 4.44 ; βραχὺ καὶ μ. φώνημα, of Nero, D.C. 61.20 . dark, obscure, enigmatical, ἱστορίη AP 11.347 ( Phil. ). of character, dark, malignant, μ. φρήν, καρδία, Sol. 42.4 , Pi. Fr. 123.4 ; μ. ἄνθρωποι Plu. 2.12d ; μ. ἦθος M. Ant. 4.28 . Comp. μελάντερος, α, ον , blacker, very black, τοῦ δ' οὔ τι μελάντερον ἔπλετο ἔσθος Il. 24.94 : prov. of thick darkness, [νέφοσ] μελάντερον ἠΰτε πίσσα (v. ἠΰτε) 4.277 : Sup. μελάντατος Hp. VC 14 , Ar. Fr. 580 , etc.:— Comp. also μελανώτερος Str. 16.4.12 : Sup. μελαινότατος AP 11.68 ( Lucill. ), Epigr.Gr. 320.4 (Thyatira). μέλαινα (sc. νοῦσος), ἡ, Medic., of diseases causing black secretions (such as melaena), Hp. Morb. 2.73 . μέλαν, τό , v. sub voc. (Cf. Skt. málam 'dirt', malinás 'dirty', Lett. melns 'black'.)

lsj_entry_text: ἐναντίος, α, ον, opposite, = ἀντίος (which is rare in Prose): of Place, on the opposite side, opposite, c.dat., ἀκταὶ ἐναντίαι ἀλλήλῃσιν Od. 10.89 ; Πάτροκλος δέ οἱ . . ἐ. ἧστο Il. 9.190 , cf. Od. 23.89 : hence, fronting, face to face, αὐτῳ οὔ πω φαίνετ' ἐναντίη 6.329 ; ὄττις ἐ. τοι ἰσδάνει Sapph. 2.2 ; δεῖξον . . τὸ σὸν πρόσωπον δεῦρ' ἐ. πατρί before him, E. Hipp. 947 ; τὰναντία τινί things open to one's sight, X. Cyr. 3.3.345 : abs., ἐ. στάνθ' E. Hipp. 1078 (but ἐ. κεῖσθαι look opposite ways, Pl. Smp. 190a ). with Verbs of motion, in the opposite direction, ἔνθα οἱ . . ἐναντίη ἤλυθε μήτηρ came to meet him, Il. 6.251 ; ἐναντίοι ἀλλήλοισιν ὄγμον ἐλαύνωσιν 11.67 ; δύο ἅμαξαι ἐ. ἀλλήλαις Th. 1.93 ; ἄνεμος ἐ. ἔπνει X. An. 4.5.3 . Astrol., in diametrical aspect, Vett.Val. 70.16 , Man. 3.360 . in hostile sense, opposing, facing in fight, c. gen., ἐναντίοι ἔσταν Ἀχαιῶν Il. 5.497 , cf. S. Aj. 1284 , X. An. 4.3.28 , etc.: c. dat., Il. 5.12 , E. Supp. 856 , IT 1415 ; οἱ ἐ. one's adversaries, A. Th. 375 , Gorg. Fr. 12 D. , etc.; the enemy, Hdt. 7.225 , Th. 4.64 , etc. generally, opposed to, τινί X. An. 3.2.10 ; τὸ ἐ. the opposite party, Id. Ath. 1.4 ; presenting obstacles, hindering, τινί S. Ph. 642 . ὁ δι ἐναντίας the opponent in a alawsuit, PFlor. 1.58.15 (iii A.D.), etc. of qualities, acts, etc., opposite, contrary, reverse, τἀναντί' εἰπεῖν A. Ag. 1373 ; δίκαια καὶ τἀναντία S. Ant. 667 : mostly c.gen., τὰ ἐ. τούτων the very reverse of these things, Hdt. 1.82 , cf. Th. 7.75 , etc.; δείξας . . ἄστρων τὴν ἐ. ὁδόν, i.e. τὴν τοῦ ἡλίου ὁδὸν ἐ. οὖσαν τοῖς ἄστροις E. Fr. 861 : also c. dat., Ὀρφεῖ δὲ γλῶσσαν τὴν ἐναντίαν ἔχεις A. Ag. 1629 ; τἀναντία πρήσσειν [τῇ ὑγιείῃ] Democr. 234 ; δύο τὰ -ώτατα εὐβουλίᾳ Th. 3.42 ; ἀγαθῷ κακὸν -ώτερον ἢ τῷ μὴ ἀγαθῷ Pl. R. 491d ; ἐναντία λέγει αὐτὸς αὑτῷ Id. Prt. 339b , cf. Ar. Ach. 493 ; τἀναντία τούτοις Pl. Prt 323d ; ἐναντία γνῶναι ταῖς πλείσταις [πόλεσιν] X. Lac. 1.2 ; τὴν ἐ. τινὶ ψῆφον θέσθαι D. 19.65 ; simply τὴν ἐ. θέσθαι τινί Pl. La. 184d : folld. by ἤ, τοὺς ἐ. λόγους ἢ ὡς αὐτὸς κατεδόκεε Hdt. 1.22 ; τοὐ. δρῶν ἢ προσῆκ' αὐτῷ ποιεῖν Ar. Pl. 14 ; τοὐ. ἔπαθεν ἢ τὸ προσδοκώμενον Pl. Lg. 966e , cf. R. 567c , etc.: freq. strengthd., πᾶν τοὐ., πάντα τἀ., quite the contrary, Lg. 967a , X. Mem. 3.12.4 ; πολὺ τοὐ. Stratt. 57 ; τὸ δὲ πολὺ ἐναντίον ἀποβήσεται Pl. Ap. 39c . τὰ ἐ. opposites in Philos., Pherecyd.Syr. 3 , Arist. Metaph. 986b3 , etc. in the Philos. of Arist. , τἀναντία (dist. fr. other ἀντικείμενα, Metaph. 1018a25 ) are contraries, esp. the two attributes within the same genus which differ most widely from each other (as hot and cold), Cat. 6a18 , al. ἐ. ἀποφάνσεις, προτάσεις, contrary propositions (All B is A, No B is A), opp. contradictory (v. ἀντιφατικῶς), Id. Int. 17b4 , APr. 63b28 . freq. in Adv. usages: from Hom. downwds., neut. ἐναντίον as Adv., opposite, facing, ἐ. ὧδε κάλεσσον here to my face, Od. 17.544 ; εἰς ὦπα ἰδέσθαι ἐ. to look one in the face, 23.107 ; ἐ. προσβλέπειν τινά E. Hec. 968 , etc.; γυναῖκας ἀνδρῶν μὴ βλέπειν ἐ. ib. 975 : abs., D. 4.40 , etc.: hence, like a Prep. c. gen., in the presence of, τῆς βουλῆς IG 12.91 ; τῶνδ' ἐ. S. OC 1002 ; μαρτύρων ἐ. Ar. Ec. 448 ; ἐ. τοῦ παιδίου Id. Lys. 907 ; ἐ. ἁπάντων λέγειν Th. 6.25 ; ἐ. Διός Plb. 7.9.2 ; also neut. pl., IG 7.1779 (Thespiae). in hostile sense, against, c. gen., ἀνέσταν . . σφοῦ πατρὸς ἐ. Il. 1.534 ; ἐ. ἰέναι τινός 21.574 ; ἐ. μάχεσθαί τινος 20.97 ; ἐ. ἵστασ' ἐμεῖο 13.448 : abs., ἐ. μίμνειν stand one's ground against, ib. 106 : c. dat., νεικεῖν ἀλλήλοισιν ἐ. 20.252 ; ἐ. θεοῖς E. Or. 624 ; ἐ. τῷ ὅρκῳ πράττειν IG 22.1258.2 . contrariwise, in Att. also with the Art., τοὐναντίον on the other hand, τοὐ. δέ . . Antiph. 80.4 ; ἢ πάλιν τοὐ. Men. 460.5 ; conversely, Pl. Men. 89e . neut. pl. ἐναντία as Adv., c. dat., Hdt. 6.32 , Th. 1.29 , etc. with Preps., ἐκ τοῦ ἐ. over against, opposite, opp. ἐκ πλαγίου, X. HG 4.5.15 , etc.; ἐξ ἐναντίας, Ion. -ίης, Hdt. 7.225 , Th. 4.33 (οἱ ἐξ ἐ. the opposing parties, prob. in PGrenf. 2.78.26 (iv A. D.)); ἐκ τῶν ἐ. on the contrary, Plb. 5.9.9 ; ἀπ' ἐναντίας Ascl. Tact. 1.2 ; ἀπ' ἐ. Χωρεῖν Procop. Arc. 4 ; κατὰ τὰ ἐ. Pl. Ti. 39a : Geom., αἱ κατ' ἐναντίον τοῦ παραλληλογράμμου πλευραί the opposite sides of the parallelogram, Archim. greek_sentence: [694] Ὅτι μὲν τὸ ὄξος τὰ νεῦρα βλάπτειν πέφυκεν ἥ τε πεῖρα μαρτυρεῖ καὶ ὁ λόγος δείκνυσιν· ἄναιμα γὰρ ὄντα καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ψυχρὰ πάσχει ῥᾳδίως ὑπὸ τοῦ ψύχοντός τε ἅμα καὶ λεπτομεροῦς φαρμάκου βλάπτεται μὲν γὰρ καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων τῶν ψυχόντων, ἀλλὰ τὸ τῆς τοῦ ὄξους οὐσίας λεπτομερὲς, εἰς τὸ βάθος αὐτῶν δύεται καὶ διεξέρχεται διὰ παντὸς μέρους, ὡς μηδὲν μηδὲ τοὐλάχιστον ἀβλαβὲς ἐᾷν.
english_sentence_A: [694] That vinegar is by nature such as to harm the sinews, both experience bears witness and reason demonstrates: for being bloodless, and on that account cold, they are easily affected by a drug that is at once cooling and fine-parted. For they are harmed also by all the other cooling agents, but the fine-parted quality of the substance of vinegar sinks into their depth and passes through every part, so as to leave nothing, not even the least portion, unharmed.
english_sentence_B: For since they are bloodless, and for this reason cold, they are readily affected by a drug that is at once cooling and composed of fine parts. They are harmed, indeed, by all the other cooling things as well; but the fine-partedness of the substance of vinegar sinks into their depth and passes through every part, so as to leave not even the smallest part unharmed.

greek_sentence: οὕτω μὲν ὄξος τὰ νευρώδη μόρια βλάπτει· τὴν μήτραν δ᾿ ἅπαντες σχεδὸν οἱ ἀνατομικοὶ λέγουσιν εἶναι νευρώδη· καὶ χωρὶς δὲ τῆς ἐκείνων ἀποφάσεως, ἣν ἐκ τῆς ἀνατομικῆς αὐτοψίας ἐποιήσαντο, πάρεστί σοι συλλογίσασθαι περὶ αὐτῆς, ὡς ἐπὶ πλεῖστον μὲν διαστελλομένης, εἰς ἐλάχιστον δὲ συνιζανούσης· ἀεὶ γὰρ ὁπηλίκον ἂν εἴη τὸ ἔμβρυον, ἐν κύκλῳ περιείληφεν αὐτὸ καὶ πεπλήρωται τὸ πᾶν κύτος ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνου, κᾂν μικρὸν ᾖ, καθάπερ καὶ ἡ γαστὴρ ὑπὸ τῶν σιτίων· ἀλλὰ ταύτης μὲν οὐ μεγάλη πρὸς τἀναντία ἡ μεταβολὴ, τῆς μήτρας δὲ μέγισται· τὸ δὲ ἐπὶ πλεῖστον [695] διαστέλλεσθαι νευρωδῶν ἴδιόν ἐστι σωμάτων, οὐ σαρκωδῶν.
english_sentence_A: Thus vinegar harms the sinewy parts; and nearly all the anatomists say that the womb is sinewy. And even apart from their pronouncement, which they made on the basis of anatomical direct inspection (autopsia), it is open to you to reason about it from the fact that it is dilated to the greatest extent and shrinks together to the least: for always, however large the embryo may be, it encloses it in a circle and its whole cavity is filled by it, even if it is small, just as the stomach also is by foods; but in the case of the stomach the change toward the opposite states is not great, whereas in the case of the womb the changes are very great; and being dilated to the greatest extent [695] is a property peculiar to sinewy bodies, not to fleshy ones.
english_sentence_B: Even apart from their pronouncement, which they made from first-hand anatomical observation, you can reason it out about the uterus, since it dilates to the greatest extent and contracts to the smallest. For however large the embryo may be at any time, the uterus always encloses it all round, and its whole cavity is filled by it even when it is small, just as the stomach is filled by foods.

greek_sentence: Οὔτε τμητικὸν ἔχει τι τὸ ὕδωρ, ὥσπερ τὸ ὄξος, ἀλλ᾿ οὔτε θερμὸν, ὥσπερ τὸ μέλι (τούτῳ μέν γε πρὸς τῷ θερμαίνειν ἔτι καὶ τὸ ῥύπτειν καὶ τέμνειν ὑπάρχει)· βραδύπορον οὖν εἰκότως ἐστὶ καὶ δύσπεπτον καὶ δυσυποβίβαστον ἅπαν τὸ ὕδωρ, κᾂν ἄλλως ἄριστόν τε καὶ ἄμεμπτον ᾖ· τὸ γὰρ ἰλυῶδες ἢ δυσῶδες ἢ ἁλικὸν ἤ τινος ἑτέρας φαρμακώδους ποιότητος ἔμφασιν ἔχον οὐχ ἁπλῶς ὕδωρ ἐστὶν, ἀλλὰ μετὰ τοιοῦδέ τινος ἐπιμιξίας φαρμάκου· καθάπερ καὶ εἰ μέλι μοχθηρὸν ἢ πτισάνην ἢ ὄξος ἢ οἶνον ἤ τι τοιοῦτον προχειρίσαιο· μέμψῃ γὰρ οὐχ ὅλον ἐπ᾿ ἐκείνου τὸ γένος, ἀλλ᾿ αὐτὸ μόνον ὃ μεταχειρίζῃ.

english_sentence_A: So far, then, as depends on these considerations, one would never use it; yet other physicians do use it, and indeed Hippocrates himself too, but he less, the others more.
english_sentence_B: So far, then, as these considerations go, one would never use it. Yet other physicians do use it, and indeed so does Hippocrates himself, but he less and the others more.

lsj_entry_text: ἀποτυχ-ία, Ion. -ιη, ἡ, failure, Democr. 243 , Din. 1.29 (as v.l.), Plb. 5.98.5 , Phld. Rh. 1.73 S. , J. AJ 16.9.1 , etc.: c. gen., failure to obtain, στεφάνου, ὕδατος, Artem. 5.78 .
greek_sentence: ἐκ γὰρ τοῦ χρῆσθαι τοῖς ἄλλοις κακῶς σφαλλόμενοι, καταφεύγουσιν ἐπὶ τὸ ὕδωρ, οὐκ ἔχον μεγάλην ἀποτυχίαν, ὅτι μηδὲ τὴν δύναμιν· οὕτω γὰρ ὁ Ἐρασίστρατος ἔλεγεν· ἰσχυραὶ δυνάμεις σίτων τε καὶ πομάτων ἐγκαίρως μὲν παραλαμβανόμεναι μεγίστην ὠφέλειαν, ἀκαίρως δὲ μεγίστην βλάβην.
english_sentence_A: For, going astray as a result of using the other drinks badly, they take refuge in water, which does not involve great failure, since it does not have great power either; for so Erasistratus used to say: strong powers of foods and drinks, when taken at the right moment, bring the greatest benefit, but when at the wrong moment, the greatest harm.
english_sentence_B: For, coming to grief through using the other things badly, they take refuge in water, which does not entail any great failure, since it does not have any great power either. For so Erasistratus used to say: strong powers of foods and drinks, when taken at the right time, bring the greatest benefit, but when taken at the wrong time, the greatest harm.

greek_sentence: ἣν δέ φημι μοχθηρὰν εἶναι χρῆσιν ὀξυμέλιτός τε καὶ μελικράτου καὶ οἴνου, γίνεται μὲν καὶ διὰ τὰς ἀθρόας μεταβολὰς, ὡς αὐτὸς ἐδίδαξεν· γίνεται δὲ καὶ διὰ τὴν μίξιν ἄκρατον ὑπὸ τῶν ἰατρῶν γιγνομένην, ὡς τὸ πολύ.
english_sentence_A: And the use of oxymel and melikraton and wine which I say is bad arises both on account of the sudden, wholesale changes, as he himself taught, and also on account of the mixture being made unmixed by the physicians, as is for the most part the case.
english_sentence_B: The use of oxymel, melicrat and wine that I say is bad comes about partly through abrupt changes, as he himself taught, and partly through the mixing, which physicians for the most part make undiluted.

lsj_entry_text: πρεσβύτης [υ], ητος, Dor. πρέσβυ-ας, ατος, ἡ, age, seniority, Test.Epict. 4.28 , 6.29 : opp. νεότας, prob. rest. in IG 5(1).1427.5 (Messene).
greek_sentence: διδόντος οὖν ἐμοῦ πρεσβύτῃ νοσοῦντι καθ᾿ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν οἴνου ὑδατώδους, παραγινόμενός τις τῶν τοιούτων ἰατρῶν, εἶτ᾿ ἰδὼν ἐλάχιστον ἐπισταζόμενον αὐτοῦ τῷ ὕδατι γελάσας ἔφη μὴ πίνειν οἴνου [699] τὸν ἄῤῥωστον, ἀλλ᾿ ὁρᾷν μόνον, οὐκ ἐννοῶν ὅτι τὸ μὲν ἡδονῆς ἕνεκα τὸν οἶνον διδόναι ἑτέραν ἔχει συμμετρίαν τῆς πρὸς ὕδωρ αὐτοῦ μίξεως, τὸ δ᾿ ὠφελείας ἄλλην.
english_sentence_A: So when I was giving an old man who was ill a watery wine each day, one of such physicians came by and, on seeing a very small amount of it being dripped into the water, laughed and said that the sick man was not drinking wine [699] but only looking at it, not understanding that giving wine for the sake of pleasure has one proportion for its mixture with water, and giving it for the sake of benefit another.
english_sentence_B: So, when I was giving an old man who was sick watery wine every day, one of physicians of this kind came by. Seeing a very small amount of it being dripped into the water, he laughed and said that the patient was not drinking the wine [699] but only looking at it.

greek_sentence: καὶ μελικράτῳ δ᾿ ἄν τις ἀκινδυνότερον χρῷτο τῷ ὑδαρεῖ· τὸ γὰρ ἄκρατον εἰ μὴ φθάσειεν ὑπαγαγεῖν τὴν γαστέρα, βλαβερώτερον γίγνεται καὶ μάλιστ᾿ ἐν τοῖς πικροχόλοις τε καὶ μεγαλοσπλάγχνοις, ἐφ᾿ ὧν καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ ἐστὶ βλαβερὸν, ὅταν ἐκχολωθῇ μεῖναν ἐπὶ πλέον ἐν τοῖς ὑποχονδρίοις· πρὸς γὰρ δὴ τούτοις ἅπασιν οἷς ἔχει κακοῖς ἔτι καὶ ἄκοπρον ὃν, οὐδ᾿ ὑπαγωγήν τινα [700] τῆς γαστρὸς ἐργάζεται.
english_sentence_A: And one would also use melikraton with less danger in its watery form; for the unmixed kind, if it does not first move the belly downward, becomes more harmful, and especially in the bitter-bilious and in those with large viscera, in whom water too is harmful, when it turns to bile after remaining too long in the hypochondria; for indeed, in addition to all the evils it has, being also free of fecal residue (ἄκοπρον), it does not even produce any downward movement [700] of the belly.
english_sentence_B: One would also use melicrat with less danger if it is watery; for the unmixed kind, if it does not first succeed in drawing the belly downward, becomes rather harmful, and especially in the bitter-bilious and in those with enlarged viscera (μεγαλοσπλάγχνοις). In these, water too is harmful, when, remaining for a longer time in the hypochondria, it turns bilious; for in addition to all the evils it has, it is also without faecal effect (ἄκοπρον) and produces no loosening [700] of the belly.

greek_sentence: ὅταν ἐπὶ μόνῳ ποτῷ ὁ κάμνων διαιτώμενος ᾖ, μηδέπω χυλὸν πτισάνης λαμβάνων· τότε γὰρ μεταξὺ τῶν ἄλλων ποτῶν ὕδωρ ἄν τις ἐν καιρῷ προσφέροι, καὶ μάλισθ᾿ ὅταν ὁ κάμνων ᾖ διψώδης.
english_sentence_A: When the patient is being kept on a regimen of drink alone, not yet taking the juice of ptisane; for then one might administer water opportunely between the other drinks, and especially when the patient is thirsty.
english_sentence_B: When the patient is being dieted on drink alone, not yet taking ptisan juice; for then one might at the right moment offer water between the other drinks, and especially when the patient is thirsty.

greek_sentence: πλημμυρίδα γάρ τινα ποιεῖν αὐτό φησι, τουτέστι πλῆθος ὑγροῦ τινος· διὸ καὶ μεταξὺ μελικράτου τε καὶ ὀξυμέλιτος δίδωσιν ὀλίγον, εἰς ὑγρότητα τοῖς ἀναπτυσθησομένοις συντελές.
english_sentence_A: For he says that it produces a certain flood (πλημμυρίδα), that is, an abundance of some moisture; for this reason he also gives a little of it between melikraton and oxymel, as contributing moistness to what is going to be expectorated.
english_sentence_B: For he says that it produces a kind of flood (πλημμυρίδα), that is, an abundance of some moisture; therefore he also gives a little between melicrat and oxymel, as it contributes moisture to what is going to be coughed up.

greek_sentence: Ὑποπτεύσαντι μέντοι ἐν ταύτῃσι τῇσι νούσοισιν ἢ καρηβαρίην ἰσχυρὴν ἢ φρενῶν ἅψιν, παντάπασιν οἴνου ἀποσχετέον, [701] ὕδατι δὲ ἐν τῷ τοιῷδε χρηστέον ἢ ὑδαρέα καὶ κιῤῥὸν παντελῶς δοτέον οἶνον καὶ ἄοσμον παντάπασι καὶ μετὰ τὴν πόσιν αὐτοῦ ὕδωρ μεταποτέον ὀλίγον· οὕτω γὰρ ἂν ἧσσον τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ οἴνου μένος ἅπτοιτο τῆς κεφαλῆς καὶ γνώμης.
english_sentence_A: If, however, in these diseases one suspects either a severe heaviness of the head or a touching of the phrenes, one must abstain from wine altogether, [701] and in such a case one must use water, or give a wine that is watery and altogether tawny and entirely without bouquet, and after the drinking of it a little water must be drunk afterwards; for in this way the force from the wine would less touch the head and the mind.
english_sentence_B: "However, if in these diseases one suspects either a severe heaviness of the head or a laying hold of the phrenes, one must abstain from wine altogether, [701] and in such a case one must use water, or else give wine that is diluted and entirely tawny and wholly without bouquet, and after the drinking of it one must drink a little water afterwards; for in this way the strength from the wine would lay hold less of the head and of the understanding." The phrenes are said to be laid hold of at the time when the patient, being feverish, is delirious; and so now too he has called delirium a "laying hold of the phrenes", in which he bids one avoid wine, and likewise also in severe headaches; about both, it has been said earlier.

english_sentence_A: As for his advice that, whenever we do at some point give wine to those in such a condition, water should be drunk immediately afterwards, he counselled this safely; for thus, he says, the strength (menos) from the wine—which is its force—would lay hold less of the head and the mind [702]; saying "would lay hold" (haptoito) in accordance with his customary usage, and making clear that he also formed the expression "laying hold of the phrenes" (hapsis of the phrenes) from this verb, which is more familiar to people than the noun "hapsis." He said that the wine lays hold of the head and the mind because, being hot, it is itself quickly carried up to the head and carries up along with it the humours that are boiling in the body.
english_sentence_B: He said that the wine lays hold of the head and the judgement because, being hot, it is itself quickly carried up to the head, and it carries up along with it the humours that are boiling in the body.

greek_sentence: Ἐν οἷσι δὲ μάλιστα αὐτῶν ὕδατι ποτῷ χρηστέον καὶ ὁκότε πολλῷ κάρτα καὶ ὅκου μετρίῳ καὶ ὅκου ψυχρῷ καὶ ὅκου θερμῷ, τὰ μέν που καὶ πρόσθεν εἰρέαται, τὰ δὲ ἐν αὐτέοισι τοῖσι καιροῖσι ῥηθήσεται.
english_sentence_A: In which of these cases water is especially to be used as a drink, and when in very great quantity, and where in moderate quantity, and where cold and where hot—some of these things have, I suppose, been stated earlier, and the others will be stated at the appropriate occasions themselves.
english_sentence_B: 'In which of these cases water should above all be used as drink, and when in very great quantity, and where in moderate quantity, and where cold, and where hot: some of this has been stated earlier, and the rest will be stated at the proper occasions themselves.'

greek_sentence: Ἐρασίστρατος μὲν ἐν τοῖς περὶ πυρετῶν κακοήθως [703] πάνυ διαβάλλει τὸν Ἱπποκράτην, τοὺς μαθητὰς αὐτοῦ δῆθεν μεμφόμενος Ἀπολλώνιόν τε καὶ Δέξιππον, οὕς φησι κηρίνους κυάθους δώδεκα ποιήσαντας εἰς τὸν ἑκτημορίτην τῆς κοτύλης κύαθον, ἕνα τούτων ἢ δύο ἀπομετρεῖν τοῖς πυρέττουσιν· ὁ δ᾿ Ἱπποκράτης οὐκ ἐνταῦθα μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἔμπροσθεν εὔδηλός ἐστι δαψιλέσι χρώμενος ἅπασι τοῖς ποτοῖς, νυνὶ δὲ καὶ διὰ τῆς λέξεως σαφῶς ἐδήλωσεν εἰπών· οἷσι δὲ μάλιστα αὐτῶν ὕδατι χρηστέον καὶ ὁπότε κάρτα πολλῷ.

english_sentence_A: But Hippocrates, not only here but also from what precedes, is quite clearly using all drinks in abundance; and now he has shown it plainly through his very wording, when he said: "in which of them especially water should be used, and when in very large quantity." For "very large quantity" (κάρτα πολλῷ) means "exceedingly large quantity"; and it would have sufficed, for the refutation of Erasistratus' malice, to say that water is sometimes given in large quantity, even without adding the "very" (κάρτα) — Erasistratus, who mentions Apollonius and Dexippus while having no book of theirs to show, yet does not hear Hippocrates himself saying plainly that one should sometimes use water in very large quantity.

And now he has also shown it plainly through his wording, saying: 'in which cases of them one should most of all use water, and when very copious.' For 'very copious' (κάρτα πολλῷ) indicates 'exceedingly copious.' To refute the malice of Erasistratus it would have been enough to say that the water is sometimes given copiously, without adding 'very.' Erasistratus mentions Apollonius and Dexippus, though he can show no book of theirs, yet does not hear Hippocrates himself saying clearly that one should sometimes use water very copiously.

greek_sentence: καὶ μέντοι καὶ ἀνωτέρω μετ᾿ ὀξυμέλιτος αὐτὸ διδοὺς ἔφη χρήσιμον εἶναι, ὅτι πλημμυρίδα τινὰ ἐμποιέει, τουτέστι πλῆθος ὑγρότητος· καὶ μελικράτου τε καὶ ὀξυμέλιτος τῶν ὑδαρῶν ἔμπροσθεν ὡς ὑγραινόντων [704] τὸ στόμα καὶ οὖρα κινούντων ἔγραψεν· οὐ δήπου κύαθον αὐτῶν διδοὺς, ἀλλὰ πλῆθος ἀξιόλογον, ἀφ᾿ οὖ καὶ τὸ στόμα δυνατὸν ὑγρανθῆναι καὶ τὰ οὖρα κινηθῆναι καὶ ἐκ πνεύμονος ἀναχθῆναι.

greek_sentence: Περὶ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων ποτῶν, οἷον τὸ κρίθινον καὶ τὰ ἀπὸ χλοίης ποιεύμενα καὶ τὰ ἀπὸ σταφίδος καὶ στεμφύλων καὶ πυρῶν καὶ κνίκου καὶ μύρτων καὶ ῥοιῆς καὶ [705] τῶν ἄλλων ὅταν οὖν ἄν τινος αὐτέων καιρὸς ᾖ χρέεσθαι, γεγράψεται παρ᾿ αὐτῷ τῷ νοσήματι, ὅκωσπερ καὶ τὰ ἄλλα τῶν συνθέτων φαρμάκων.
english_sentence_A: Concerning the other drinks, such as the barley drink and those made from green herbage (χλοίης), and those from raisins and grape-pressings and wheat and safflower and myrtle-berries and pomegranate and [705] the others—whenever, then, there is an occasion to use any of them, it will be written under the disease itself, just as also the other compound medicines.
english_sentence_B: "Concerning the other drinks, such as the barley drink, and those made from green shoots, and those from raisins and grape-pressings and wheat and safflower and myrtle-berries and pomegranate and [705] the rest, whenever the right moment comes to use any of them, it will be written in connection with the disease itself, just as the other compound remedies also will be." This passage too contains an announcement of a separate instruction for each of the diseases individually.

greek_sentence: Περὶ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων ποτῶν, οἷον τὸ κρίθινον καὶ τὰ ἀπὸ χλοίης ποιεύμενα καὶ τὰ ἀπὸ σταφίδος καὶ στεμφύλων καὶ πυρῶν καὶ κνίκου καὶ μύρτων καὶ ῥοιῆς καὶ [705] τῶν ἄλλων ὅταν οὖν ἄν τινος αὐτέων καιρὸς ᾖ χρέεσθαι, γεγράψεται παρ᾿ αὐτῷ τῷ νοσήματι, ὅκωσπερ καὶ τὰ ἄλλα τῶν συνθέτων φαρμάκων.
english_sentence_A: Concerning the other drinks, such as the barley drink and those made from green herbage (χλοίης), and those from raisins and grape-pressings and wheat and safflower and myrtle-berries and pomegranate and [705] the others—whenever, then, there is an occasion to use any of them, it will be written under the disease itself, just as also the other compound medicines.
english_sentence_B: "Concerning the other drinks, such as the barley drink, and those made from green shoots, and those from raisins and grape-pressings and wheat and safflower and myrtle-berries and pomegranate and [705] the rest, whenever the right moment comes to use any of them, it will be written in connection with the disease itself, just as the other compound remedies also will be." This passage too contains an announcement of a separate instruction for each of the diseases individually.

Spir.Praef. , Papp. 70.4 . Math. also, of the transformation of a ratio componendo, Arist. EN 1131b8 ( Pass. ), Euc. 5.18 , 24 ( Pass. ). Logic, combine the terms of a proposition, Arist. Rhet., accumulate, joined with ἐποικοδομεῖν (to form a climax), ib. 1365a16 . ς. λόγον make up an account, PHib. 1.48.15 (iii B.C.). put together constructively, so as to make a whole, πεντηκοντέρους καὶ τριήρεας (as a bridge) Hdt. 7.36 ; λίθους, of builders, Th. 4.4 , IG 42(1).103.59 (Epid., iv B.C.); πλίνθους, ξύλα, X. Mem. 3.1.7 , etc.; τὰ ὄστρακα IG 42(1).121.82 (Epid., iv B.C.); τὰ κομισθέντα Sor. 2.64 ; ἐκ τούτων τὰ μέγιστα . . συνθεὶς τοῦτον . . τὸν λόγον ποιήσομαι Hippias Eleus 6 D. ; συλλαβάς Pl. Cra. 424e . construct, frame, τὸ θνητὸν γένος Pl. Ti. 69d ; ὁ συνθείς the creator, ib. 33d :— Pass. , to be constructed, of the material universe, opp. διαλύεσθαι, Arist. Cael. 304b30 . ς. τι ἀπό τινος compose or make one thing of or from another, Hdt. 4.23 ; τὸ ἐκ τῶν νεῶν καὶ τοῦ πεζοῦ πλῆθος συντιθέμενον Id. 7.184 ; ἐξ ὧν [συλλαβῶν] τὰ ὀνόματα συντίθενται Pl. Cra. 425a , cf. 434a ; συνθεὶς πρᾶγμα πράξει δι' ὀνόματος καὶ ῥήματος Id. Sph. 262e ; εἴδωλον οὐρανοῦ ξυνθεῖσ' ἄπο (Reiske for ὕπο) E. Hel. 34 : metaph., συντιθεὶς γέλων πολύν S. Aj. 303 ; δυοῖν ἅμιλλαν ξ. strive for two things at once, E. El. 95 . construct or frame a story, συνθέντες λόγον Id. Ba. 297 , cf. Ar. Ra. 1052 (anap.), Pl. Phdr. 260b ; οἱ τὰς τέχνας τῶν λόγων συντιθέντες Arist. Rh. 1354a12 ; narrate in writing, τὰ Ἑλληνικά Th. 1.97 , cf. 21 ; compose, ς. μύθους, ποίησιν, μελῳδίαν, ὄρχησιν, Pl. R. 377d , Phdr. 278c , Lg. 812d , 816c ; αἴνιγμα Id. Ap. 27a ; ὁ τὴν ἐνθάδε συνθεὶς ἀνατομήν Gal. 15.147 :— Pass. , pf. συντέθειται ib. 797 ; περὶ ὀλίγας οἰκίας αἱ . . τραγῳδίαι συντίθενται Arist. english_sentence_A: This passage too contains a promise of another teaching, for each of the diseases separately.
english_sentence_B: It is therefore evident that either the therapeutic books he wrote on each of the acute diseases in particular have not been preserved, or they were not written at all; for those now in circulation are not worthy of Hippocrates.

lsj_entry_text: ἐξήγ-ησις, εως, ἡ, statement, narrative, ἐ. ποιήσασθαι Th. 1.72 ; ὑπέρ τινος Plb. 6.3.1 . explanation, interpretation, περὶ τοὺς νόμους Pl. Lg. 631a ; ἐνυπνίων D.S. 2.29 ; Ἐ. τῶν Ἐμπεδοκλέους, title of a work by Zeno Eleaticus; so in Gramm., Sch. Il. 8.296 .
greek_sentence: πρόδηλον οὖν ὡς ἢ οὐ σώζεται τὰ γραφέντα ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ βιβλία θεραπευτικὰ τῶν ὀξέων νοσημάτων ἑκάστου κατὰ μέρος ἢ ὅλως οὐκ ἐγράφη· ταυτὶ γὰρ τὰ νῦν φερόμενα τῆς Ἱπποκράτους ἀξίας οὐκ ἔστιν· ἔχει μέντοι πολλὰ τῆς γνώμης αὐτοῦ, καθάπερ καὶ ταῦτα αὐτὰ τὰ προσκείμενα τῷδε τῷ βιβλίῳ, τὰ μετὰ τὸ λουτρόν· κάλλιον δ᾿ ὡς ἔφην ὑπὲρ ἑκάστου σκεψόμεθα, κατὰ τὰς ἐξηγήσεις αὐτῶν.
english_sentence_A: It is therefore evident either that the books written by him on the treatment of each of the acute diseases in particular are not preserved, or that they were not written at all; for the ones now in circulation are not of Hippocrates' worth. They do, however, contain much of his thought, just as also these very things appended to this book, the ones after the bath; but, as I said, we shall examine each of them better in the course of their exegeses.
english_sentence_B: They do, however, contain much of his thinking, just as do these very passages appended to this book, those after the section on the bath. But, as I said, we shall examine each of them better in the exegeses of them.

greek_sentence: Λουτρὸν δὲ συχνοῖσι τῶν νουσημάτων ἀρήγοι ἂν χρεομένοισιν, ἐς τὰ μὲν ξυνεχέως, ἐς τὰ δὲ οὔ· ἔστι δ᾿ ὅτε ἧσσον χρηστέον, διὰ τὴν ἀπαρασκευασίην τῶν ἀνθρώπων.
english_sentence_A: The bath would help in many of the diseases for those who use it, in some continuously, in others not; but there are times when it should be used less, because of the lack of preparation among people.
english_sentence_B: "A bath would benefit many of the diseases for those who use it, in some continuously, in others not; but there are times when it should be used less, because of people's lack of preparation."

greek_sentence: Καὶ μᾶλλον μὲν μὴ σμήχεσθαι· ἢν δὲ σμήχηται, θερμῷ χρέεσθαι αὐτέῳ καὶ πολλαπλασίῳ ἢ ὡς νομίζεται σμήγματι· καὶ προσκαταχεῖσθαι μὴ ὀλίγῳ καὶ ταχέως μετακαταχεῖσθαι.
english_sentence_A: And it is better not to use a detergent; but if one does use a detergent, to use it warm and with many times more detergent than is customary; and to pour on in addition no small quantity and quickly to pour on again afterwards.

english_sentence_B: And preferably he should not be cleansed with detergent; but if he is cleansed with detergent, use the detergent warm and in a quantity many times greater than is customary; and let him have not a little poured over him besides, and quickly have it poured over him again.

lsj_entry_text: δακν-ώδης, ες, biting, pungent, Hp. Aph. 5.20 , Gal. 6.237 ; painful, Mich. in EN 499.3 .
greek_sentence: χρῄζουσι γὰρ οἱ κάμνοντες ἀκοπώτατα καὶ ἀοχλητότατα διαβραχῆναι τῷ ὕδατι· τὸ δὲ σμήξασθαι διὰ ῥυμμάτων γίγνεται δακνωδῶν ὄντων αὐτῶν καὶ ξηραντικῶν, ὥστε ἐναντιώτατόν ἐστι τοῦτο τῇ δυνάμει τε καὶ χρείᾳ τοῦ λουτροῦ.
english_sentence_A: For the sick need to be thoroughly soaked with the water in the manner freest of fatigue and of disturbance; but scouring with detergent takes place by means of cleansing agents (ῥύμματα), these being biting and drying, so that this is most contrary to both the power and the use of the bath.
english_sentence_B: For patients need to be soaked through by the water with the least fatigue and the least disturbance possible; but cleansing with detergent is done by means of washing agents, which are biting and drying, so that this is most contrary to both the power and the use of the bath.

lsj_entry_text: ἐναντίος, α, ον, opposite, = ἀντίος (which is rare in Prose): of Place, on the opposite side, opposite, c.dat., ἀκταὶ ἐναντίαι ἀλλήλῃσιν Od. 10.89 ; Πάτροκλος δέ οἱ . . ἐ. ἧστο Il. 9.190 , cf. Smp. 190a ). with Verbs of motion, in the opposite direction, ἔνθα οἱ . . ἐναντίη ἤλυθε μήτηρ came to meet him, Il. 6.251 ; ἐναντίοι ἀλλήλοισιν ὄγμον ἐλαύνωσιν 11.67 ; δύο ἅμαξαι ἐ. ἀλλήλαις Th. 1.93 ; ἄνεμος ἐ. ἔπνει X. An. 3.2.10 ; τὸ ἐ. the opposite party, Id. Ath. 1.4 ; presenting obstacles, hindering, τινί S. Ph. 642 . ὁ δι ἐναντίας the opponent in a alawsuit, PFlor. 1.58.15 (iii A.D.), etc. of qualities, acts, etc., opposite, contrary, reverse, τἀναντί' εἰπεῖν A. Ag. 1373 ; δίκαια καὶ τἀναντία S. Ant. 667 : mostly c.gen., τὰ ἐ. τούτων the very reverse of these things, Hdt. 1.82 , cf. Th. 7.75 , etc.; δείξας . . ἄστρων τὴν ἐ. ὁδόν, i.e. τὴν τοῦ ἡλίου ὁδὸν ἐ. οὖσαν τοῖς ἄστροις E. Pl. 14 ; τοὐ. ἔπαθεν ἢ τὸ προσδοκώμενον Pl. Lg. 966e , cf. R. 567c , etc.: freq. strengthd., πᾶν τοὐ., πάντα τἀ., quite the contrary, Lg. 967a , X. Mem. 3.12.4 ; πολὺ τοὐ. Metaph. 986b3 , etc. in the Philos. of Arist. , τἀναντία (dist. fr. other ἀντικείμενα, Metaph. 1018a25 ) are contraries, esp. the two attributes within the same genus which differ most widely from each other (as hot and cold), Cat. 6a18 , al. ἐ. ἀποφάνσεις, προτάσεις, contrary propositions (All B is A, No B is A), opp. contradictory (v. ἀντιφατικῶς), Id. greek_sentence: δεομένου μέντοι σμήχεσθαι τοῦ κάμνοντος ἢ διὰ ῥύπον ἢ διὰ κνησμὸν, ἐκλύειν [708] δύναμιν τοῦ σμηκτικοῦ φαρμάκου μίξει πλείονος ὕδατος, ἐπεμβάλλοντας καὶ τοῦ ἐλαίου· καὶ διὰ τοῦτ᾿ εἶπεν ὁ Ἱπποκράτης, πολλαπλασίῳ δεῖ χρῆσθαι ἢ ὡς νομίζεται τῷ σμήγματι, τουτέστιν ἢ ὡς εἴθισται πρὸς τῶν ὑγιαινόντων.
english_sentence_A: If, however, the patient does need to be cleansed with a detergent, either because of dirt or because of itching, one must weaken [708] the power of the detergent drug by the admixture of more water, adding some oil as well; and it is for this reason that Hippocrates said that one must use the detergent in a quantity many times greater than is customary, that is, than is habitually used by the healthy.
english_sentence_B: When, however, the patient needs to be scrubbed, either on account of dirt or on account of itching, one must weaken [708] the potency of the detergent drug by an admixture of more water, adding in some of the oil as well. And for this reason Hippocrates said that one must use a many times greater quantity of the cleansing agent than is customary, that is, than is the habit among the healthy.

greek_sentence: Ἔνεστι μὲν καὶ ὑφ᾿ ἓν ἀναγνῶναι μετακέρασμα, δυνατὸν δὲ καὶ καθ᾿ αὑτὴν ἀκοῦσαι τὴν μετὰ πρόθεσιν, ἰδίᾳ δὲ πάλιν τὸ κέρασμα· καὶ γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ τῷ βιβλίῳ καὶ ἐν ἄλλοις [711] Ἱπποκράτης φαίνεται χρώμενος τῇ μετὰ προθέσει κατὰ τὸ τῶν Ἰώνων ἔθος ἐλλειπτικῶς· ἔστι δὲ τὸ πλῆρες τοιοῦτο καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα κέρασμα πολὺ ἡτοιμάσθαι.
english_sentence_A: It is possible to read μετακέρασμα as a single word, but it is also possible to understand the preposition μετά on its own, and again κέρασμα separately; for both in this book and in others [711] Hippocrates evidently uses the preposition μετά elliptically, in accordance with the usage of the Ionians; and the full expression is as follows: "and after these things let a large quantity of mixture be prepared." Whether one understands μετακέρασμα as a single word, or, dividing it, as standing for "after these things, a mixture", there is one meaning common to both readings; for he wishes a mixture to be prepared which is to be poured over the one being bathed, after he has made use of the bath in the tub.

english_sentence_A: It is possible to read μετακέρασμα as a single word, but it is also possible to understand the preposition μετά on its own, and again κέρασμα separately; for both in this book and in others [711] Hippocrates evidently uses the preposition μετά elliptically, in accordance with the usage of the Ionians; and the full expression is as follows: "and after these things let a large quantity of mixture be prepared." english_sentence_A: The word "quick" should be understood both with reference to the very action that takes place in the pouring, and no less also with reference to the time between the actions, so that the second affusion does not leave a long interval after the first; which, if one were naming it properly, one would say is to make the affusions not quick but frequent. Nevertheless, among the ancients the use of the terms "frequent" and "quick" is confused, and there are times when they call frequent actions quick.
english_sentence_B: The word 'quick' should be understood both with reference to the action itself that takes place in the pouring-down, and no less with reference to the time between the actions, so that the second affusion does not leave a long interval after the first. Someone using the terms in their proper sense would say that the affusions should be made not 'quick' but 'frequent'.

greek_sentence: Τὸ ταχείας ἀκούειν προσήκει καὶ κατ᾿ αὐτῆς μὲν τῆς γιγνομένης ἐνεργείας ἐν τῷ καταχεῖν, οὐδὲν δὲ ἧττον καὶ κατὰ τοῦ μεταξὺ τῶν ἐνεργειῶν χρόνου, ὡς μὴ διαλείπειν πολὺ τὴν δευτέραν ἐπάντλησιν ἀπὸ τῆς προτέρας· ὅπερ ὀνομάζων τις κυρίως οὐ ταχείας, ἀλλὰ πυκνὰς ποιεῖσθαι τὰς ἐπαντλήσεις εἴποι· συγκέχυταί γε μὴν παρὰ τοῖς παλαιοῖς ἡ χρῆσις τῶν ὀνομάτων, τοῦ τε πυκνοῦ καὶ τοῦ ταχέος, ἔστιν ὅτε τὰς πυκνὰς ἐνεργείας ταχείας ὀνομάζουσιν.
english_sentence_A: The word "quick" should be understood both with reference to the very action that takes place in the pouring, and no less also with reference to the time between the actions, so that the second affusion does not leave a long interval after the first; which, if one were naming it properly, one would say is to make the affusions not quick but frequent. Nevertheless, among the ancients the use of the terms "frequent" and "quick" is confused, and there are times when they call frequent actions quick.
english_sentence_B: The word 'quick' should be understood both with reference to the action itself that takes place in the pouring-down, and no less with reference to the time between the actions, so that the second affusion does not leave a long interval after the first. Someone using the terms in their proper sense would say that the affusions should be made not 'quick' but 'frequent'.

greek_sentence: Καὶ σπόγγοισι χρέεσθαι ἀντὶ στλεγγίδος.
english_sentence_A: And use sponges instead of a strigil.
english_sentence_B: Among the ancients, however, the use of the terms 'frequent' and 'quick' is confused: sometimes they call frequent actions 'quick'. And use sponges instead of a strigil.

greek_sentence: Οὐδὲ οἱ νῦν ἰατροὶ χρῶνται στελεγγίσιν ἐπὶ τῶν ἀσθενούντων, οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ σπόγγῳ, ἀλλ᾿ ἐνειλίττουσιν αὐτοὺς μετὰ τὸ λουτρὸν εἰς ὀθόνην· οἱ δὲ εἰς ἱμάτια καὶ μάλιστά [714] γε τὰ ἄγναπτα, περιστέλλουσι πανταχόθεν, ὡς ἱδρῶσι πλεῖστον.
english_sentence_A: Nor do physicians nowadays use strigils on the sick, nor indeed a sponge either, but after the bath they wrap them in a linen cloth; others wrap them in cloaks, and especially [714] unfulled ones, covering them on every side, so that they may sweat as much as possible.
english_sentence_B: Nor do the physicians of the present day use strigils on the sick, nor indeed a sponge, but after the bath they wrap them up in linen cloth; others wrap them in cloaks, and especially [714] unfulled ones, covering them round on all sides, so that they may sweat as much as possible.

greek_sentence: ἔστι δ᾿ οὐκ ἀεὶ χρεία τοῦ πλεῖστον ἱδροῦν μετὰ τὸ λουτρὸν τὸν κάμνοντα· πολλάκις γὰρ οὐ τοῦ κενῶσαι τὸ σῶμα χάριν ἐπὶ τὸ λουτρὸν τὸν κάμνοντα ἄγομεν, ἀλλὰ τοὐναντίον ἅπαν ὑγρᾶναί τε καὶ τέγξαι διόλου, κατεξηρασμένον ἀμετρότερον.
english_sentence_A: But there is not always need for the patient to sweat a great deal after the bath; for often we bring the patient to the bath not for the sake of evacuating the body, but for the complete opposite, to moisten it and wet it throughout, when it has been dried out beyond due measure.
english_sentence_B: But there is not always need for the patient to sweat a great deal after the bath; for often we bring the patient to the bath not for the sake of evacuating the body, but, quite the contrary, in order to moisten it and soak it through and through, when it has been dried out beyond due measure.

greek_sentence: ἐπὶ τῶν τοιούτων οὖν οὔτ᾿ ἔνδον κατὰ τὸ βαλανεῖον ἱδρῶτας ἀναμένειν χρὴ πολλοὺς, ἀλλ᾿ ὅτι τάχιστα τῷ κατὰ τὴν πύελον ἐμβαλεῖν ὕδατι καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ἐξελθόντας ἐκ τοῦ λουτροῦ διὰ ταχέων ἐκμάττειν.
english_sentence_A: In such cases, then, one should neither wait inside in the bath-house for copious sweats, but as quickly as possible put them into the water in the tub, and after this, when they have come out of the bath, wipe them off speedily.
english_sentence_B: In such cases, then, one ought not to wait inside the bath-house for copious sweats, but should put him as quickly as possible into the water in the tub, and after this, once they have come out of the bath, wipe them dry quickly.

english_sentence_A: For after the bath, Hippocrates, having sponged off the water [715] — it is unclear whether he also anointed at all, but it is evident that he anoints the patient even while the body is still thoroughly wet, unless someone says this, that he wipes off again this very oil together with the water.
english_sentence_B: For after the bath Hippocrates, having sponged off the water, [715] leaves it unclear whether he also anointed at all; but it is evident that he anoints the patient even while the body is thoroughly moist, unless someone says this: that he afterwards wipes off this very oil together with the water.

greek_sentence: ἔστι μὲν οὖν χρήσιμον ἐσκέφθαι καὶ περὶ τῆς κατὰ τὸ λουτρὸν χρήσεως τοῦ λίπους· ἀναγκαιότερον δὲ τὸ περὶ τοῦ κατὰ τὸ λουτρὸν, εἴθ᾿ ἱδρώσαντι τῷ λουομένῳ περιχεῖν προσήκει τὸ ἔλαιον, εἴτε καὶ πρὶν ἱδρῶσαι, ξηρῷ παραχρῆμα μετὰ τὸ ἀποδύσασθαι, ἢ τούτων μὲν οὐδέτερον, ὅταν δ᾿ ἄρξηται νοτίζεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: It is useful, then, to have considered also the use of oil in the bath; but more necessary is the question concerning the bath, whether it is fitting to pour the oil over the bather once he has sweated, or even before he sweats, when he is dry, immediately after undressing, or neither of these, but when he has begun to become moist.
english_sentence_B: It is useful, then, to have considered also the use of fat in connection with the bath; but more necessary is the question about its use in the bath: whether it is proper to pour the oil over the bather after he has sweated, or also before he sweats, while he is dry, immediately after undressing, or at neither of these times but when he begins to grow moist.

english_sentence_A: This seems to me to have been said as something too trivial for him. For it is obvious to everyone that no part should be left bare for long, [717] at the time when they wipe off from those who have bathed the water that remains after the bath; for everyone knows that parts thus bared are quickly chilled.
english_sentence_B: This he seems to me to have said as a small matter, or as something standing on its own. For it is plain to everyone that no part ought to be left uncovered for long [717] at the time when they wipe off from those being bathed the water that remains after the bath; for all know that parts uncovered in this way are quickly chilled.

greek_sentence: καὶ γὰρ ὀδύνης τῆς κατὰ πλευρὴν καὶ στῆθος [719] καὶ μετάφρενον παρηγορικόν ἐστι τὸ λουτρὸν καὶ πτυέλου πεπαντικὸν καὶ ἀναγωγὸν καὶ εὔπνοον καὶ ἄκοπον (μαλθακτικὸν γὰρ καὶ ἄρθρων καὶ τοῦ ἐπιπολαίου δέρματος) καὶ οὐρητικὸν δὲ καὶ καρηβαρίην λύει καὶ ῥῖνας ὑγραίνει.
english_sentence_A: For the bath is soothing of pain in the side and chest [719] and back, and it concocts sputum and brings it up, and it makes breathing easy and relieves fatigue (for it is softening both of the joints and of the superficial skin), and it is also diuretic, and it dissolves heaviness of the head and moistens the nostrils.

greek_sentence: Ἥκιστα δὲ λούειν καιρὸς τούτοισιν, οἷσιν ἡ κοιλίη ὑγροτέρη τοῦ καιροῦ ἐν τῇσι νούσοισιν· ἀτὰρ οὐδὲ οἶσιν ἑστήκει μᾶλλον τοῦ καιροῦ καὶ μὴ προεληλύθει.

english_sentence_B: It is least of all the right moment to bathe those whose bowel is moister than is proper in their diseases; nor, again, those in whom it has been arrested more than is proper and has not passed beforehand.

english_sentence_A: But neither should one bathe those who are [721] enfeebled (γεγυωμένους), nor indeed those who are nauseous or prone to vomiting, nor those who belch up bilious matter, nor those who bleed from the nostrils, unless it flows less than the due measure (and you know the due measures); but if it flows less than the due measure, bathe them, whether the whole body is in need of it with respect to the other things, or the head alone.
english_sentence_B: But neither should one bathe those who are [721] enfeebled (γεγυωμένους), nor indeed those who are nauseous or inclined to vomit, nor those who belch up bilious matter, nor those haemorrhaging from the nostrils, unless the flow be less than is due (you know the due measures). But if it flows less than is due, bathe them, either the whole body, should that help in respect of the other matters, or the head alone.

greek_sentence: Οἶς μὲν ὑπέρχεται τὰ κατὰ τὴν γαστέρα πλείονα, τὸ βαλανεῖον ἵστησιν, ἀντισπῶν αὐτὰ πρὸς ὅλον τὸ σῶμα καὶ ταύτῃ βλάπτεται· τοῖς δὲ μηδ᾿ ὅλως διακεχωρηκόσιν ὅτι προεκκενῶσαι βέλτιόν ἐστι τὴν παλαιὰν κόπρον οὐδεὶς ἀγνοεῖ, καθάπερ οὐδ᾿ ὅτι τοὺς γεγυωμένους, τουτέστι τοὺς καταλελυμένους τὴν δύναμιν, ἐπικαταλύει τὸ βαλανεῖον.
english_sentence_A: In those in whom the contents of the belly pass off in greater quantity, the bath checks them, drawing them by revulsion toward the whole body, and in this way the patient is harmed; while in those who have had no evacuation at all, no one is unaware that it is better first to empty out the old faeces, just as no one is unaware that the bath further breaks down those who are enfeebled (γεγυωμένους), that is, those whose faculty has been broken down.
english_sentence_B: In those in whom the contents of the belly pass down in too great quantity, the bath-house checks them by drawing them away by revulsion towards the whole body, and in this way the patient is harmed. In those who have had no evacuation at all, no one is unaware that it is better to evacuate the old faeces beforehand, just as no one is unaware that the bath-house further breaks down those who are γεγυωμένοι, that is, those whose strength has been broken down.

greek_sentence: Οἶς μὲν ὑπέρχεται τὰ κατὰ τὴν γαστέρα πλείονα, τὸ βαλανεῖον ἵστησιν, ἀντισπῶν αὐτὰ πρὸς ὅλον τὸ σῶμα καὶ ταύτῃ βλάπτεται· τοῖς δὲ μηδ᾿ ὅλως διακεχωρηκόσιν ὅτι προεκκενῶσαι βέλτιόν ἐστι τὴν παλαιὰν κόπρον οὐδεὶς ἀγνοεῖ, καθάπερ οὐδ᾿ ὅτι τοὺς γεγυωμένους, τουτέστι τοὺς καταλελυμένους τὴν δύναμιν, ἐπικαταλύει τὸ βαλανεῖον.
english_sentence_A: In those in whom the contents of the belly pass off in greater quantity, the bath checks them, drawing them by revulsion toward the whole body, and in this way the patient is harmed; while in those who have had no evacuation at all, no one is unaware that it is better first to empty out the old faeces, just as no one is unaware that the bath further breaks down those who are enfeebled (γεγυωμένους), that is, those whose faculty has been broken down.
english_sentence_B: In those in whom the contents of the belly pass down in too great quantity, the bath-house checks them by drawing them away by revulsion towards the whole body, and in this way the patient is harmed. In those who have had no evacuation at all, no one is unaware that it is better to evacuate the old faeces beforehand, just as no one is unaware that the bath-house further breaks down those who are γεγυωμένοι, that is, those whose strength has been broken down.

english_sentence_A: For it is indeed reasonable, if they haemorrhage too deficiently, to bathe them; and these are also the ones who need a vigorous (λαύρου) bath, for the sake of a more vehement movement of the blood in the head; and likewise we shall bathe them if, while needing a haemorrhage, they do not haemorrhage at all.
english_sentence_B: For it is indeed reasonable, if they bleed rather deficiently, to bathe them; and these are also the ones who need a copious bath, for the sake of a more vigorous movement of the blood in the head. Likewise we shall bathe them if, though they need a haemorrhage, they do not bleed at all.

greek_sentence: Καὶ ταύτην τὴν ῥῆσιν ὁ δοὺς ἰατρὸς [723] Βίκτωρι τῷ Ῥώμης ὑπάρχῳ τὸ περὶ τῆς καθ᾿ Ἱπποκράτην διαίτης καὶ ἄλλας τινὰς ἐξ ἡμισείας ἐνέγραψε τῷ βιβλίῳ, καθάπερ κᾀκείνην ἐν ᾗ φησιν ὅτι οὐχ ὑστερητέαι αἱ πρῶται ἡμέραι τοῦ ῥοφήματος· ἔτι δὲ πρὸς αὐτῇ καὶ τοῖσι μέν γε εἰθισμένοισι δὶς σιτεῖσθαι τῆς ἡμέρης δὶς δοτέον.

greek_sentence: Χρέεσθαι δὲ λουτροῖσι τοῖσιν ὅλῃσι πτισάνῃσι χρεομένοισι παρὰ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἐνδέχεται ἢ τοῖσι χυλῷ μούνῳ χρεομένοισι· ἐνδέχεται δὲ καὶ τούτοισιν ἐνίοτε, ἥκιστα δὲ καὶ τοῖσι ποτῷ μούνῳ χρεομένοισιν.
english_sentence_A: 'To use baths is permissible to a far greater degree for those who use whole ptisan than for those who use the juice alone; it is permissible sometimes also for these, but least of all for those who use drink alone.'
english_sentence_B: 'It is admissible to use baths far more for those who are taking whole ptisans than for those who are taking the juice alone; it is admissible sometimes for these too, but least of all for those who are taking drink alone.'

greek_sentence: πτισάνας γὰρ ὅλας δίδωσι τοῖς ἐπιεικῶς ἔχουσιν, ὅσοι δ᾿ αὐτῶν φαυλότερον διάγουσι, χυλὸν μόνον· ὅσοι δὲ καὶ τούτων ἔτι σφαλερώτερον ἢ ὀξύτερον νοσοῦσι, μόνα τὰ ποτά.
english_sentence_A: For he gives whole ptisane to those who are in a reasonably good condition, but to those among them who are faring worse, the juice alone; and to those who are ill in a still more precarious or more acute manner than these, the drinks alone.

greek_sentence: τοῖς οὖν οὕτως ἔχουσιν, ὅταν καὶ ἡ ἀπὸ ἔθους ἔνδειξις προσέλθῃ, διπλασιάσαι τὸ λουτρὸν οὐδὲν κωλύει· τοῖς μέντοι ποτῷ μόνῳ χρωμένοις ἥκιστά φησιν ἁρμόττειν τὸ λουτρὸν, ὅπερ σημαίνει [725] τὸ ἐλάχιστον καὶ οὐχ ὡς ἔνιοί φασι τὸ οὐδαμῶς· ἐπιφέρων γοῦν ἐρεῖ· Ἔστι δ᾿ οἷσι καὶ τουτέων μὲν ἐνδέχεται· τεκμαίρεσθαι δὲ χρὴ τοῖσι προγεγραμμένοισι, οὕς τε μέλλει λουτρὸν ὠφελέειν ἐν ἑκάστοισι τῶν τρόπων τῆς διαίτης οὕς τε μή.
english_sentence_A: For those, then, who are in this condition, whenever the indication derived from habit is also added, nothing prevents doubling the bath; to those, however, who are using drink alone he says that the bath is least fitting, which signifies [725] the least and not, as some people say, not at all; at any rate, continuing, he will say: "There are some even of these for whom it is admissible; but one must judge by the things written above both whom the bath is going to benefit in each of the modes of regimen and whom not.
english_sentence_B: For those, then, who are in this condition, when the indication from habit is also added, nothing prevents doubling the bath. For those, however, who take drink alone, he says the bath is 'least of all' suitable, which signifies [725] 'very little', and not, as some people say, 'not at all'.

greek_sentence: Οὐ προσέθηκε δὲ τὸ πότε τούτους ἐνδέχεται χρῆσθαι λουτρῷ· λεκτέον οὖν ἡμῖν ἐστιν ἑπομένοις αὐτοῦ τῇ ὅλῃ διανοίᾳ.
english_sentence_A: For those in whom there is a strong further need of some one of those things which a bath does as a good, not to bathe, and whatever things would be benefited by a bath; but those in whom there is further need of none of these, and in whom there are present some of the signs upon which it is advantageous to bathe, these one must bathe." He did not add, however, when it is admissible for these to use the bath; so it must be stated by us, following his overall intention.
english_sentence_B: For those who stand in great need of any of these things which a bath makes good, not to bathe, and whatever would be benefited by a bath; but for those who need none of these, and in whom some of the signs are present on which it is beneficial to bathe, one must bathe.' He did not add when these persons may use a bath; so it must be stated by us, following his thought as a whole.

english_sentence_A: Hippocrates regulates the regimen of those who are acutely ill with drinks alone, whenever he expects their strength to suffice until the acme of the disease, which sometimes occurs together with the concoction, [726] as in the case of the affections of the thorax and lung; for once the humours that produce the affections have been concocted, they straightway expectorate; and if they merely begin to spit up what they should, the disease will no longer increase in either of the two ways, neither in respect of the condition nor in respect of the symptoms.
english_sentence_B: Hippocrates regulates the diet of those who are acutely ill with drinks alone when he expects that their strength will hold out until the acme of the disease, which sometimes comes about together with coction, [726] as in the diseases of the thorax and lung. For once the humours that produce the affections have been concocted, the patients at once bring them up; and if they merely begin to spit up such matter as they ought, the disease will no longer increase in either of the two ways, neither in respect of the condition nor in respect of the symptoms.

greek_sentence: ποτοῖς μόνοις διαιτᾷ ὁ Ἱπποκράτης τοὺς ὀξέως νοσοῦντας, ὅταν ἐλπίζῃ τὴν δύναμιν αὐτῶν ἐξαρκέσαι εἰς τὴν τοῦ νοσήματος ἀκμὴν, ἥτις ἐνίοτε ἅμα τῇ πέψει γίνεται, [726] καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν κατὰ θώρακα καὶ πνεύμονα· πεφθέντων γὰρ τῶν ἐργαζομένων τὰ πάθη χυμῶν εὐθέως ἀναπτύσουσιν· ἂν δὲ ἄρξωνται μόνον πτύειν οἶα δεῖ, κατ᾿ οὐδέτερον ἔτι τῶν τρόπων ἡ νόσος αὐξηθήσεται, οὔτε κατὰ τὴν διάθεσιν οὔτε κατὰ τὰ συμπτώματα.
english_sentence_A: Hippocrates regulates the regimen of those who are acutely ill with drinks alone, whenever he expects their strength to suffice until the acme of the disease, which sometimes occurs together with the concoction, [726] as in the case of the affections of the thorax and lung; for once the humours that produce the affections have been concocted, they straightway expectorate; and if they merely begin to spit up what they should, the disease will no longer increase in either of the two ways, neither in respect of the condition nor in respect of the symptoms.
english_sentence_B: Hippocrates regulates the diet of those who are acutely ill with drinks alone when he expects that their strength will hold out until the acme of the disease, which sometimes comes about together with coction, [726] as in the diseases of the thorax and lung. For once the humours that produce the affections have been concocted, the patients at once bring them up; and if they merely begin to spit up such matter as they ought, the disease will no longer increase in either of the two ways, neither in respect of the condition nor in respect of the symptoms.

english_sentence_A: Hence, among those who are ill with ardent fever, it will suit only those who are ill without a phlegmonous or erysipelatous swelling, the bile throughout their whole body being in a state of boiling; and if they also have signs of concoction, it will suit them much more.

greek_sentence: Μέμνημαι κατὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ἐξηγήσεως τοῦ βιβλίου τούτου πρὸς τοὺς Κνιδίους ἰατροὺς εἰπόντος Ἱπποκράτους· ὁκόσα δὲ προκαταμαθεῖν δεῖ τὸν ἰατρὸν μὴ λέγοντος τοῦ [728] κάμνοντος, τούτων τὰ πολλὰ παρεῖται.
english_sentence_A: I recall that at the beginning of the exegesis of this book Hippocrates said, against the Cnidian physicians: "But of all the things that the physician must learn beforehand without the [728] patient telling him, most have been omitted." Those who consider Hippocrates to be a Dogmatist said that these things are the affected places and their conditions and the causes; those who consider him an Empiricist, that they are seasons and regions and ages, habits and the constitutions of the air surrounding us.
english_sentence_B: I remember that at the beginning of my exposition of this book, where Hippocrates, speaking against the Cnidian physicians, said: 'but as for the things the physician must learn beforehand without the [728] patient telling him, most of these have been passed over', some, believing Hippocrates to be a Dogmatist, said that these things were the affected places and their dispositions and their causes; others, believing him an Empiricist, said that they were seasons and regions and ages, habits, and the constitutions of the air surrounding us.

greek_sentence: καὶ πάλιν ἐφεξῆς· εἰ δὲ μὴ ὑπεληλύθει ὁ παλαιότερος νεοβρώτῳ ἐόντι, εἰ μὲν ἰσχύει τε καὶ ἀκμάζει τὴν ἡλικίαν, κλύσαι· ἢν δὲ ἀσθενέστερος ᾖ, βαλάνῳ προσχρῆσθαι, ἢν μὴ αὐτόματα διεξίῃ καλῶς.
english_sentence_A: And again in what follows: but if the older [food] has not passed down in one who has recently eaten, if he is strong and in the prime of life, administer a clyster; but if he is weaker, make use of a suppository, unless the contents pass through well of their own accord.
english_sentence_B: whichever of these it indicates; but if you give ptisans to people in this state, [730] the deaths of such patients come about quickly.' After this, again drawing distinctions, he says: 'If the fever begins when he has recently eaten and the bowel has not yet passed anything, whether with pain or without pain, withhold the giving of the gruel until one supposes that the food has passed down into the lower part of the intestine.' And again, next: 'If the older food has not passed down while he has recently eaten, then, if he is strong and in the prime of life, give an enema; but if he is weaker, make use of a suppository as well, unless it passes through well of its own accord.' Here, then, he has added the indication taken from the strength, as he often does in what follows too, at the same time bidding us also to consider what cause and condition it is that is bringing down the strength; and there he also added that these things are unknown to physicians.

greek_sentence: ἐμνημόνευσε δὲ καὶ περὶ τῆς πέψεως τοῦ νοσήματος πολλάκις, οὐ μικρὸν σκοπὸν οὐδὲ τοῦτον ποιούμενος ὅλης τε τῆς διαίτης καὶ τῶν ἐν ταύτῃ μεταβολῶν· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ περὶ ἀκμῆς νοσήματος εἶπέ τι καὶ πρὸς τοῦτον ἀποβλέπων, τρέφει οὐχ ὡς πρὸς τὸν φαυλότατον σκοπὸν ἐν διαίτῃ.
english_sentence_A: He also made mention many times of the concoction of the disease, making this too no small indication both for the whole regimen and for the changes within it; and similarly he also said something about the acme of the disease, and looking to this as well, he nourishes (τρέφει), not as toward the most trivial indication in regimen.
english_sentence_B: He also mentioned the concoction of the disease many times, making this too no small aim of the whole regimen and of the changes within it. Likewise he said something about the peak of the disease too, and with an eye to this he gives nourishment, treating it not as the most trivial aim in regimen.

greek_sentence: Ἐν τῷ περὶ διαίτης τὰ μετὰ τὸν περὶ λουτρῶν λόγον εἰρημένα προσηκόντως ὑπώπτευσαν οὐκ ὀλίγοι τῶν ἰατρῶν ὡς οὐχ Ἱπποκράτους ὄντα· καὶ γὰρ τῇ τῆς ἑρμηνείας δυνάμει καὶ τῇ τῶν θεωρημάτων ἀκριβείᾳ λείπεται πολὺ τῶν ἔμπροσθεν.
english_sentence_A: In the work On Regimen, the things said after the discussion of baths have been suspected, and fittingly so, by not a few physicians as not being by Hippocrates; for both in the power of the expression and in the precision of the theorems they fall far short of what precedes.

english_sentence_A: Yet neither were those who held that these parts too are Hippocrates' moved without reason; for the thought of what has been written [733] accords with that man's doctrinal position, so that one would suspect that some pupil of his wrote it.

greek_sentence: τεσσάρων οὖν ὡς εἴποι τις εἰδῶν ὄντων ἐν αὐτῷ, τοῦ μὲν ἀξίου καὶ [734] κατὰ τὴν λέξιν καὶ κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν Ἱπποκράτους, τοῦ δὲ καθ᾿ ἕτερον μόνον, ἤτοι τὴν λέξιν ἢ τὴν διάνοιαν, ἐνίων δὲ κατ᾿ οὐδέτερον, σημανοῦμεν τοῦτ᾿ αὐτὸ καθ᾿ ἑκάστην τῶν προχειριζομένων εἰς τὴν ἐξήγησιν λέξεων.

lsj_entry_text: φλέβιον, τό, Dim. of φλέψ, any one of the smaller vessels, Hp. VC 1 , Pl. Ti. 65c , 84e , Arist. HA 514a19 , b27 ; φλεβίου ῥῆξις Hp. Aph. 4.78 . of veins in the earth, Str. 8.6.21 .

greek_sentence: Καῦσος δὲ γίνεται, ὁκόταν ἀναξηρανθέντα τὰ φλεβία ἐν θερινῇ ὥρῃ ἐπισπάσηται δριμέας καὶ χολώδεας ἰχῶρας ἐς ἑαυτά.
english_sentence_A: "Causus arises whenever the small veins, having been dried up in the summer season, draw to themselves pungent and bilious ichors." greek_sentence: ἐπιδέδεικται δὲ καὶ ὅτι τῆς κατὰ φύσιν τε καὶ συμμέτρου καταστάσεως ἐξιστάμενον τὸ σῶμα, καθότι ἂν ἐξίστηταί τε καὶ μεταβέβληται, κατὰ τοῦτο καὶ τῆς οἰκείας ἐπικουρίας δεῖται, ξηραινόμενον μὲν ὑγραίνεσθαι, ὑγραινόμενον δὲ ξηραίνεσθαι, θερμαινόμενον δὲ ψύχεσθαι, ψυχόμενον δὲ θερμαίνεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: And it has also been demonstrated that the body, when it departs from its natural and proportionate constitution, in whatever respect it departs and has been changed, in that same respect also requires the appropriate assistance: when it is being dried, to be moistened; when being moistened, to be dried; when being heated, to be cooled; when being cooled, to be heated.
english_sentence_B: It has further been demonstrated that the body, when it departs from its natural and well-proportioned state, requires the assistance appropriate to it in the very respect in which it has departed and been altered: when dried, it needs to be moistened; when moistened, to be dried; when heated, to be cooled; when cooled, to be heated.

english_sentence_A: If, then, the moistures carried into the dried veins, just as they have a moist nature in their consistency, so also have a moistening power, the part recovers its natural good mixture; but if the moisture is pungent in quality and drying in power, the body is set ablaze, just as if one of us ourselves, having become thirsty, were to gulp down greedily either unmixed wine treated with sea-water or [736] salty water.
english_sentence_B: If, then, the moistures carried into the dried-out veins have a moistening power just as they have a moist nature in their consistency, the part recovers its natural good mixture (eukrasia). english_sentence_B: I at any rate know this myself: once, having become thirsty from a summer journey, I drank a single cup of old wine that was a little too unmixed, and by it I increased my thirst rather than stopped it.

greek_sentence: ὥσπερ οὖν ἡμεῖς καίτοι τὸν λογισμὸν ἔχοντες ἐπιστατοῦντα ταῖς ὀρέξεσιν ἐνίοτε μὲν ἀμελέστερον, ἐνίοτε δὲ προπετέστερον, ἔστι δ᾿ ὅτε τῷ μὴ παρεῖναι βέλτιον, ἠναγκάσθημεν ἐπί τι τῶν ἁλμυρῶν καὶ δριμέων ἀφικέσθαι ποτῶν, οὕτως καὶ ἡ ἐν ταῖς φλεψὶ δύναμις ἑλκτικὴ διὰ παντὸς ἐπισπᾶται τὴν ἐκ τῶν πλησιαζόντων ὑγρότητα, μὴ διακρίνουσα τὴν οὐσίαν αὐτῆς ὁποία τίς ἐστιν· οὐ γὰρ ἔχει λογισμὸν ὡς σκέψασθαί τι περὶ τοῦ βελτίονος, ἀλλ᾿ ὥσπερ τὰ παιδία καὶ τὰ βοσκήματα τὸ προστυχὸν ὑγρὸν αἱρεῖται διψῶντα, κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον κᾀκείνη.
english_sentence_A: Just as we, then, although we have reason presiding over our appetites, sometimes through greater carelessness, sometimes through greater rashness, and sometimes because something better was not at hand, have been compelled to resort to one of the salty and pungent drinks, so too the attractive faculty in the veins continually draws in the moisture from the neighbouring parts, without discriminating what sort of thing its substance is; for it does not possess reason so as to consider anything about what is better, but just as children and grazing animals, when thirsty, take whatever liquid happens to be at hand, in the same way does that faculty too.
english_sentence_B: Just as we, then, although we have reasoning presiding over our appetites, have been compelled to resort to some salty and acrid drink, sometimes through rather great carelessness, sometimes through rather great rashness, and at times because nothing better was at hand, so too the attractive faculty in the veins continually draws in the moisture from the neighbouring parts without discerning what kind of thing its substance is. For it does not possess reasoning so as to consider anything about what is better.

greek_sentence: ἀλλ᾿ ὅ γε καῦσος ἰδίως καλούμενος οὐ μόνον τῇ σφοδρότητι τῆς καθ᾿ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα γιγνομένης θερμασίας διαφέρει, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ δίψει· βίαιόν τε γάρ ἐστιν ἐν τούτῳ καὶ ἄπαυστον.
english_sentence_A: But the kausos properly so called differs not only in the vehemence of the heat that arises throughout the whole body, but also in the thirst; for in this it is violent and unceasing.
english_sentence_B: The kausos properly so called, however, differs not only in the intensity of the heat that arises throughout the whole body, but also in the thirst; for in this the thirst is violent and unceasing.

lsj_entry_text: δίψα, ης, ἡ, thirst, δ. τε καὶ λιμός Il. 19.166 ; πεῖνα καὶ δ. Pl. R. 585a ; δίψῃ ξυνέχεσθαι Th. 2.49 , etc.; of trees, Antiph. 231.6 , PFlor. 176.12 (iii A. D.): pl., Arist. EN 1154b3 . c. gen., thirst for, ποτοῦ Pl. R. 437d : metaph., ἀοιδᾶν δ. Pi. P. 9.104 .—The form δίψη occurs in Opp. C. 4.339 , and in codd. of A. Ch. 756 ; cf. δίψος.
greek_sentence: ἐνίοτε μὲν γὰρ καθ᾿ ἓν ὁτιοῦν, ἐνίοτε δὲ καὶ καθ᾿ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα καῦσος γίγνεται· ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ καθ᾿ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα γενομένου, ἐξ ἅπαντος δίψαν ἐργάζεται· ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν καθ᾿ ἕν τι μέρος, οὐκ ἐξ ἀνάγκης εἰ μὴ αὐτὸ τὸ μέρος τὴν δίψαν ἐργάζεται, πάντων μὲν πρῶτον καὶ μάλιστα τὸ στόμα τῆς γαστρὸς, ἐφεξῆς δὲ ἡ γαστὴρ καὶ μετὰ ταύτην ὁ στόμαχος, εἶτα πνεύμων, εἶτα νῆστις.
english_sentence_A: For sometimes kausos arises in any one part whatever, sometimes also throughout the whole body. In the case of the one arising throughout the whole body, it produces thirst in every instance; but in the case of those in some one part, not necessarily, unless the part itself is one that produces thirst—first and most of all the mouth of the stomach, next the stomach, and after this the gullet (stomachos), then the lung, then the jejunum.
english_sentence_B: For sometimes kausos arises in any one part whatever, sometimes throughout the whole body. In the case of the kausos that arises throughout the whole body, it produces thirst in every instance; in the case of those in some one part, not necessarily, unless the part itself is one that produces thirst: first and foremost of all the mouth of the stomach, next the stomach, and after it the oesophagus, then the lung, then the jejunum.

greek_sentence: ἆρ᾿ οὖν οὕτως μόνον γίγνεται καῦσος, ὡς εἶπεν, ὅταν ἐπισπάσηται τὰ φλεβία δριμεῖς καὶ χολώδεις ἰχῶρας ἐς ἑαυτά;
english_sentence_A: Does kausos, then, arise only in this way, as he said, when the small veins draw pungent and bilious ichors into themselves?
english_sentence_B: Is it then only in this way that kausos arises, as he said, when the small veins draw acrid and bilious ichors into themselves?

lsj_entry_text: ἰχώρ [ι], ῶρος, ὁ , ichor, the juice, not blood, that flows in the veins of gods, Il. 5.340 ,etc.: Ep. acc. ἰχῶ ib. 416 : in pl., of the Giants, Str. 6.3.5 ; later simply, blood, A. english_sentence_B: For it was shown that the flesh too has a faculty that attracts the things it lacks.
