greek_sentence: ὅτι μὲν ὁ τοιοῦτος ἐξ ἀνάγκης τεθνήξεται πρόδηλον ἐκ τοῦ τῶν κακῶν ἀθροίσματος σημείων· τὸ δὲ καὶ πνευματωθήσεται τῇ τελευτῇ τῆς ῥήσεως ὥσπερ αἴνιγμα προσέῤῥιπται ταύτης, ὥς τι τῶν ἐξ ἀνάγκης ὡμολογημένων ἔσεσθαι ὅ τί περ ἂν σημαίνῃ τὸ πνευματωθήσεται, εἴτε τὸ τῶν κατὰ τὴν γαστέρα πνευμάτων πλῆθος, ὡς ἐνὸν γαστέρα φυσηθῆναι πᾶσαν αὐτὴν, εἴτε τὴν μεγάλην καὶ πυκνὴν ἀναπνοήν· ἀλλὰ καὶ ταύτην ἐμάθομεν, αἷς ἔσεσθαι διαθέσεσιν οὐκ ἀγαθὸν, ὥσπερ γε καὶ τὴν τῆς γαστρός.
english_sentence_A: That such a person will of necessity die is evident from the accumulation of bad signs; but the words 'and he will become pneumatic' (πνευματωθήσεται) have been tossed in at the end of this passage like a riddle, as though it were one of the things agreed to be going to happen of necessity—whatever 'he will become pneumatic' may signify, whether the abundance of winds (πνεύματα) in the belly, it being possible that the whole belly itself be inflated, or the large and frequent respiration; but we have learned about this too, in which dispositions it will occur, [and that it is] not good, just as also that of the belly.
english_sentence_B: But the phrase 'and he will be filled with pneuma' has been tossed onto the end of this passage like a riddle, as though it were one of the things agreed to occur of necessity, whatever 'he will be filled with pneuma' may signify: whether the quantity of winds in the belly, since it is possible for the belly to be blown up with wind as a whole, or the large and frequent respiration. But we have learned that this too is not good in the conditions in which it will occur, just as indeed we have learned the same of the inflation of the belly.

english_sentence_A: In whomever during fevers the legs become full of phymata and, lingering on, do not ripen while they are still in the fevers, and a choking falls upon the pharynx, the parts about the pharynx being lean, and this too does not ripen but is quenched, for such a person blood is apt to flow from the nostrils; and if much flows, it signifies resolution of the disease; if not, a long one; and the less flows, the worse, and length as well.

If much flows, it signifies resolution of the disease; if not, a long one; and the less flows, the worse it is, and the length too.

greek_sentence: ἢν δὲ τἄλλα ῥήϊστα γένηται, προσδέχεσθαι τῷ τοιῷδε ἐς πόδας ἀλγήματα· ἢν δ᾿ ἅψηται τοῦ ποδὸς καὶ ἐπώδυνος γενόμενος παραμένει, πυριφλεγὴς γενόμενος καὶ μὴ λυθῇ, κατὰ σμικρὸν ἥξει καὶ ἐς αὐχένα ἀλγήματα καὶ ἐς κληῖδα καὶ ἐς ὦμον καὶ ἐς στῆθος καὶ ἐς ἄρθρον καὶ τοῦτο δεήσει φυματῶδες γενέσθαι.
english_sentence_A: And if everything else goes most easily, expect for such a person pains in the feet; and if it takes hold of the foot and, having become painful, persists, having become fiery-hot, and is not resolved, little by little pains will come also to the neck and to the collarbone and to the shoulder and to the chest and to the joint, and this will have to become full of phymata.
english_sentence_B: If everything else becomes very easy, one should expect pains in the feet in such a person. If it fastens on the foot and, having become painful, persists, having become fiery-hot, and is not resolved, then little by little pains will come also to the neck, to the collarbone, to the shoulder, to the chest and to a joint, and this will have to become tumour-like.

lsj_entry_text: ὀφρῦς, ύος, ἡ, acc. ὀφρῦν, in late Poets ὀφρύα, AP 12.186 ( Strat. ), Opp. C. 4.405 , Q.S. 4.361 : acc. pl. ὀφρύας (in the fourth foot) Od. 9.389 ; but ὀφρῦς (before caesura) Il. 16.740 , and so in Att. (v. infr.). [υ in nom. and acc., which are accented ὀφρῦς, -ῦν by Hdn.Gr. 2.937 : the accentuation ὀφρύς, ὀφρύν may be admitted in late writers: compds. have υ , εὔοφρυς, λεύκοφρυς, etc.] (Cf. Skt. bhrūs, gen. bhruvas, Slav. br[ucaron]v[icaron], O E. brú 'brow'.):—brow, eyebrow, τὸν . . ὑπ' ὀφρύος οὖτα Il. 14.493 ; ἡ ὀ. ἡ δεξιά, ἡ ἀριστερά, Arist. PA 671b32 , cf. Pr. 878b28 : elsewh. in pl., ὑπ' ὀφρύσι δάκρυα λεῖβον Il. 13.88 , al.; ὑπ' ὀ. πῦρ ἀμάρυσσεν Hes. Th. 827 , etc.: freq. of signs, ἐπ' ὀφρύσι νεῦσε Κρονίων, i.e. ἐπένευσε ὀφρύσι, nodded assent, Il. 1.528 , etc.; ἡ δ' ἄρ' ἐπ' ὀ. νεῦσε nodded to him to do a thing, Od. 16.164 ; ἀνὰ δ' ὀφρύσι νεῦον ἑκάστῳ made a sign not to do, 9.468 ; ὀφρύσι νευστάζων 12.194 : in various phrases expressing emotions, τὰς ὀ. ἀνασπᾶν, in token of grief, τὰς ὀφρῦς ἀνεσπακώς, ὥσπερ τι δεινὸν ἀγγελῶν Ar. Ach. 1069 ; ἀνασπάσας τις τὰς ὀφρῦς οἴμοι λαλεῖ Men. 556.3 ; of pride (cf. ὀφρυόομαι), D. 19.314 ; οἱ τὰς ὀφρῦς αἴροντες Men. 39 ; ὀφρῦν ἐπαίρειν E. Fr. 1040 , cf. Amphis 13 ; τὰς ὀ. ἔχειν ἐπάνω τῆς κορυφῆς Alex. 16.6 ; ὑπὲρ αὐτοὺς κροτάφους ὑπεραίρειν Luc. Am. 54 ; ὀφρῦς ἔχειν Ar. Ra. 925 ; ὀφρῦν ἐφέλκεσθαι AP 7.440.6 ( Leon. , interpol.?); ἐρύσσαι ib. 5.215 ( Agath. ); ἀνελκταῖς ὀφρύσι σεμνός Cratin. 355 : contrariwise, τὰς ὀφρῦς συνάγειν knit the brows, frown, Ar. Nu. 582 , Pl. 756 , etc.; τὰς ὀ. συνέλκειν Antiph. 307 ; συσπᾶν Luc. Vit.Auct. 7 ; κατεσπακώς Alciphr. 3.3 : on the other hand, καταβαλεῖν, λῦσαι, μεθεῖναι τὰς ὀ. or τὴν ὀ., let down or unknit the brow, become calm or cheerful again, E. Cyc. 167 , Hipp. 290 , IA 648 ; ὀ. μὴ καθειμένη Zeno Stoic. 1.58 ; σχάζεσθαι τὰς ὀ. Pl.Com. 32 ; καθέσθαι Plu. 2.1062f : the brow was also the seat of smiles and joy, ἀγανᾷ χλοαρὸν γελάσσαις ὀφρύϊ Pi. P. 9.38 , cf. h.Cer. 358 ; or gravity, στυγνὸν ὀφρύων νέφος E. Hipp. [172] ; ὁρᾶτε ὡς σπουδαῖαι μὲν αὐτοῦ αἱ ὀφρύες X. Smp. 8.3 ; on their physiognomical character, v. Arist. HA 491b14 , Phgn. 812b26 . ὀφρῦς alone, scorn, pride, AP 7.409 (Antip.), 9.43 ( Parmen. ), 10.122 ( Lucill. ), etc. from like ness of shape, brow of a hill, crag, Il. 20.151 , Pi. O. 13.106 ; embankment, ὀ. ἀπότομος Plb. 36.8.3 ; overhanging bank of a river, Id. 2.33.7 , etc.; ἐπ' ὀφρύων ποταμοῦ PAmh. 2.68.9 (i A. D.); of the sea, A.R. 1.178 , etc.; of a ditch, Str. 5.3.7 (cf. ὀφρύη); of the rim of joint-cavities, Gal. UP 1.15 , al.; of the woodwork enclosing the bore of a torsion-engine, Ph. Bel. 57.7 : in Archit., architrave, Procop.Gaz. p.157 B. a plant, Plin. HN 26.164 .
greek_sentence: σβεννυμένων δὲ τούτων, ἢν αἱ χεῖρες ἐφέλκωνται ἢ τρομεραὶ γένωνται, σπασμὸς [835] τὸν τοιόνδε ἐπιλαμβάνει καὶ παραφροσύνη· ἀτὰρ καὶ φλυζάκια ἐπὶ τὴν ὀφρὺν καὶ ἐρυθήματα ἴσχει καὶ βλέφαρον τὸ ἕτερον παρὰ τὸ ἕτερον παραβλαστάνει καὶ σκληρὴ φλεγμονὴ κατέχει καὶ οἰδέει ἰσχυρῶς ὁ ὀφθαλμὸς καὶ παραφροσύνη μέγα ἐπιδιδοῖ· αἱ δὲ νύκτες μᾶλλον ἐπισημαίνουσιν ἢ αἱ ἡμέραι τὰ περὶ τὴν παραφροσύνην.
english_sentence_A: And when these are extinguished, if the hands are drawn up or become tremulous, spasm [835] seizes such a person, and delirium (paraphrosyne). Moreover he also gets pustules (phlyzakia) on the eyebrow and rednesses, and the one eyelid sprouts out beside the other, and a hard inflammation (phlegmone) takes hold and the eye swells strongly, and the delirium greatly increases; and the nights rather than the days show the signs relating to the delirium.
english_sentence_B: But when these are extinguished, if the hands are drawn or become tremulous, convulsion [835] and derangement seize such a person. Moreover he also has small pustules on the eyebrow, and rednesses; and one eyelid sprouts out alongside the other, and a hard inflammation (phlegmonē) takes hold, and the eye swells violently, and the derangement increases greatly.

Ag. 15 , Th. 3 ; of weeping, δάκρυ χαμαὶ βάλεν ἐκ βλεφάροιϊν Od. 17.490 , cf. 23.33 ; of death, λύειν β. S. Ant. 1302 : in Prose, Antipho Soph. 81a , Pl. Ti. 45d , PPetr. 3p.23 (iii B. lsj_entry_text: περισσός, Att. περιττός, ή, όν, (from περί, as ἔπισσαι from ἐπί, μέτασσαι from μετά) beyond the regular number or size, prodigious, δῶρα Hes. Th. 399 (never in Hom. ); ῶʼμος Trag.Adesp. 458.3 ; στάθμα, dub.sens., v. ἕλκω B. 3 . out of the common, extraordinary, strange, ἔ τι περισσὸν εἰδείη if he has any signal knowledge, Thgn. 769 ; εἴ τι φρονεῖς καί τι περισσὸν ἔχεις Philisc.( PLG 2.327 ); π. λόγος S. OT 841 ; ἄγρα E. Ba. 1197 (lyr.); πάθος Id. Supp. 791 (lyr.); βίος οὐδὲν ἔχων π. ἀλλὰ πάντα σμικρά Antipho Soph. 51 ; οὐ γὰρ π. οὐδὲν οὐδ' ἔξω λόγου πέπονθας E. Hipp. 437 ; περισσότερα παθήματα Antipho 3.4.5 ; τὰ π. τῶν ἔργων καὶ τερατώδη Isoc. 12.77 ; ἴδια καὶ π. Id. 15.145 ; π. καὶ θαυμαστά Arist. EN 1141b6 ; πρᾶξις π. Id. Pol. 1312a27 ; οὐθὲν δὴ λέγοντες π. φαίνονταί τι λέγειν Id. Metaph. 1053b3 ; τί π. ποιεῖτε; Ev.Matt. 5.47 ; περιττοτάτη φύσις Arist. HA 531a9 ; συνανθρωπίζον . . πάντων περισσότατον, of the dog, Ath. 13.611c , cf. Clearch. 24 ; in Literature, striking, τὸ περιττόν, as a quality of οἱ τοῦ Σωκράτους λόγοι, Arist. Pol. 1265a11 ; τὰ σοφὰ καὶ τὰ π. refinements, Epicur. Fr. 409 ; opp. κοινὸς καὶ δημώδης, Longin. 40.2 (but also, elaborate, π. καὶ πεποιημένος Id. 3.4 ; in bad sense, far-fetched, D.H. Pomp. 2 , Dem. 56 ). of persons, extraordinary, remarkable, esp. for great learning, π. ὢν ἀνήρ E. Hipp. 948 ; τοὺς . . π. καί τι πράσσοντας πλέον Id. Fr. 788 ; δυστυχεῖς εἶναι τοὺς π. Arist. Metaph. 983a2 ; π. γένος τῶν μελιττῶν Id. GA 760a4 : freq. with the manner added, π. κατὰ φιλοσοφίαν Id. Pr. 953a10 ; περὶ τὸν ἄλλον βίον περιττότερος somewhat extravagant or eccentric, Id. Pol. 1267 b24 ; τῇ φύσει π. Id. HA 622b6 ; κάλλει Plu. Demetr. 2 ; ἐν ἅπασι Id. Dem. 3 ; τὴν ὥραν Alciphr. 1.12 : c. inf., D.H. Comp. 18 . c. gen., περισσὸς ἄλλων πρός τι beyond others in . . , S. El. 155 ; θύσει τοῦδε περισσότερα greater things than this, AP 6.321 (Leon. Alex. ); περιττότερος προφήτου one greater than . . , Ev.Matt. 11.9 . more than sufficient, superfluous, αἱ π. δαπάναι X. Mem. 3.6.6 ; περιττὸν ἔχειν to have a surplus, Id. An. 7.6.31 ; οἱ μὲν . . περιττὰ ἔχουσιν, οἱ δὲ οὐδὲ τὰ ἀναγκαῖα . . Id. Oec. 20.1 : c. gen., τῶν ἀρκούντων περιττά more than sufficient, Id. Cyr. 8.2.21 ; τὰ π. τῶν ἱκανῶν Id. Hier. 1.19 : freq. in military sense, οἱ π. ἱππεῖς the reserve horse, Id. Eq.Mag. 8.14 ; οἱ π. τῆς φυλακῆς ib. 7.7 ; π. σκηναί spare tents, Id. Cyr. 4.6.12 (but τοῖς περιττοῖς χρήσεσθαι their superior numbers, Id. An. 4.8.11 , cf. Cyr. 6.3.20 ); τὸ π. the surplus, residue, Inscr. ap. eund. An. 5.3.13 (but τὸ π. τοῦ Ἰουδαίου the advantage of the Jew, Ep.Rom. 3.1 ); Ἁρπυιῶν τὰ π. their leavings, AP 11.239 ( Lucill. ); τὸ π. τῆς ἡμέρας the remainder of the day, X.Eph. 1.3 ; π. γράμματα supplementary provisions in a will, BGU 326ii9 (ii A.D.). in bad sense, superfluous, useless, οὐδέ τι τοῦ παντὸς κενεὸν πέλει οὐδὲ π. Emp. 13 ; μόχθος π. A. Pr. 385 , cf. S. Ant. 780 ; π. κἀνόνητα σώματα Id. Aj. 758 ; βάρος π. γῆς ἀναστρωφώμενοι Id. Fr. 945 ; ἄχθος Id. El. 1241 (lyr.); τὰ γὰρ π. πανταχοῦ λυπήρ' ἔπη Id. Fr. 82 ; αὐδῶ σε μὴ περισσὰ κηρύσσειν A. Th. 1048 ; π. πάντες οὑν μέσῳ λόγοι E. Med. 819 ; π. φωνῶν Id. Supp. 459 . excessive, extravagant, μηχανᾶσθαι περισσά commit extravagances, Hdt. 2.32 ; περισσὰ δρᾶν, πράσσειν, to be over-busy, S. Tr. 617 , Ant. 68 ; π. φρονεῖν to be over-wise, E. Fr. 924 (anap.); ἡ π. αὕτη ἐπιμέλεια τοῦ σώματος Pl. R. 407b ; μῆκος πολὺ λόγων π. Id. Lg. 645c ; redundant, overdone, οἱ καρτεροὶ καὶ π. λόγοι Id. Ax. 365c , etc.; of dress, ἐσθὴς π. Plu. 2.615d ; περισσοτέρα λύπη 2 Ep.Cor. 2.7 ; τοῦ τὰ δέοντ' ἔχειν περιττὰ μισῶ I hate extravagance in comparison with moderation, Alex. 254 , etc. of persons, over-wise, over-curious, περισσὸς καὶ φρονῶν μέγα E. Hipp. 445 , cf. Ba. 429 (lyr.); ὁ πολυπράγμων καὶ π. Plb. 9.1.4 ; τὴν περὶ τὸ σῶμα θεραπείαν ἀκριβὴς καὶ π. Plu. Cic. 8 ; so, of speakers, π. ἐν τοῖς λόγοις Δημοσθένης Aeschin. 1.119 . as a term of praise, subtle, acute, ἀκριβὴς καὶ π. διάνοια Arist. Top. 141b13 . Arith., ἀριθμὸς π. an odd, uneven number, opp. ἄρτιος, Epich. 170.7 , Philol. 5 , Pl. Prt. 356e , etc.; π. ἡμέραι Hp. Aph. 4.61 ; τὸ π. καὶ τὸ ἄρτιον the nature of odd and even, Pl. Grg. 451c , etc.; π. χῶραι the odd places in a verse, Heph. 5.1 ; ἀρτιάκις π. ἀριθμός a number divisible by an odd number an even number of times, as 2 , 6 , 10 , Euc. 7 Def. 9 . περισσότεροι more in number, extra, Carnead. ap. S.E. M. 9.140 . περιττόν, τό, = στρύχνος μανικός, θρύον 11 , Thphr. HP 9.11.6 ; περισσόν Dsc. 4.73 ; περίσκον Orib. 12.8.56 . Adv. περισσῶς extraordinarily, exceedingly, θεοσεβέεες π. ἐόντες Hdt. 2.37 ; ἐπαινέσεται π. E. Ba. 1197 (lyr.); π. παῖδας ἐκδιδάσκεσθαι to have them educated overmuch, Id. Med. 295 ; περιττοτέρως τῶν ἄλλων far above all others, Isoc. 3.44 ; περισσότερον τοῦ ἑνός Luc. Pr.Im. 14 ; also περισσά Pi. N. 7.43 , E. Hec. 579 , etc. remarkably, περισσότερον τῶν ἄλλων θάψαι τινά more sumptuously, Hdt. 2.129 ; οἴκησις π. ἐσκευασμένη Plb. 1.29.7 ; περιττότατα ἔχειν to be most remarkable, Arist. HA 589a31 ; κοσμουμένη π. καὶ σεμνῶς Plu. 2.145e ; περισσότατα ἀνθρώπων θρησκεύειν in the most singular way, D.C. 37.17 ; ἡδέως καὶ π. in an uncommon manner, D.H. Comp. 3 ; εἰπεῖν στρογγύλως καὶ π. Id. Is. 20 ; ἰδίως καὶ π. Plu. Thes. 19 ; τὰ καινῶς ἱστορούμενα καὶ π. Id. 2.30d . abundantly, ἐχέτω π. τῆς κρόκης Alciphr. 3.41 . with a neg., οὐδὲν περισσὸν τούτων nothing more than or beyond these, Antipho 3.4.6 ; οὐδὲν τῶν ἄλλων περιττότερον πραγματεύεσθαι Pl. Ap. 20c ; οὐδὲν π. ἢ εἰ . . no otherwise than if . . , Id. Smp. 219c ; περισσόν alone, furthermore, LXX Ec. 12.12 ,al. τὰ περισσά in vain, AP 12.182 ( Strat. ). ἐκ περιττοῦ superfluously, uselessly, Pl. Prt. 338c , Sph. 265e ; but ὑπερέχειν ἐκ π. to be far superior, Id. Lg. 734d , cf. 802d ; ἡ κάμινος ἐκαύθη ἐκ π. Thd. Da. 3.22 ; ἐκ π. χρησάμενος τῇ παρρησίᾳ Luc. Pro Merc.Cond. 13 ; cf. ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ.
lsj_first_sense_gloss: beyond the regular number or size
greek_sentence: τὰ δὲ σημεῖα μάλιστα γίνεται πολλὰ ἐπὶ τὸν περισσὸν ἀριθμὸν ἢ ἐπὶ τὸν ἄρτιον· ὁκοτέρῳ δ᾿ ἂν τούτων τῶν ἀριθμῶν γίνηται, ὀλέθριοι ἐπιγίνονται.
english_sentence_A: And the signs occur in greater number mostly on the odd number than on the even; but in whichever of these numbers they occur, they turn out deadly.
english_sentence_B: The nights give signs of what concerns the derangement more than the days do. The signs occur for the most part in great number on the odd number rather than on the even; but on whichever of these numbers they occur, they supervene as deadly.

lsj_entry_text: πυρετώδης, ες, feverish, ῥίγεα Hp. Fract. 34 ; inflamed, ἕλκος ib. 25 ( v.l. πυρῶδες ). subject to fever, κύστις Id.Aër. 9 . of a sickly season, π. θέρος ib. 10 ; π. νότοι Arist. Pr. 862a17 , etc. Comp. -έστερος Hp. Art. 49 .
greek_sentence: γεγενήσθω [836] γάρ τινι φυματώδη τὰ σκέλη καὶ μὴ πεπαινέσθω, προσυποκείσθω δὲ καὶ πυρετώδης εἶναι καὶ πνιγώδης γενόμενος παυσάσθω· προσδοκήσειεν ἄν τις ἄνω γεγονέναι μετάστασιν τῶν ἐν σκέλεσι χυμῶν, ἥτις ἐν ταῖς παρόδοις πνιγώδη τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐποίησεν, ἐὰν οὖν ὁ τοιοῦτος, ὡς Ἱπποκράτης εἶπεν, ἐστὶ περιεστηκὼς, αἱμοῤῥαγῆσαι δυνήσεται διὰ ῥινῶν· καὶ ἐὰν πολὺ ᾖ τὸ αἷμα, λύσει τὴν νόσον· εἰ δ᾿ οὐ, χρονίσει, καὶ εἰ τἄλλα καλῶς γένοιτο, πάλιν εἰς τοὺς πόδας ἀλγήματα τούτῳ κατασκῆψαι δυνατόν ἐστιν.
english_sentence_A: For let it be supposed [836] that someone's legs have become tumorous and do not come to maturation; let it further be supposed that he is also feverish, and that, having become suffocative, he has ceased to be so. One would then expect that a transference upward of the humours in the legs has taken place, which in its passages made the man suffocative.
english_sentence_B: One would expect that a transfer upwards of the humours in the legs has taken place, which in its passages made the person suffocated. If, then, such a person, as Hippocrates said, has survived, he will be able to haemorrhage through the nostrils; and if the blood is copious, it will resolve the disease; but if not, the disease will become chronic, and, if everything else goes well, it is possible for pains to descend again into his feet.

greek_sentence: ὑποκείσθω δὲ καὶ τοῦτο γεγονέναι, καθάπερ καὶ τὸ πυριφλεγῆ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐπὶ τούτοις γενέσθαι, ὅπερ ἤτοι θερμασίαν πολλὴν περὶ τὸν πόδα δηλοῦν εἴωθεν ἢ πυρετὸν πολὺν καὶ πυρώδη· καὶ εἰ ἐπὶ τούτοις μὴ λυθείη τὰ συμπτώματα, πάλιν ἀναχωρῆσαν ἄνω μᾶλλον τὸ πλῆθος, ἀλγήματα γεννήσει κατὰ τοὺς αὐχένας καὶ κλεῖς καὶ τὸν ὦμον καὶ τὸ στῆθος.
english_sentence_A: If, then, such a person, as Hippocrates said, is one who is going to survive, he will be able to have a haemorrhage through the nostrils; and if the blood is abundant, it will resolve the disease; but if not, it will become chronic, and even if the other things turn out well, it is possible for pains to settle down again into this man's feet. And let it be supposed that this too has happened, as also that the man became burning-hot (πυριφλεγῆ) after these things, which is wont to indicate either much heat about the foot or a great and fiery fever; and if after these the symptoms are not resolved, the plethora, again withdrawing further upward, will generate pains in the neck and collar-bones and the shoulder and the chest.
english_sentence_B: Let this too be supposed to have happened, as also that the person became fire-hot upon these things, which is wont to indicate either much heat about the foot or a great and fiery fever. And if upon these the symptoms are not resolved, the plethos, withdrawing once more rather upwards, will produce pains in the neck and collarbones and the shoulder and the chest.

english_sentence_A: If, then, such a person, as Hippocrates said, is one who is going to survive, he will be able to have a haemorrhage through the nostrils; and if the blood is abundant, it will resolve the disease; but if not, it will become chronic, and even if the other things turn out well, it is possible for pains to settle down again into this man's feet. And let it be supposed that this too has happened, as also that the man became burning-hot (πυριφλεγῆ) after these things, which is wont to indicate either much heat about the foot or a great and fiery fever; and if after these the symptoms are not resolved, the plethora, again withdrawing further upward, will generate pains in the neck and collar-bones and the shoulder and the chest.
english_sentence_B: Let this too be supposed to have happened, as also that the person became fire-hot upon these things, which is wont to indicate either much heat about the foot or a great and fiery fever. And if upon these the symptoms are not resolved, the plethos, withdrawing once more rather upwards, will produce pains in the neck and collarbones and the shoulder and the chest.

greek_sentence: ὡς δὲ πάντα συνέβη ταῦτα αὐτῷ ἀλόγως (τοῦτο γὰρ ἦν τὸ σβεσθῆναι) τὰς χεῖρας ὑποκείσθω γενέσθαι τρομώδεις, ἔπειτα σπασμὸν ἐπακολουθῆσαι, τοῦ πλήθους [837] ἀποσκήψαντος εἰς τὰ νευρώδη μόρια καὶ αὐτὴν τὴν ἀρχὴν αὐτῶν καταλαβόντος, ἐντεῦθεν γὰρ αἱ παραφροσύναι.
english_sentence_A: And when all these things have befallen him without reason (for this is what 'to be quenched' meant), let it be supposed that the hands become tremulous, and then that a spasm follows, the plethora [837] having settled upon the sinewy parts and seized their very origin; for from there come the deliria.
english_sentence_B: And when all these things had happened to him unaccountably (for this was what 'being extinguished' meant), let it be supposed that his hands became tremulous, and that then a spasm followed, the plethos [837] having settled upon the sinewy parts and having seized their very origin; for it is from this that the deliria arise. The writer, then, having seen one of those who had been ill in this way with blisters on the eyebrow (for this is what 'phlyzakia' means), rashly declared that this symptom would occur in all who are in this condition.

greek_sentence: τούτων δὲ τὰ μὲν ἄλλα σαφῆ, τὸ δὲ παραβλαστάνει τὸ βλέφαρον τὸ ἕτερον, ἀσαφὲς ἐστι πότερον ἐκ μέρους αὐτῶν τινα γινομένην σύμφυσιν ἢ σαρκῶδές τι βλάστημα, θατέρου μὲν ἐκφυόμενον, ἐπὶ δὲ θάτερον ἐκτεινόμενον ἠβουλήθη δηλῶσαι.
english_sentence_A: Of these, the rest are clear, but 'the one eyelid grows out beside' is unclear—whether he wished to indicate some coalescence of them arising in part, or some fleshy outgrowth growing out from the one and extending toward the other.
english_sentence_B: Of these, the rest are clear. But 'the one eyelid grows out alongside' is unclear: did he wish to indicate a partial adhesion arising between them, or some fleshy outgrowth springing from the one and extending onto the other?

greek_sentence: Ὁκόταν πυρέσσοντι τεσσαρεσκαιδεκαταίῳ ἐόντι ἀφωνίη προσγένηται, οὐ φιλέει λύσις ταχείη, οὐδ᾿ ἀπαλλαγὴ τοῦ νοσήματος γίγνεσθαι, ἀλλὰ χρόνον τῷ τοιῷδε σημαίνει· ὁκόταν δὲ φανῇ ἐπὶ τῇ ἡμέρῃ ταύτῃ, μακρότερον ξυμπίπτει.
english_sentence_A: Whenever voicelessness supervenes in a patient who is febrile and in the fourteenth day, a swift resolution is not wont to occur, nor a release from the disease, but it signifies length of time for such a patient; and whenever it appears on this day, it turns out longer.
english_sentence_B: When loss of voice supervenes in someone who is feverish and on the fourteenth day, a swift resolution, or deliverance from the disease, is not wont to occur; rather, it signifies length of time for such a person; and when it appears on this day, the illness turns out longer.

english_sentence_A: This statement is superfluous for those who have learned that bad symptoms have a greater power when they appear on critical days; for the writer of the book has here too made use of this universal principle in the case of one of the particular matters pertaining to the fourteenth day.
english_sentence_B: This statement is superfluous for those who have learned that bad symptoms have greater force when they appear on critical days. For the writer of the book has now too employed this universal rule, applied to one of the particular cases, that of the fourteenth day.

english_sentence_A: For just as on the other critical days, so also on this one, if some bad symptom appears, it has greater power.

greek_sentence: Θερινῆς καὶ μετοπωρινῆς ὥρης ἐπὶ τῶν ὀξέων, αἵματος ἀπόσταξις ἐξαπίνης, συντονίην καὶ πολλὴν φλεγμασίην κατὰ τὰς φλέβας δηλοῖ καὶ ἐς τὴν ὑστεραίην λεπτῶν οὔρων ἐπιφάσιας· καὶ ἢν ἀκμάζῃ τῇ ἡλικίῃ καὶ τὸ σῶμα ἐκ γυμνασίων ἢ εὐσαρκώσιος ἔχῃ ἢ μελαγχολικὸς ἢ ἐκ πόσιος χεῖρες τρομεραὶ, καλῶς ἔχει παραφροσύνην προειπεῖν ἢ σπασμόν.
english_sentence_A: In the summer and autumnal season, in acute diseases, a sudden dripping of blood indicates tension and much inflammation in the veins, and, on the following day, appearances of thin urines; and if he is in the prime of life and has his body in a condition from exercises or from good fleshiness, or is melancholic, or his hands are tremulous from drinking, it is well to foretell derangement of mind or spasm.
english_sentence_B: "In the summer and autumn season, in acute diseases, a sudden dripping of blood indicates tension and much inflammation in the veins, and, for the following day, appearances of thin urines; and if the patient is at the prime of life and has his body in condition from exercises or from good fleshiness, or is melancholic, or has trembling hands from drinking, it is well to predict derangement or convulsion." This passage too, again, contains a combination of many symptoms that do not occur together in every sick person; and for this reason things written in this way are useless, since useful teaching proceeds through universals, as Hippocrates is accustomed to do.

greek_sentence: θερινῆς καὶ μετοπωρινῆς ὥρης ἐπὶ τῶν ὀξέων αἵματος ἀπόσταξις ἐξαπίνης συντονίην καὶ πολλὴν φλεγμασίην κατὰ τὰς φλέβας δηλοῖ καὶ ἐς τὴν ὑστεραίην λεπτῶν οὔρων ἐπιφάσιας· καὶ ἢν ἀκμάζῃ τῇ ἡλικίῃ καὶ τὸ σῶμα ἐκ γυμνασίων ἢ εὐσαρκώσιος ἔχῃ ἢ μελαγχολικὸς ἢ ἐκ πόσιος χεῖρες τρομεραὶ, καλῶς ἔχει παραφροσύνην προειπεῖν ἢ σπασμόν.
english_sentence_A: "In the summer and autumn season, in acute diseases, a sudden dripping of blood indicates tension (syntonia) and much inflammation in the veins, and for the following day appearances of thin urines; and if he is in the prime of life and has his body in a condition resulting from exercises or from good flesh, or is melancholic, or his hands are tremulous from drinking, it is well to predict delirium or convulsion." It would have been better, then, to say that the tension indicates that the veins need treatment; and we know that he says that drippings of blood from the nostrils are always something bad, because nature strives to excrete the superfluity but is unable to do so, on account of its own weakness, or thickness of the blood, or condensation of the parts, or some of these, or all of them together.

english_sentence_A: "In the summer and autumn season, in acute diseases, a sudden dripping of blood indicates tension (syntonia) and much inflammation in the veins, and for the following day appearances of thin urines; and if he is in the prime of life and has his body in a condition resulting from exercises or from good flesh, or is melancholic, or his hands are tremulous from drinking, it is well to predict delirium or convulsion." It would have been better, then, to say that the tension indicates that the veins need treatment; and we know that he says that drippings of blood from the nostrils are always something bad, because nature strives to excrete the superfluity but is unable to do so, on account of its own weakness, or thickness of the blood, or condensation of the parts, or some of these, or all of them together.
english_sentence_B: We know that he says that drippings of blood from the nostrils are always something bad, because nature seeks to excrete the superfluity but is unable to, owing to its own weakness, or the thickness of the blood, or the condensation of the parts, or some or all of these coming together.

greek_sentence: Δύο γραφαί εἰσι τῆς ἐπιγίνεσθαι λέξεως· μία μὲν διὰ τοῦ τ στοιχείου τῆς τρίτης συλλαβῆς γεγραμμένης, ἄλλη δὲ διὰ τοῦ γ.
english_sentence_A: "And if it supervenes on even days, it is better; but on critical days it is deadly, unless blood, rushing forth abundantly and in sufficient quantity, makes outlets for the excess through the nostrils or through the seat, or suppurations, or metastases, or abscessions, or pains of the hypochondria, or into the testicles or into the legs; and when these have been concocted, there come about discharges of sputa, of thick urines or of smooth white ones." There are two readings of the word ἐπιγίνεσθαι: one in which the third syllable is written with the letter τ, the other with the letter γ.
english_sentence_B: "And if it supervenes on even days, it is better; but on critical days it is deadly, unless blood, rushing forth in great abundance, makes outlets for the excess through the nostrils, or there are suppurations at the seat, or metastases, or apostases, or pains of the hypochondria, or into the testicles or into the legs; and when these have been concocted, there come outlets of sputa, of thick urines, or of smooth, white ones." There are two readings of the word epiginesthai ('to supervene'): one with the third syllable written with the letter tau, the other with gamma.

greek_sentence: ἀλλ᾿ ἐάν τε κατὰ τὴν προτέραν ἐπιτείνεσθαι λέγῃ τοὺς κάμνοντας ἐν ἀρτίαις ἡμέραις, ἐάν τε κατὰ τὴν δευτέραν ἐπιγίνεσθαι τὰ εἰρημένα συμπτώματα κατὰ τὰς ἀρτίας ἡμέρας, οὐκ εὐθέως ἐστὶ καὶ βέλτιον (τοῦτο δ᾿ αὐτὸς [845] εἶπεν) οὐδὲ γὰρ εἰ ἄρτιοι προσήκει σκοπεῖν, ἀλλ᾿ εἰ καὶ κρίσιμοι· τὴν γοῦν τετάρτην ἡμέραν ἀρτίαν οὖσαν καὶ αὐτὸς ἑξῆς ὀλίγον ἔμπροσθεν εἶπεν, ὅτι μεγίστην δύναμιν ἔχει.
english_sentence_A: But whether, according to the former reading, he says that the patients are intensified on even days, or, according to the second, that the symptoms mentioned supervene on the even days, it is not immediately also better (this he himself [845] said); for it is not proper to consider whether the days are even, but whether they are also critical. At any rate, of the fourth day, which is even, he himself said a little earlier in sequence that it has the greatest power.
english_sentence_B: But whether, according to the first reading, he says that the patients are exacerbated on the even days, or, according to the second, that the aforementioned symptoms supervene on the even days, it is not on that account straightway also better (this is what he himself [845] said). For one ought not to consider whether the days are even, but whether they are also critical.

greek_sentence: διαφέρει δ᾿ ἀλλήλων τῷ τὴν μὲν ἀπόστασιν αὐτὴν τὴν κρίσιν ἐπιφέρειν καὶ ἀπαλλάττειν ἁπάντων τῶν ὀχληρῶν τὸν κάμνοντα, τὴν δὲ μετάστασιν ἑτέρων ἴσχειν ἀρχὴν παροξυσμῶν τε καὶ πόνων, ὡς δεῖσθαι πάλιν ἄλλου χρόνου πρὸς τὴν πέψιν τὸν τόπον τοῦ σώματος, εἰς ὃν ἡ μετάστασις ἐγένετο τῶν λυπούντων χυμῶν· διὸ καὶ προσέθηκε, πεφθέντων δὲ τούτων, αἱ διέξοδοι γίγνονται πτυσμῶν ἢ παχέων οὔρων, λείων, λευκῶν· σημεῖα διδάσκων τοῦ πεπέφθαι τὴν μετάστασιν ἐκ τῶν πεπεμμένων πτυσμάτων τε καὶ οὔρων.
english_sentence_A: They differ from one another in that the abscession brings on the crisis itself and frees the patient from all troubles, whereas the metastasis contains the beginning of other paroxysms and pains, so that the part of the body into which the metastasis of the offending humours has taken place needs again another period of time for concoction; wherefore he also added, 'and when these have been concocted, the discharges of sputa occur, or of thick urines, smooth, white', teaching the signs that the metastasis has been concocted, from the concocted sputa and urines.
english_sentence_B: These differ from one another in this: the apostasis brings on the crisis itself and frees the patient from all that troubles him, whereas the metastasis contains the beginning of other paroxysms and pains, so that the region of the body into which the metastasis of the troublesome humours took place again requires further time for coction. For this reason he also added: 'when these have been concocted, there come the evacuations of sputa or of thick urines, smooth, white'.

greek_sentence: ἄφυκτος δ᾿ ὁ τοιοῦτος, ἢν μὴ ἱδρῶτες κριτικοὶ καὶ ὕπνοι ὁμαλοὶ ἐπιγένωνται καὶ οὖρα παχέα καὶ δριμέα καταδράμῃ ἢ εἰς ἀπόστασιν στηρίζῃ.
english_sentence_A: Such a case is inescapable unless critical sweats and even sleep supervene, and thick and acrid urine run down, or it settles into an abscession.
english_sentence_B: Such a patient is not to escape, unless critical sweats and even sleep supervene, and thick and acrid urine runs down, or the disease settles into an apostasis.

greek_sentence: Τὰς λύγγας εἰώθασι καὶ λυγμοὺς ὀνομάζειν· εἰσὶ δὲ κινήσεις τινὲς τοῦ στομάχου σπασμώδεις· γίνεσθαι δέ φασι δι᾿ ἄμετρον κένωσιν ἢ πλήρωσιν.
english_sentence_A: They are accustomed to call hiccups (lynges) also lygmoi; these are certain spasmodic movements of the stomach (stomachos); and they say they arise through immoderate evacuation or repletion.
english_sentence_B: The lynges (hiccups) they are accustomed to call also lygmoi; they are certain spasmodic movements of the stomach, and they say that they arise through immoderate evacuation or repletion.

lsj_entry_text: δῆξις, εως, ἡ, (δάκνω) bite, biting, Arist. HA 623a1 ; δήξιες σπλάγχνων gnawings, Hp. VM 19 : metaph., of mental anguish, pangs, Zeno Stoic. 1.51 (pl.), Chrysipp.ib. 3.119 , Phld. D. 3 . Fr. 22 ; also, biting jokes, Plu. Lyc. 14 .
greek_sentence: φαίνεται δὲ νῦν ἡ δῆξις αὕτη γιγνομένη καὶ διὰ δριμύτητα δάκνουσαν τὸν στόμαχον, ὡς ἐπειδάν τις πέπερι πλέον ἤ τι τοιοῦτον καταπίῃ· καὶ μέντοι καὶ τῶν πυρεσσόντων ἔνιοι λύγξαντες ἤμεσαν [847] διαβρωτικὸν καὶ δριμύτατον χυμὸν, ἐφ᾿ ᾧ τελέως ἐπαύσαντο τοῦ συμπτώματος· ἀλλ᾿ ὅ γε τοιοῦτος πυρετὸς οὐ καλεῖται λυγγώδης, ἐπὶ πλέον γὰρ δεῖ παραμένειν τὸν λυγμὸν ἢ καὶ δι᾿ ὅλου τοῦ νοσήματος εἶναι συμπαροξυνόμενον τοῖς πυρετοῖς, ἵνα λυγγώδης ὀνομασθῇ.
english_sentence_A: But now this biting appears to arise also through a pungency that bites the orifice of the stomach (stomachos), as when someone swallows too much pepper or something of that kind; and indeed some of those with fever, after hiccuping, have vomited up [847] a corrosive and most pungent humour, upon which they were completely freed of the symptom; but such a fever is not called hiccup-fever (lyngodes), for the hiccup must persist for a longer time, or even be present throughout the whole disease, being exacerbated along with the fevers, in order that it be named hiccup-fever.
english_sentence_B: But now it is evident that this biting also arises through an acridity that bites the stomach, as when someone swallows too much pepper or something of that kind; and indeed some of those in fever, after hiccuping, have vomited [847] a corrosive and extremely acrid humour, upon which they were completely relieved of the symptom. Such a fever, however, is not called hiccuping, for the hiccup must persist for a longer time, or even be exacerbated together with the fevers throughout the whole disease, for the fever to be named hiccuping.

greek_sentence: τὸν τοιοῦτον πυρετὸν ὑφ᾿ ἱδρώτων κρισίμων καὶ ὕπνων ὁμαλῶν καὶ οὔρων δριμέων καὶ παχέων ἐκκενωθέντων θεραπεύεσθαί φησιν, ἤτοι γε ἐκκριθέντων τῶν τοιούτων ἢ εἰ εἰς ἀπόστημα στηριχθῇ.
english_sentence_A: Such a fever, he says, is cured by critical sweats and even sleeps and by the evacuation of pungent and thick urines, that is, either when such things are excreted or if it is fixed in an abscess (apostema).
english_sentence_B: Such a fever, he says, is cured by critical sweats, by even sleep, and by acrid and thick urines being evacuated, that is, when such things are excreted, or if it settles into an abscess.

greek_sentence: Τὰ δὲ περιπνευμονικὰ καὶ πλευριτικὰ ὧδε χρὴ σκέπτεσθαι· ἢν ὀξύς τε ὁ πυρετὸς ᾖ καὶ τὰ ὀδυνήματα τοῦ πλευροῦ τοῦ ἑτέρου ἢ καὶ ἀμφοῖν καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος ἄνω φερομένου, ἢν πονέῃ καὶ βῆχες ἐνέωσι καὶ πτύσματα ἀνείη πυῤῥὰ ἢ πελιὰ ἢ καὶ λεπτὰ καὶ ἀφρώδεα καὶ ἀνθηρὰ καὶ εἴ τι ἄλλο διαφέρον ἔχῃ παρὰ τὰ μεμαθηκότα τούτοισιν· οὕτω χρὴ διάγειν.
english_sentence_A: "Peripneumonic and pleuritic cases must be considered as follows: if the fever is acute and there are pains of one side or indeed of both, and if, when the breath is carried upward, he suffers pain, and coughs are present and he brings up sputa that are tawny or livid, or also thin and frothy and florid, and if he has anything else that differs from what is usual in these cases; one must manage (them) in the following way."
english_sentence_B: "Peripneumonic and pleuritic cases should be examined thus: if the fever is acute and there are pains of one side, or of both, and if the patient is in pain when the breath is carried upward, and coughs are present, and he brings up sputa that are tawny or livid, or also thin and frothy and florid, and if they have anything else that differs from what is customary for them: thus one must manage the regimen."

english_sentence_B: "Peripneumonic and pleuritic cases should be examined thus: if the fever is acute and there are pains of one side, or of both, and if the patient is in pain when the breath is carried upward, and coughs are present, and he brings up sputa that are tawny or livid, or also thin and frothy and florid, and if they have anything else that differs from what is customary for them: thus one must manage the regimen."

greek_sentence: πυρετὸς οὖν ὀξὺς καὶ ὀδύνη πλευροῦ θατέρου ἢ ἀμφοτέρων, μάλιστα κατὰ τὴν ἐκπνοὴν γιγνομένη (τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος ἄνω φερομένου, ἢν πονέῃ) καὶ βῆχες καὶ πτύελα πυῤῥὰ ἢ πελιδνὰ καὶ λεπτὰ καὶ ἀφρώδη καὶ ἀνθηρὰ καὶ ὁπωσοῦν ἄλλως ἐξηλλαγμένα παρὰ τὰ εὐήθη (τοῦτο γὰρ δηλοῖ λέγων καὶ εἴ τι ἄλλο διαφέρον ἔχει παρὰ τὰ μεμαθηκότα) ταῦτα πάντα τοῖς πλευριτικοῖς τε καὶ περιπνευμονικοῖς ἐμφαίνεσθαί φησι συμβαίνοντα.
english_sentence_A: An acute fever, then, and pain of one side or of both, arising especially during expiration (for this is the meaning of 'and if he suffers when the breath is carried upward'), and coughs, and sputa that are tawny or livid and thin and frothy and florid, and in whatever other way altered from the customary ones (for this is what he indicates in saying 'and if it has anything else differing from what has been learned')—all these, he says, are seen to occur in pleuritics and peripneumonics.
english_sentence_B: First he gives what the old Empiricists name the 'syndrome' (syndromē); the ancients called such symptoms 'those that sit together with' the affections (synedreuonta). So: acute fever, and pain of one side or of both, occurring especially during expiration (for this is the meaning of 'and when the breath is carried upward, if he suffers'), and coughs, and sputa that are tawny or livid, thin, frothy and florid, or altered in any other way from the customary (for this is what he indicates by saying 'and if it has anything else differing from what is usual').

greek_sentence: πυρετὸς οὖν ὀξὺς καὶ ὀδύνη πλευροῦ θατέρου ἢ ἀμφοτέρων, μάλιστα κατὰ τὴν ἐκπνοὴν γιγνομένη (τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος ἄνω φερομένου, ἢν πονέῃ) καὶ βῆχες καὶ πτύελα πυῤῥὰ ἢ πελιδνὰ καὶ λεπτὰ καὶ ἀφρώδη καὶ ἀνθηρὰ καὶ ὁπωσοῦν ἄλλως ἐξηλλαγμένα παρὰ τὰ εὐήθη (τοῦτο γὰρ δηλοῖ λέγων καὶ εἴ τι ἄλλο διαφέρον ἔχει παρὰ τὰ μεμαθηκότα) ταῦτα πάντα τοῖς πλευριτικοῖς τε καὶ περιπνευμονικοῖς ἐμφαίνεσθαί φησι συμβαίνοντα.
english_sentence_A: An acute fever, then, and pain of one side or of both, arising especially during expiration (for this is the meaning of 'and if he suffers when the breath is carried upward'), and coughs, and sputa that are tawny or livid and thin and frothy and florid, and in whatever other way altered from the customary ones (for this is what he indicates in saying 'and if it has anything else differing from what has been learned')—all these, he says, are seen to occur in pleuritics and peripneumonics.
english_sentence_B: First he gives what the old Empiricists name the 'syndrome' (syndromē); the ancients called such symptoms 'those that sit together with' the affections (synedreuonta). So: acute fever, and pain of one side or of both, occurring especially during expiration (for this is the meaning of 'and when the breath is carried upward, if he suffers'), and coughs, and sputa that are tawny or livid, thin, frothy and florid, or altered in any other way from the customary (for this is what he indicates by saying 'and if it has anything else differing from what is usual').

Ba. 701 ); Dor. μασδός Theoc. 3.16 , 48 ; later μασθός LXX Is. 32.12 (cod.A), al., Asclep. ap. Gal. 13.934 , Apoc. 1.13 (v.l.), IG 3.238 b, PMag.Lond. 121.208 , etc., also in codd. of A. Ch. 545 :—usage contradicts the statement of Gramm. that μαζός is the man's breast, μαστός the woman's:— breast, δεξιτερὸν κατὰ μαζόν Il. 5.393 ; of men's breasts, βάλε δουρὶ στέρνον ὑπὲρ μαζοῖο 4.528 ; βάλε στῆθος παρὰ μαζόν 8.121 , cf. Od. 22.82 , X. An. 1.4.17 , 4.3.6 . more freq. of a woman's breast, μαζὸν ἀνέσχε, of Hecuba pleading with Hector, Il. 22.80 ; εἴ ποτέ τοι λαθικηδέα μαζὸν ἐπέσχον ib. 83 ; γυναῖκά τε θήσατο μαζόν sucked her breast, 24.58 ; πάϊς δέ οἱ ἦν ἐπὶ μαζῷ Od. 11.448 ; σὺ δέ μ' ἔτρεφες . . τῷ σῷ ἐπὶ μαζῷ 19.483 ; so φαίνουσαι τοὺς μαζούς Hdt. 2.85 ; τοὺς μ. ἀποταμοῦσα Id. 4.202 ; ἐπὶ τοῦ μαστοῦ ἔφυ φῦμα Id. 3.133 ; προὔκειτο μαστῶν περονίς S. Tr. 925 ; προσέσχε μαζόν, of the mother, A. Ch. 531 ; μαστὸν ἀμφέχασκε, of the child, ib. 545 , cf. 897 ; μαστῶν ἀποστάς S. El. 776 ; πῶλον ἀφέλξων σῶν ἀπὸ μαστῶν E. Hec. 142 (anap.), etc. rarely of animals, udder, Id. Cyc. 55 (lyr.), 207 , Call. Jov. 48 . generally, of the breasts of all mammalia, Arist. HA 521b21 , PA 688a18 sq., GA 752b23 . metaph., any round, breast-shaped object: round hill, knoll, Pi. P. 4.8 , X. An. 4.2.6 , Call. Del. 48 . round piece of wool fastened to the edge of nets, X. Cyn. 2.6 , cf. Poll. 5.29 . at Paphos, breast-shaped cup, Apollod. Cyren. ap. Ath. 11.487b , cf. IG 7.3498 (Oropus), 11(4).1307.21 (Delos).
greek_sentence: Ἢν μὲν ὀδύνη ἄνω περαίνῃ πρὸς κληῖδα ἢ περὶ μαζὸν καὶ [852] βραχίονα, τέμνειν χρὴ τὴν ἐν τῷ βραχίονι φλέβα τὴν εἴσω, ἐφ᾿ ὁκότερον ἂν ᾖ τῶν μερῶν, κατὰ τόδε.

Cyr. 4.2.37 . as indirect interrog., Ζεὺς οἶδε . . , ὁπποτέρῳ θανάτοιο τέλος πεπρωμένον ἐστίν Il. 3.309 , cf. 22.130 , 23.487 ; περὶ τοῦ ὁκότερος ἡμέων πλέω ἀγαθὰ . . ἐργάσεται about the question, which of us two . . , Hdt. 8.79 ; ὥστε μὴ γνῶναι ὁπότερος . . N. 4.32 ; δρᾶν καὶ πάσχειν, v. δράω ; πολλὰ μὲν . . πείσεσθαι, πολλὰ δὲ ποιήσειν Hdt. 5.89 , etc. : hence used as Pass. of ποιέω (cf. Arist. Cat. 2a4 , Metaph. 1017a26 , Plot. 3.6.8 , etc.), π. τι ὑπό τινος to be treated so and so by another, suffer it at his hands, ἃ πάσχοντες ὑφ' ἑτέρων ὀργίζεσθε, ταῦτα τοὺς ἄλλους μὴ ποιεῖτε Isoc. 3.61 , cf. Hdt. 1.44 , 124 ,al. ; ἐξ ἐμοῦ μὲν ἔπαθες οἷα φῂς παθεῖν, δρᾷς δ' οὐδὲν ἡμᾶς εὖ E. Hec. 252 ; οἷα πρὸς θεῶν πάσχω θεός A. Pr. 92 , cf. V. 946 ; ὁρᾶτε μὴ ταὐτὸ πάθητε τῷ ἵππῳ see that it be not with you as with the horse in the fable, Arist. Rh. 1393b20 , cf. Pl. R. 488a ; παραπλ ήσιον π. ὥσπερ ἂν εἰ . . Isoc. 1.27 ; ὁμοιότατον πεπονθέναι ὥσπερ ἂν εἴ τις . . Pl. Phd. 98c . of the influence of passion or feeling, to be affected in a certain way, be (or come to be) in a certain state of mind, οἱ Καμαριναῖοι ἐπεπόνθεσαν τοιόνδε Th. 6.88 , cf. 1.80 , D. 20.56 ; ὅ τι μὲν ὑμεῖς πεπόνθατε ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμῶν κατηγόρων οὐκ οἶδα Pl. greek_sentence: Κᾀνταῦθα πάλιν ἐξεργάζεται τὴν τοῦ γνησίου μέρους γνώμην· ἐπεὶ παρελέλειπτο τὸ συνεπινοούμενον τοῖς εἰρημένοις αὐτῷ, προστιθεῖ, οἷον καὶ τοῦτο, κατ᾿ εὐθὺ τῆς πεπονθυίας πλευρᾶς ποιεῖσθαι τὴν φλεβοτομίαν, ὅπερ ἐδήλωσεν εἰπών· τέμνειν χρὴ τὴν ἐν τῷ βραχίονι φλέβα τὴν εἴσω, ἐφ᾿ ὁκότερον ἂν ᾖ τῶν μερῶν, κατὰ τόδε.

english_sentence_A: Plainly, in abbreviating, he is careless of the expression; for whereas he ought to have said the vein at the elbow, he says the one in the upper arm.
english_sentence_B: He made this clear by saying: 'one must cut the inner vein in the arm, on whichever of the two sides it may be, on that side.' Plainly, in abbreviating, he neglects his exposition; for when he ought to have said 'the vein at the elbow', he says 'the one in the arm'.

greek_sentence: Ἀφαιρέειν δὲ κατὰ τὴν τοῦ σώματος ἕξιν καὶ ὥρην καὶ ἡλικίην καὶ χροιὴν πλέον· καὶ θαρσέων, ἢν ὀξὺ τὸ ἄλγημα ᾖ, ἀγαγεῖν πρὸς λειποψυχίην· ἔπειτα ὑποκλύζειν μετὰ τοῦτο.
english_sentence_A: And one should remove more according to the habit of the body, the season, the age and the complexion; and boldly, if the pain is acute, carry it to the point of fainting; then after this administer a clyster.
english_sentence_B: Withdraw more according to the habitus of the body, the season, the age and the colour; and, if the pain is acute, boldly bring the patient to a swoon; then after this administer a clyster.

greek_sentence: [853] Ἐνταῦθα πάλιν πλέον τοῦ μέτρου τοὺς σκοποὺς τῆς φλεβοτομίας ἅπαντας εἰπεῖν φιλοτιμηθεὶς, ὅμως παραλέλοιπέ τινας· οὔτε γὰρ τῆς δυνάμεως ἐμνημόνευσεν |οὔτε τῆς μεταβολῆς τοῦ αἵματος, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ χώρας ἢ καταστάσεως.
english_sentence_A: [853] Here again, although he was ambitious to state all the indications for phlebotomy more fully than the measure requires, he has nevertheless omitted some; for he mentioned neither the faculty nor the change of the blood, nor indeed the region or the constitution of the air.
english_sentence_B: [853] Here again, having been ambitious beyond due measure to state all the indications of phlebotomy, he has nevertheless left some out: for he made no mention of the strength, nor of the change of the blood, nor yet of the country or of the constitution [of the weather].

greek_sentence: πλέον δ᾿ ἀφαιρεῖν κελεύων καὶ θαῤῥεῖν μέχρι λειποθυμίας ἄγειν, ἥμαρτεν ἐν τῇ λέξει προσθεὶς δι᾿ ὃ θαῤῥεῖν προσήκει· διὰ μὲν γὰρ τὴν ὀξύτητα τοῦ ἀλγήματος ἐπὶ τὸ πλέον ἐκκενοῦν τοῦ αἵματος ἀφικνούμεθα· τὸ δ᾿ ἐᾷν ῥεῖν, οὐκ ἐκ τῆς ὀξύτητος, ἀλλ᾿ ἐξ ἄλλων ἔχομεν, ἐὰν ἥ τε δύναμις ἐῤῥωμένη καὶ ἡ τῶν ἀκμαζόντων ἡλικία καὶ τὸ πλῆθος αἱματικὸν καὶ ἡ τοῦ κάμνοντος φύσις πυκνοτέρα τε καὶ σκληροτέρα καὶ δυσδιαφορητοτέρα καὶ πολύαιμος, ἥ τε ὥρα τοῦ ἔτους καὶ ἡ κατάστασις εὔκρατος, οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ἡ χώρα· τὸ γὰρ ἄχρι λειποθυμίας ἄγοντα θαῤῥεῖν, ἐκ τούτων ἡμῖν προσγίνεται.
english_sentence_A: And in ordering to remove more and to be bold in carrying it as far as fainting, he erred in his wording by adding the reason on account of which it is fitting to be bold; for it is because of the acuteness of the pain that we come to evacuating more of the blood, but our allowing it to flow we derive not from the acuteness but from other things: if the faculty is strong, and the age is that of those in their prime, and the plethos is sanguineous, and the nature of the patient is denser and harder and less easily dispersed by transpiration and full of blood, and the season of the year and the constitution are well-tempered, and likewise the region too; for being bold in carrying it to the point of fainting accrues to us from these.
english_sentence_B: And in bidding us to remove more and to be confident in leading [the patient] to fainting, he erred in the wording by adding the reason for which one ought to be confident. For it is on account of the acuteness of the pain that we come to evacuate more of the blood; but letting it flow [until fainting] we take not from the acuteness but from other things: if the strength is robust, and the age is that of those in their prime, and the plethora is sanguineous, and the nature of the patient is denser and harder and less easily dispersed, and abounding in blood, and the season of the year and the constitution are well tempered, and so too the country.

greek_sentence: πλέον δ᾿ ἀφαιρεῖν κελεύων καὶ θαῤῥεῖν μέχρι λειποθυμίας ἄγειν, ἥμαρτεν ἐν τῇ λέξει προσθεὶς δι᾿ ὃ θαῤῥεῖν προσήκει· διὰ μὲν γὰρ τὴν ὀξύτητα τοῦ ἀλγήματος ἐπὶ τὸ πλέον ἐκκενοῦν τοῦ αἵματος ἀφικνούμεθα· τὸ δ᾿ ἐᾷν ῥεῖν, οὐκ ἐκ τῆς ὀξύτητος, ἀλλ᾿ ἐξ ἄλλων ἔχομεν, ἐὰν ἥ τε δύναμις ἐῤῥωμένη καὶ ἡ τῶν ἀκμαζόντων ἡλικία καὶ τὸ πλῆθος αἱματικὸν καὶ ἡ τοῦ κάμνοντος φύσις πυκνοτέρα τε καὶ σκληροτέρα καὶ δυσδιαφορητοτέρα καὶ πολύαιμος, ἥ τε ὥρα τοῦ ἔτους καὶ ἡ κατάστασις εὔκρατος, οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ἡ χώρα· τὸ γὰρ ἄχρι λειποθυμίας ἄγοντα θαῤῥεῖν, ἐκ τούτων ἡμῖν προσγίνεται.
english_sentence_A: And in ordering to remove more and to be bold in carrying it as far as fainting, he erred in his wording by adding the reason on account of which it is fitting to be bold; for it is because of the acuteness of the pain that we come to evacuating more of the blood, but our allowing it to flow we derive not from the acuteness but from other things: if the faculty is strong, and the age is that of those in their prime, and the plethos is sanguineous, and the nature of the patient is denser and harder and less easily dispersed by transpiration and full of blood, and the season of the year and the constitution are well-tempered, and likewise the region too; for being bold in carrying it to the point of fainting accrues to us from these.
english_sentence_B: And in bidding us to remove more and to be confident in leading [the patient] to fainting, he erred in the wording by adding the reason for which one ought to be confident. For it is on account of the acuteness of the pain that we come to evacuate more of the blood; but letting it flow [until fainting] we take not from the acuteness but from other things: if the strength is robust, and the age is that of those in their prime, and the plethora is sanguineous, and the nature of the patient is denser and harder and less easily dispersed, and abounding in blood, and the season of the year and the constitution are well tempered, and so too the country.

english_sentence_A: For none at all of such remedies [855] is to be applied to the patient by making a number of days one's aim; rather, as Hippocrates said, order purging either right at the beginning, before the humours have become fixed, or later, when they have been concocted; so that we too have purged around the first day, sometimes also on the second and the fourth, and sometimes also on the fifth, not on the fourth only, as this writer has written.
english_sentence_B: For in principle none of such remedies [855] is to be applied to the patient with the number of days made one's guide; rather, as Hippocrates said, bid him (?) administer the purgative drug either at the beginning, immediately, before the humours have become fixed, or later, when they have been concocted. So we have administered purgative drugs around the first day, sometimes also on the second and the fourth, and sometimes also on the fifth, and not on the fourth only, as this man wrote.

greek_sentence: Ἢν δὲ μὴ ῥηϊδίως ἀπαλλαγῇ, ἔλασσόν τε τὸ πόμα καὶ τὸ ῥόφημα ὀλίγον, χυλὸν λεπτὸν καὶ ἅπαξ, ἐν ὁκοτέρῃ ἂν ὥρῃ βέλτιον διάγῃ· γνώσῃ δὲ ἐκ τῶν οὔρων.
english_sentence_A: But if he is not easily relieved, [give] both less drink and little gruel, a thin juice and once only, at whichever of the two times of day he fares better; and you will know this from the urines.
english_sentence_B: If he is not easily freed of it, let the drink be less and the gruel little, thin juice and once a day, at whichever hour he fares better; you will know this from the urine.

greek_sentence: δεῖ δὲ ῥόφημα προσφέρειν τοῖσιν ἐκ τῶν νοσημάτων μὴ πρότερον ἢ πέπονα τὰ οὖρα ἢ πτύσματα ἴδῃς γεγενημένα.
english_sentence_A: One should offer gruel to those [recovering] from diseases not before you see that the urines or the sputa have become concocted.
english_sentence_B: Gruel should not be given to those emerging from the diseases before you see that the urine or the sputa have become concocted.

greek_sentence: ἢν δὲ φαρμακευθεὶς συχνὰ καθαρθῇ, ἀναγκαῖον διδόναι, ἔλασσον δὲ καὶ λεπτότερον· οὐ γὰρ δυνήσεται ὑπὸ κενεαγγείης ὑπνώσσειν, οὐδὲ πέσσειν ὁμοίως, οὐδὲ τὰς κρίσιας ὑπομένειν· [856] ἀλλ᾿ ἐπειδὰν ξυντήξιες ὠμῶν γένωνται καὶ τὰ ἀντέχοντα ἀποβάλλῃ, ἀνθέξει οὐδέν.
english_sentence_A: But if, having been treated with a drug, he is purged copiously, it is necessary to give [nourishment], but less and thinner; for because of emptiness of the vessels he will not be able to sleep, nor to concoct in the same way, nor to endure the crises; [856] but when colliquations of crude [humours] occur and he casts off what holds out, nothing will hold out.
english_sentence_B: [856] but when colliquations of raw matters occur and he casts off the things that offer resistance, nothing will hold out. Hippocrates, in considering the particular occasion for nourishment, and indeed this very man who wrote these things, in what he wrote above, thought it right to attend to the heat in the thorax and the feet.

lsj_entry_text: θερμασία, ἡ, warmth, heat, Hp. Aph. 5.63 , Arist. Pr. 860a19 , Epicur. Ep. 2p.40U. , Thphr. HP 8.11.7 . LXX Je. 28(51).39 , D.S. 3.34 , Paus. 2.34.6 ; heating, opp. ψῦξις, Arist. GA 764b7 : pl., Plu. 2.128f . (The pure Att. words are θερμότης and θέρμη, Thom.Mag. p.179R. , but θερμασία is used by X. An. 5.8.15 .)
greek_sentence: Περὶ τοῦ κατὰ μέρος καιροῦ τῆς τροφῆς ἐπισκοπούμενος ὁ Ἱπποκράτης καὶ αὐτὸς δὲ οὗτος ὁ ταῦτα γράψας ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω γεγραμμένοις αὐτῷ θερμασίᾳ προσέχειν ἠξίου τῇ κατὰ τὸν θώρακα καὶ τοὺς πόδας.
english_sentence_A: In considering the particular occasion for nourishment, Hippocrates—and this very man too who wrote these things, in what was written above by him—deemed it right to attend to the heat in the region of the thorax and the feet.
english_sentence_B: For the examination of the urine is useful for the regimen as a whole, not for that of the particular part of the nourishment. So he did not speak correctly here when he said to give thin juice once, at whichever hour the patient fares better, and that one will recognise that hour from the urine.

greek_sentence: ἡ γὰρ τῶν οὔρων ἐπίσκεψις εἰς τὴν καθόλου δίαιταν, οὐκ εἰς τὴν τοῦ μερικοῦ μέρους τῆς τροφῆς ἐστι χρήσιμος· ὥστε οὐκ ὀρθῶς εἶπε νῦν, χυλὸν λεπτὸν ἅπαξ διδόναι καθ᾿ ἣν ὥρην βέλτιον διάγει, γνώσεσθαι δ᾿ ἐκείνην ἐκ τῶν οὔρων· εἰ γὰρ καὶ ὅτι μάλιστα βραχεῖαν ῥοπὴν ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον ἴσχει τὰ οὖρα κατὰ τοὺς μερικοὺς παροξυσμοὺς, ἀλλ᾿ οὐχ οὕτως γε μακρὸς ὁ χρόνος ἐκεῖνός ἐστιν, ὡς ἀποθέσθαι ταῦτα ἡμᾶς καὶ περιμεῖναι, πότερον νεφέλας ἐπαιωρουμένας ἢ κάτω χωρούσας ἴσχει· ταῦτα γὰρ ἐν πολλῷ χρόνῳ γίγνεται, τρέφεσθαι δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς ὀξέσι νοσήμασι τοὺς κάμνοντας ἐνίοτε ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι καὶ ἐν ἀρχῇ τῆς παρακμῆς.
english_sentence_A: For the examination of the urine is useful for the regimen as a whole, not for the particular portion of nourishment; so that he did not speak correctly now, [saying] to give thin juice once at whichever hour he fares better, and that one will know that hour from the urine; for even if the urine does most certainly have a slight inclination toward the better during the particular paroxysms, still that time is not so long that we should set these matters aside and wait to see whether it has clouds suspended or moving downward; for these things come about over a long time, whereas in acute diseases it is sometimes necessary for the patients to be nourished even at the beginning of the decline.
english_sentence_B: For even if the urine shows, at most, a slight inclination toward the better during the particular paroxysms, that time is still not so long that we should put these things off and wait to see whether it has clouds suspended in it or moving downward. For these things come about over a long time, whereas in acute diseases it is sometimes necessary to nourish the patients even at the beginning of the decline.

greek_sentence: ἡ γὰρ τῶν οὔρων ἐπίσκεψις εἰς τὴν καθόλου δίαιταν, οὐκ εἰς τὴν τοῦ μερικοῦ μέρους τῆς τροφῆς ἐστι χρήσιμος· ὥστε οὐκ ὀρθῶς εἶπε νῦν, χυλὸν λεπτὸν ἅπαξ διδόναι καθ᾿ ἣν ὥρην βέλτιον διάγει, γνώσεσθαι δ᾿ ἐκείνην ἐκ τῶν οὔρων· εἰ γὰρ καὶ ὅτι μάλιστα βραχεῖαν ῥοπὴν ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον ἴσχει τὰ οὖρα κατὰ τοὺς μερικοὺς παροξυσμοὺς, ἀλλ᾿ οὐχ οὕτως γε μακρὸς ὁ χρόνος ἐκεῖνός ἐστιν, ὡς ἀποθέσθαι ταῦτα ἡμᾶς καὶ περιμεῖναι, πότερον νεφέλας ἐπαιωρουμένας ἢ κάτω χωρούσας ἴσχει· ταῦτα γὰρ ἐν πολλῷ χρόνῳ γίγνεται, τρέφεσθαι δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς ὀξέσι νοσήμασι τοὺς κάμνοντας ἐνίοτε ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι καὶ ἐν ἀρχῇ τῆς παρακμῆς.
english_sentence_A: For the examination of the urine is useful for the regimen as a whole, not for the particular portion of nourishment; so that he did not speak correctly now, [saying] to give thin juice once at whichever hour he fares better, and that one will know that hour from the urine; for even if the urine does most certainly have a slight inclination toward the better during the particular paroxysms, still that time is not so long that we should set these matters aside and wait to see whether it has clouds suspended or moving downward; for these things come about over a long time, whereas in acute diseases it is sometimes necessary for the patients to be nourished even at the beginning of the decline.
english_sentence_B: For even if the urine shows, at most, a slight inclination toward the better during the particular paroxysms, that time is still not so long that we should put these things off and wait to see whether it has clouds suspended in it or moving downward. For these things come about over a long time, whereas in acute diseases it is sometimes necessary to nourish the patients even at the beginning of the decline.

greek_sentence: ἡ γὰρ τῶν οὔρων ἐπίσκεψις εἰς τὴν καθόλου δίαιταν, οὐκ εἰς τὴν τοῦ μερικοῦ μέρους τῆς τροφῆς ἐστι χρήσιμος· ὥστε οὐκ ὀρθῶς εἶπε νῦν, χυλὸν λεπτὸν ἅπαξ διδόναι καθ᾿ ἣν ὥρην βέλτιον διάγει, γνώσεσθαι δ᾿ ἐκείνην ἐκ τῶν οὔρων· εἰ γὰρ καὶ ὅτι μάλιστα βραχεῖαν ῥοπὴν ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον ἴσχει τὰ οὖρα κατὰ τοὺς μερικοὺς παροξυσμοὺς, ἀλλ᾿ οὐχ οὕτως γε μακρὸς ὁ χρόνος ἐκεῖνός ἐστιν, ὡς ἀποθέσθαι ταῦτα ἡμᾶς καὶ περιμεῖναι, πότερον νεφέλας ἐπαιωρουμένας ἢ κάτω χωρούσας ἴσχει· ταῦτα γὰρ ἐν πολλῷ χρόνῳ γίγνεται, τρέφεσθαι δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς ὀξέσι νοσήμασι τοὺς κάμνοντας ἐνίοτε ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι καὶ ἐν ἀρχῇ τῆς παρακμῆς.
english_sentence_A: For the examination of the urine is useful for the regimen as a whole, not for the particular portion of nourishment; so that he did not speak correctly now, [saying] to give thin juice once at whichever hour he fares better, and that one will know that hour from the urine; for even if the urine does most certainly have a slight inclination toward the better during the particular paroxysms, still that time is not so long that we should set these matters aside and wait to see whether it has clouds suspended or moving downward; for these things come about over a long time, whereas in acute diseases it is sometimes necessary for the patients to be nourished even at the beginning of the decline.
english_sentence_B: For even if the urine shows, at most, a slight inclination toward the better during the particular paroxysms, that time is still not so long that we should put these things off and wait to see whether it has clouds suspended in it or moving downward. For these things come about over a long time, whereas in acute diseases it is sometimes necessary to nourish the patients even at the beginning of the decline.

english_sentence_A: When the peripneumonia is at its height, it is beyond help if he does not clear [the chest] by expectoration, and it is bad if he is dyspnoeic and the urines are thin and pungent and sweats occur about the neck and head; for such sweats are bad, the diseases prevailing by way of suffocation and rupture and violence, unless urine copious and thick rushes forth and concocted sputa come; and whichever of these occurs spontaneously resolves the disease.
english_sentence_B: When the peripneumonia is at its peak, it is beyond help if the patient is not being cleared upwards, and it is bad if he is short of breath and the urine is thin and acrid and sweats occur about the neck and head; for such sweats are bad, arising from choking and rupture and violence, as the diseases prevail, unless copious and thick urine bursts forth and concocted sputa come up; whichever of these occurs spontaneously resolves the disease.

greek_sentence: Ὁκόταν δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν τενόντων σφοδρῶς ἔμπροσθεν ἀντισπῶνται καὶ περὶ τὸν τράχηλον καὶ πρόσωπον ἱδρῶτες, ὑπὸ τοῦ πόνου δακνομένων καὶ ξηραινομένων τῶν τενόντων καὶ τῶν οὐρωδέων, οἳ παχύτατοι μὲν τὴν ῥάχιν ξυνέχουσιν, ᾗ οἱ μέγιστοι σύνδεσμοι καταπεφυκότες, ἕως εἰς πόδας ἀποτελευτῶσι· τῷ τοιῷδε ἢν μὴ πυρετὸς καὶ ὕπνος ἐπιγένηται καὶ ἑπόμενα οὖρα πέψιν ἔχοντα ἔλθῃ καὶ ἱδρῶτες [862] κριτικοὶ, πίνειν οἶνον Κρητικὸν οἰνώδεα καὶ ἄλητον ἑφθὸν ἐσθίειν καὶ κηρωτῇ ἀλείφειν καὶ ἐγχρίειν, τά τε σκέλεα περιελίσσειν ἕως τῶν ποδῶν, θερμῷ προσβρέχων ἐν σκάφῃ καὶ βραχίονας ἕως δακτύλων κατελίσσειν καὶ ὀσφὺν ἀπὸ τοῦ τραχήλου ἕως τῶν ἰσχίων, σίαλον ἐγκηρώσας μαλακῷ δέρματι, ὅκως καὶ τὰ ἔμπροσθεν περιέξῃ καὶ διαλείπων πυρία τοῖσιν ἀσκίοισι θερμὸν ὕδωρ ἐγχέων καὶ περιτείνων σινδόνιον,ἐπανάκλινε αὐτόν.
english_sentence_A: But when they are violently drawn forward from the tendons, and there are sweats about the neck and face, the tendons being bitten and dried by the pain, and also the tail-ward ones (οὐρώδεες), which, being the thickest, hold the spine together, where the greatest ligaments, having grown down, terminate at the feet: for such a patient, if fever and sleep do not supervene and urines following with concoction do not come, and [862] critical sweats, he is to drink Cretan wine of vinous character and eat boiled meal, and one should anoint and rub him in with cerate, and wrap round the legs as far as the feet, fomenting with warm water in a tub, and wrap down the upper arms as far as the fingers and the loin from the neck as far as the hips, having worked grease (σίαλον) with wax into a soft skin, so that it may also enclose the front parts; and at intervals apply fomentations with the small skins, pouring in hot water and stretching a linen cloth around, and lay him back.
english_sentence_B: When they are violently drawn forward from the tendons, and there are sweats about the neck and face, the tendons being bitten and dried by the pain, and also those of the tail region (οὐρωδέων), which, being very thick, hold the spine together, where the greatest ligaments have grown down until they terminate in the feet: for such a person, if fever and sleep do not supervene, and urine following upon them showing concoction does not come, and critical [862] sweats, give vinous Cretan wine to drink and boiled meal to eat, anoint and smear him with cerate, and wrap the legs round as far as the feet, first bathing them with hot water in a tub, and wrap the arms down as far as the fingers, and the back from the neck to the hips, having spread lard worked up with wax on soft leather, so that it encloses the front parts as well; and at intervals foment him with small skins into which you pour hot water, and, stretching a linen cloth round them, lay him back upon it.

greek_sentence: καὶ ἢν μέν τί σοι ἐπιδιδῷ ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον· εἰ δὲ μὴ, τοῦ μόδου τῆς ῥίζης τρίβων ἐν οἴνῳ εὐώδει καὶ δαῦκον πίνειν δίδου πρωῒ νήστει πρὸ τοῦ βρέχειν καὶ ταχὺ ἐπὶ τούτοισι τὸ ἄλευρον ἑφθὸν χλιαρὸν ἐσθιέτω ὡς πλεῖστον καὶ οἶνον ὁκόταν βούληται εὔκρητον ἐπιπινέτω.
english_sentence_A: And if anything in your patient makes progress toward the better, well; but if not, grinding some of the root of modos (μόδος) in fragrant wine, and daucus, give it to drink early in the morning, fasting, before the soaking, and quickly after these let him eat the boiled flour lukewarm, as much as possible, and let him drink after it well-mixed wine whenever he wishes.
english_sentence_B: And if he makes some progress towards the better for you, well; if not, pound some of the root of modos (μόδου) in fragrant wine and give it to drink, with daucus, early in the morning while fasting, before the bathing; and soon after these let him eat as much as possible of the boiled wheaten meal, lukewarm, and afterwards drink well-mixed wine whenever he wishes.

greek_sentence: [863] Καὶ ὁ λόγος ἀδιορίστως εἴρηται μετὰ τοῦ καὶ ἀκύρως ἔνια τῶν ὀνομάτων γεγράφθαι· τὸ γὰρ ὑπὸ τοῦ πόνου δάκνεσθαι τοὺς τένοντας ἀκύρως λέλεκται, δριμέσι χυμοῖς πρέποντος τοῦ δάκνειν ῥήματος, οὐ τοῖς πόνοις.

greek_sentence: εἰ δ᾿ ἀμφότερα τὰ μέρη δηλῶσαι βούλεται τεινόμενα καὶ περὶ τὰ πρόσω καὶ ὀπίσω, τέτανον ἐπιτείνασθαι δυνατὸν, καθάπερ ὀλίγον ἔμπροσθεν ἔφη, τετάνοισι δὲ ὀσφύος.
english_sentence_A: But if he wishes to indicate both parts being stretched, both toward the front and toward the back, it is possible that a tetanus is set up (ἐπιτείνασθαι), just as a little earlier he said, 'and in tetanus of the loins.' Nor does he safely foreknow the relief of the affections from the concoction of the urines; for the lack of concoction of a feverish disease is clearly shown through the urines, but for the affections of the muscles the indication through the urines is not safe.
english_sentence_B: But if he wishes to indicate that both parts are stretched, both in front and behind, it is possible for a tetanus to be intensified, as he said a little before, 'and in tetanus of the loin'.

english_sentence_A: And that it is not fitting to give hellebore either to those who have become purulent from such a cause, or to those who have become so from abscesses, or from any other cause, is quite clear; but those who are purulent through intemperance have been wrongly stated in the present enumeration, since the intemperance itself, by itself, harms the intemperate—such as repletion, lack of concoction, wine-bibbing, much sexual intercourse and sleeplessness, and all other such things.

greek_sentence: προειπὼν δὲ τίσιν ἐλλέβορον οὐ χρὴ διδόναι φησίν· ἢν διαλύηται τὸ σῶμα, τουτέστιν ἐὰν ἔκλυτον ἱκανῶς γένηται, χωρὶς προφάσεως δηλονότι ἢ πόνος ἐν κεφαλῇ χρόνιος καὶ δύσλυτος (ὑπακοῦσαι γάρ σε τοῦτο κᾀν τῷ τῆς κεφαλῆς χρὴ πόνῳ καὶ τοῖς ἐφεξῆς εἰρημένοις ἅπασι, τοῖς ἐμπεπλασμένοις ὠσὶ καὶ ῥινὶ καὶ τῷ πτυαλισμῷ) προστίθησι δὲ γονάτων βάρος καὶ πόνον καὶ σώματος ὄγκον παρὰ [867] τὸ ἔθος· ἐπὶ πάντων γὰρ τούτων ἄνευ φανερᾶς αἰτίας γενομένων ἐλλεβορίζειν συμβουλεύει, διελών τε τὸν καθόλου τοῦτον λόγον εἰς τὰ κατὰ μέρος ἔφη, μήθ᾿ ὑπ᾿ ἀφροδισίων, μήθ᾿ ὑπὸ λύπης, μήθ᾿ ὑπὸ φροντίδος ἢ ἀγρυπνιῶν, τῶν εἰρημένων γεγονότων· εἰ γὰρ ἐκ τούτων τινὸς εἴη γεγονότα, πρὸς τὸ ποιῆσαν αἴτιον ἁρμόττεσθαι κελεύει.
english_sentence_A: Having first said to whom one must not give hellebore, he says: if the body be dissolved, that is, if it become sufficiently slack, obviously without a manifest cause, or a pain in the head that is chronic and hard to resolve (for you must understand this both in the case of the pain of the head and in all the things said next, the stopped-up ears and nose and the salivation); and he adds heaviness and pain of the knees and a bulk of the body beyond [867] what is customary; for in all these cases, when they have come about without an evident cause, he advises giving hellebore, and dividing this general statement into its particulars he said, "neither from sexual intercourse, nor from grief, nor from anxiety or sleeplessness," the aforesaid things having come about; for if they should have come about from any one of these, he bids the treatment be fitted to the cause that produced them.
english_sentence_B: Having first said to whom one ought not to give hellebore, he says: "if the body is dissolved", that is, if it becomes considerably slack, without an occasioning cause (prophasis), evidently; "or pain in the head", chronic and hard to resolve (for you must understand this also in the case of the pain of the head and of all the things mentioned next, the blocked-up ears and nose and the ptyalism).

greek_sentence: προειπὼν δὲ τίσιν ἐλλέβορον οὐ χρὴ διδόναι φησίν· ἢν διαλύηται τὸ σῶμα, τουτέστιν ἐὰν ἔκλυτον ἱκανῶς γένηται, χωρὶς προφάσεως δηλονότι ἢ πόνος ἐν κεφαλῇ χρόνιος καὶ δύσλυτος (ὑπακοῦσαι γάρ σε τοῦτο κᾀν τῷ τῆς κεφαλῆς χρὴ πόνῳ καὶ τοῖς ἐφεξῆς εἰρημένοις ἅπασι, τοῖς ἐμπεπλασμένοις ὠσὶ καὶ ῥινὶ καὶ τῷ πτυαλισμῷ) προστίθησι δὲ γονάτων βάρος καὶ πόνον καὶ σώματος ὄγκον παρὰ [867] τὸ ἔθος· ἐπὶ πάντων γὰρ τούτων ἄνευ φανερᾶς αἰτίας γενομένων ἐλλεβορίζειν συμβουλεύει, διελών τε τὸν καθόλου τοῦτον λόγον εἰς τὰ κατὰ μέρος ἔφη, μήθ᾿ ὑπ᾿ ἀφροδισίων, μήθ᾿ ὑπὸ λύπης, μήθ᾿ ὑπὸ φροντίδος ἢ ἀγρυπνιῶν, τῶν εἰρημένων γεγονότων· εἰ γὰρ ἐκ τούτων τινὸς εἴη γεγονότα, πρὸς τὸ ποιῆσαν αἴτιον ἁρμόττεσθαι κελεύει.
english_sentence_A: Having first said to whom one must not give hellebore, he says: if the body be dissolved, that is, if it become sufficiently slack, obviously without a manifest cause, or a pain in the head that is chronic and hard to resolve (for you must understand this both in the case of the pain of the head and in all the things said next, the stopped-up ears and nose and the salivation); and he adds heaviness and pain of the knees and a bulk of the body beyond [867] what is customary; for in all these cases, when they have come about without an evident cause, he advises giving hellebore, and dividing this general statement into its particulars he said, "neither from sexual intercourse, nor from grief, nor from anxiety or sleeplessness," the aforesaid things having come about; for if they should have come about from any one of these, he bids the treatment be fitted to the cause that produced them.
english_sentence_B: Having first said to whom one ought not to give hellebore, he says: "if the body is dissolved", that is, if it becomes considerably slack, without an occasioning cause (prophasis), evidently; "or pain in the head", chronic and hard to resolve (for you must understand this also in the case of the pain of the head and of all the things mentioned next, the blocked-up ears and nose and the ptyalism).

greek_sentence: Τὰ δὲ ἐκ πορείης ἀλγήματα πλευρέων, νώτου, ὀσφύος, ἰσχίων καὶ ὁκόσα ἀναπνέοντες ἀλγέουσι πρόφασιν ἔχοντες· πολλάκις γὰρ μεμάθηκε φοιτᾷν ἐκ κραιπαλέων καὶ βρωμάτων φυσωδέων ἀλγήματα καὶ εἰς ὀσφὺν καὶ ἐς ἰσχίον.
english_sentence_A: The pains from walking, of the sides, the back, the loins, the hips, and whatever pains they feel in breathing, having a manifest cause; for pains have often been known to come, from drunken debauches and flatulent foods, both to the loins and to the hip.
english_sentence_B: Which of all the things he mentioned have been stated truly and precisely, and which not, you have learned both from the books of Hippocrates and from our own treatises. Pains from walking, of the sides, back, loins, hips, and whatever pains people feel when breathing, have an occasioning cause; for pains are often wont to come, from bouts of crapulence and from flatulent foods, both to the loins and to the hip.

english_sentence_A: It is beneficial for these persons to sleep after having bathed, and, having slept, to walk slowly over a long circuit; and if the bowel is loosened, [869] to dine and to drink a smaller quantity of wine, more unmixed; but if it is not loosened, to anoint the body with warm oil; and if he is thirsty, to drink in addition watery white or sweet wine and then rest; and if he does not fall asleep, to rest longer, and in other respects let him be dieted in the same way as those recovering from a drinking-bout (kraipalē).
english_sentence_B: It is beneficial for these, after bathing, to sleep, and after sleeping to walk slowly over a long circuit; and if the belly is loosened, [869] to dine and to drink less wine, less diluted; but if it is not loosened, to anoint the body with something warm; and if he is thirsty, he should drink watery white or sweet wine and rest; and if he does not fall asleep, he should rest longer, and in other respects let him follow the same regimen as those suffering from crapulence.

english_sentence_B: It is beneficial for these, after bathing, to sleep, and after sleeping to walk slowly over a long circuit; and if the belly is loosened, [869] to dine and to drink less wine, less diluted; but if it is not loosened, to anoint the body with something warm; and if he is thirsty, he should drink watery white or sweet wine and rest; and if he does not fall asleep, he should rest longer, and in other respects let him follow the same regimen as those suffering from crapulence.

english_sentence_A: As for the affections arising from drinks: those that are watery are slower in passing, and circulate and float about the hypochondria and do not run down into urination; and one who has been filled with such a drink should accomplish no task sharply, of the sort which it befalls the body to labour at when it is strained by force or by speed; rather let him keep as quiet as possible, until it has been concocted together with the food.
english_sentence_B: As for the effects of drinks: those that are watery pass through more slowly, and they circulate and float on the surface about the hypochondria and do not run down to urination; and when filled with such drink he should perform quickly none of the tasks in which one happens to toil with the body strained by force or by speed; let him keep as quiet as possible until it has been digested together with the food.

english_sentence_A: But those who take a single meal a day [870] are both weak and pass hot urine contrary to their custom, since their vessels are emptied; the mouth also becomes salty and bitter, they tremble in every activity and are strained at the temples, and they cannot concoct the dinner as they would if they had taken a midday meal.
english_sentence_B: Those who eat only one meal a day [870] are weak and pass hot urine, contrary to what is customary, their vessels being empty; the mouth also becomes salty and bitter, and they tremble in every task, and they are drawn tight at the temples, and they are not able to digest their dinner as they would if they had taken a morning meal.

greek_sentence: Σκόροδον φῦσαν καὶ θέρμην περὶ τὸν θώρηκα καὶ κεφαλῆς βάρος καὶ ἄσην καὶ εἴ τι ἄλλο ἄλγημα εἴη μεμαθηκὸς πρόσθεν, παροξύνειεν ἄν· οὐρητικὸν δὲ καὶ τοῦτο ἔχει ἀγαθόν.
english_sentence_A: Garlic would exacerbate flatus and heat about the chest and heaviness of the head and asē (restless distress) and whatever other pain one had been accustomed to before; but it also has this good quality, that it is diuretic.
english_sentence_B: 'Garlic [produces] flatus and heat about the thorax, heaviness of the head and asē (distress), and would exacerbate any other pain that had previously become habitual; but it also has this good, that it is diuretic.

lsj_entry_text: φυσώδης, ες, (φῦσα) full of wind, windy, τὸ φ. Pl. Cra. 427a : metaph., bombastic, Longin. 28.1 . flatulent, causing flatulency, Hp. Acut. 50 , Arist. HA 522b32 , 588a7 , Sor. 2.85 ; φ. νοσήματα Arist. HA 605a23 .
greek_sentence: Εἰ τῇ πείρᾳ χρὴ κρίνειν ἓν ἕκαστον τῶν ἐσθιομένων, οὐκ ἂν ὀρθῶς λέγοιτο φυσῶδες εἶναι τὸ σκόροδον, οὐδὲ θέρμης πλείονος ἢ κατὰ κρόμμυον, αἴσθησιν φέρον τοῖς φαγοῦσιν, οὔτ᾿ ἐν ἄλλῳ τινὶ μέρει τοῦ σώματος οὔτ᾿ ἐν τῷ [872] θώρακι· κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον οὐδ᾿ ἄσης, καὶ μάλιστα, ἄν τις αὐτὸ βραχὺ προαποζέσας προσάρηται.
english_sentence_A: If one must judge each single one of the things eaten by experience, garlic would not rightly be said to be flatulent, nor to bring to those who have eaten it a sensation of greater heat than in the case of onion, either in any other part of the body or in the [872] thorax; and in the same way not a sensation of nausea either, and especially if one takes it after having first boiled it briefly.
english_sentence_B: If one must judge each single one of the things that are eaten by experience, it would not rightly be said that garlic is flatulent, nor that it brings to those who have eaten it a perception of heat greater than onion does, either in any other part of the body or in the [872] chest; and in the same way not of nausea either, especially if one takes it after first boiling it briefly.

greek_sentence: κάκιστον δὲ, φησὶ, καὶ πεπληρωμένον μετὰ πόματος φαγεῖν αὐτὸ, ὅπερ εὔδηλόν ἐστι καὶ τοῖς ἰδιώταις· ἔστι μὲν γὰρ καὶ ἄλλως οὐκ ἀγαθὸν ἔδεσμα τυρὸς, ὡς ἂν παχύχυμος καὶ δύσπεπτος ὑπάρχων· εἰ δ᾿ ἐν τῷ πίνειν αὐτῷ τις χρήσαιτο πεπληρωμένος ὢν, χείριστος ἁπάντων τῶν ἐδεσμάτων γίνεται, βαρύνων τε τὸ στόμα τῆς γαστρὸς, αὐτός τε πρῶτος διαφθειρόμενος, εἶθ᾿ ἑαυτῷ συνδιαφθείρων καὶ τἄλλα.
english_sentence_A: But 'raw and unconcocted' is inserted parenthetically in the middle of the passage, not [874] carefully expressed; at any rate it indicates that everything raw and unconcocted that forms in the body among the humours naturally arises from foods of such a kind as cheese also is, a raw and unconcocted food—as if he were saying this: 'cheese produces both flatulence and costiveness of the belly and is burning, and further it is a raw and unconcocted food and generative of such humours.' And it is worst, he says, for one who is already filled to eat it together with drink—which is quite clear even to laymen; for in other respects too cheese is not a good food, inasmuch as it is thick-juiced and hard to concoct; but if someone makes use of it while drinking, being already filled, it becomes the worst of all foods, weighing down the mouth of the stomach, being itself the first to be corrupted, and then corrupting the rest along with itself.
english_sentence_B: For cheese is in any case not a good food, since it is thick-humoured and hard to concoct. But if someone should make use of it while drinking when he is already full, it becomes the worst of all foods: it weighs down the mouth of the stomach, is itself corrupted first, and then corrupts the other things along with itself.

greek_sentence: συμβουλεύει τοίνυν ἄνευ σιτίων ὀσπρίοις μὴ χρέεσθαι· σιτία δηλονότι μάλιστα μὲν τοὺς ἐκ πυρῶν ἄρτους λέγων ἢ ἁπλῶς ἅπαντα τὰ ὁπωσοῦν σκευαζόμενα, τάχα δὲ καὶ τἄλλα πάντα ἐξ ὅσων ἄρτοι γίνονται, ζειὰς καὶ [876] τίφας καὶ κριθάς· οἱ δ᾿ ἀγροῖκοι καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν κέγχρων ἄρτους ποιοῦνται.

lsj_entry_text: ἐρέβινθ-ος (proparox.), ὁ, chick-pea, Cicer arietinum, κύαμοι ἢ ἐ. Il. 13.589 , cf. Pl. R. 372c ; eaten as dessert, Xenoph. 22.3 , Ar. Pax 1136 , Crobyl. 9 , etc. ; χρύσειοι ἐ. greek_sentence: Ἐρέβινθος φῦσαν μὲν ὠμὸς καὶ πεφρυγμένος καὶ πόνον ἐμποιέει.
english_sentence_A: The chickpea, raw and roasted, produces flatus and pain.
english_sentence_B: The chickpea, raw and roasted, produces wind and pain.

lsj_entry_text: ὠμός, ή, όν: (v. sub fin.):— raw, crude (cf. Arist. Mete. 380b5 ): prop. of flesh, raw, uncooked, Il. 22.347 , al.; opp. ὀπταλέος, Od. 12.396 ; ὠμὸν καταφαγεῖν τινα or ὠμοῦ ἐσθίειν τινός to eat one raw, prov. of savage cruelty, X. An. 4.8.14 , HG 3.3.6 ; so ὠμὸν βεβρώθοις Πρίαμον Il. 4.35 , cf. Od. 18.87 , etc. of eggs, Thphr. Vert. 2 ; of vegetables, μύκητας ὠμοὺς . . φαγεῖν Antiph. 188 ; κριθαί Luc. Asin. 17 ; cf. ὠμήλυσις. of water, crude, opp. ἄπεφθος, Alex. 198 ; also of milk, Arist. Mete. 380b8 . of fruit, uncooked by the sun, unripe, opp. πέπων, Ar. Eq. 260 (troch.), cf. X. Oec. 19.19 ( Comp. ), Arist. Mete. 380b7 . of pitch, opp. ἑφθή, Gp. 6.5.5 , cf. Plb. 5.89.6 ; of pottery, unbaked, χύτραι Dsc. 1.68 , Gp. 10.21.1 ; κέραμος ὠμός Arist. Mete. 380b8 , cf. GA 743a9 : even of soil which needs to be exposed to the sun, ὡς ἡ ὠμὴ αὐτῆς ὀπτῷτο X. Oec. 16.15 . of food, undigested, Anon.Lond. 25.7 , al., Plu. 2.131c , 133d ; of a person, suffering from indigestion, Philostr. Gym. 54 ; also οὖρα, ὑποχωρήσεις, κατάρροι, Arist. Mete. 380b5 . metaph., savage, fierce, cruel, [ δεσπόται] ὠμοί τε δούλοις A. Ag. 1045 ; ὠ. φρόνημα Id. Th. 536 ; ὠμῇ ξὺν ὀργῇ Id. Supp. 187 ; δαίμων S. OT 828 ; τὰ . . Ἀγαμέμνονος κλύεις ὠμὰ καὶ πάντολμ' E. IA 913 (troch.); ὠμὸς ἔς τινα Id. Hipp. 1264 ; and so in Prose, ὠμὸν τὸ βούλευμα . . ἐγνῶσθαι Th. 3.36 ; οὕτως ὠμὴ <ἡ> στάσις προὐχώρησε ib. 82 ; θηρευταὶ ὠμοὶ καὶ ἄνομοι Pl. Lg. 823e ; ὠμὴ ψυχή ib. 718d ; χαλεπὸς καὶ ὠ. X. An. 2.6.12 ; τὸν οὕτως ὠμόν, τὸν οὕτως ἀγνώμονα D. 21.97 ; ὠμοὶ χρόνοι hard times, IG 3.1372 (metr.). Adv., ὠμῶς καὶ ἀπαραιτήτως Th. 3 . [84] , cf. X. Vect. 5.6 ; ὠ. καὶ σχετλίως ἔχειν Isoc. 19.31 ; ὠ. καὶ πικρῶς D. 29.2 ; ὠ. ἀποκτείνειν Lys. 13.63 codd. ὁμοίως Lipsius): Sup. , ὠμότατα διακεῖσθαι πρός τινα Isoc. 9.49 . harsh, rough, cruel, νόμοι S. Aj. 548 ; δηλοῖ τὸ γέννημ' ὠμὸν ἐξ ὠμοῦ πατρός Id. Ant. 471 ; πῶς ἂν ὠμότερος συκοφάντης γενοιτ'; a more coarse, more unmitigated sycophant, D. 18.212 . Adv. ὠμῶς rudely, coarsely, παρελθεῖν ὠ. καὶ ἀναιδῶς ib. 285 . (from 1.4 ) ὠμὸν γῆρας an unripe, premature old age, Od. 15.357 , Hes. Op. 705 (but ὠμότατον καὶ ἀγριώτατον γῆρας in signf. 11.1 , Plu. Mar. 2 ), cf. ὠμογέρων : ὠμὸς τόκος an untimely birth, Philostr. VS 2.1.8 . (Cf. Skt. āmás 'raw, uncooked'.)

lsj_entry_text: φυσώδης, ες, (φῦσα) full of wind, windy, τὸ φ. Pl. Cra. 427a : metaph., bombastic, Longin. 28.1 . flatulent, causing flatulency, Hp. Acut. 50 , Arist. HA 522b32 , 588a7 , Sor. 2.85 ; φ. νοσήματα Arist. HA 605a23 .
greek_sentence: Τινὲς γράφουσι διὰ τοῦτ᾿ αὐτὸν φυσώδη, ὡς ἐντείνοντα τὰ αἰδοῖα, τὸν ἐρέβινθον· διὰ μέντοι τὸν ὑπογεγραμμένον τῆς λέξεως τὸν πόνον φέρομεν ἐπὶ τὴν διὰ τὴν ἐμφύσησιν ὀδύνην.
english_sentence_A: Some write that the chickpea is flatulent for this reason, as distending the genitals; however, on account of what is written after this in the text, we refer the "pain" to the pain arising from inflation.
english_sentence_B: Some write that for this very reason the chickpea is flatulent, as distending the genitals; however, on account of the 'pain' written next in the phrase, we refer it to the ache caused by the inflation.

greek_sentence: Φακὸς δὲ στύφει καὶ ἄραδον ἐμποιέει, ἢν μετὰ τοῦ φλοιοῦ ᾖ.
english_sentence_A: Lentil astringes and produces arados (disturbance), if it is together with its husk.
english_sentence_B: The lentil is astringent and produces disturbance (arados), if it is taken with its husk.

lsj_entry_text: ταραχή, also τάρχη ( Hsch. ), ἡ, disorder, physiological disturbance or upheaval, Sor. 1.105 , 2.59 ; τοῦ πνεύματος Id. 1.46 ; ἡ ἀπὸ τῆς φλεβοτομίας τ. Id. 2.11 ; esp. of the bowels, τῆς κοιλίης Hp. Coac. 205 ; οὐδὲ θόρυβόν τινα ἢ τ. ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ ποιεῖ Gal. 6.825 . of the mind, αἱ φρενῶν ταραχαί Pi. O. 7.30 ; ἀνωμαλία καὶ τ.
