greek_sentence: Τὴν ἄραδον φωνὴν ἔφην σημαίνειν ταραχήν τινα καὶ οἷον μάχην ἐν τῇ γαστρὶ γινομένην ἐκ τῶν διαφόρων ταῖς [877] δυνάμεσι σιτίων· ὥσπερ καὶ νῦν ὅταν μετὰ τοῦ φλοιοῦ προσενέγκηται, πολὺ τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτῆς ἐστι δυσπεπτοτέρα.
english_sentence_A: I said that the word arados signifies a certain disturbance and, as it were, a battle arising in the belly from foods that differ in their [877] powers; just as here too, when it is taken together with the husk, it is far harder to digest than its flesh itself.
english_sentence_B: I said that the word arados signifies a certain disturbance and, as it were, a battle taking place in the belly from foods that differ in their [877] powers; so also now, whenever it is taken with its husk, it is much harder to digest than its flesh itself.

greek_sentence: Τὴν ἄραδον φωνὴν ἔφην σημαίνειν ταραχήν τινα καὶ οἷον μάχην ἐν τῇ γαστρὶ γινομένην ἐκ τῶν διαφόρων ταῖς [877] δυνάμεσι σιτίων· ὥσπερ καὶ νῦν ὅταν μετὰ τοῦ φλοιοῦ προσενέγκηται, πολὺ τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτῆς ἐστι δυσπεπτοτέρα.
english_sentence_A: I said that the word arados signifies a certain disturbance and, as it were, a battle arising in the belly from foods that differ in their [877] powers; just as here too, when it is taken together with the husk, it is far harder to digest than its flesh itself.
english_sentence_B: I said that the word arados signifies a certain disturbance and, as it were, a battle taking place in the belly from foods that differ in their [877] powers; so also now, whenever it is taken with its husk, it is much harder to digest than its flesh itself.

greek_sentence: ταύτην δέ φησι καὶ προσέτι [878] τὸν ὀπὸν τῆς πόας τοῖς ἀπείροις, τουτέστι τοῖς ἀήθεσι, ξηρὰν ἐργάζεσθαι χολέραν· ἥτις δ᾿ ἐστὶν αὕτη μετ᾿ ὀλίγον αὐτὸς διδάξει γράφων ὡδί· χολέρης δὲ ξηρῆς ἡ γαστὴρ πεφύσηται καὶ ψόφοι ἔνεισιν.

greek_sentence: τὴν ξηρὰν χολέρην αὐτῷ κεκλημένην μάλιστα γίγνεσθαί φησι τοῖς τὸ σίλφιον ἅμα τῷ τυρῷ πλέον προσενεγκαμένοις ἢ βοείοις κρέασιν ἡ γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ σιλφίου γεννωμένη φῦσα τοῖς ἐμπλαστικοῖς καὶ βραδυπόροις ἐδέσμασι μιχθεῖσα μένει κατὰ τὴν γαστέρα μὴ διεξερχομένη.
english_sentence_A: 'And it occurs most of all if it should be mixed with much cheese or with the eating of beef.' He says that what he has called dry cholera occurs most of all in those who have taken silphium together with a good deal of cheese or with beef; for the flatus generated from the silphium, when mixed with emplastic and slow-passing foods, remains in the belly and does not pass through.
english_sentence_B: "It happens most of all if it is mixed with much cheese or with an eating of beef." He says that what he has called dry cholera happens most of all to those who have taken silphium together with cheese in rather large quantity, or with beef. For the flatus generated from the silphium, when mixed with emplastic and slow-passing foods, stays in the belly and does not pass through.

greek_sentence: [879] Τὰ μὲν γὰρ μελαγχολικὰ καὶ παροξυνθείη ἂν παθήματα ὑπὸ βοείων κρεῶν ἐδωδῆς· ἀνυπέρβλητος γὰρ ἡ φύσις αὐτέων καὶ οὐ τῆς τυχούσης κοιλίης καταπέψαι· βέλτιστα δὲ ἂν ἀπαλλάσσοιεν, εἰ διέφθοισί τε χρέοιντο καὶ ὡς παλαιοτάτοισι.
english_sentence_A: [879] For the melancholic affections too would be exacerbated by the eating of beef; for their nature is not to be overcome, and it is not for just any belly to digest them; but they would come off best if they used them thoroughly boiled and as old as possible.
english_sentence_B: [879] "For melancholic affections too might be exacerbated by the eating of beef; for their nature is unsurpassable, and it is not for any ordinary stomach to concoct them; but they would fare best if they used them thoroughly boiled and as old as possible." His discussion was about the power of silphium, but he mixed in with this the eating of beef, and after this, passing on in sequence to the melancholic affections themselves, he says that they will be exacerbated by them.

greek_sentence: [879] Τὰ μὲν γὰρ μελαγχολικὰ καὶ παροξυνθείη ἂν παθήματα ὑπὸ βοείων κρεῶν ἐδωδῆς· ἀνυπέρβλητος γὰρ ἡ φύσις αὐτέων καὶ οὐ τῆς τυχούσης κοιλίης καταπέψαι· βέλτιστα δὲ ἂν ἀπαλλάσσοιεν, εἰ διέφθοισί τε χρέοιντο καὶ ὡς παλαιοτάτοισι.
english_sentence_A: [879] For the melancholic affections too would be exacerbated by the eating of beef; for their nature is not to be overcome, and it is not for just any belly to digest them; but they would come off best if they used them thoroughly boiled and as old as possible.
english_sentence_B: [879] "For melancholic affections too might be exacerbated by the eating of beef; for their nature is unsurpassable, and it is not for any ordinary stomach to concoct them; but they would fare best if they used them thoroughly boiled and as old as possible." His discussion was about the power of silphium, but he mixed in with this the eating of beef, and after this, passing on in sequence to the melancholic affections themselves, he says that they will be exacerbated by them.

greek_sentence: ἐχρῆν μὲν οὖν ὅσον ἐπὶ τῇ ὥρᾳ φαυλότατα διὰ τὴν κρᾶσιν εἶναι συμβαίνει δὲ βελτίονα τὴν τροφὴν αὐταῖς κατὰ τὸ θέρος εἶναι καθάπερ τὰ ποηφάγα τῶν ζώων μοχθηρὰ, διὰ τὸ μηκέτι ἔχειν τὴν πόαν χλωράν· ταῖς δ᾿ αἰξὶν ἐπιτηδειοτάτη τροφή τῶν δένδρων οἱ βλαστοὶ καὶ καυλοί ἐστιν, οὓς ἐπὶ τῇ τελευτῇ τοῦ ἦρος ἔχει δαψιλεῖς κατὰ τὸ θέρος.
english_sentence_A: Now, so far as concerns the season, it ought to be worst on account of the temperament; but it turns out that their nourishment is better during the summer, even as (καθάπερ) the grass-eating animals are bad, because they no longer have the grass green; but for goats the most suitable nourishment is the shoots and stalks of trees, which they have in abundance at the end of spring and during the summer.
english_sentence_B: But it happens that their food is better for them in summer, whereas for the grass-eating animals it is poor, because they no longer have green grass. For goats the most suitable food is the shoots and stems of trees, which the trees have in abundance from the end of spring through the summer.

greek_sentence: φθινοπώρου τοίνυν αἱ αἶγες ἀποροῦσαι τροφῆς ἐπιτηδείου χειρίστην καὶ ἰσχνοτάτην ἔχουσι τὴν σάρκα· κατὰ δὲ τὸν χειμῶνα πάλιν ἀμείνω τὴν τοῦ σώματος ἕξιν ἴσχουσι, τὴν φυσικὴν δυσκρασίαν ὑπὸ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ὥραν κράσεως ἐπανορθούμεναι.
english_sentence_A: In autumn, therefore, the goats, being without suitable nourishment, have the worst and leanest flesh; but in winter in turn they acquire a better habit of body, their natural dyskrasia being corrected by the krasis belonging to the season.
english_sentence_B: In autumn, then, goats, lacking suitable nourishment, have the worst and leanest flesh; but in winter they again possess a better condition of the body, their natural dyscrasia being corrected by the krasis that belongs to the season.

An. 7.8.5 , D. 54.39 , Henioch. 2 . generally, = ὗς, σῦς , swine, ἤδη δέλφακες, χοῖροι δὲ τοῖσιν ἄλλοις Cratin. l.c., cf. Mnesim. 4.47 (anap.), Plu. Cic. 7 , Ev.Matt. 8.30 . pudenda muliebria, freq. in Com. poets, who are always punning on the word and its compds., Ar. Ach. 773 sq., etc.; said to be a Corinthian usage, Suid. a fish of the Nile, Str. 17.2.4 , Ath. 7.312a , Gp. 20.7.1 , 13 tit. (Perh. for ĝhoryo- 'grey', cf. Norse griss 'sucking-pig', OHG grīs 'grey', or cf. Alb. de[rmacr ] 'pig'.)
greek_sentence: Χοίρου δὲ πονηρὰ, ὁκόταν ᾖ ἐνωμότερα καὶ περικαῆ· χολερώτερα δ᾿ ἂν εἴη καὶ ἐκταρακτικά.
english_sentence_A: Those of the young pig are bad whenever they are rather underdone and scorched; they would be more productive of cholera and disturbing to the bowels.
english_sentence_B: The meats of a piglet are bad when they are rather underdone and scorched on the outside; they would be more bilious and liable to cause disturbance.

greek_sentence: ὕεια βέλτιστα τῶν κρεῶν ἁπάντων· κράτιστα δὲ τὰ μήτ᾿ ἰσχυρῶς πίονα μήτε πάλιν ἰσχυρῶς λεπτὰ, μήθ᾿ ἡλικίην φέροντα ἱερείου παλαιοῦ.

english_sentence_A: [883] The ancients called 'choiros' in a special sense the very small pig, as one may find in the poet: "Eat now, stranger, what is at hand for servants, piglets; but the suitors eat fattened hogs." The suitors indeed—I do not know how they ate the fattened hogs (for they gave that name to those beyond full-grown age)—the suitors were of all men the most lacking in perception for the discernment of foods that are at once easy to digest and pleasant, just as also in their eating the stomachs of goats stuffed with blood and fat, than which what food could you find harder to digest?

greek_sentence: κάλλιστον δὲ κρέας εἰς ἡδονὴν καὶ πέψιν ἐστὶ τὸ τῶν μέσων κατὰ τὴν ἡλικίαν, τὸ δὲ καὶ γεννητικόν ἐστιν αἵματος χρηστοῦ· χείριστον δέ ἐστι τὸ τοῦ παλαιοτάτου καὶ τὸ τοῦ μετὰ τὴν ἀποκύησιν εὐθέως ἐσθιομένου.
english_sentence_A: The best flesh for pleasure and for digestion is that of pigs of middle age, and this is also generative of good blood; the worst is that of the very oldest and that of the one eaten immediately after birth.
english_sentence_B: The finest meat, both for pleasure and for digestion, is that of animals of middle age, and this is also productive of good blood; the worst is that of the oldest animal, and that of the one eaten immediately after its birth.

lsj_entry_text: εὔσαρκ-ος, ον, (σάρξ) fleshy, in good condition, Hp. Aph. 4.7 , X. Lac. 5.8 , Arist. HA 583a9 , Phld. Mort. 30 , etc.; of meat, Amphis 16 ; opp. σαρκώδης on the one hand, and ἄσαρκος on the other, Gal. 6.30 .
greek_sentence: τῷ δ᾿ αὐτῷ τούτῳ λόγῳ καὶ τὴν τῶν ὑῶν λιπαρωτάτην οὖσαν σάρκα χείρονα νομίζει τῆς τῶν μέσων εὐσάρκων, ὑποπτεύων αὐτῆς τὴν ὑγρότητα, δι᾿ ἣν καὶ πᾶσα πιμελὴ τῆς ὁμογενοῦς σαρκὸς χείρων ἐστὶν, εἰς πέψιν τε καὶ θρέψιν.
english_sentence_A: By this same reasoning he also considers the flesh of pigs that is very fat to be worse than that of those of middle age that are well-fleshed, being suspicious of its moisture, on account of which all fat too is worse than the flesh of the same kind, for both concoction and nourishment.
english_sentence_B: By this same reasoning he also considers the flesh of swine, when it is fattest, to be worse than that of the middling, well-fleshed ones, suspecting its moisture, on account of which all fat, too, is worse than the flesh of the same kind, both for digestion and for nourishment.

greek_sentence: καὶ τὰ περικεκαυμένα δὲ κατὰ τὴν ὄπτησιν ἀνεπιτήδεια πρὸς εὐχυμίαν τε καὶ πέψιν ἐστὶ καὶ χολέρας ποιητικὰ, διὰ τὴν προσελθοῦσαν αὐτοῖς δριμύτητα· κοινὴ γὰρ αὕτη κακία τῶν χολερωδῶν ἐδεσμάτων ἐστὶν, ὅταν ὑγρά τε εἴη καὶ δριμέα.
english_sentence_A: And the parts charred in roasting are unsuitable for good humour and for concoction, and are productive of cholera, because of the pungency that has accrued to them; for this is the common vice of cholera-producing foods, whenever they are both moist and pungent.
english_sentence_B: And things that have been scorched all round in roasting are unsuitable both for good humours and for digestion, and are productive of cholera, on account of the acridity that has been added to them; for this is the common vice of choleric foods, whenever they are both moist and acrid.

lsj_entry_text: αἴγειος, α, ον, of a goat, α<*>γσιον κνῆ τυρόν Il. 11.639 , Hp. Nat.Mul. 38 ; ἀσκῷ ἐν αἰγείῳ in a goat's skin, Il. <*>. 247 ; αἰγείη κυνέη a helmet of goatskin, Od. 24.231 ; γάλα αἴ. Arist. HA 522a23 ; κρέα αἴ. Hp. Acut. (Sp.) 49 .
greek_sentence: ἐγὼ δ᾿ ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν αἰγείων κρεῶν, ὅσα τε ἄλλα φύσει θερμὰ, προσίεμαι τὸν λόγον· ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν εὐκράτων κατὰ θερμότητα καὶ ψύξιν, οἷα τῶν ὑῶν ἐστιν, ἁπλῶς οὕτως λεγόμενον ἀδιορίστως, οὐ προσίεμαι· διορισαμένῳ γὰρ ἐπιτηδειότερα γένοιτο τὰ θερμὰ τῶν ψυχρῶν.
english_sentence_A: For my part, in the case of goat's meat and whatever else is hot by nature, I accept the argument; but in the case of meats that are well-tempered in respect of heat and cold, such as those of pigs are, stated thus simply and without distinction, I do not accept it; for to one who makes the distinction, the hot would prove more suitable than the cold.
english_sentence_B: I for my part accept the argument in the case of goats' meat, and of whatever other meats are hot by nature; but in the case of those that are well-tempered with respect to heat and cold, such as the meat of pigs is, I do not accept it when it is stated thus simply and without qualification; for, once a distinction has been drawn, the hot would prove more suitable than the cold.

greek_sentence: Τὴν ἁπλῶς ὀνομαζομένην ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων χολέραν ὑγρότητι διορίζει τῆς ξηρᾶς· ὀνόματι δὲ κοινῷ κατ᾿ ἄμφω κέχρηται, πρὸς τὸν τῆς γενέσεως τρόπον ἀποβλέπων ὄντα κοινόν.
english_sentence_A: The cholera that is named simply by people he distinguishes by moisture from the dry one; and he has used a common name for both, looking to the mode of their generation, which is common.
english_sentence_B: The condition which men call simply cholera he distinguishes from the dry by its moistness; yet he has used a common name for both, looking to the manner of their generation, which is common to them.

greek_sentence: ὡς γὰρ ὑγρὴ χολέρα γίνεται δριμέων χυμῶν ἐκ τῆς διαφθορᾶς τῶν ἐδηδεσμένων γεννηθέντων, οὕτως ἡ ξηρὰ πνεύματος φυσώδους δριμέος· διὸ καὶ τὰ πλησιάζοντα τῇ [886] γαστρὶ νευρώδη σώματα δακνόμενά τε καὶ τεινόμενα πόνον ποιοῦσι.
english_sentence_A: For just as moist cholera arises from pungent humours generated out of the corruption of the foods that have been eaten, so the dry arises from pungent flatulent pneuma; wherefore also the sinewy bodies adjoining the [886] belly, being bitten and stretched, produce pain.
english_sentence_B: For just as moist cholera arises when acrid humours have been generated from the corruption of what has been eaten, so the dry arises from an acrid, flatulent pneuma. This is also why the sinewy bodies lying close to the [886] stomach cause pain, being bitten and stretched.

english_sentence_A: But since these pneumata are able sometimes to be retained and sometimes to pass through, I am not able to say that it is on account of the retained pneumata that dry cholera is engendered; for it would have been more plausible to give this name to those that pass out.

english_sentence_A: Administer a clyster, then, as quickly as possible, warm and as oily as possible, and, anointing him, seat him in as much warm water as possible, laying him down in a tub, and pour in the warm water little by little; and if, as he is being warmed, the bowel passes, he is relieved.
english_sentence_B: Administer a clyster, then, as quickly as possible, hot and as oily as possible; and, anointing him as abundantly as possible, seat him in hot water, laying him down in a tub, and pour on some of the hot water little by little; and if the bowel passes while he is being warmed, he is set free.

english_sentence_A: [887] To administer a clyster as quickly as possible and to prevent vomiting are precepts common to all things contained in the belly contrary to nature which we are eager to have excreted downward; and in the same way also the clystering with a warm clyster, for what is warm is provocative, just as what is cold is repellent.

greek_sentence: [887] Τὸ μὲν ὅτι τάχιστα κλύζειν καὶ κωλύειν ἐμεῖν, κοινὰ παραγγέλματα πάντων τῶν ἐν κοιλίᾳ περιεχομένων παρὰ φύσιν, ἃ σπουδάζομεν ἐκκριθῆναι κάτω· κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον καὶ τὸ θερμῷ κλύζειν κλύσματι, προκλητικὸν γὰρ τὸ θερμὸν, ὥσπερ ἀποκρουστικὸν τὸ ψυχρόν· τὸ δὲ λιπαρὸν εἶναι τὸ κλύσμα τῆς ξηρᾶς ἴδιον ἴαμα, διότι καὶ τὴν δύναμιν ἐναντίον ἐστὶν, ὑγραῖνον τὴν ξηρότητα, παρηγοροῦν τε τὴν δῆξιν.
english_sentence_A: [887] To administer a clyster as quickly as possible and to prevent vomiting are precepts common to all things contained in the belly contrary to nature which we are eager to have excreted downward; and in the same way also the clystering with a warm clyster, for what is warm is provocative, just as what is cold is repellent.
english_sentence_B: [887] To give a clyster as quickly as possible and to prevent vomiting are general precepts for all things contained in the belly contrary to nature which we are eager to have excreted downwards. In the same way, too, is the precept to give the clyster as a warm clyster, for what is warm is provocative, just as what is cold is repellent.

english_sentence_A: "It is beneficial also for such a person to sleep." It is unclear whether he bids him sleep while being fomented in the tub, or also apart from it; but to one considering the matter in and of itself it is evident that it is most beneficial for all those [suffering] from lack of concoction.

greek_sentence: οἶνον μὲν ὡς τῇ πέψει συντελοῦντα δίδωσι· λεπτὸν δὲ ὡς μὴ μένοι κατὰ τὴν γαστέρα· παλαιὸν δὲ καὶ ἀκρατέστερον ἕνεκα τοῦ θερμαίνειν μᾶλλον· ἅπας γὰρ οἶνος θερμαίνει τὴν ἕξιν, μᾶλλον δὲ ὁ παλαιός.
english_sentence_A: "And to drink wine that is thin and old and more undiluted." Wine he gives as contributing to concoction; thin, so that it may not remain in the stomach; old and more undiluted for the sake of warming more; for all wine warms the bodily condition, but old wine more so.
english_sentence_B: 'And to drink wine that is thin, old and less diluted.' He gives wine as contributing to concoction; thin, so that it may not remain in the stomach; old and less diluted for the sake of warming more. For all wine warms the bodily condition, but old wine more so.

Nu. 1273 , cf. Pl. Lg. 701d . ὄνος ὕεται an ass in the rain, of being unmoved by what is said or done, Cratin. 52 , cf. greek_sentence: ἢν δὲ μὴν ἀνῇ ὁ πόνος, ὄνου γάλα δίδου πίνειν ἕως καθαρθῇ.
english_sentence_A: But if the pain does not abate, give ass's milk to drink until he is purged.
english_sentence_B: But if the pain does not [μὴν, read μὴ] let up, give ass's milk to drink until he is purged.

greek_sentence: Ἢν δὲ ὑγρὴ ἡ κοιλίη ᾖ καὶ χολὴ ὑποχωρέῃ καὶ στρόφοι [889] καὶ ἔμετοι καὶ πνιγμοὶ, τούτοισι κράτιστον ἀτρεμίζειν, πίνειν δὲ μελίκρητον καὶ ἐξεμέειν.
english_sentence_A: If the belly is moist and bile passes downward, and there are gripings [889] and vomitings and chokings, for these it is best to keep still, and to drink melikraton and vomit it up.

It is unclear whether the discussion is even now still about dry cholera, or whether these words should be understood on their own.

greek_sentence: Ἄδηλον εἴτε περὶ τῆς ξηρᾶς χολέρας ἔτι καὶ νῦν ἐστιν ὁ λόγος ἢ τούτων ἀκούειν χρὴ καθ᾿ ἑαυτά· ὁποτέρως δ᾿ ἂν ἔχῃ, φαίνεται δὴ χολὴ δριμεῖα δυσεκνιπτοτέρα περιέχεσθαι κατὰ τὴν γαστέρα· ταύτην δὲ ὑπάγειν πειρᾶται μετρίως, ἅμα τῷ συμπέττειν τὰ περιεχόμενα κατ᾿ αὐτήν· ὑπαχθήσεται μὲν οὖν μετρίως τῷ μελικράτῳ, πεφθήσεται δὲ τῇ ἡσυχίῃ.
english_sentence_A: It is unclear whether the discourse is still even now about dry cholera, or whether one must understand these things on their own; but whichever way it may be, it is evident that acrid bile, rather hard to wash out, is contained in the stomach; and this he attempts to bring down moderately, together with concocting the matters contained in it. It will, then, be brought down moderately by the melikraton, and concocted by the rest.
english_sentence_B: Whichever way it may be, it does appear that acrid bile, rather difficult to wash out, is contained in the stomach. This he tries to draw off moderately, while at the same time concocting the matters contained in it.

english_sentence_A: Often, however, in such dispositions one who gives aid in a combative manner purges out the bad humour (kakochymia) all at once with a strong drug, having first additionally considered the strength and the habit of body of the sick person, and the season, and the age, and the prevailing state (katastasis).

english_sentence_A: Of the other of the two dropsies, however, which he says comes about with inflations, he writes a treatment, which has one part common to all dropsies, as at the beginning he wrote exertion and fomentation and self-restraint, advising to eat hot and dry things; and another part belonging only to the dropsy throughout the flesh, which he left aside as incurable; for this one alone, when it is beginning, sometimes requires phlebotomy, when at any rate it is formed having begun from a suppression of a haemorrhoid, or of the menses in women, or from some plethoric cause of this kind; but the tympanites or the ascites dropsy no one has dared to cure by means of phlebotomy. At any rate, in the case of the one that requires phlebotomy the subsequent treatment would be heating and drying.

For this one alone, when it is beginning, sometimes requires phlebotomy, namely when it is established after starting from the suppression of a haemorrhoid, or of the menses in women, or from some such plethoric cause.

greek_sentence: τοῦ γε μὴν ἑτέρου τῶν ὑδρώπων, ὃν μετ᾿ ἐμφυσημάτων φησὶ γίγνεσθαι, θεραπείαν γράφει, τὸ μέν τι κοινὸν ἔχουσαν πάντων ὑδέρων, ὡς κατὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἔγραψε ταλαιπωρίαν καὶ πυρίαν καὶ ἐγκράτειαν, συμβουλεύων ἐσθίειν θερμὰ καὶ ξηρά· τὸ δέ τι μόνου τοῦ ἀνὰ σάρκα, ὃν ὡς ἀθεράπευτον ἀπέλιπεν· οὗτος γὰρ μόνος ἀρχόμενος, ἐνίοτε δεῖται φλεβοτομίας, ὅταν γ᾿ ἐξ αἱμοῤῥοΐδος ἐπισχέσεως ἢ καταμηνίων ταῖς γυναιξὶν ἤ τινος οὕτω πληθωρικῆς αἰτίας ἀρξάμενος συνίσταται· τὸν δὲ τυμπανίαν ἢ τὸν ἀσκίτην ὕδερον, οὐδεὶς ἐτόλμησε διὰ φλεβοτομίας ἰάσασθαι· ἐπὶ γοῦν τοῦ δεομένου τῆς φλεβοτομίας ἡ ἐφεξῆς θεραπεία θερμαίνουσα καὶ ξηραίνουσα γίγνοιτ᾿ ἄν.
english_sentence_A: Of the other of the two dropsies, however, which he says comes about with inflations, he writes a treatment, which has one part common to all dropsies, as at the beginning he wrote exertion and fomentation and self-restraint, advising to eat hot and dry things; and another part belonging only to the dropsy throughout the flesh, which he left aside as incurable; for this one alone, when it is beginning, sometimes requires phlebotomy, when at any rate it is formed having begun from a suppression of a haemorrhoid, or of the menses in women, or from some plethoric cause of this kind; but the tympanites or the ascites dropsy no one has dared to cure by means of phlebotomy. At any rate, in the case of the one that requires phlebotomy the subsequent treatment would be heating and drying.

For this one alone, when it is beginning, sometimes requires phlebotomy, namely when it is established after starting from the suppression of a haemorrhoid, or of the menses in women, or from some such plethoric cause.

greek_sentence: ταῦτα μὲν οὖν γράψας τοῦ προσήκοντος ἐστοχάσθαι φαίνεται καὶ ὁ ταῦτα γράψας· [893] οὐ μὴν ὀρθῶς γε εἶπεν, ἢν δὲ δύσπνοος ᾖ ὁ κάμνων, φλεβοτομίας χρῄζει, μὴ διὰ πληθώραν ὄντως ἰσχυρὰν εἰς τὸν ὕδερον ἐμπίπτων, κινδυνευούσης δηλονότι σβεσθῆναι τῆς ἐμφύτου θερμασίας ὥσπερ τὸ πῦρ.
english_sentence_A: Having written these things, then, the one who wrote them too appears to have aimed at what is fitting; [893] he did not, however, speak correctly when he said, 'but if the patient is dyspnoeic, he needs phlebotomy', if the patient is not falling into the dropsy on account of a genuinely strong plethora, the innate heat being obviously in danger of being extinguished, like fire.
english_sentence_B: In writing these things, then, the man who wrote them also appears to have aimed at what is fitting. [893] He was not, however, correct in saying 'if the patient is short of breath, he requires phlebotomy', unless the patient has fallen into the dropsy through a plethora that is truly severe, in which case, evidently, the innate heat is in danger of being extinguished, as a fire is.

greek_sentence: ὡς γὰρ τὸ πῦρ κινδυνεύει σβεσθῆναι, ἐπιβληθέντων αὐτῷ ξύλων ὑγρῶν πολλῶν, εἰ μή τις τοῦ πλήθους ὑφέλοιτο, οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ διὰ πλῆθος αἵματος ψυχροτέρου σβεσθῆναι κινδυνεύοντος ἐμφύτου θερμοῦ μέγιστόν ἐστιν ἴαμα ἡ φλεβοτομία, καθ᾿ ἣν ὥραν ὁ κίνδυνος οὕτως καταλάβῃ.
english_sentence_A: For just as fire is in danger of being extinguished when much wet wood has been thrown upon it, unless someone removes some of the quantity, so too in the case of the innate heat that is in danger of being extinguished through an abundance of colder blood, phlebotomy is the greatest remedy, at whatever season the danger thus takes hold.
english_sentence_B: For just as a fire is in danger of being extinguished when many moist logs have been thrown onto it, unless someone takes away some of the quantity, so too in the case of the innate heat that is in danger of being extinguished through a quantity of rather cold blood, phlebotomy is the greatest remedy, at whatever season the danger thus overtakes the patient.

Metaph. 1026a5 : neut. pl. as Adv., συμμανῆναι ἔνια δεῖ Men. 421 ; ἔστι καὶ ταὐτόματον ἔνια χρήσιμον Id. 486 .
greek_sentence: ἔνιοι δὲ ὥσπερ καὶ Διοσκορίδης οὐ θερινὴν ὥραν, ἀλλ᾿ ἐαρινὴν ἔγραψαν, ὑποπτεύοντες τῆς μὲν θερινῆς τὴν διάλυσιν τῆς δυνάμεως, τῆς δὲ χειμερινῆς τὴν προσγενησομένην τῷ πάθει ψύξιν.
english_sentence_A: Some people, however, like Dioscorides, wrote not 'the summer season' but 'the spring', suspecting, in the case of summer, the dissolution of the faculty, and in the case of winter, the chilling that would be added to the affection.
english_sentence_B: Some, however, Dioscorides among them, wrote not 'summer season' but 'spring', suspecting in the summer the dissolution of the strength, and in the winter the chilling that would be added to the affection.

greek_sentence: μέλας γὰρ οἶνος πλεῖστον αἷμα γεννᾷ, τοσοῦτον δὲ ὡς περιττὸν καὶ μελαγχολικὸν γενέσθαι ἐκείνῳ· βέλτιον δ᾿ ἐστὶ κιῤῥὸν οἶνον διδόναι, λεπτὸν μὲν τὴν σύστασιν, ὅπως καὶ τὴν οὔρησιν κινῇ, τὴν δ᾿ ἡλικίαν μὴ νέον, ὥσπερ οὖν καὶ τὰ πολλὰ συμβαίνει· τῶν νέων γὰρ οἴνων οὐδεὶς ἔσται κιῤῥὸς, ἀλλ᾿ ἤτοι λευκὸς ἢ ἐρυθρὸς ἢ μέλας, παλαιούμενοι δὲ κιῤῥοί τε γίνονται καὶ ξανθοί.

english_sentence_A: And pork flesh, eaten in the manner that has been stated, would not be badly given to those in their prime and strong; but of the others none would be able to concoct it well, being already in danger of having the innate heat extinguished; it is better, then, to give to those who are in such a condition whatever they will concoct well.
english_sentence_B: Pig's flesh, eaten in the manner described, would not be badly given to those in their prime and strong; but none of the others could digest it well, since he is already in danger of having his innate heat extinguished. It is better, then, to give those in this condition whatever they will digest well.

english_sentence_B: [895] "Those who have the lower bellies hot, and whose excrements are acrid and pass irregularly because of colliquation: if they are strong, draw [the matter] away by revulsion with white hellebore; if not, [give] the juice of sitaneian wheat, thick and cold, and lentil pottage, and loaves baked in the ashes, and fish, boiled for one who is feverish, roasted for one who is without fever; and dark wine for one without fever.

english_sentence_B: But if, while the acridity prevails, the person is unable for any reason whatever to take hellebore, he bids us give foods and drinks that are astringent and cooling; and to the foods he also adds those capable of drying, such as the loaves baked under the ashes and the roasted fish.

english_sentence_B: But if, while the acridity prevails, the person is unable for any reason whatever to take hellebore, he bids us give foods and drinks that are astringent and cooling; and to the foods he also adds those capable of drying, such as the loaves baked under the ashes and the roasted fish.

english_sentence_A: These things having been said thus reasonably, one must examine what he means by the upper cavity; for sometimes the ancients, naming the thorax the upper cavity, call the whole vessel of nourishment below the diaphragm the lower cavity; but sometimes, naming as the upper cavity that into which we swallow the food, they at one time call all the parts after it the lower cavity, and at another time only the thick intestines; and there are some who name the colon alone the lower cavity.
english_sentence_B: These things having been said thus reasonably, we must consider what he calls the upper cavity. For sometimes the ancients, calling the thorax the upper cavity, give the name lower cavity to the whole receptacle of nourishment after the diaphragm; and sometimes, calling upper cavity that into which we swallow our food, they call the lower cavity at one time everything after it, and at other times only the thick parts of the intestines; and there are those who call the colon alone the lower cavity.

greek_sentence: Ἢν δὲ πυρετὸς μὴ ἔχῃ καὶ στρόφοι ἔωσι, γάλα ὄνειον θερμὸν ὀλίγον τὸ πρῶτον, ἔπειτα ἐκ προσαγωγῆς πλεῖον καὶ λινόσπερμον καὶ πύρινα ἄλφιτα καὶ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων κυάμων ἐξελὼν τὰ πικρὰ, καταλεπίσας, ἐπιπάσσων πινέτω· ἢ ὠὰ ἡμιπάγεα ἐσθιέτω ὀπτὰ καὶ σεμίδαλιν καὶ κέγχρον καὶ χόνδρον ἑφθὸν ἐν γάλακτι, ἑφθὰ ψυχρὰ ἐσθίειν· καὶ τὰ τούτοισιν ὅμοια καὶ ποτὰ καὶ ἐδέσματα προσφερέσθω.
english_sentence_A: If there is no fever and there are gripings, let him drink warm ass's milk, a little at first, then gradually more, together with linseed and wheaten meal and Egyptian beans, having removed their bitter parts and peeled them, sprinkling these on; or let him eat half-set roasted eggs, and fine wheat flour and millet and groats boiled in milk, eating them boiled and cold; and let him take drinks and foods similar to these.
english_sentence_B: "If fever is not present and there are gripings, give warm ass's milk, a little at first, then more by gradual increase; and linseed and wheaten groats; and of Egyptian beans, having taken out the bitter parts and having husked them, let him drink them, sprinkling them in; or let him eat half-set eggs, roasted, and fine wheat flour and millet and groats boiled in milk, to eat boiled things cold; and let him take both drinks and foods similar to these."

greek_sentence: τὸ μὲν οὖν γάλα τὸ ὄνειον καθαίρειν δύναται καὶ ἐπικεραννύναι, τὸ δὲ τοῦ λίνου σπέρμα ξηραίνειν τε καὶ ψύχειν· τὰ δ᾿ ἐκ τῶν πυρῶν ἄλφιτα τὸ ἐπικεραστικὸν ἔχει· καλῶς δ᾿ αὐτοῖς ἀναμέμικται καὶ τὰ κρίθινα, ξηραίνοντά τε καὶ ψύχοντα.
english_sentence_A: The aim in these prescriptions is partly to purge the bad humours (κακοχυμία), partly to temper, partly to dry up, and partly to cool. Asses' milk, then, is able to purge and to temper, while linseed is able to dry and to cool; the alphita made from wheat possess the tempering quality; and the barley ones too are well mixed in with them, drying and cooling.
english_sentence_B: Their aim is partly to purge away some of the bad humour (kakochymia), partly to temper it, partly to dry it, partly to cool it. Now asses' milk is able to purge and to temper, and the seed of flax to dry and to cool; the groats made from wheat have the tempering property; and barley groats too are fittingly mixed in with them, since they dry and cool.

greek_sentence: οἱ δὲ Αἰγύπτιοι κύαμοι μετρίως ψῦξαι δύνανται· τὰ δὲ ὠὰ καὶ ἡ σεμίδαλις καὶ ὁ χόνδρος παχύχυμα καὶ εὔχυμα καὶ ἐπικρατητικά· καὶ ξηραίνει δὲ ἱκανῶς ὡς ἐν ἐδέσμασιν ἡ κέγχρος, ὥσπερ γε καὶ ψύχει.
english_sentence_A: The Egyptian beans are able to cool moderately; the eggs, the fine wheat flour (σεμίδαλις) and the groats (χόνδρος) are thick-juiced, of good juice, and ἐπικρατητικά (prevailing, overpowering); and millet dries sufficiently, as far as foods go, just as it also cools.
english_sentence_B: Egyptian beans are able to cool moderately; eggs, fine wheat-meal (semidalis) and groats (chondros) are productive of thick humour and of good humour, and are capable of prevailing (ἐπικρατητικά; the reading is doubtful, perhaps 'tempering'). And millet dries considerably, as foods go, just as it also cools.

greek_sentence: Τῆς διαιτητικῆς ἐστι μέγιστον παρατηρεῖν καὶ φυλάσσειν, ὥσπερ ἐν τοῖς ὀξέσι καὶ ἐν τοῖσι μακροῖσιν ἀῤῥωστήμασι καὶ τὰς ἐπιτάσιας τῶν πυρετῶν καὶ τὰς [899] ἀνέσιας, ὥστε τοὺς καιροὺς διαφυλάττειν, ὁκότε μὴ δεῖ τὰ σιτία προσενεγκεῖν καὶ ἀσφαλέως, ὁκότε δέῃ προσενεγκεῖν εἰδέναι· ἔτι δὲ| ὁκότε πλεῖστον ἀπέχωσι τῆς ἐπιτάσεως.
english_sentence_A: It is the greatest part of dietetics to observe and to keep watch, as in acute so also in long illnesses, over both the intensifications of the fevers and the [899] remissions, so as to preserve the right moments—when one must not administer food, and to know securely when one must administer it; and further, when they are farthest removed from the intensification.
english_sentence_B: It is of the greatest importance in dietetics to observe carefully and to watch, both in acute and in long illnesses, the intensifications of the fevers and their [899] abatements, so as to keep to the right moments: when one must not offer food, and to know when one may safely offer it; and further, when they are farthest from the intensification. He says that the greatest thing in the dietetic art is to recognise the particular right moment for nourishment.

greek_sentence: Τῆς διαιτητικῆς τέχνης μέγιστον εἶναί φησι τὸ τὸν κατὰ μέρος καιρὸν γνῶναι τῆς τροφῆς· αὐτὸς οὖν ἕνα σκοπόν φησι πλεῖστον ἀπέχειν τὸν καιρὸν ἐκεῖνον, ἐν ᾧ τὴν τροφὴν δεῖ διδόναι τῆς ἐπιτάσεως· εἴη δ᾿ ἂν ἐπίτασιν λέγων τὴν ἀρχὴν τοῦ παροξυσμοῦ.
english_sentence_A: He says that the greatest thing in the dietetic art is to recognise the particular right moment for nourishment; he himself, then, states one indicator: that the moment at which one must give nourishment is farthest removed from the intensification; and by 'intensification' he would be meaning the beginning of the paroxysm.
english_sentence_B: He himself, then, states one indication: that the moment at which nourishment must be given should be farthest from the intensification. By 'intensification' he would mean the beginning of the paroxysm.

greek_sentence: ἐπὶ γὰρ τῶν ὀξέων αὔταρκες ἦν γνώρισμα καιροῦ τροφῆς καταλαβεῖν τὴν θέρμην εἰς τοὺς πόδας, οὐ μὴν ἐπὶ τῶν χρονίων γε θρεπτέον οὕτως, ἀλλὰ περιμένειν προσήκει τὰ βέλτιστα τῆς ἀνέσεως· κατὰ γὰρ τὰς ὀξείας νόσους ἀναμένειν οὐκ ἐγχωρεῖ, φόβῳ τῆς μελλούσης διὰ ταχέων ἐπιτάσεως ἔσεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: For in acute diseases it was a sufficient sign of the right moment for nourishment that the heat had come down to the feet, yet in chronic diseases one must certainly not give nourishment in this way, but it is fitting to wait for the best part of the remission; for in acute diseases it is not possible to wait, out of fear of the intensification that is going to come shortly.
english_sentence_B: For in acute diseases it was a sufficient sign of the right moment for nourishment that the heat had come down into the feet; in chronic diseases, however, one should not feed in this way, but one ought to wait for the best part of the abatement. For in acute diseases it is not possible to wait, for fear of the intensification that is going to come on quickly.

english_sentence_A: Some people, however, write the text thus: "Of dietetics [900] the greatest part is to observe and watch carefully, as in acute diseases, so also in chronic ones, the knowing of when one must give nourishment." greek_sentence: Εἰδέναι δὲ τοὺς κεφαλαλγικοὺς ἐκ γυμνασίων ἢ δρόμων ἢ πορειῶν ἢ κυνηγεσιῶν ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς πόνου ἀκαίρου ἢ ἐξ ἀφροδισίων· τοὺς ἀχρόους, τοὺς βραγχαλέους, τοὺς σπληνώδεας, τοὺς λειφαίμους, τοὺς πνευματώδεας καὶ ξηρὰ βήσσοντας καὶ διψώδεας, τοὺς φυσώδεας καὶ φλεβῶν ἀπολήψιας, ἐντεταμένους ὑποχόνδρια καὶ πλευρὰ καὶ μετάφρενον καὶ τοὺς ἀπονεναρκωμένους καὶ ἀμαυρὰ βλέποντας [901] καὶ οἷς ἦχοι τῶν οὐάτων ἐμπίπτουσι καὶ τὰς οὐρήθρας ἀκρατῶς διακειμένους, τοὺς ἰκτερώδεας καὶ ὧν αἱ κοιλίαι ὠμὰ ἐκβάλλουσιν, αἱμοῤῥαγέοντας ἐκ ῥινῶν ἢ καθ᾿ ἕδρην σφοδρῶς ἢ ἐν ἐμφυσήμασιν ἐόντας, ἢν πόνος αὐτοῖς ἐπιτρέχει σφοδρὸς καὶ μὴ ἐπικρατέωσι· τῶν τοιούτων μηδένα φαρμακεύειν· κίνδυνόν τε γὰρ ἕξεις καὶ οὐδὲν ὀνήσεις, τάς τε ἀπὸ ταυτομάτου ἀπαλλάξιας καὶ κρίσιας ἀφαιρήσεις.
english_sentence_A: One must know those who suffer headache from exercises or runnings or journeys or hunting or some other untimely exertion, or from sexual intercourse; those who are of bad colour, the hoarse, the splenetic, those deficient in blood, the pneumatic and those who cough dry and are thirsty, the flatulent and those with interceptions of the veins, those tense in the hypochondria and sides and back, and those who are benumbed and see dimly [901] and those upon whom ringings of the ears fall and those who are incontinent in their urethras, the jaundiced and those whose bellies cast out crude matters, those bleeding violently from the nostrils or by the seat, or those who are in a state of inflations, if a violent pain runs upon them and they do not master it: to none of such persons should one administer a drug; for you will incur danger and will do no good, and you will take away the spontaneous releases and crises.
english_sentence_B: And one must know about those who suffer from headache as a result of exercises, or runs, or journeys on foot, or hunts, or some other untimely exertion, or from sexual intercourse; those who are without colour, those who are hoarse, those who are splenic, those deficient in blood, those who are short of breath and cough dry and are thirsty, those who are flatulent and have interceptions of the veins, who are distended in the hypochondria and the sides and the upper back, and those who are numbed and see dimly [901], and those into whose ears ringing sounds fall, and those whose urethras are in a state of incontinence, those who are jaundiced, and those whose bellies discharge raw matter, those who bleed violently from the nostrils or at the seat, or who are in states of inflation, if a violent pain runs over them and they do not get the better of it: none of such persons should you purge with a drug; for you will incur danger and will do no good, and you will take away the releases and crises that come of their own accord.

english_sentence_A: That everything in this book has been written in a disorderly fashion and in the manner of a memorandum of preparation is, I think, obvious to everyone; many things, however, as I said, are well said in it, on account of which some people have been persuaded also by the things not correctly said, and more so all those who were conscious in themselves that they do not possess a critical knowledge of what has been written.
english_sentence_B: That everything in this book has been written in no order and in the manner of a preparation for a memorandum is, I think, plain to everyone; but many things in it, as I said, are well stated, on account of which some people have been persuaded even by what is stated incorrectly, and the more so those who were conscious in themselves that they do not possess a critical knowledge of what has been written.

english_sentence_A: Those with headache, he says, from gymnastic exercises or some other untimely exertion. Taking it concisely, then, understand it thus: do not purge those who have become subject to headache from untimely exertions.

greek_sentence: ἀναμνήσω δέ σε νῦν εἰς πολλὰ χρησίμου πράγματος, οὗ διὰ παντὸς ἀξιῶ μεμνῆσθαι· τοῦ σώματος ἡμῶν παρασκευῆς μετέχοντος, ἐγγὺς τοῦ συμπληρωθῆναι, τῶν ἔξωθέν τι προσιὸν ἐξήλεγξε τὴν διάθεσιν αὐτοῦ, πυρετὸν ἀνάψαν ἢ κεφαλαλγίαν ἢ κατάῤῥουν ἢ βῆχα κινῆσαν, ἤ τι τοιοῦτον ἄλλο· κᾄπειτα ἐκ τούτου κατὰ τὸ συνεχὲς ἐπὶ τὴν παρασκευὴν τῆς νοσώδους διαθέσεως ἀσθενοῦσιν ἐπικινδύνως, οὔτε δρόμου τὴν νόσον γεννήσαντος ἢ ὅλως τῆς ἰσχυρᾶς κινήσεως, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τῆς ἀκρασίας ἢ τῆς ψύξεως ἤ τινος ἄλλου τῶν τοιούτων.
english_sentence_A: Untimely exertions are in every case those which the disposition of the body present at that time is unable to bear. I shall now remind you of a matter useful for many purposes, which I think you should keep in mind throughout: when our body partakes of a preparation (for disease) that is close to being completed, something approaching from outside exposes its disposition, kindling a fever or stirring up headache or catarrh or cough, or some other such thing; and then, as a consequence of this, in continuity with the preparation of the morbid disposition, they fall dangerously ill, though it was not the running that generated the disease, nor the violent motion in general, just as it was not the intemperance or the chilling or any other of such things.
english_sentence_B: When our body has a share of a preparation, near to its being completed, something coming at it from outside exposes its condition, kindling a fever or setting in motion a headache or a catarrh or a cough, or some other such thing. And then, from this, in unbroken continuity, they fall dangerously ill on account of the preparation of the morbid condition, though it was not running that generated the disease, nor vigorous movement in general, just as it was not intemperance or chilling or any other such thing either.

english_sentence_A: Next after these he mentions those deficient in blood, that is, those who have blood in deficient quantity, even if they are not yet clearly colourless.
english_sentence_B: In this he seems to me not to speak correctly, for these, if any others do, need to be purged of black [bile]. Next after these he mentions those lacking in blood, that is, those who have deficient blood, even if they are not yet clearly colourless.

lsj_entry_text: εἰσπνοή, ἡ, inspiration, inhalation, opp. ἐκπνοή, Arist. Resp. 471a8 , cf. Str. 3.5.7 ; μιᾷ ἐσπνοῇ θνῄσκουσι Aret. SA 1.7 .
greek_sentence: ἔστι δ᾿ οὐδὲ καθ᾿ ἓν ἕκαστον αὐτῶν λεγόμενον σαφὲς, ὡς καὶ πρόσθεν ἤδη λέλεκται· πνευματώδεις γὰρ ὡς πολὺ μόνον ὀνομάζουσι τοὺς κατὰ τὴν εἰσπνοὴν ἀέρος δεομένους, ἔστι δ᾿ ὅτε καὶ τοὺς ἐμπνευματουμένους· ἀλλ᾿ ἑκάτερον αὐτῶν πολλὰς αἰτίας ἔχει, καὶ εἰ πάσας ἐπεξίω, μακρότερος ὁ λόγος ἔσται πρὸς τῷ καὶ φανῆναί τινας μὲν αὐτῶν φλεβοτομίας δεομένους, τινὰς δὲ καθάρσεως, τινὰς δ᾿ ἄλλου βοηθήματος.
english_sentence_A: Nor is each of them, taken singly, clear in the way it is stated, as has already been said before; for they call 'pneumatic', for the most part, only those who are in need of air in inhalation, but sometimes also those who are filled with wind. But each of these has many causes, and if I were to go through them all, the discussion would become too long, besides the fact that some of them would be shown to need phlebotomy, others purgation, and others some other remedy.
english_sentence_B: For by pneumatōdeis they mostly mean only those who are in need of air in inhalation, but sometimes also those who are inflated with wind (empneumatoumenoi). Yet each of these has many causes, and if I were to go through them all the discussion would become too long; besides, it would also become apparent that some of them need phlebotomy, some purging, and some another remedy.

english_sentence_A: So too those who cough dry do not come about through a single condition, nor do the thirsty among them.

lsj_entry_text: ἀπύρετος [υ], ον, free from fever, Hp. Aph. 4.20 , Luc. Philops. 25 , POxy. 1582.9 (ii A.D.); not inducing fever, δίαιτα Hp. Art. 69 ; βίος Antiph. 226.6 ; relieving fever, ἀντίδοτος Archig. ap. Gal. 13.173 :— perh. to be read for ἀπύρευτος f.l. in Thphr. Char. 3.6 .
greek_sentence: οὕτως δὲ οὐδ᾿ εἰ περὶ τῶν πυρεσσόντων διψωδῶν ὁ λόγος ἐστὶν αὐτῷ, ἐπίστασθαι νῦν ἡμᾶς ἢ περὶ τῶν ἀπυρέτων ἢ ἀμφοτέρων· κᾂν γὰρ ἑνὸς αὐτῶν μνημονεύσω κατὰ τοὺς ἀφορισμοὺς εἰρημένου, τὸ καθόλου διαβεβλήσεται· λέλεκται δὲ ἐν ἀφορισμοῖς ὧδε· ἀπυρέτῳ ἐόντι ἀποσιτίη καὶ καρδιωγμὸς καὶ σκοτόδινος καὶ στόμα ἐκπικρούμενον, ἄνω φαρμακείης [906] δεῖσθαι σημαίνει· ἐὰν δὲ ἐκπικροῦται τὸ στόμα, διψώδεις εἰσίν.
english_sentence_A: And so too we cannot know now whether his statement concerns thirsty patients who are feverish, or those without fever, or both; for even if I mention one of them that is stated in the Aphorisms, the universal statement will be discredited. It is said in the Aphorisms thus: "In one who is without fever, loss of appetite, cardialgia, vertigo with darkening of vision and a mouth turning bitter indicate a need of purging upward" [906]; and if the mouth turns bitter, they are thirsty.
english_sentence_B: In the same way, we cannot now know whether his account concerns thirsty patients who are feverish, or those who are without fever, or both; for even if I mention just one of them, stated in the Aphorisms, the universal statement will be discredited. And if the mouth turns bitter, they are thirsty.

english_sentence_A: [908] If it is beneficial to take blood from someone, first make the belly firm and then take it away; and starve him and withhold wine from him, then treat the remainder of these cases with the appropriate regimen and with moist fomentations.

greek_sentence: τὸ δὲ καὶ ταῖς πυρίαις ταῖς ἐνίκμοις θεραπεύειν, εἰ μὲν ἐπὶ πάντων λέγοιτο τῶν ἀφαιρουμένων αἷμα, ψεῦδός ἐστιν· εἰ δ᾿ ἐπί τινων, ἐχρῆν εἰπεῖν.

greek_sentence: Ὡς προειρηκὼς τὸ πάθος ἐφ᾿ οὗ κελεύει ταῦτα πράττεσθαι τὸν λόγον ποιεῖται, καίτοι οὐδὲν προείρηκεν· ἢ οὖν ἀπόλωλέ τις ῥῆσις, ἐν ᾗ τὸ πάθος ἐδηλοῦτο, ἢ ἐπιλήσμων [910] ἦν ὁ ταῦτα γράψας καὶ τοιοῦτος οἷος ὁ νῦν ὀνομαζόμενος ὑπὸ τῶν πολλῶν μετέωρος.
english_sentence_A: He makes his statement as though he had already spoken of the affection in which he orders these things to be done, and yet he has said nothing beforehand. Either, then, some passage has been lost in which the affection was indicated, or the one who wrote these things was forgetful, [910] and such a person as the one nowadays called by most people 'up in the air'.
english_sentence_B: He frames his account as though he had already stated the affection for which he orders these things to be done, and yet he has stated nothing beforehand. greek_sentence: Κράτιστον δὲ ἐς οὔρησιν καὶ ἐς ἱδρῶτας καὶ ἐς περιπάτους ἄγειν, καὶ τρίψει ἡσύχῳ χρέο, ἵνα μὴ πυκνώσῃς τὴν ἕξιν· ἢν δὲ κλινοπετὴς ᾖ, ἄλλοι τριβέτωσαν αὐτόν.
english_sentence_A: It is best to lead towards urination and towards sweats and towards walks, and use gentle rubbing, so that you do not condense the habit of the body; but if he is bedridden, let others rub him.

english_sentence_A: And if the affection troubles him in the thorax, above the diaphragm, [he is] to sit up as often as possible, and let them recline as little as possible [911], to whatever extent they are able, and while he is sitting up one should rub him down for a long time with much warm [water]; but if he has the pains in the lower belly, beneath the diaphragm, it is beneficial to lie back, and it is beneficial for such a body to make no movement whatever, apart from the rubbing.

But if he has the pains in the lower belly below the diaphragm, it is beneficial to lie back, and it is beneficial for such a body to be moved with no movement at all, apart from the rubbing down.

greek_sentence: [913] Ταύτην τις ἀναγνοὺς τὴν ῥῆσιν ἰατρὸς τολμηρὸς ἀφελὼν τὰ προειρημένα μόρια τῶν κανθαρίδων ἔδωκεν ὑδρωπιῶντι· καὶ μετὰ μίαν ἡμέραν ἀπόστημά τι σχὼν ὁ ἄνθρωπος εἰς τὴν γαστροκνημίαν, εἶτα μετὰ τρεῖς ἄλλας τμηθεὶς ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ, πλείστου ῥυέντος ὕδατος, ἔδοξε τεθεραπεῦσθαι· προσεστάλη γὰρ ἐν τῷ παραυτίκα τὸ πλεῖστον τοῦ παρὰ φύσιν ὄγκου· ἀλλ᾿ ὅμως ἀπέθανεν οὐ μετὰ πολλὰς ἡμέρας.
english_sentence_A: [913] A certain bold physician, having read this passage, removed the aforesaid parts of the cantharides and gave them to a dropsical patient; and after one day the man developed an abscess in the calf, then after three more days, when he had been incised by him and a very great quantity of water had flowed out, he seemed to have been cured; for the greater part of the swelling contrary to nature subsided at once. But nonetheless he died not many days later.
english_sentence_B: [913] Having read this passage, a certain bold physician removed the aforementioned parts of the cantharides and gave them to a man suffering from dropsy. After one day the man developed an abscess in the calf of the leg; then, after three more days, he was incised by him, a very great quantity of water flowed out, and he seemed to have been cured, for the greater part of the swelling contrary to nature subsided at once.

english_sentence_A: And the haemorrhoids you will transfix in the same manner with the needle, passing through a [915] thread of greasy (unwashed) wool as thick as possible, and tying off as large a portion as possible (for the treatment becomes safer); then, having squeezed it out, apply the septic and do not wet it before it falls off; and always leave one behind. english_sentence_A: And the haemorrhoids you will transfix in the same manner with the needle, passing through a [915] thread of greasy (unwashed) wool as thick as possible, and tying off as large a portion as possible (for the treatment becomes safer); then, having squeezed it out, apply the septic and do not wet it before it falls off; and always leave one behind. And after this, having restored the patient, give hellebore; then let him take exercise and sweat, and let there be much rubbing by way of exercise from early dawn; but let him abstain from running and from drunkenness and from pungent things, apart from oregano.
english_sentence_B: And you will pass the needle through the haemorrhoids in the same way, carrying as thick a thread of greasy wool as possible, [915] and, having tied them off as large as possible (for the treatment becomes safer), then, having pressed them off, use the septic [medicament]; and do not foment them before they fall off; and always leave one behind. And after this, having restored the patient, give hellebore; then let him exercise and sweat it off, and let there be much rubbing as part of the exercise from early dawn; but let him abstain from running and from drunkenness and from acrid things, except marjoram.

lsj_entry_text: σκίλλα, ης, ἡ, squill, Urginea maritima, Thgn. 537 , Arist. HA 556b4 , Thphr. HP 7.9.4 , Theoc. 7.107 , Dsc. 2.171 ; used in purificatory rites, Hippon. 5 , Diph. 126.3 , Thphr. Char. 16.14 , SIG 968v i(Mytil., iii B.C.), D.Chr. 48.17 .
greek_sentence: τοῖσι δὲ ἐμπύοισι σκίλλης καταταμὼν κυκλίσκους ἑψεῖν ὕδατι καὶ ἀποζέσας εὖ μάλα ἀπόχεον καὶ ἐπιχέας ἄλλο ἕψεε, ἕως ἂν ἁπτομένῳ δίεφθον καὶ μαλθακὸν φανῇ.
english_sentence_A: For those suppurating internally (empyics), having cut squill into little round slices, boil them in water, and when you have boiled it thoroughly, pour the water off and, pouring on other water, boil until it appears to the touch thoroughly cooked and soft.
english_sentence_B: For empyematic patients, cut squill into small discs and boil them in water; and when it has boiled thoroughly, pour off the water, pour on fresh, and boil it again, until to the touch it appears thoroughly boiled and soft.

greek_sentence: ῥοφήματα δὲ, μήκωνος τῆς λευκῆς ὑποτρίψας ὁκόσον λεκίσκιον, ὕδατι διεὶς σητανίου πλύματι ἀλεύρου, ἑψήσας, μέλι ἐπιχέας, χλιηρὸν ἐπιῤῥοφέων, οὕτω διαγέτω τὴν ἡμέρην· εἶτα ἐς τὰ ἀποβαίνοντα [916] λογιζόμενος τὸ δεῖπνον δίδου.
english_sentence_A: And as gruels: having pounded white poppy, as much as a small dish-full, and diluted it with water, with the washings of this-year's wheat flour, having boiled it and poured on honey, let him sip it lukewarm and so pass the day; then, reckoning according to the results, [916] give the dinner.
english_sentence_B: As gruels: grind up white poppy, about a lekiskion's measure; dilute it with water, with the washing of setanion flour; boil it, pour honey over it, and let him sip it warm.

english_sentence_A: Washed spodos, kneaded richly like tallow, not moist; having ground it smooth, moistened it with omphakion, the juice of the bitter unripe grape, and dried it in the sun, moisten it so that it can be used as an ointment; and when it has become dry, anoint the eyes with the dry, smoothly ground powder and sprinkle it on the corners of the eyes.

Pi. N. 5.2 , E. Med. 1036 , etc.; γλυκύ [ἐστι], c. inf., A. Pr. 698 , Alex. 210 ; θανεῖν γλύκιστον B. 3.47 ; ὅτῳ . . μηδὲν ἦν ἰδεῖν γλυκύ S. greek_sentence: Ἐβένου δραχμὴν, χαλκοῦ κεκαυμένου ἐννέα ὀβολοὺς ἐπ᾿ ἀκόνης τρίβων, κρόκου τριώβολον, ταῦτα τρίψας λεῖα, παράχεε οἴνου γλυκέος κοτύλην Ἀττικὴν, κᾄπειτα ἐς τὸν ἥλιον θεὶς, κατακαλύψας, ὁκόταν συνεψηθῇ, τούτῳ χρέο.
english_sentence_A: A drachma of ebony, nine obols of burnt copper, grinding it on a whetstone, three obols of saffron; having ground these smooth, pour on an Attic kotyle of sweet wine, and then, having set it in the sun, covered, when it has been boiled down together, use this.
english_sentence_B: For moist eyes: a drachm of ebony, and nine obols of burnt copper, grinding it on a whetstone, and three obols of saffron. Grind these smooth, pour in an Attic kotyle of sweet wine, and then set it in the sun, covered.

lsj_entry_text: περιωδυν-ία, ἡ, excessive pain, Pl. R. 583d ; opp. περιχάρεια, Id. Lg. 732c ; of headache, Hp. Aff. 2 : in pl., αἱ ἀπὸ τῶν φρενῶν π. Id.Acut. (Sp.) 34 ; ἥπατος π. ib. 4 ; οἱ θάνατοι καὶ π. Arist. Po. 1452b12 .
greek_sentence: πρὸς τὰς περιωδυνίας.
english_sentence_A: For severe pains.
english_sentence_B: When it has been boiled together, use this. For severe pains.

english_sentence_A: Let there be a drachm of chalcitis; of grape, when two parts have been left, having pressed it out, having ground myrrh and saffron and mixed in the must, boil it in the sun, and anoint with this those who are suffering severe pain; and let it be in a bronze [917] vessel.
english_sentence_B: Let there be a drachm of chalcitis; of the grape, when two parts are left, having pressed it out, and having ground myrrh and saffron, mix in the must, boil it in the sun, and with this anoint those suffering violent pains; let it be kept in a copper [917] vessel.

english_sentence_A: Recognition of women being suffocated by uterine (hysterical) affections: press with the two fingers, and if she perceives it, it is the uterine affections; but if not, it is spasmodic.
english_sentence_B: Diagnosis of women suffocated by uterine affections: press with the two fingers, and if she feels it, the condition is uterine; if not, it is convulsive.

english_sentence_A: Into dried figs drip juice of spurge (tithymallos), about seven times into each, for the one mentioned; then, having put them together into a new vessel, store them, and give to the one mentioned before food.
english_sentence_B: Onto dried figs drip juice of tithymallos, about seven times onto each, with the aforesaid; then, putting them together into a new vessel, store them, and give them to the aforesaid patient before food.

lsj_entry_text: αἱμο-ρραγία, ἡ, haemorrhage, Hp. Art. 69 , Aph. 7.21 ; any violent bleeding, ib. 5.16 ; nose-bleeding, Gal. 17(1).50 , etc.
greek_sentence: [918] Φανερῶς ἐκ τῶν τοιούτων δηλοῦται τοῦτο τὸ βιβλίον ὑπόμνημα συμμίκτων εἶναι θεωρημάτων, ἀτάκτως τῆς μεταβάσεως ἀπ᾿ ἄλλων πρὸς ἄλλα γιγνομένης, ὥσπερ καὶ νῦν ἐπὶ τῆς ἐκ τῶν μυκτήρων αἱμοῤῥαγίας γέγραπται βοηθήματα, τὰ μὲν αὐτῷ τῷ μέρει τῷ αἱμοῤῥαγοῦντι προσφερόμενα, τὰ δὲ ἀντισπαστικὰ, καθάπερ ἡ γαστὴρ λυομένη, τὰ δὲ τῆς κεφαλῆς πυκνωτικὰ καὶ στυπτικὰ, καθάπερ τὰ ψύχοντα.
english_sentence_A: [918] It is clearly shown from such passages that this book is a memorandum of mixed theorems, the transition from one subject to another taking place without order, just as here too, in the case of haemorrhage from the nostrils, remedies have been written down, some applied to the haemorrhaging part itself, others revulsive, such as loosening the belly, others condensing and astringent of the head, such as the cooling ones.
english_sentence_B: [918] From passages such as these it is plainly shown that this book is a memorandum of miscellaneous doctrines (θεωρημάτων), the transition from some matters to others taking place without order.
